### 7.28 QUICK SKIP (HIGH-SPEED SKIP)

#### 7.28.1 Overview

Quick Skip (High-Speed Skip) allows you to store the position of the robot when the skip conditions are met in programmed position registers.

Digital servo control stops the robot quickly by developing the maximum torque of the motor when the robot detects that the skip conditions are met.

# Warning

Due to the impact of servo quick stop when Quick Skip condition is satisfied, Quick Skip will not exceed motion speeds greater than 100mm/sec. If the max speed is exceeded "MOTN-560 Hspd.skip speed limit(G:g)" warning is posted and the speed is limited internally set to 100 mm/sec.

#### 7.28.2 Execution

The quick skip function can be used in program teaching. There is no need to set system variables.

- The skip conditions for the quick skip function are taught in the same way as the ordinary skip function.
- Teach a quick skip instruction (an additional operation instruction) in the same way as the ordinary line skip instruction. Select the high-speed skip instruction from the additional operation instruction menu.

Motion modify JOINT 30%
1 Skip, LBL, PR <-Quick skip instruction
3 Skip, LBL, <-Ordinary skip instruction

- Specify the label, position register, and position storage format.

Skip, LBL[10], PR[5]=LPOS or JPOS

<!-- PDF page 667 -->

Sample Program

8: SKIP CONDITION SDI[3]=ON
10: LP[2]500mm/sec FINE
11: LP[3]100mm/sec
: SKIP, LBL[10], PR[5]=LPOS
30: LBL[10]

- When SDI[3] is turned on during execution of the 11th line, the current position is stored in a form of Cartesian coordinates.
- When SDI[3] is not turned on during execution of the 11th line, a branch to LBL[10] is made after the execution of the 11th line ends. In this case, no position data is stored in PR[5].

#### 7.28.3 Limitations

<1> Position read error

As the programmed operation speed is faster, the position read accuracy under skip conditions becomes lower. (As a guideline, an error of about 1.5 mm is generated for 100 mm/sec. The error is proportional to the speed.)

### 7.29 REGISTER INSTRUCTIONS

Aregister stores one number. Up to 999 registers are available for all the programs in the controller combined. The default number of registers is 32. Registers are identified by numbers. You can increase the number of registers during a controlled start. Refer to the “System Operations” Appendix in the Setup and Operations Manual for information on performing a Controlled start. Register instructions manipulate register data arithmetically.

# Register Addressing

Many instructions employ direct or indirect addressing techniques. When direct addressing is used, the actual value is entered into the instruction. For example, if the register instruction R[2]=5 is used, the current contents of register 2 is replaced with the value 5.

When indirect addressing is used, the instruction contains a register within a register. This indicates that the actual value of the internal register becomes the register number of the external register. See Figure 7–199.

<!-- PDF page 668 -->

Figure 7–199. Direct and Indirect Addressing Example

> **Image description -- img-452.jpeg:** The diagram illustrates the relationship between direct and indirect register addressing. It shows two registers: an Internal Register and an External Register. The Internal Register is labeled 'R[3] = 2', indicating that register 3 holds the value 2. An arrow labeled 'Direct' points from the Internal Register to the value 2, signifying direct addressing where the register's value is accessed directly. Another arrow labeled 'Indirect' points from the Internal Register to the External Register, which is labeled '[R[3]] = 5', indicating that the value stored at the address pointed to by register 3 (which is 2) is 5. This demonstrates indirect addressing, where the value in the register (2) is used as a pointer to another memory location (External Register) containing the value 5.

In Figure 7–199, the first instruction illustrates direct addressing. This instruction causes the current contents of register 3 to be replaced with the value 2.

The second instruction in Figure 7–199 illustrates indirect addressing. In this instruction, R[3] is the internal register and R[R[3]] is the external register. Since in the previous instruction the value of the internal register R[3] is 2, the external register number becomes R[R[3]=2] or R[2]. Therefore, the result of the second instruction is that the contents of the external register, R[2], is to be replaced with the value 5.

R[x] = [value]

The R[x] = [value] instruction stores a value in a register. See Figure 7–200.

Figure 7–200. R[x] = [value]

R[...] = ...

<!-- PDF page 669 -->

> **Image description -- img-453.jpeg:** The image is a table that defines the notation and usage of the register R[x] in a programming or control system context. It includes two main sections: Direct and Indirect addressing modes. 

1. **Direct (1-32)**:
   - R[x] represents the contents of the analog input signal x.
   - A[x] represents the contents of the analog output signal x.
   - D[x] represents the contents of the analog output signal x.

2. **Indirect**:
   - R[x] is used as a pointer to another register or memory location.
   - The table lists various indirect references:
     - G[x]: Group input signal x.
     - GO[x]: Group output signal x.
     - DI[x]: System digital input signal x.
     - DO[x]: System digital output signal x.
     - RI[x]: Robot digital input signal x.
     - RO[x]: Robot digital output signal x.
     - S[x]: SOP digital input signal x.
     - SO[x]: SOP digital output signal x.
     - UI[x]: UOP digital input signal x.
     - UO[x]: UOP digital output signal x.
     - PR[x,y]: Position register element x,y.
     - R[x]: Direct register.
     - R[R[x]]: Indirect register (system variable name).

3. **TIMER[x]**:
   - Represents the timer value, with the value of program timer x being the contents of R[x]. The units of the value are seconds.

4. **TIMER_OVERFLOW[x]**:
   - Represents the timer overflow flag, with the contents of timer overflow flag x being the contents of R[x]. A value of 0 indicates no overflow, and 1 indicates an overflow.

5. **NOTE**:
   - The result of the overflow is cleared when a timer reset instruction is executed.

# R[x]=[value][operator][value ]

The R[x] = [value] [operator] [value] instructions store the result of an arithmetic operation in a register. The arithmetic operations are

- Addition
- Subtraction
- Multiplication
- Division
- Whole number division (DIV)
- Remainder division (MOD)

<!-- PDF page 670 -->

See Figure 7–201.

You can use multiple arithmetic operators in a single instruction. However, there are the following limitations:

- You can mix + and - in the same instruction. Arithmetic operations within an instruction that mixes + and - will be performed from left to right. You cannot mix * or / in an instruction that already contains + or -.
- You can mix * and / in the same instruction. Arithmetic operations within an instruction that mixes + and - will be performed from left to right. You cannot mix + or - in an instruction that already contains * or /.
- The maximum number of arithmetic operators you can have in the same instruction is 5.

Figure 7–201. R[x] = [value] [operator] [value]

R[...] = ... + ...
R[...] = ... - ...
R[...] = ... * ...
R[...] = ... / ...
R[...] = ... DIV ...
R[...] = ... MOD ...
R[...] = ...+...-...+..
R[...] = ...*.../...*..

<!-- PDF page 671 -->

> **Image description -- img-454.jpeg:** The image is a table that defines the syntax and possible values for the register operation R[x] in a programming or control system context. The table is divided into two main columns, each with two sub-columns: one for the left-hand side (LHS) and one for the right-hand side (RHS) of the operation. 

- The LHS column describes the register number or its indirect contents, with possible values including direct register numbers (1 to 32), indirect register numbers (contents of R[x]), and specific system inputs/outputs such as analog input (AI[x]), analog output (AO[x]), group input (GI[x]), group output (GO[x]), system digital input (DI[x]), robot digital input (RI[x]), system digital output (DO[x]), robot digital output (RO[x]), position register element (PR[x,y]), SOP input (SI[x]), SOP output (SO[x]), UOP input (UI[x]), UOP output (UO[x]), timer value (TIMER[x]), and timer overflow flag (TIMER_OVERFLOW[x]).

- The RHS column describes the value or operator applied to the register, with possible values including addition (+), subtraction (-), multiplication (*), division (/), whole number division (DIV), remainder division (MOD), carriage return without termination (cr*), and direct assignment without an operator. It also lists the same system inputs/outputs as the LHS, along with registers (R[x]) and position register elements (PR[x,y]).

# Error Number

ERR_NUM =aaabbb

aaa : Error ID (decimal); bbb : Error number (decimal)

Refer to the “Error Codes and Recovery” appendix in the Setup and Operations Manual.

If 0 is specified as error number "aaabbb," when any kind of error occurs, the condition is satisfied.

For example,

This specifies the "SRVO-006 Hand broken" error because SRVO ID number is 11.

# Operators

For the SKIP instruction, you can connect conditions using AND or OR operators, as follows:

- AND operator

SKIP CONDITION [cond1] AND [cond2] AND ...

For example,

1: SKIP CONDITION R[1]=1 AND R[2]=2

- OR instruction

SKIP CONDITION [cond1] OR [cond2] OR ...

For example,

1: IF DI[10]=ON OR R[7]=R[8], JMP LBL[2]

1: SKIP CONDITION R[1]=1 OR R[2]=2

Note You cannot mix AND and OR in the same operation.

If you replace the operator between AND and OR, any other operators taught in the same line are also replaced automatically and the following message is displayed:

TPIF-062 AND operator was replaced to OR

PIF-063 OR operator was replaced to AND

<!-- PDF page 674 -->

The maximum number of logical conditions that can be taught in the same operation is 5.

SKIP CONDITION [cond1] OR [cond2] OR [cond3]OR[cond4] OR [cond5] (Maximum of five logical conditions)

### 7.31 STRING REGISTER INSTRUCTIONS

#### 7.31.1 Overview

A string register stores alphanumeric character strings. Each string register can hold a maximum of 254 characters. The default number of string registers is 25.

You can increase the number of string register at controlled start. Refer to the “System Operations” appendix of the Setup and Operations Manual for information on performing a controlled start.

There are several kinds of string register instructions:

- String register assignment, SR[x]=
- String register concatenation, SR[x]+
- String register comparison, SR[x]<, >, =, <>, <=, >=
- String register length, R[y]=STRLEN SR[x]
- String register substring search, R[y]=FINDSTR SR[x], SR[z]
- String register substring cut, SR[x]=SUBSTR SR[n],R[y],R[z]

String registers can be addressed using direct and indirect techniques. Please see Figure 6.46 in the Register Instructions section for more information.

#### 7.31.2 String Register Assignment and Concatenation

SR[x] string register instructions manipulate the string register. The string register supports assignment and concatenation.

<!-- PDF page 675 -->

Figure 7-206. String Register Assignment

The table also includes a notation at the top: 'SR[x] = [value]', where 'x' is a placeholder for the register number or argument register index. The table uses clear labels to distinguish between direct and indirect register references, showing how the value of SR[x] is accessed or interpreted in each case.

### 7.31.3 String Conversion and Precedence

String and numeric data are automatically converted when using any register instruction.

Conversion from either integer or floating point numeric data is allowed. Floating point data will be rounded to 6 decimal places.

Examples of conversions from numeric to string data:

Table 7–41. SR[x]=R[y]

[tbl-175.md](tbl-175.md)

Conversion from strings to numeric data is allowed. An overflow alarm can occur if the maximum value for a floating point number is exceeded in the string representation. Conversion from string to numeric data will stop when the first alpha character is found.

Examples of conversions from string to numeric data:

Table 7–42. R[x]=SR[y]

[tbl-176.md](tbl-176.md)

There is data type conversion precedence when multiple conversions occur within an instruction. The data is converted to the data type of the left instruction for each operation.

Examples of conversion precedence:

Table 7–43. SR[x]=R[y]+SR[z]

[tbl-177.md](tbl-177.md)

Table 7–44. SR[x]=SR[y]+R[z]

[tbl-178.md](tbl-178.md)

The first row contains headers: 'SR[x]', 'SUDSTR[value],[value],[value]', and 'SR[x]'. The second row describes the components of the instruction: 'String Register' for 'SR[x]', 'String Register' for the first 'SUDSTR[value]', 'Constant Value' for the second 'SUDSTR[value]', and 'Argument Register' for the third 'SUDSTR[value]'. The third row repeats the structure with 'R[x]' as the register type for the first and third columns, and 'AR[x]' as the argument register type for the middle column. Example of SUBSTR usage:

Table 7–47. SR[n]=SUBSTR SR[x],R[y],R[z]

[tbl-181.md](tbl-181.md)

An overflow alarm will occur in any of the following conditions:

- Starting point is less than or equal to zero
- Length is less than zero
- Starting point is greater than the target string length

<!-- PDF page 679 -->

- Starting point plus length is greater than the target string length

If an argument register, AR[x], is used as the target string and whose data type is not a string, a type mismatch alarm will occur. If an argument register, AR[x], is used as the starting point or length and whose data type is not a numeric type mismatch alarm will occur.

### 7.32 TOOL OFFSET CONDITION INSTRUCTION

A tool offset condition instruction specifies the offset condition used in a tool offset instruction. Execute a tool offset condition instruction before executing the corresponding tool offset instruction. After the tool offset conditions have been specified, they remain in effect until the program terminates or the next tool offset condition instruction is executed. See the following screen for an example.

Instruction
1 Miscellaneous 5 Tool_Offset
2 Program control 6 MACRO
3 Skip 7
4 Offset 8 ---next page---

- The position register specifies the direction in which the target position shifts, as well as the amount of shift.
- The tool coordinate system is used for specifying offset conditions.
- When the number of a tool coordinate system is not specified, the currently selected tool coordinate system is used.
- When the position data is given as joint coordinates, an alarm is issued and the program pauses.

A tool offset instruction moves the robot from the target position (that was originally recorded in the position data) to another position by the amount specified using the tool offset condition instruction. The tool offset condition instruction specifies the condition when the offset is applied. See Figure 7–211.

Figure 7-211. Tool Offset Condition Instruction

TOOL_OFFSET CONDITION PR[i] ( UTOOL[j])
Position register number
(1 to 10)
Tool frame number
(1 to 5)
Example
1: TOOL_OFFSET PR[1]
2: J P[1] 100% FINE
3: L P[2] 500mm/sec FINE Tool_Offset

<!-- PDF page 680 -->

### 7.33 VIA INSTRUCTION

The VIA instruction is an additional motion instruction. This instruction makes it easy for the user to teach motion that goes up to the intended height, goes horizontally, and then goes down to the target position without directly going to the target position.

(This instruction is for the SCARA robot. It has been supported since software version 9.10P/20)

### 7.33.1 How to Use

While teaching, the VIA instruction is used after a motion statement as in the following example:

L P[1] 4000mm/s FINE VIA(FINE,Z=150)

The VIA instruction has three types, DEFAULT, FINE, and CNT.

### 7.33.1.1 Default

VIA(DEFAULT)

Robot goes up to the maximum height. This is FINE motion.

Figure 7–212. VIA (DEFAULT)

> **Image description -- img-462.jpeg:** The image is a simple diagram illustrating a vertical movement between two positions. It features two circles labeled 'Current position' on the left and 'Target position' on the right, connected by a vertical double-headed arrow indicating movement. The arrow points upward to a dashed horizontal line labeled 'Maximum height,' representing the peak of the movement. The diagram visually conveys the concept of an object moving from a starting point (current position) to a higher point (target position) and reaching a maximum height during this motion.

<!-- PDF page 681 -->

### 7.33.1.2 FINE

VIA(FINE,Z=n)

The robot goes up to the height that is specified by the Z value. This is FINE motion.

Note The Z value is related to the World Frame of the robot, not relative to any user frame or tool frame.

Figure 7–213. VIA (FINE, Z=n)

> **Image description -- img-463.jpeg:** The image depicts a simple two-dimensional coordinate system diagram. It shows two labeled points: "Current position" and "Target position." The "Current position" is marked with an open circle at the origin of the coordinate system, with an upward-pointing arrow indicating the positive direction along the vertical axis. The "Target position" is marked with another open circle located to the right of the current position along the horizontal axis, with a rightward-pointing arrow indicating the positive direction along the horizontal axis. A dashed line labeled "Z" extends horizontally from the target position to the right, suggesting a reference or measurement direction. The diagram implies a movement or transition from the current position to the target position along the horizontal axis.

### 7.33.1.3 CNT

VIA(CNT,Z=n1,RT_LD=n2,AP_LD=n3)

Robot goes up to the height that is specified by the Z value, goes horizontally, and then goes down to the target position using the CNT motion.

<!-- PDF page 682 -->

Figure 7–214. VIA (CNT, Z=n1, RT_LD=n2, AP_LD=n3)

> **Image description -- img-464.jpeg:** The image depicts a curved path or trajectory labeled 'Z' between two points: 'Current position' on the left and 'Target position' on the right. The path starts at the 'Current position' and smoothly curves upward before descending to the 'Target position'. The curve is symmetric, with the highest point approximately midway between the two positions. Both the 'Current position' and 'Target position' are marked with small circles, and the path between them is a dashed line, indicating a planned or theoretical route rather than a physical one.

By specifying the distance to RT_LD, the robot moves straight up from the current position to the specified distance.

By specifying the distance to AP_LD, the robot moves straight down from the specified distance to the target position.

Figure 7–215. Specifying the Distance

> **Image description -- img-465.jpeg:** The image is a simple schematic diagram illustrating a process involving two positions labeled 'Current position' and 'Target position'. The 'Current position' is represented by an open circle with an upward-pointing arrow labeled 'RT_LD' above it. The 'Target position' is represented by another open circle with a downward-pointing arrow labeled 'AP_LD' above it. A curved arrow connects the 'Current position' to the 'Target position', indicating a directional flow or transition from the current state to the target state. The diagram suggests a movement or transition process between these two positions, with the labels 'RT_LD' and 'AP_LD' likely representing specific states, actions, or parameters associated with the current and target positions, respectively.

Note For more information regarding RT_LD and AP_LD see Section 7.3.3. Even if AP_LD and RT_LD have the same values, the approach and retreat path around the current position and target position may not be identical due to many factors (speed, acceleration, cycle time priority, ITP resolution etc.), but it will never provide a linear distance less than what is specified.

<!-- PDF page 683 -->

### 7.33.2 Specifications

- The Z axis, or quill, is near the floor when Z=0 and fully retracted when Z reaches its maximum value. It always uses the Z value in world frame for specifying the quill height regardless of whether the motion type is linear or joint.
- This instruction is usable with joint or linear motion. (It is unusable with circular or circle arc motion)
- RT_LD and AP_LD are usable with linear motion. (It is unusable with joint motion.)
- Program name in execution shows when robot moves by VIA instruction.
- In single-step mode, the robot stops not only at the target point but also at the two relay points that are created automatically by the VIA instruction.
- Backward execution to a motion statement with the VIA instruction is not allowed.
- The following additional motion instructions are usable with the VIA instruction:

- Acceleration override instruction (ACC)
- Time before/after instruction (TB/TA)
- Distance before instruction (DB)
- Signal output motion option (DO[]=, RO[]=, GO[]= and AO[]=)

(The other additional motion instructions such as the Offset condition instruction (Offset) are unusable with the VIA instruction.)

## 7.34 VISION INSTRUCTIONS

### 7.34.1 Overview

This page contains help for the Vision Instruction Set. When editing the teach pendant program, press the F1,[INST] key for a list of teach pendant instructions. The iRVision instructions are under the group heading VISION ( not to be confused with PC VISION - which is used with a PC based vision system).

After selecting the VISION group the vision instructions will be displayed. Select one of the desired instructions:

- RUN_FIND
- GET_OFFSET
- SET_REFERENCE
- CAMERA_CALIB
- VR[].OFFSET
- VR[].MODELID

<!-- PDF page 684 -->

### 7.34.2 RUN_FIND

VISION RUN_FIND '...' CAMERA_VIEW[...]

This instruction begins with a request to acquire the image. After the image has been acquired, control returns to the robot and the robot can move. The vision process continues to process.

# **Parameters**

Vision Process Name: This indicates the name of the vision process. The name can be selected from the list of valid vision processes.

Camera View Number: An option that is used with a vision program with more than one camera image and the images can not be acquired at the same time. For example, suppose there is one overhead camera, and the robot is holding a part with two target holes. The target holes are too far apart to be in the same FOV. Hole one is acquired, the robot moves and hole two is acquired. In this case there would be two RUN_FIND instructions — one for each hole.

### 7.34.3 GET_OFFSET

VISION GET_OFFSET 'VP1' VR[2] JMP LBL[99]

This command provides a destination vision register for the vision process. After the vision process has completed and the data has been transferred to the appropriate vision register, control returns to the robot.

# **Parameters**

Vision Process Name: Type the name of the vision process.

Vision Register Index: Type the index of the vision register to receive the data.

Jump Label: Type the label of a jump statement. The program jumps to this label in the event the vision program fails or no parts are found.

### 7.34.4 GET_PASSFAIL

# **Syntax**

VISION GET_PASSFAIL 'VP1' R[99]

This instruction transfers the vision pass fail result of a vision process to a general register.

<!-- PDF page 685 -->

# Parameters

Vision Process Name: The name of the vision process. The name can be selected from the list of inspection vision processes.

Pass Fail Register : This register contains the pass fail result.

- 0 indicates the test failed.
- 1 indicates the test passed.
- 2 indicates a parent tool failed and the child tool could not be tested.

# Example

VISION GET_PASSFAIL 'INSPECTVP' R[5] ;

### 7.34.5 GET_NFOUND

# Syntax

VISION GET_NFOUND 'VP1' R[...] [CAMERA_VIEW[...] ]

This instruction returns the number of targets found in the specified view. If the camera view is omitted it defaults to one.

# Parameters

Vision Process Name: The name of the vision process. The name can be selected from the list of valid vision processes.

Number Found Register Number:

Camera View Number: (1 – 4)

# Example

VISION GET_NFOUND 'FINDVP' R[6] CAMERA_VIEW[2] ;

### 7.34.6 SET_REFERENCE

VISION SET_REFERENCE 'VP1'

Use this instruction to set the reference position from a program. The steps for training a vision process are to train and find a vision target. Set this vision position to be the zero or reference position thus Set Reference. Vision will return a zero result for the offset. Record the pick/place robot position without an offset. The vision position and the robot position have been linked.

<!-- PDF page 686 -->

# Parameters

Vision Process Name: Use the [CHOICE] key to select the vision process from a list of vision processes.

### 7.34.7 OVERRIDE

# Syntax

VISION OVERRIDE 'AST' value

This instruction changes a value in the vision process as defined by the Application Setup Tool. The Application Setup Tool specifies a vision process name, a tool in the vision process, and a field value in the tool. The value is used only once. The user must reset the override value to be used with the next VISION RUN_FIND instruction, otherwise the original vision process value is used.

# Parameters

VISION OVERRIDE 'AST' Value

AST: Application Setup Tool Name

Value: Input value passed to the vision process

# Example

VISION OVERRIDE 'EXPOSURE' 45.0 ;

In this example an Application Setup tool (EXPOSURE) was created to set the exposure time in the vision process to .045 seconds.

### 7.34.8 CAMERA_CALIB

VISION CAMERA_CALIB 'TWOPTCAL' Request=1

This instruction allows you to calibrate the system from a teach pendant program. This is especially useful for a robot mounted camera. Checks can be made periodically. When calibration is required, the calibration program can be run to re-calibrate vision. This is useful after the camera has been bumped or replaced.

# Parameters

Camera Name : Type the name of the camera calibration.

<!-- PDF page 687 -->

Request Number: Type the plane number for the grid to be calibrated when used with grid calibration.

### 7.34.9 VR[. MODELID

R[33]=VR[2].MODELID

This instruction transfers the vision process model ID from the Vision Data register to a register so that it can be used to determine which model was found.

# **Parameters**

Register Index: Specify an integer to indicate the index of the destination register.

Vision Register Index: Specify an integer to indicate the source vision register.

### 7.34.10 VR[.MES]

# **Syntax**

R[RN]=VR[VRN].MES[MN]

This instruction retrieves a measurement value from a specified vision register. A vision register contains ten measurement results. The measurement value is 0.0 by default.

# **Parameters**

Register Number: Destination register

Vision Register Number: (1-10)

Measurement Number :(1-10)

# **Example**

R[5]=VR[1].MES[2] ;

This sets R[5] with the contents of the 2nd measurement value in Vision register 1.

<!-- PDF page 688 -->

### 7.34.11 VR[.FOUND_POS]

#### Syntax

PR [PRN] = VR [VRN]. FOUND_POS [VN] ;

This instruction returns the found position result of a specified view number of a vision register. When a view is not used the FOUND_POS is $NILPOS.

#### Parameters

PRN: The destination Position Register Number

VRN: Vision Register Number (1–10).

VN: View Number (1-4)

#### Example

PR[3]=VR[2].FOUND_POS[1];

Load PR[3] with view 1 found position of VisionRegister 2.

### 7.34.12 VR[.OFFSET]

PR[1]=VR[2].OFFSET

This instruction transfers the vision offset from the Vision Data register to a position register so that it can be used with a Move instruction with an offset clause.

#### Parameters

Position Register Index: Specify an integer to indicate the index of the destination position register.

Vision Register Index: Specify an integer to indicate the source vision register.

### 7.34.13 VR[.ENC]

#### Syntax

R [RN] = VR [VRN].ENC ;

This instruction transfer the vision register encoder value to a destination register. It is used with visual tracking. The encoder value is recorded at the time the camera image is acquired.

<!-- PDF page 689 -->

# Parameters

RN : Register Number

VRN: Vision Register Number: (1-10)

# Example

R[4]=VR[2].ENC ;

Set R[4] with the encoder value of VR[2].

# 7.34.14 RUN_FIND SR[]

# Syntax

VISION RUN_FIND SR[SRN] {CAMERA_VIEW[CVN] }

This instruction requests a vision view image to be acquired. The vision process name is passed by a string register. If the camera view is omitted the default value is 1. Also see RUN_FIND.

# Parameters

SRN: The String Register number (1- 4) the Vision Process Name

CVN: The Camera View Number (1 – 4) , defaults to 1 when omitted.

# Example

VISION RUN_FIND SR[1] CAMERA_VIEW[2]

# 7.34.15 GET_OFFSET SR[]

# Syntax

VISION GET_OFFSET SR[SRN] VR[VRN] JMP LBL[JL] ;

This instruction transfers the vision process result data to a vision register. The string register contains the vision process name. Also see the GET_OFFSET instruction..

# Parameters

SRN: String register number (1- 4) contains the Vision Process Name

VRN : Destinaiton Vision Register Number (1 – 10)

JL: Jump Label Number for no part or error.

<!-- PDF page 690 -->

# Example

VISION GET_OFFSET SR[1] VR[2] JMP LBL[998]

# 7.34.16 SET_REF SR[]

# Syntax

VISION SET_REFERENCE SR[SRN]

This instruction sets the reference position in the vision process. The vision process name is passed by a string register. Also see the SET_REFERENCE instruction.

# Parameters

String register number: (1- 4) the string register contains the vision process name

# Example

VISION SET_REFERENCE SR[2]

# 7.34.17 CAMERA_CAL SR[]

# Syntax

VISION CAMERA_CALIB SR[SRN] Request=RN

This instruction finds the plane data for a camera calibration tool. It allows the user to re-calibrate vision from a TP program. The camera calibration name is passed by a string register. Also see the CAMERA_CALIB instruction.

# Parameters

SRN: String register number (1- 4) contains the camera calibration name.

RN: Request number

# Example

VISION CAMERA_CAL SR[2] REQUEST=1

<!-- PDF page 691 -->

### 7.34.18 GET_PASSFAIL SR[]

# Syntax

VISION GET_PASSFAIL SR[SRN] R[PFN] ;

This instruction transfers the pass fail result of a vision process to a general register. Also See the GET_PASSFAIL instruction.

# Parameters

SRN: The String Register number (1- 4) contains the vision process name.

PFN: Pass Fail Register Number contains the vision result.

- 0 indicates the test failed
- 1 indicates the test passed
- 2 indicates a parent tool failed and the child tool could not be tested.

# Example

GET_PASSFAIL SR[2] R[5] ;

### 7.34.19 GET_READING

# Syntax

VISION GET_READING 'BARCODEVP' SR[1] R[2] JMP LBL[997]

The get barcode instruction returns the barcode value in a string register. The number of characters is returned in the supplied register. Note In case of an overflow, there is no error and the overflow characters are lost. The string register maximum size is 128. The user should check the register for number of characters read.

# Parameters

# Parameters

# Example

VISION GET_READING 'BARCODEVP' SR[1] R[2] JMP LBL[997]

### 7.34.20 SAMPLE PROGRAM

The following example illustrates how the vision instructions are used together:

<!-- PDF page 692 -->

Line 2 finds the vision process VP1

Line 3 the results are stored in Vision register 5. If there were no parts found, the program will jump to LBL 999.

Line 4 the offset is transferred to PR[1]

Line 5 the model ID is saved in R[4]

Line 7 is the approach point

Line 8 is the pick position

Line 9 actuates the gripper

Line 10 Move through approach.

1: LBL[1]
2: VISION RUN_FIND 'VP1'
3: VISION GET_OFFSET 'VP1' VR[5]
: JMP LBL[999]
4: PR[1]=VR[5].OFFSET
5: R[4]=VR[1].MODELID
6:
7:L @P[1] 500MM/SEC CNT75 Offset,PR[1]
8:L @P[2] 100MM/SEC FINE Offset,PR[1]:
9: CALL PICK
10:L @P[1] 300mm/sec CNT75 Offset,PR[1]
: Offset,PR[1]
11: END
12:
13: LBL[999:NO PART]
14: UALM[1]
[End]

#### 7.34.21 Re-Calibration and Verification Sample Program

In this example the user re-calibrates and verifies its accuracy (.05 mm). The camera is mounted on the robot. The calibration grid is the same frame as the application frame (uframe 1).

Lines 1-6 moves the camera to calibrate plane 1
Lines 7-9 moves the camera to calibrate plane 2
Lines 11-12 returns the robot to plane 1 and prepares to find the Big circle of
Lines 15-16 tests for number of circles (must be 4)
Lines 17-22 Loads R[9] and R[10] with X and Y
Lines 23-52 Verified the circle centers are correct.
1: !Re-Calib Robot Mounted Cam ;
2: UFRAME_NUM=1 ;
3: UTOOL_NUM=1 ;
4:L P[1:Plane 1] 2000mm/sec FINE ;

<!-- PDF page 693 -->

5: WAIT .25(sec) ;
6: VISION CAMERA_CALIB 'WTICALB' Request=1 ;
7:L P[2:Plane 2] 2000mm/sec FINE ;
8: WAIT .25(sec) ;
9: VISION CAMERA_CALIB 'WTICALB' Request=2 ;
10: !Test for valid calibration ;
11:L P[1:Plane 1] 2000mm/sec FINE ;
12: R[6:Window index]=0 ;
13: LBL[20] ;
14: VISION RUN_FIND 'BIGCIRCLE' ;
15: VISION GET_NFOUND 'BIGCIRCLE' R[7] ;
16: IF R[7:N Big Circles]<>4,JMP LBL[999] ;
17: LBL[50:Loop] ;
18: VISION GET_OFFSET 'BIGCIRCLE' VR[1] JMP LBL[200] ;
19: R[8]=VR[1].MODELID ;
20: PR[6]=VR[1].FOUND_POS[1] ;
21: R[9:X]=PR[6,1:Found Pos] ;
22: R[10:Y]=PR[6,2:Found Pos] ;
23: SELECT R[8:MODEL ID]=1,JMP LBL[110] ;
24: =2,JMP LBL[120] ;
25: =3,JMP LBL[130] ;
26: =4,JMP LBL[140] ;
27: ELSE,JMP LBL[999] ;
28: LBL[110:Origin Circle] ;
29: IF R[9:X]>.05,JMP LBL[999] ;
30: IF R[9:X]<-.05,JMP LBL[999] ;
31: IF R[10:Y]>.05,JMP LBL[999] ;
32: IF R[10:Y]<-.05,JMP LBL[999] ;
33: JMP LBL[50] ;
34: LBL[120:Inner X Circle] ;
35: IF R[9:X]>15.05,JMP LBL[999] ;
36: IF R[9:X]<14.95,JMP LBL[999] ;
37: IF R[10:Y]>.05,JMP LBL[999] ;
38: IF R[10:Y]<-.05,JMP LBL[999] ;
39: JMP LBL[50] ;
40: LBL[130:Outer X Circle] ;
41: IF R[9:X]>30.05,JMP LBL[999] ;
42: IF R[9:X]<29.95,JMP LBL[999] ;
43: IF R[10:Y]>.05,JMP LBL[999] ;
44: IF R[10:Y]<-.05,JMP LBL[999] ;
45: JMP LBL[50] ;
46: LBL[140:Y Circle] ;
47: IF R[9:X]>.05,JMP LBL[999] ;
48: IF R[9:X]<-.05,JMP LBL[999] ;
49: IF R[10:Y]>-14.95,JMP LBL[999] ;
50: IF R[10:Y]<-15.05,JMP LBL[999] ;
51: JMP LBL[50] ;
52: LBL[200:Success] ;
53: END ;
54: LBL[999:Error]
55: UALM[1]

<!-- PDF page 694 -->

This programs read a barcode using the “Barcode” VP .The value of the barcode label is placed in SR[1]. Register [1] has been programmed to indicate the result.

5: R[1]=0 ;
6: END ;
7: ;
8: LBL[20:SR Overflow] ;
9: R[1]=2 ;
10: END ;
11: ;
12: LBL[999:Error] ;
13: R[1]=(-1) ;

#### 7.34.23 Inspection Sample Program

R[1] indicates the result of the InspectPart vision process. If R[1] contains a 1 it was successful, If R[1] is a 0 it failed. If R[1] is a 2, the test could not be preformed because a parent tool failed to locate the test area.

1: VISION RUN_FIND 'INSPECTPART' ;
2: VISION GET_PASSFAIL 'INSPECTPART' R[1] ;

#### 7.34.24 2D Single Multi-View Vision Process

Use Multi View 1 camera robot to pick a part. Hole One can not be larger than 1 inch Lines 1-6 The robot moves to view 1 to find a target. If not found skip going to view 2.

Lines 19 Skip pick if hole too large

#### 7.34.25 Calling Vision by String Register Sample Program

The first program provides a simple method to load a string value into a string register.

PROGRAM GetPartName

1: !Set SR[1] to passed str ;
2: SR[1]=AR[1] ;

Lines 1-5 load the appropriate vision process name into SR[1] using routine GetpartName.

Lines 6-7 call vision by the contents of SR[1]

Lines 8-9 moves to the approach position (using a tool offset)

Assume PR[3] is (0,0,50,0,0,0), and then the pick position

1: SELECT R[20:VP Name Index]=1,CALL GETPARTNAME('FindPart1');
2:    =2,CALL GETPARTNAME('FindPart2');
3:    =3,CALL GETPARTNAME('FindPart3');
4:    =4,CALL GETPARTNAME('FindPart4');
5:    ELSE,JMP LBL[999];
6: VISION RUN_FIND SR[1];
7: VISION GET_OFFSET SR[1] VR[1] JMP LBL[998];

9:L P[1] 2000mm/sec FINE VOFFSET,VR[1];

### 7.35 WAIT INSTRUCTIONS

Wait instructions delay program execution for a specified time or until a specified condition is true. When a wait instruction is executed, the robot does not execute any motion instructions. There are two kinds of wait instructions:

- WAIT time - delays program execution for a specified time.
- WAIT condition - delay program execution until specified conditions are true.

<!-- PDF page 696 -->

Note Using WAIT instructions in line- or rail-tracking paths is NOT recommended. If an E-STOP occurs during the execution of a WAIT instruction, the robot might not continue to track the part until the next position comes into bounds.

# WAIT time

The WAIT time instruction delays program execution for a specified time. The time in a WAIT time instruction is specified in seconds, with a minimum unit of 0.01 seconds. See Figure 7–216.

Figure 7–216. Wait Time

WAIT ... (sec)

# WAIT time

Direct: Time in seconds, with a minimum unit of 0.01 seconds
Indirect: R[x], where time in seconds = contents of R[x]

# WAIT [item] [operator] [value] [time]

WAIT condition instructions delay program execution until specified conditions are true or until an amount of time elapses (a timeout occurs). The timeout can be specified as one of the following:

- Forever - the program will wait until the condition is true.
- Time out, LBL[i] - the program will wait for the time specified in Timeout. If the condition is still not true, the program will branch to the specified label.

Specify the timeout by setting the system variable $WAITTMOUT to a time, in 100ths of a second. The default timeout value is 3000 hundredths of a second. You can set $WAITTMOUT using the parameter name instruction. Refer to Section 7.16.10 for information on the parameter name instruction.

See Figure 7–217 to Figure 7–220 for examples.

The third column describes the operator parameter, which includes options such as = (equal), <> (not equal), < (less than), <= (less than or equal), > (greater than), and >= (greater than or equal). Figure 7-220. WAIT Condition

WAIT ERR_NUM = ...

WAIT ERR_NUM = [value] [time]

Constant value
Forever
TIMEOUT -
LBL[x]

# Error Number

Where:

ERR_NUM =aaabbb

aaa : Error facility code (decimal); bbb : Error number (decimal)

Refer to the “Error Codes and Recovery” appendix in the Setup and Operations Manual.

If 0 is specified as the error number "aaabbb" when an error occurs, the condition is satisfied.

For example, the instruction

WAIT ERR_NUM=11006, CALL PROG_A

Will cause the program PROG_A to be called when a "SRVO-0 06 HAND BROKEN" error occurs. (SRVO errors are facility code 11.)

# Operators

For WAIT instructions, logical instruction editing can contain multiple logical statements connected by AND or OR operators.

- AND operator

WAIT [cond1] AND [cond2] AND ...

<!-- PDF page 699 -->

For example,1: WAIT DI[1]=ON AND DI[2]=ON, TIMEOUT,LBL[1]

- OR instruction

WAIT [cond1] OR [cond2] OR ...

For example,1: WAIT DI[10]=ON OR R[7]=R[8], TIMEOUT,LBL[2]

Note You cannot mix the AND and OR operators in the same operation.

If an instruction contains multiple ORs or ANDs, and you change one of them, the others will also change. In this case, the following message is displayed:

TPIF-062 AND operator was replaced to OR

TPIF-063 OR operator was replaced to AND

The maximum number of logical conditions that you can teach in the same operation is 5. For example

WAIT [cond1] OR [cond2] OR [cond3] OR [cond4]OR [cond5] (Maximum of five logical conditions)

WAIT Mixed Logic Instruction

Figure 7-221. Mixed Logic WAIT Example

WAIT (DI[1] AND (!DI[2] OR DI[3]))

- Mixed Logic expressions can be specified in the condition of a WAIT statement
- The result of the expression must be boolean.
- The WAIT statement waits until the result of the expression becomes ON.
- “On+”, “Off-” and “ERR_NUM” cannot be specified in mixed logic instructions. You must use normal logic instructions to specify them.
- The maximum number of items (data or operators) in a WAIT statement is approximately 20. The exact maximum number of items varies according to the data type.

Refer to Section 7.17 for more information on mixed logic instructions.

#### Output when WAITing on Input

The Output when WAITING on Input feature allows you to turn on a digital output that indicates that a WAIT instruction in a teach pendant program has been waiting on a specified digital input for longer than a specified time. This item is set on the SYSTEM Configuration menu. Refer to “SYSTEM Configuration Setup,” in your application-specific Setup and Operations Manual for more information.

## 8.1 OVERVIEW

A program is used to tell your robot what to do and how to do it. You must first create a program, and then you can add instructions to it that your robot can follow to perform a task. For example, a program can direct the robot and controller to:

- Move the robot in an appropriate way to required locations in the workcell.
- Perform an application-specific operation
- Send output signals to other equipment in the workcell.
- Recognize and respond to input signals from other equipment in the workcell.
- Keep track of time, part count, or job number.

Note This chapter assumes some knowledge of instructions. Refer to Chapter 7 PROGRAM INSTRUCTIONS for more information.

## 8.2 PLANNING A PROGRAM

### 8.2.1 Overview

This section provides hints that will help you program specific tasks more efficiently. It contains:

- Hints for programming robot motion
- Information regarding special positions
- Application program guidelines

### 8.2.2 Robot Motion

#### 8.2.2.1 Overview

Use the guidelines in this section to help you program certain kinds of robot motion. Refer to Section 7.2 for help deciding what kind of motion to use. Below is a brief reminder as to the characteristics of various components of a typical motion instruction.

**Joint Motion**

Use joint motion type for the fastest moves and the shortest cycle time.

**Linear Motion**

Linear motion type may result in slower moves. Use linear motion type when it is the only way to move to a certain position.

<!-- PDF page 704 -->

# FINE Termination

Using a FINE termination type as part of a motion instruction ensures that the robot will terminate at the precise point that you taught as part of the motion instruction. From this stopped position, if there are other points, the robot will then continue to the next position. FINE is useful, therefore, when the robot must stop at a point to perform a function.

# Continuous Termination

Using Continuous termination type as part of a motion instruction provides flexibility for termination of robot motion at a certain position. Based upon a user-defined value, the robot can come to a complete stop at the position or can move on to the next position before completely coming to a stop at the position. Continuous is useful, therefore, when the robot is using positions as guidance around an obstacle. Program the position near the obstacle and then adjust the termination type value as needed.

### 8.2.3 Special Positions

#### 8.2.3.1 Overview

You can use *special positions* in a program. A special position is a position you define that can be used several times in a program or in other programs. For example, *special positions* might include a position for maintenance, a perch position, or a user-defined "safe" position.

Positions or position registers can be programmed as *special positions*. In addition, Reference Positions can be used to set an output signal that can also be used to indicate that the robot has reached the special position. See Section 14.44 for information about reference positions.

# Caution

Recorded positions and position registers are affected by UFRAME, and UFRAME has an affect during playback. If you change UFRAME, any recorded positions and position registers will also change.

**Note** If the position register is to be shared between two programs, both programs must have the same tool frame and user frame in order to move the robot to the same position in space.

Common *special positions* are:

- Home Position
- Repair Position
- Pounce Position
- Safe Position

<!-- PDF page 705 -->

### 8.2.3.2 Home Position

The *home position* is a position away from the workpiece transfer area. Program the robot to move to home before the first position, between cycles, and any time the robot must be away from workcell activity.

For fastest cycle time, record the home position close to the first position in the path, in line with the first position in the path, and with the same wrist orientation as the first position. Also, the MOVE TO HOME macro can be used to move the robot to the home position.

In HandlingTool, "Home Position" is an input signal in UOP, not a special position. It can be one of the Reference Positions, but these are not utilities or built-ins used to send the robot to the "HOME" position.

### 8.2.3.3 Repair Position

The *repair position* is a position where robot repair operations are performed. Program the robot to move to the repair position any time repair operations must be performed. Record the repair position away from other equipment and the transfer area.

Table 8–1 shows an example of a repair position.

In HandlingTool, the "Repair Position" is not a special position, but you can use one of the *reference positions* for this purpose. A user program with the same trained position must be run to move the robot to "REPAIR" position

Table 8–1. Rack 1

[tbl-183.md](tbl-183.md)

### 8.2.3.4 Pounce Position

The *pounce position* is a position closer to the workpiece than the home position, but not at a position where the application begins. Using a pounce position can improve cycle time slightly, if the workcell is set up so that it is safe for the robot to move closer to the workpiece when the workpiece is almost in place.

The pounce position should be set up for each job, in a position appropriate for that job. After reaching the pounce position, the robot should wait for a "go ahead" signal from the cell controller, informing the robot that the workpiece is now completely in position and the job can proceed.

<!-- PDF page 706 -->

### 8.2.3.5 Safe Position

The safe position is away from fixtures and the workpiece transfer area. Program the robot to move to the safe position any time it is necessary to move the robot away from other workcell activities.

In HandlingTool, the "Safe Position" is not a special position, but you can use one of the reference positions for this purpose. A user program with the same trained position must be run to move the robot to "SAFE" position.

### 8.2.3.6 Position Registers

Position registers can be used as special positions. Each position register can only contain one robot position.

Refer to Section 7.24 for more information about position registers.

Caution

Position registers and reference positions are global positions. Any changes to position registers that are used as special positions in a program will change the special position location. Make sure you do not change position registers used as special positions; otherwise, unexpected results might occur.

To set up a position register as a special position,

1. Press DATA.
2. Press F1, [TYPE].
3. Select Position Reg.
4. Move the cursor to the position register you want to set up.
5. Jog the robot to the position you want to define.
6. Hold down the SHIFT key and press F3, RECORD.

To use a position register as a special position in a program, include the position register you set up in a motion instruction. For example, if you selected PR[2] in Step 4, you could use the following motion instruction in your program.

L

PR[2]

50mm/sec FINE

<!-- PDF page 707 -->

Caution

Recorded positions and position registers are affected by UFRAME, and UFRAME has an affect during playback. If you change UFRAME, any recorded positions and position registers will also change.

**Note** If the position register is to be shared between two programs, both programs must have the same tool frame and user frame in order to move the robot to the same position in space.

8.2.3.7 Other Positions

You can define any other positions to be *special positions*. Define any position that the program uses more than once as a special position. This minimizes the time it takes to create and modify your program.

8.3 CREATING AND NAMING A PROGRAM

8.3.1 Naming a Program

Four choices are available to you when you try to name a program.

- Words
- Upper Case
- Lower Case
- Options

Each choice corresponds to a different set of function keys as shown in the following four sections.

8.3.1.1 Words

This method provides a list of words on the function keys that you can use to build a program name.

**Note** Since each Application Tool has its own program names, the words shown below might not be the same for your robot.

[tbl-184.md](tbl-184.md)

<!-- PDF page 708 -->

### 8.3.1.2 Upper Case

This method lets you use upper case letters and any numbers.

> **Image description -- img-470.jpeg:** The image displays a horizontal row of seven black rectangular buttons arranged side by side. Each button contains a distinct set of characters or symbols. From left to right, the buttons are labeled as follows: the first button shows three asterisks (***), the second button shows the letters ABCDEF, the third button shows the letters GHIJKL, the fourth button shows the letters MNOPQR, the fifth button shows the letters STUVWX, the sixth button shows the letters YZ, and the seventh button shows the symbols @ and *. The buttons appear to be part of a user interface, likely representing a keyboard layout or input method, where each button corresponds to a group of characters or symbols for selection or input.

### 8.3.1.3 Lower Case

This method lets you use lower case letters and any numbers. For the program name, lower case letters are automatically converted to upper case after you enter them.

> **Image description -- img-471.jpeg:** A grayscale image showing a sequence of seven rectangular blocks arranged horizontally. Each block contains a distinct set of characters or symbols. From left to right, the blocks display the following: 1) Three asterisks (***), 2) The lowercase letters 'abcdef', 3) The lowercase letters 'ghijkl', 4) The lowercase letters 'mnopqr', 5) The lowercase letters 'stuvwx', 6) The lowercase letters 'yz', and 7) A combination of the underscore symbol '_', the at symbol '@', and a period '.'. The blocks are evenly spaced and appear to be part of a structured layout, possibly representing a font, keyboard layout, or character encoding reference.

### 8.3.1.4 Options/Keybd

Allows you to change whether you are overwriting, inserting, or clearing the program name or comment information. The screen will display the choices on the function keys as shown below. In addition, KEYBOARD brings up a touchable keyboard on the screen for entering data.

> **Image description -- img-472.jpeg:** A black rectangular keyboard overlay with six labeled buttons arranged horizontally. From left to right, the buttons are labeled: '###' (with three hash symbols), 'OVRSTRK', 'INSERT', 'CLEAR', 'SPACE', and 'KEYBOARD'. The buttons are evenly spaced and appear to be part of a virtual or overlay keyboard interface, likely used for text input or editing in a software application.

The total length of the program name must be no more than thirty-six characters. You can combine words, upper case letters, and lower case letters to form the program name. The name must start with a letter. Give the program a unique name that indicates the purpose of the program.

Note Do not use the asterisk * symbol in program names.

Note Any program name that is longer than 12 characters is abbreviated on the SELECT screen and displayed with a > at the end. When the program name is selected, the entire program name is displayed at the bottom of the screen.

Note If you have common characters in long program names, you can set $UI_CONFIG.$PROG_COMMON[1–3] to contain the common characters. For instance, if your program name is TEST111_PLANT1_ROBOT15467_A and TEST111 is a common prefix, then set $UI_CONFIG.$PROG_COMMON = TEST111. When the system needs to truncate the program name, it will remove the common portion and replace it with a tilde (~) character.
