### 8.4 ADDING INSTRUCTIONS AND EDITING A PROGRAM

#### 8.4.1 Overview

Once a program has been created, instructions must be added to tell the robot how to perform a task. Instructions that tell the robot how, where, and at what speed to move are called motion instructions. Instructions that tell the robot what to do once it arrives at a programmed point are called non-motion instructions.

**Default Motion Instructions**

A list of default motion instructions is provided for your convenience. These motion instructions can be modified according to your need. Default motion instructions can include within them application-specific instructions to perform your work, as well as other motion options.

After you have defined the default instructions you can add them to the program. You select one of the available default instructions to be the current default instruction by moving the cursor to that instruction. You can define and change default instructions any time while you write or modify a program.

**Non-motion Instructions**

Non-motion instructions typically include instructions that tell the robot what to do after moving into position. For example, once it arrives at a position you may want the robot to wait for a period of time, turn on an output, or increment a counter. Many non-motion instructions have been provided for your convenience.

Procedure 8-2 steps you through the adding of both motion and non-motion instructions to a program.

#### 8.4.2 Adding Instructions to a Program

**Procedure 8-2 Adding Instructions to a Program**

You can use iHMI Guides to perform a similar procedure.

**Note** If you want to edit a program with the teach pendant off, this is called Background Program Editing. **Refer to Section 8.10 for more information.**

**Note** To use the Icon Editor, refer to Section 8.9.

**Conditions**

- All personnel and unnecessary equipment are out of the workcell.

<!-- PDF page 714 -->

##### Steps

1. Press the SELECT key. A list of created programs will display as follows:

Select
702566 bytes free 7/7
No. Program name Comment
1 -BCKEDT- [ ]
2 HOME_IO [SET AT HOME I-O ]
4 TEST1 [TEST1 ]
5 TEST111_PLAN> [ ]
6 UOP_ROBOT_12> [ ]
TEST111_PLANT1_ROBOT15467_A

Note Any program name that is longer than 12 characters is abbreviated on the SELECT screen and displayed with a > at the end. When the program name is selected, the entire program name is displayed at the bottom of the screen.

2. Cursor to the program that you would like to edit and press the ENTER key.

3. To define default motion instructions:

a. Continuously press the DEADMAN switch and turn the teach pendant ON/OFF switch to ON.
b. Press F1, POINT. If POINT is not visible, press the NEXT key until it appears at F1.

You will see a list of default motion instructions similar to the following.

Default Motion
1: J P[] 100% FINE
2: J P[] 100% CNT100
3: L P[] 100 mm/sec FINE
4: L P[] 100 mm/sec CNT100

Note If the instructions listed are the ones you want to use, do not modify them. Go to Step 5

c. To modify the default motion instructions, press F1, ED_DEF.
d. Move the cursor to a component in the default instruction you want to modify.
e. Use the appropriate arrow and function keys to modify the component and press ENTER.

If the [CHOICE] function key is displayed, press F4 to display a list of values for the selected component.

<!-- PDF page 715 -->

For example, to change the speed value, move the cursor to 100%. Type a new value and press ENTER. The new value will be displayed. Each time you add this instruction to the program the new value will be used.

f. Repeat Step 3d through Step 3e for each default instruction that you want to define.
g. When you are finished defining default motion instructions, move the cursor to the instruction you want to be the current default instruction and press F5, DONE.

4. Turn the teach pendant ON/OFF switch to OFF and release the DEADMAN switch.

5. To record a position using the current default motion instruction:

a. Jog the robot to the location in the workcell where you want to record the motion instruction.
b. Press and hold in the SHIFT key and press F1, POINT. The instruction will be added to the program automatically.

Note The @ indicator will be displayed on the screen at the current line in the program indicating that the robot is near the current position.

6. To record the position using one of the other three default motion positions:

a. Jog the robot to the location in the workcell where you want to record the motion instruction.
b. Press F1, POINT.
c. Move the cursor to a new default position.
d. Press ENTER and the position is recorded. This then becomes the current default position.

Note The @ indicator will be displayed on the screen at the current line in the program indicating that the robot is near the current position.

7. To add other instructions:

a. Press NEXT until F1, [INST] is displayed, then press F1, [INST].
b. Select the kind of instruction you want and use the appropriate selections on the screen to build the instruction.

Refer to Chapter 7 PROGRAM INSTRUCTIONS for details about each instruction.

8. When you are finished, turn the teach pendant ON/OFF switch to OFF and release the DEADMAN switch.

Note To test the program, refer to the “Testing a Program and Running Production,” chapter.

Note If the system variable $BACKGROUND is FALSE, the teach pendant must remain on during programming. If you want to turn the teach pendant off, you must edit the program in the background. Refer to "Modifying a Program in the Background," for more information.

<!-- PDF page 716 -->

### 8.4.3 Editing a Program

You can modify an existing program any time you want to change the content of the program. Modifying a program includes

- Selecting a program
- Modifying motion instructions
- Modifying application-specific instructions
- Modifying other instructions
- Inserting instructions
- Deleting instructions
- Copying and pasting an existing instruction or program element
- Finding and replacing an existing instruction or program element
- Renumbering positions after instructions have been added, removed, or moved
- Undoing operations, such as modifying instructions, inserting instructions, and deleting instructions
- Remarking instructions, so they are disabled (commented out)
- Displaying comments on the teach pendant program screen
- Displaying instructions in color
- Displaying status in IO instructions

Note You cannot modify details if the program is set up as a system level macro. These macros are identified with the letter "s" at the far right side of the Macro Setup screen.

#### 8.4.3.1 Selecting a Program

You select a program by choosing the program name from a list of existing programs in controller memory. Refer to Chapter 12 PROGRAM AND FILE MANIPULATION for more information on loading programs.

#### Procedure 8-3 Selecting a Program

You can use iHMI Guides to perform a similar procedure.

- All personnel and unnecessary equipment are out of the workcell.
- The program has been created and all detail information has been set correctly (refer to Section 8.5).

#### Steps

1. Press SELECT. You will see a screen similar to the following.

<!-- PDF page 717 -->

Select
702566 bytes free 7/7
No. Program name Comment
1 -BCKEDT- [ ]
2 HOME_IO [SET AT HOME I-O ]
4 TEST1 [TEST1 ]
5 UOP_ROBOT_12> [ ]
UOP_ROBOT_12436

Note Any program name that is longer than 12 characters is abbreviated on the SELECT screen and displayed with a > at the end. When the program name is selected, the entire program name is displayed at the bottom of the screen.

2. Press F1, [TYPE].

If F1, [TYPE], is not displayed on the screen, press >, NEXT, until it is displayed.

3. Select the list you want:

- Recent displays the most recent programs.
- All displays all programs.
- Collections displays any programs that have been added to a Collection.
- TP Programs displays all teach pendant programs.
- KAREL Progs displays all KAREL programs.
- Macro displays all macro programs.
- Cond displays all conditional programs.

4. Move the cursor to the name of the program you want to modify and press ENTER.

5. Your program should now be selected and ready for editing.

##### 8.4.3.2 Modify and Touching up Motion Instructions

Each of the five components of a motion instruction can be changed by moving the cursor to the component and pressing F4, [CHOICE], or entering new numeric data.

When you touch up a motion instruction, only the positional data at that memory location is changed. Other components of the motion instruction are unchanged.

# Procedure 8-4 Modifying and Touching Up Motion Instructions

1. Move the cursor to the line number of the motion instruction you want to modify.
2. To change only the position component of the motion instruction, jog the robot to the new position, press and hold in the SHIFT key and press F5, TOUCHUP. If F5, TOUCHUP, is not displayed, press >, NEXT.

<!-- PDF page 718 -->

# Warning

If you change the motion type of a positional instruction from linear to joint you can cause the speed value to change from mm/sec to a default value as high as 100%. Be sure to check the speed value before you execute the instruction; otherwise, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

3. To change other motion instruction components, move the cursor to the component using the arrow keys, and press the appropriate function keys to modify the component:

- If function key labels are available, press the appropriate one.
- If no function key labels are available, press F4, [CHOICE], and select a value.
- To change the position value, move the cursor to the position number and press F5, POSITION. The position screen will be displayed showing the Cartesian coordinates or joint angles of the selected position. Move the cursor to the component you want to change and enter the new value using the number keys. To make other changes, use the function keys, described here.

[tbl-186.md](tbl-186.md)

— To change the motion group number, press F1, GROUP. This applies only to systems that have been set up for multiple groups.
— To display components for extended axes, press F2, PAGE. This only applies to systems that include extended axes.
— To change the configuration between flip (F) and no-flip or normal (N), press F3, CONFIG, and then use the up and down arrow keys to change F to N and N to F.

Note Joint angles are useful for zero-positioning the robot or for non-kinematic motion control such as controlling the motion of a positioning table.

— To change the format of the position from Cartesian coordinates to joint angles or from joint angles to Cartesian coordinates, press F5, [REPRE] and select the coordinate system. The position is converted automatically.

— When you are finished, press F4, DONE.

<!-- PDF page 719 -->

# Caution

When you change the representation from Cartesian to joint, the user frame and tool frame values currently in effect will be used to calculate the joint angles. After you have changed from Cartesian to joint, if you modify user frames and tool frames, these changes will have no effect on the position with joint representation, regardless of the motion type of the motion instruction that contains the position.

— To change the comment associated with the position, move the cursor to the position value and press ENTER. Follow the information on the screen to enter the position comment. Press ENTER when you are finished changing the comment.

4. Repeat Step 1 through Step 3 for each motion instruction you want to modify.
5. It may help to visualize positions that you intend to modify. This can be done by viewing taught positions in 4D Graphics:

a. Bring up the 4D Edit Node Map related view

- Press i+EDIT from any user interface screen
- From i+MENU and select 4D Edit Node Map from the 4D screen
- Press i+FCTN and select 4D Edit Node Map in the editor screen
- Press the graphical i in the status bar and select 4D Edit Node Map in the editor screen
- See Section 4.4.

##### 8.4.3.3 Modifying Application-specific Instructions

Modifying arc welding instructions changes any element of the Arc Start, Arc End, Weave, or Weave End instructions.

Modifying spot welding instructions changes any element of the Spot and Backup instructions.

Modifying dispensing instructions changes any element of the seal start and seal end instructions.

##### 8.4.3.4 Modifying Other Instructions

When you modify other instructions, you change any element of the instruction.

# Procedure 8-5 Modifying Other Instructions

1. Move the cursor to the line number of the instruction you want to modify.
2. Move the cursor to the component you want to modify and press the appropriate key:
- If function key labels are available, press the appropriate one.

<!-- PDF page 720 -->

- If no function key labels are available, press F4, [CHOICE], and select a value.

3. Repeat Step 1 and Step 2 for each instruction you want to modify.

### 8.4.3.5 Inserting Instructions

When you insert instructions, you place a specified number of new instructions between existing instructions. When you insert an instruction, the instructions that follow the new instruction are automatically renumbered.

### Procedure 8-6 Inserting Instructions

1. Decide where you want to insert the instruction. Move the cursor to the line following that point. The cursor must be on the **line number**. For example, if you want to insert between lines 5 and 6 place the cursor on line 6.
2. Press NEXT, >, until F5, [EDCMD] is displayed.
3. Press F5, [EDCMD].
4. Select Insert.
5. Type the number of lines to insert and press ENTER. A blank line will be inserted into the program for each line you want inserted. All lines in the program will be renumbered automatically. Your program will look similar to the following.

5: J P[4] 50% CNT50
6:
7:
8:
9: J P[5] 50% CNT10

6. Move the cursor to the line number of any inserted line and add any instruction.

### 8.4.3.6 Deleting Instructions

When you delete instructions, you remove them from the program permanently. When you remove an instruction the remaining instructions are automatically renumbered.

### Procedure 8-7 Deleting Instructions

1. Move the cursor to the line number of the instruction you want to delete. If you want to delete several instructions in consecutive order, move the cursor to the first line to be deleted.

<!-- PDF page 721 -->

# Caution

If you delete an instruction, it will be permanently removed from the program. Be sure you want to remove an instruction before you continue; otherwise, you could lose valuable information.

2. Press NEXT, >, until F5, [EDCMD] is displayed.
3. Press F5, [EDCMD].
4. Select Delete.
5. To delete a range of lines, move the cursor to select the lines to be deleted. The line number of each line to be deleted will be highlighted as you move the cursor.
6. Delete the line or lines:

- If you do not want to delete the selected line(s), press F5, NO.
- To delete the selected line(s) press F4, YES.

##### 8.4.3.7 Copying and Pasting Instructions

When you copy and paste, you select a group of instructions, make a copy of the group, and insert the group at one or more locations in the program. You can paste copied program instructions using the methods described in Table 8–3.

Table 8–3. Paste Methods

[tbl-187.md](tbl-187.md)

<!-- PDF page 722 -->

[tbl-188.md](tbl-188.md)

<!-- PDF page 723 -->

[tbl-189.md](tbl-189.md)

<!-- PDF page 724 -->

[tbl-190.md](tbl-190.md)

<!-- PDF page 725 -->

Note When you use RM-POS-ID and RM-POS, motion instructions that contain the following motion options are only copied in reverse order and cause a warning to be displayed:

- Application commands
- SKIP
- INC (incremental motion)
- Continuous turn
- TIME BEFORE/AFTER

Note You can copy instructions from one program and paste them within that program or into another program.

### Procedure 8-8 Copy and Paste

1. Press NEXT, > until F5, [EDCMD] is displayed.
2. Press F5, [EDCMD].
3. Select Copy.
4. Move the cursor to the first line to be copied.
5. Press F2, COPY.
6. Move the cursor to select the range of lines to be copied.

The line number of each line to be copied will be highlighted as you move the cursor.

7. Press F2, COPY, again.

8. Decide where you want to paste the lines. Move the cursor to the line following that point. The cursor must be on the line number.

9. Press F5, PASTE.

10. Press the function key that corresponds to the way you want to paste the copied lines (refer to Table 8–3 for details and examples of each paste method).

11. Repeat Step 8 through Step 10 to paste the same set of instructions as many times as you want.

Note When you use RM-POS-ID and RM-POS, motion instructions that contain the following motion options are only copied in reverse order and cause a warning to be displayed:

- Application commands
- SKIP
- INC (incremental motion)
- Continuous turn
- TIME BEFORE/AFTER

12. When you are finished copying and pasting instructions, press PREV.

<!-- PDF page 726 -->

### 8.4.3.8 Finding and Replacing Instructions

When you find and replace, you find specific instructions and, if desired, replace those instructions with new instructions. This function is useful, for example, when setup information that affects the program is changed. It is also useful when you need to find a specific area of a long program quickly.

### Procedure 8-9 Finding Instructions

1. Move the cursor to the line number of any instruction.
2. Press NEXT, >, until F5, [EDCMD], is displayed.
3. Press F5, [EDCMD].
4. Select Find.
5. Select the kind of instruction to find.
6. When prompted, enter the necessary information.

The system searches forward from the current cursor position for the item you want. If it finds an instance of the item, it highlights it on the screen.

7. To find the next instance of the item, press F4, NEXT.
8. When you are finished finding items, press F5, EXIT.
9. If you pressed F5, EXIT, press PREV. You do not need to press PREV if you pressed F4, NEXT, until all instances had been found.

Note In ArcTool and HandlingTool, you can not use the Find command to locate track/offset instructions or touch sense instructions.

### Procedure 8-10 Replacing Instructions

1. Move the cursor to the line number of any instruction.
2. Press NEXT, > until F5, [EDCMD], is displayed.
3. Press F5, [EDCMD].
4. Select Replace.
5. Select the instruction you want to replace from the list of instructions. Follow the information on the screen to specify the instruction.

The system finds the first instance of the existing instruction and highlights it.

6. Select the replacement item and enter the necessary information.

7. Decide how to replace the instruction:

- To replace the existing instruction with a new instruction in all instances, press F2, ALL. The system will prompt you to confirm that you want to replace all instances of the instruction.
- To replace the existing instruction with the new instruction, press F3, YES. The system will prompt you to search for the next one.

<!-- PDF page 727 -->

- To ignore this instance and find the next, press F4, NEXT, and the system will find the next instance, if there is one.
- To stop the cancel and replace operation, press F5, EXIT.

# Caution

In ArcTool and HandlingTool, you cannot use the Replace command to replace a motion instruction with a touch sense or track/offset instruction. Doing so causes a memory write failure error. If you want to replace the motion instruction, first delete the motion instruction and then insert the touch sense or track instruction.

### 8.4.3.9 Renumbering Positions

You can renumber positions in the program. When you add positions in a program, the first available position number is assigned to the position, regardless of its place in the program. When you delete motion instructions, all remaining positions keep their current numbers. Renumbering reassigns all position numbers in the program so that they are in sequential order.

# Procedure 8-11 Renumbering Positions

1. Move the cursor to the line number of any instruction.
2. Press NEXT, >, until F5, [EDCMD], is displayed.
3. Press F5, [EDCMD].
4. Select Renumber.
5. Renumber the positions:

- If you do not want to renumber positions press F5, NO.
- To renumber positions press F4, YES.

### 8.4.3.10 Undoing Operations

You can undo an operation to recover from the last incorrect or faulty operation. You can undo the previous operation to edit the program, and you can redo the last Undo operation. Several modifications for one line can be recovered with a single Undo operation if you have not modified any other line in between modifications.

You cannot Undo an operation when any of the following conditions exist:

- The controller has been turned off and turned on
- Another program has been selected
- You are using a keyboard
- The teach pendant ON/OFF switch is OFF

<!-- PDF page 728 -->

- The program is write-protected
- The teach pendant does not have enough available memory

Also, you cannot Undo an operation in HandlingTool when any of the following conditions exist:

- Modifying palletizing command
- Deleting program lines that include palletizing instructions.
- Copying program lines that include palletizing instructions.
- Pasting lines that include palletizing instruction.
- Replacing or re-numbering at the place in the program that has palletizing instructions.

In addition, Undo will not work if you have executed any of the following instructions in a program:

- Palletizing instructions (HandlingTool)
- Line tracking instructions
- On-line touch up

Note If power fails in the process of performing an Undo operation, unexpected results can occur, and the desired modification is not guaranteed to have taken effect when power is restored.

### Procedure 8-12 Undoing an Operation

1. Press NEXT, >, until F5, [EDCMD], is displayed.
2. Press F5, [EDCMD].
3. Select Undo.
4. Undo the operation. The recovered operation is displayed.

- If you do not want to undo the operation, press F5, NO.

- To undo the operation, press F4, YES.

5. To cancel the undo operation, press F5, [EDCMD], then press Undo. Press F4, YES, to redo the operation.

# Warning

If you have used Undo, you should thoroughly test the modified program at a low motion speed before allowing it to run continuously. Otherwise, you could injure personnel or damage equipment. Refer to Chapter 9 TESTING A PROGRAM AND RUNNING PRODUCTION for more information on testing a program.

<!-- PDF page 729 -->

### 8.4.3.11 Remarking Instructions

When you remark an instruction, you disable the instruction by commenting it out. // is shown at the beginning of the instruction. You cannot remark just a portion of the instruction. You will not be able to edit the instruction until you unremark it. You can perform other modifications on the instruction such as delete, copy and paste, find and replace, and renumber.

# Procedure 8-13 Remarking/Unremarking Instructions

1. Move the cursor to the line number of the instruction you want to remark or unremark. If you want to change several instructions in consecutive order, move the cursor to the first line to be changed.
2. Press NEXT, >, until F5, [EDCMD] is displayed.
3. Press F5, [EDCMD].
4. Select Remark.
5. To remark/unremark a range of lines, move the cursor to select the lines to be changed. The line number of each line to be changed will be highlighted as you move the cursor.
6. Remark or unremark the line or lines:

- To remark the selected line(s) press F4, REMARK
- To unremark the selected line(s) press F5, UNREMARK

Note When remarking lines, any lines already remarked are skipped. When unremarking lines, any lines not remarked are skipped. You will not be able to edit a line if it is remarked.

### 8.4.3.12 Displaying Comments on the Teach Pendant Program Screen

This function displays comments of I/O and registers on the teach pendant program screen. This gives you the ability to confirm comments while you edit a teach pendant program, without having to display another screen.

You can only display comments for the following instructions while you are editing a teach pendant program. You cannot change the comments on the teach pendant program screen.

- I/O instructions (DI[i:COMMENT], DO[i:COMMENT], RI[i:COMMENT], RO[i:COMMENT], GI[i:COMMENT], GO[i:COMMENT], AI[i:COMMENT], AO[i:COMMENT], UI[i:COMMENT], UO[i:COMMENT], SI[i:COMMENT], SO[i:COMMENT])
- Register instructions (R[i:COMMENT])
- Position register instructions (PR[i:COMMENT])
- Position register element instructions (PR[i.j:COMMENT])

The display of the comments is turned on and off when you select the [Comment] by pressing F5, [EDCMD].

<!-- PDF page 730 -->

Note Instructions that include indirect addressing do not display the comments, as in the following example: R[R[i]], DO[R[i]], ...

# Procedure 8-14 Displaying Comments on the Teach Pendant Program Screen

1. To display comments on the teach pendant program screen, see the following screen for an example.

PNS0001
1: R[2:COUNTER1]=DI[3:HAND1]
2: DO[1:HAND1ACK]=ON
[END]

2. Press F5, [EDCMD].

PNS0001
1/3
1: R[2:COUNTER1]=DI[3:HAND1]
2: DO[1:HAND1ACK]=ON +---+
| 1 Insert |
[END] | 2 Delete |
| 3 Copy/Cut |
| 4 Find |
| 5 Replace |
| 6 Renumber |
| 7 Comment |
| 8 Undo |
| 9 Remark |
| 0 -- NEXT -- |

3. If you select Comment, the comments turn off.

PNS0001
1/3
1: R[2]=DI[3]
2: DO[1]=ON
[END]

4. Press F5, [EDCMD], again. If you select Comment, the comments turn on.

<!-- PDF page 731 -->

PNS0001
1: R[2:COUNTER1]=DI[3:HAND1]
2: DO[1:HAND1ACK]=ON
[END]

##### 8.4.3.13 Displaying instructions in color

The application instructions and the remark instructions can be displayed in color. The application instructions are displayed in red. The remark instructions are black on a yellow background. The use of color can be turned on or off by pressing F5, [EDCMD] and selecting [Color].

# Procedure 8-15 Displaying Instructions in Color

1. To display some instructions in color press F5 [EDCMD] and select [Color]. Repeat this step to turn off using color.

##### 8.4.3.14 Displaying status in IO instructions

The current status of an IO signal can be displayed within an IO instruction in a TPE program. The status display can be turned on and off by pressing F5, [EDCMD] and selecting [IO Status].

# Procedure 8-16 Displaying Status in IO Instructions

1. Press F5 [EDCMD] and select [IO Status]. Repeat this step to turn off the IO status display. In the example program below DI[3] is currently ON and DO[1] is currently OFF. ON will have a green background and OFF will have a red background if color is enabled.

PNS0001
1: R[2:COUNTER1]=DI[3:ON :HAND1]
2: DO[1:OFF:HAND1ACK]=ON
[END]

If the comment display is turned off the program can still display the IO status, as shown in the program below.

PNS0001
1: R[2]=DI[3:ON]
2: DO[1:OFF]=ON
[END]

<!-- PDF page 732 -->

The Comment, Color, and IO Status commands within EDCMD can be used independently.

## 8.5 PROGRAM DETAIL INFORMATION

### 8.5.1 Overview

Program detail information, also known as program header information, is specific information that identifies and classifies the program. Once a program has been created, the program detail information can be reviewed and/or changed.

To access program detail information, follow procedure Procedure 8-17

Accessing the program detail information reveals the following items and their operations

Table 8–4. Program DETAIL Screen Items and Operations

[tbl-194.md](tbl-194.md)

** For PaintTool, this applies to process programs only.

### 8.5.2 Creation Date

Creation date is the date on which the program name was created.

### 8.5.3 Modification Date

Modification date is the date, according to the calendar in the controller, when the file was last displayed in the editor. This information can be displayed using the [ATTR] function key on the SELECT menu.

### 8.5.4 Copy Source

Copy source is the name of the file from which the file was copied. This field is empty if the file is an original file. This information can be displayed using the [ATTR] function key on the SELECT menu.

<!-- PDF page 737 -->

### 8.5.5 Positions and Program Size

The positions item indicates whether the program contains recorded robot positions. When you first create a program, positions is always set to FALSE.

Program size is the size of the program in bytes. The program size can be displayed using the [ATTR] function key on the SELECT menu.

### 8.5.6 Program Name

A program name identifies the program. When you create a new program, you must give it a unique program name. The program name differentiates the programs stored on the controller.

**Length**

The name can be from one to 36 characters long.

**Available Characters**

**Letters** : A through Z. A program name must start with a letter.

**Numbers** : 0 through 9; a program name cannot start with a number.

**Symbols** : _ (underscore) only; **do not use** @ (at), * (asterisk), or space.

**Content**

The name should be descriptive and it should tell you what the program does.

**Note** Any program name that is longer than 12 characters is abbreviated on the SELECT screen and displayed with a > at the end. When the program name is selected, the entire program name is displayed at the bottom of the screen.

**Note** If you have common characters in long program names, you can set $UI_CONFIG.$PROG_COMMON[1–3] to contain the common characters. For instance, if your program name is TEST111_PLANT1_ROBOT15467_A and TEST111 is a common prefix, then set $UI_CONFIG.$PROG_COMMON[1] = TEST111. When the system needs to truncate the program name it will remove the common portion and replace it with a tilde (~) character. See the following screen for an example.

<!-- PDF page 738 -->

Select
702566 bytes free 7/7
No. Program name Comment
1 -BCKEDT- [ ]
2 HOME_IO [SET AT HOME I-O ]
4 TEST1 [TEST1 ]
5 ~_PLANT1_ROBOT1>[ ]
6 UOP_ROBOT_12> [ ]
TEST111_PLANT1_ROBOT15467_A

Note If you are writing a program for production operation using RSR or PNS, name the program as follows:

- An RSR program must be RSRnnnn, wherennnn is a four-digit number. For example, if you want your program numbered 23, you would enter RSR0023.
- A PNS program must be PNSnnnn, wherennnn is a four-digit number. For example, if you want your program numbered 23, you would enter PNS0023.

For RSR and PNS programs, use the program comment to indicate what the program does. Refer to Section 8.5.8.

#### 8.5.7 Sub Type

Sub type identifies the kind of program you want to write. These are:

- None
- Macro
- Cond
• Collection - see Section 8.6

# None

If you select none, the program will be created as a .TP program, which can include any instructions in your teach pendant program.

# Macro

A macro program created as a .MR program can contain any instruction and function as a normal .TP program. However, only macro programs can be set up to be executed in a variety of ways including from operator panel buttons, teach pendant keys, and the Manual Functions menu. They can also be assigned a name in the macro table and be called with this name in a macro program.

<!-- PDF page 739 -->

Macro programs can also be called by a program when the MACRO instruction is used. Refer to the "Program Elements" chapter of this manual for more information.

# **Cond**

A "ch" program has a Cond (Condition Handler) sub type. Refer to the "Advanced Functions" chapter of this manual for more information on the condition monitor function.

These programs are created for you so that you can move to the positions you define in these programs using the Move Menu. Refer to the “Planning and Creating a Program” chapter for details on how to define and use predefined positions.

### 8.5.8 Program Comment

When you create a new program, you can also add a *program comment* to the name. A program comment includes additional information that you want to further identify the program. This information can be displayed using the [ATTR] function key on the SELECT menu, and also from the DETAIL function key.

# **Length**

One to 16 characters

# **Available Characters**

**Letters** : a through z and A through Z

**Numbers** : 0 through 9

**Symbols** : _ (underscore), @ (at), * (asterisk)

# **Blank spaces**

**Punctuation**: ; (semicolon),: (colon), " (quotation marks),( ) (left and right parentheses), . (period)

# **Content**

Should be descriptive and provide additional information, if necessary.

### 8.5.9 Group Mask

When you create a program, you define the *group mask* that identifies the group of axes, or *motion group*, that the program will control. Motion groups define different groups of axes that can be used for independent pieces of equipment, positioning tables, opening devices, and other axes.

There are eight motion groups available. The controller can operate a maximum of 40 axes, however, only nine axes can belong to a single motion group.

<!-- PDF page 740 -->

Note In HandlingTool and ArcTool, multiple motion groups must be set up before they can be used. Refer to the Software Installation Manual.

If a system has only one motion group, the default motion group is 1. An asterisk indicates the group is not used. You can specify a program to use all eight motion groups, but only two motion groups can perform Cartesian interpolated motion within a single program. If you disable all groups, you cannot add motion instructions to your program.

Note In HandlingTool and SpotTool+, when you add a motion instruction that has a motion type, the following appears on the screen:

Group mask: 1, *, *, *, *, *, *, *

You cannot change the group mask after you have added motion instructions to your program. You will not be able to select group mask in the program DETAIL screen.

Note For system level macro programs, the group mask cannot be changed.

#### 8.5.10 Write Protection

Write protection allows you to specify whether the program can be modified.

- When write protection is set to ON, you cannot add or modify any element in the program. When you have finished creating a program and are satisfied with how it works, you should set write protection to ON so that you or someone else does not modify it.
- When write protection is set to OFF, you can create the program and add or modify any element in the program. By default, write protection is set to OFF.

This information can be displayed using the [ATTR] function key on the SELECT menu.

##### Caution

When write protection is set to ON, you cannot modify any program detail information (program name, sub type, program comment, group mask, ignore pause) except write protection.

#### 8.5.11 Ignore Pause

If the program type has been set to NONE, you can use ignore pause to specify whether the program will continue to run even when an error occurs, a command is issued (such as pushing EMERGENCY STOP or HOLD), or the teach pendant is enabled. Ignore pause is allowed only in programs that do not have motion groups specified such as an I/O monitoring program. This means that programs that use ignore pause cannot contain any motion instructions.

<!-- PDF page 741 -->

# Warning

If ignore pause is set to ON, the program MUST NOT issue any motion instructions; otherwise, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

- When ignore pause is set to ON, the program continues to run even when an error occurs, a command is issued, or the teach pendant is enabled. This allows the program to continue any monitoring function, such as monitoring I/O.
- When ignore pause is set to OFF, the program pauses when an error occurs, a command is issued, or the teach pendant is enabled.

### 8.5.12 Stack Size

When a program is executed, a stack of 500 long words (1200 bytes) is allocated unless you specify a stack size. The stack is allocated from available user RAM.

If a stack overflow alarm occurs, the program needs more stack. Options such as TCPMate and Cell Finder require that teach pendant programs have increased stack size.

The minimum and default stack size is 500. The maximum stack size is 4000.

### 8.5.13 Collection

Collections are used to collect programs together to simplify program maintenance. Collections are shown as a [TYPE] in the Select Menu. They are created as a new TP program type, CO. Collection names must be unique among all programs. Use the SYSTEM Configuration menu to setup collection names for CREATE. Refer to Section 8.6.

### 8.5.14 No-Disp Sub-Program

The feature allows you to make a teach pendant program not to display while the program is CALLED as a sub-program or as a macro. While running the program, the teach pendant display will not display the contents of the sub-program with the “No-Display” attribute set. When you press the ENTER key while the cursor is at the CALL statement, or when the program is paused (e.g. HOLD key is pressed), you can see the contents of the sub-program where the program is currently executing.

You can press the PREV key to return to “No Display” mode. The system also goes back to “No Display” mode when the sub-program returns.

<!-- PDF page 742 -->

### 8.5.15 Application Mask

If you have enabled more than one application (such as spot welding, dispensing, or material handling) during software installation, you must set the application mask item to the application you want to use in your program. After you specify the application to use in your program, the program instructions and function key labels will change to reflect the application you specified.

Set the application mask as follows:

- To select an application to use in your program, set the application you want to TRUE on the application process DETAIL screen.
- To write a program that includes no application instructions, set all applications to FALSE on the application process DETAIL screen. This sets the application process to NONE.

[tbl-195.md](tbl-195.md)

Note You can use Spot Welding and Material Handling in a program by selecting Spot Welding.

The available applications are defined at Controlled start during software installation. You can enable up to two applications at one time if you have purchased the Multi Application Enable option and have enabled it at Controlled start. Refer to the Software Installation Manual for more information.

All teach pendant keys and LED indicators correspond to the currently selected application. The currently selected application is displayed in the middle of the screen name line on the teach pendant screen. If more than one application has been enabled during a controlled start, you can toggle between them by pressing FCTN and selecting Change APPL-Tool. The character abbreviations are as follows: DI for dispensing, HT for material handling, and SW for spot welding. Refer to Section for more information on defining the currently selected application. Refer to Section for more information on the teach pendant keys and LED indicators for the currently selected application.

Note If a software application is using the multiple equipment option, then you will see only the first letter of the application in its character abbreviation, and the number of the equipment assigned to it. D1 corresponds to "Dispensing equipment 1," and S2 corresponds to "Spot welding equipment 2."

### Calling Programs when Application Masks are Used

The following rules dictate the kinds of programs you can CALL (using the program CALL instruction) when application masks are used:

<!-- PDF page 743 -->

- A program with an application mask set to NONE can CALL a program that has an application mask set to an application or NONE.
- A program with an application mask set to an application can CALL a program that has an application mask set to NONE.
- A program with an application mask set to an application cannot CALL a program that has a different application mask.

### 8.5.16 Program Type

The program type indicates the kind of Multi-Arm program being used. This should always be set to Normal Program.

### 8.5.17 Multi-Arm Main

This item indicates the status of the Multi-Arm program in the Family. It can be set to No, independent program, if it is not the main program of the Multi-arm family, Yes, Head of Family if it is the head of a family program, or Yes, Family Member if it is the main program of a family program.

### 8.5.18 Head of Family

This item indicates which robot is the head of the family for this job in a Multi-Arm application.

### 8.5.19 Family Members

This item indicates which robots are included as family members in a Multi-Arm application.

## 8.6 COLLECTIONS

### 8.6.1 Overview

Collections are used to collect programs together to simplify program maintenance. Collections are shown as a [TYPE] in the Select Menu. They are created as a new TP program type, CO. Collection names must be unique among all programs. Use the SYSTEM Configuration menu to setup collection names for CREATE.

Collections are enabled by default but can be disabled by setting $COLLECT_ENB to FALSE. Collections are backed up and restored same as other TP programs.

To create a collection, press CREATE in the Select menu and enter a name. In the DETAIL screen, verify the Sub type field is Collection.

### 8.6.2 Adding to a Collection

Select the collection in the Select Menu. While you are displaying the programs (if any) in the collection, you can cursor to the collection itself and press ENTER. You will enter the Collection Editor. You may also use the DETAIL screen, cursor to the Collection field and press ENTER.

The Collection Editor is used to add or remove existing programs to or from the selected collection. Programs can be in multiple collections. If $COLLECT_CFG.$MULTI_PROG is FALSE, then a program can only be in 1 collection at a time. All types of programs can be added except Process. Process should always belong to a Job which can be added. If $COLLECT_CFG.$ALLOW_PROC is TRUE, then Process can be directly added to a collection.

### 8.7 LINE NUMBER AND PROGRAM END MARKER

A line number is automatically inserted next to each instruction you add to a program. If you remove an instruction or move an instruction to a new position in the program, the program instructions will be renumbered automatically so that the first line is always line 1, the second line 2, and so forth. You use line numbers to identify which lines to move, remove, and mark when you modify a program.

The program end marker ( [End] ) automatically appears after the last instruction in a program. As new instructions are added, the program end marker moves down on the screen, retaining its position as the last line in the program.

<!-- PDF page 750 -->

## 8.8 MACROS

### 8.8.1 Overview

A macro is typically an easily initiated, concise program used to perform an often repeated function. Macro programs can be executed from

- Specific teach pendant keys
- The MACROS screen
- Specific operator panel buttons
- The MANUAL FCTNS macro screen
- Within a program using the MACRO COMMAND instruction
- Issuing an input signal: DI, RI, and UI

Refer to Section 7.14 for information on using macro command instructions in a program.

To use a macro, you must

- Write the macro program
- Set up the macro to define how it will be executed
- Execute the macro

**Note** System level macros are application-specific instructions that are predefined and cannot be changed by the user. These macros are identified with the letter "s" at the far right side of the Macro SETUP screen. You cannot change instruction name or program for system level macros on any screen.

### 8.8.2 Writing a Macro

Other than typically being concise, macros are not initially any different from any other program. Therefore, they are not created any differently. Refer Procedure 8-1 to see how to create a program.

### 8.8.3 Setting Up Macros

Macro commands must be set up before they can be used.

You can select an instruction name and assign a program from the Macro Command screen.

<!-- PDF page 751 -->

Table 8–5. Macro Command Screen Items

[tbl-196.md](tbl-196.md)

### Teach Pendant User Keys

You can set up a macro command to run when a teach pendant user key is pressed alone or with the SHIFT key. If you want to execute a program that contains robot motion when a user key is pressed, you must set it up to run when the SHIFT key is pressed.

# Caution

Make certain that your application has not already assigned functions to the teach pendant user keys; otherwise, execution problems can occur.

When you set up macro commands, you can define up to seven macro commands to run when the user key is pressed alone (UK[1] - UK[7]), and seven macro commands to run when the user key is pressed with the SHIFT key (SU[1] - SU[7]). The macro commands that require the user key to be pressed alone (UK[1] - UK[7]) cannot contain any instructions that move the robot, and the group mask must be set to [*,*,*,*,*] in the program header information.

Note In the following table, UK indicates that only the key must be pressed - for macro commands that do not include robot motion. SU indicates that SHIFT and the key must be pressed.

# MANUAL FCTNS Macro Screen Items

You can set up a macro command program to be executed from the MANUAL FCTNS Macros screen. After you set up a macro command to run from this screen, you can then select a manual functions menu item and press the SHIFT key and the EXEC function key to execute the macro command. Refer to Section 8.8.4 to execute a macro command from the MANUAL FCTNS menu.

# Operator Panel Buttons

You can set up a macro command program to run when a button on the operator panel is pressed.

# Input Signals

You can set up a macro command program to be executed when the input signal you specify is received. You can assign a macro command to a digital input (DI), robot input (RI) and, in some cases, a user operator panel input (UI). By default, you can assign up to ten macro commands as input signals, or UOP input signals. You can change the number of signals by modifying the value of the $MACROMAXDRI system variable.

For digital input signals, indexes 0 through 999 (or the number of digital input signals configured on your system) are available. An index of 0 indicates that no macro is assigned. You can assign

### 8.8.4 Executing Macros

#### 8.8.4.1 Overview

As mentioned, after you have set up macros you can run them, using one of the following methods:

- Press a teach pendant user key
- Press the SHIFT key and a teach pendant user key
- Select a MANUAL FCTNS (MANUAL Macros in DispenseTool) screen item
- Press an operator panel button (if available)
- Execute a macro program from within another program using the macro command instruction
- Receive an input signal (DI, RI, or UI)
- Execute a macro program by selecting the program, then pressing Shift-FWD on the teach pendant.

The method you use depends on how you set up the macro command to execute. This section describes how to execute a macro command from the MANUAL FCTNS Macros screen (MANUAL Macros screen in DispenseTool). Refer to Section 7.14 for information about the macro command instruction.

<!-- PDF page 757 -->

# Warning

Before you copy a program with embedded macros from one controller to another, compare the SETUP screen macro lists of the two controllers. Be sure that the list on the first controller matches the list on the second controller. If they are not identical, DO NOT copy the program; otherwise, when you run a program that uses those macros, the robot could injure personnel or damage equipment.

### 8.8.4.2 Teach Pendant User Keys

Use Procedure 8-19 to execute a macro command that has been assigned to a teach pendant user key.

# Procedure 8-19 Executing a Macro Command from a Teach Pendant User Key

# Conditions

- The program you want to use as a macro command has been tested.
- The macro command has been set up to execute when a teach pendant user key is pressed.

# Steps

1. Make sure the teach pendant is ON and the DEADMAN switch is pressed.

# Warning

In the next step, the robot could move. Make sure that personnel and unnecessary equipment are out of the workcell; otherwise, the robot could injure personnel or damage equipment.

2. Press the teach pendant user key that corresponds to the macro command you assigned. If you assigned the key to be pressed with the SHIFT key, press and hold SHIFT and press the user key. Refer to Procedure 8-18.

### 8.8.4.3 MANUAL FCTNS Menu Items

You can execute preassigned macros from the MANUAL Macros screen.

Refer to Table 8–8 for a description of the Manual Macros Screen Items. Use Procedure 8-20 to execute a macro command that has been assigned to a MANUAL FCTNS menu item.

### 8.9.2.5 Configuring the CUSTOM Toolbar

Pressing the CUSTOM icon displays a selection of icons specific to your application. The custom toolbar can be configured using the XML file, FR:\TPEINS.XML. This file will be backed up and restored as Application Data.

An example syntax for a toolbar button is shown below:

<!-- Require Multi-Pass -->
<BUTTON pos='24'
REQUIRE='MPAS'
TEXT='MP OFFSET'
TEXTKN='Insert KANJI here'
IMAGE='mp_ofst.gif'
LINE='MP Offset PR[...] RPM[...]'
/>

- The BUTTON element begins a new button. The pos attribute is optional. It is the relative position of the button when it is displayed. The toolbar will reorder the buttons based on the

<!-- PDF page 770 -->

position number. When the position number changes, it forces a line feed. If the pos attribute is omitted, then it defaults to 0 which is the top of the list.

- The REQUIRE element is optional. It is the entry in $FEATURE.$MOD[] which must exist for the button to display. There can be multiple REQUIRE statements which are OR'd together. Typically a single REQUIRE statement is sufficient if the order name which loads the instruction is used, such as 'MPAS' for Multi-Pass. If the REQUIRE element is omitted, then the button is always displayed.
- The TEXT element is optional. It is the text shown on the button for any languages which are not explicitly stated. If the TEXT element is omitted, then the button has no default text.
- The TEXTKN element is optional. It is the text for Japanese and KANJI languages. It supports either Katakana or KANJI characters. Any language can be specified using TEXTXX where XX is the language suffix. When the language changes, the editor is notified and the toolbar changes the language automatically. Other language suffixes supported are "FR", "GR", "SP", "CH", "TW", and "OT" for other.
- The IMAGE element is optional. It is the button icon. Icons are typically installed in FRH:\GUI\ directory. If the icon is elsewhere the path can be specified, such as '/frh/cgtp/tcyc_sb.gif'. If the IMAGE element is omitted, then the button has no icon.
- The LINE element is the ascii line which will be inserted into the program. It should be in English. This works even if English is not loaded on the controller. If the LINE element is omitted, then the button does nothing when pressed.

### 8.10 MODIFYING A PROGRAM IN THE BACKGROUND (BACKGROUND EDITING)

### 8.10.1 Overview

Background editing is used to modify a program when the teach pendant is off. This can also be used to edit a program while another program is running. You do not have to stop the robot to modify or check another program. This option can improve the efficiency of production and maintenance.

Warning

If the teach pendant is off, make sure you are at a safe distance (outside of the robot workcell) when you edit a program while another program is running. The teach pendant is not in control of the robot during this time. Otherwise, the robot could injure personnel or damage equipment.

During background editing, you can

- Create and delete programs.
- Add new program instructions.

<!-- PDF page 771 -->

- Add new motion instructions.

The position recorded will be the current position of the robot.

— If the robot is currently executing a motion instruction in another program, the robot position at the time you add the motion instruction will be the recorded position.
— If the robot is not executing a motion instruction in another program, the current robot position will be the recorded position.

- Modify existing program instructions.

During background editing, you **cannot** move the robot. You cannot move the robot unless the teach pendant is enabled.

If you add motion instructions during background program editing, you must remember to touch up the positions using TOUCHUP in the foreground, before you run the program.

Use Procedure 8-26 to modify a program in the background.

# Caution

You cannot edit system level macros in the foreground or the background. If you attempt to do so, you will not be able to save your changes.

### 8.10.2 Background Edit Process Flow

Figure 8–9 and Figure 8–10 show how the Background Edit process flows.

<!-- PDF page 772 -->

Figure 8–9. Background Edit Process

> **Image description -- img-487.jpeg:** The image is a flowchart illustrating the process for managing background editing of programs. The flowchart begins with a decision box asking, 'Is background edit already in progress for a program?' If the answer is 'YES,' the process loops back to the start. If 'NO,' it proceeds to a selection box where a program for background editing is chosen from a list labeled 'AAA' and 'BBB.' The next step instructs to declare the end of editing using the 'End_edit.in' command. A decision box then asks, 'Is a program in background editing?' If 'NO,' the process moves to enable TP (Test Program) and disable TP, leading to a final state where the program is listed under 'BBB' with background editing enabled. If 'YES,' it checks if TP is enabled. If TP is enabled, it loops back; if not, it enables TP and proceeds to the final state. The flowchart includes labels such as 'TP enabled?', 'Enable TP,' 'Disable TP,' and 'EDIT key,' indicating the operational steps and conditions for managing background editing. The overall process ensures that background editing is properly declared and managed, with TP being enabled or disabled as necessary.

<!-- PDF page 773 -->

Figure 8–10. Background Edit Process (Continued)

> **Image description -- img-488.jpeg:** The image is a flowchart illustrating the process of ending background editing in a program. The flowchart begins with a box labeled 'End Background Editing' leading to a decision box asking if the user wants to implement modifications edited in the background. If 'YES', it asks for the original program name and checks if the program was running or paused. If the program was running or paused, it displays a message stating that the modification cannot be implemented and returns to the start. If the program was aborted, it asks if the user wants to discard the modification. If 'YES', it proceeds to a box labeled 'AAA PAUSED' with options to select, back out, or end, indicating that background editing has ended. If 'NO' at any decision point, the flow returns to the start. The flowchart uses arrows to indicate the direction of the process flow and includes labels such as 'Select', 'End, edit, EOCMD', and 'Background Editing Ended' to guide the user through the steps.

### 8.10.3 Background Editing Using the iPendant

When you use background edit on the iPendant, you must remember the following guidelines:

- Background edit is supported in each window. There will be a background edit program unique for each window so multiple edit sessions will not affect each other.
- The background edit program for dual window is –BCKED2- and for third window is –BCKED3-.
- When a program is selected for background edits, then the comment for the background edit program will show the selected program.

<!-- PDF page 774 -->

- The same program cannot be background edited in multiple edit sessions. If you select the same program already being background edited in another window, then the warning “TPIF-167 Program already in background edit” is posted. You need to End_edit the background session in the other window first.
- Background edit programs are retained during cycle power.

- If you do not want to save the changes you made, move the cursor to NO and press ENTER. You will be given the option to disregard the changes or be returned to the current background edit session.

Note You cannot implement the changes you made if the currently selected program is running or paused. You must first select OK and press ENTER before you can save the program. The background editing session will be resumed.

### 8.11 DISPLAYING A PROGRAM IN THE BACKGROUND (BACKGROUND LOOK)

Background look is used to view a program while another program is running. You can also view the running program. This is useful if you want to use related views and do not want the editor to follow the running program.

To enter background look, follow the steps for Background Edit, but after cursoring to the background program, press F4 LOOK instead of ENTER. You will see "<BACKGROUND LOOK>> on the title line. If you try to modify the program, you will get Memory protect violation. The [ INST ] function key will be replaced with END_LOOK.

To exit background look, press END_LOOK. You may also press [EDCMD] End_edit. It acts the same as END_LOOK during background look.

### 8.12 SETTING PROGRAM STORAGE CONFIGURATION

This option “R798 DRAM File Storage” provides for storage of TP programs outside of CMOS. This allows for an order of magnitude larger program space when using SHADOW DRAM and virtually unlimited space when using files.

The LARGEST TPP program supported is dependent on CMOS size. So without this feature you get ONE 7000 point program. With this feature you can get 8000 7000 point programs. The total number of points loaded into memory at any one time depends on memory configuration. However, with 1GB DRAM almost 150,000 points in memory at the same time is feasible. More points than that requires the use of the FILE type or ONDEMAND type. For these cases not all points are in DRAM at the same time.

In general this enhanced capacity is provided through SHADOW programs. The user model for SHADOW is the same as CMOS. However, the storage for the programs consumes DRAM rather than limited CMOS. So any system configuration with unused DRAM can take advantage of this feature

<!-- PDF page 779 -->

This feature also provides the option that not ALL programs are in DRAM at the same time. Many applications which have thousands of TP programs but only 100 are used on any given day. Both FILE and SHADOW ONDEMAND provide this capability. The disadvantage of this approach is that there is a hesitation when loading the program. To minimize the impact ALL called programs are loaded when a program is called for execution.

For SHADOW ONDEMAND programs are loaded as needed from internal FlashROM. The only limitation of this option is that the user programs are on the internal FlashROM only. So this option doesn't support memory card or other storage devices. This is just a way to structure a system where all the programs don't need to be loaded all the time. When a SHADOW ONDEMAND program is loaded there is a slight hesitation. However, the load times for SHADOW ONDEMAND are ten times faster than FILE type programs and the limitations above do not apply.

The file option can use external storage but the user model is different. The users 1000's of programs might be on a memory card, FlashROM or other storage device. The storage device can be Network storage which provides almost unlimited storage. As FILE programs are called on to be executed they get moved into memory. This loading into memory can be time consuming but in a lot of cases on systems this is not a constraint. Once it's moved into memory it stays in memory until some user action is taken to remove it.

Note The FILE option has limitations. Please consider carefully whether this is the best option for you to use.

- The file is just an ordinary TP file that can be shared among robots or even directly shared with ROBOGUIDE.
- Programs of this type can be edited using the TP editor just like other programs.
- Programs of type FILE may not be compatible with certain applications.

Certain utilities like "Program Adjust" and "On the fly" do not work efficiently with FILE programs. These utilities are designed to be able to modify the program while it is running. The system must temporarily move a program from FILE to CMOS to do these adjustments and then move the program back to FROM. It is better to use the SHADOW and SHADOW ONDEMAND storage for applications requiring constant adjustments.

- FILE programs are generally not part of the file backup. By default it is expected that the user will take care of maintaining these backups since they can be quite large. This behavior can be changed with a setting but care must be taken not to use auto backup when using FILE programs because there may not be room in internal FROM for these programs.
- Mixing FILE programs and other storage types can provide unexpected behaviors. For example program hesitation could occur when a file program is loaded.
- Deleting programs of type file requires that the actual file be deleted.
- The default storage cannot be FILE
- The files which result from editing a FILE program have default storage characteristic. If loaded they will load to the default storage.
- If there are FILE programs and non-file programs of the same name the FILE programs will be ignored.

<!-- PDF page 780 -->

- In order to know ANYTHING about a file program that program must be loaded. For example if it is a MACRO is not known until the program is actually loaded. Only the program name is known.

The key is the STORAGE states that a program can take on. The “permanent” states are:

Table 8–11. Permanent Program Storage States

[tbl-204.md](tbl-204.md)

Programs in SHADOW behave the same way as CMOS. There is no difference in the user model. There is a time lag when a user first EDIT’s a program because it is moved to CMOS for editing. This is noticeable if the program is large. For example a 1000 point program takes about 1 second to be moved into CMOS for editing. Other operations such as program header updates do not require that the program be moved to CMOS so there is no time lag.

Programs in SHADOW ONDEMAND differ from SHADOW programs in that they are loaded when required. This can save startup time as it may take several minutes to load several thousand SHADOW programs. The system will never unload SHADOW ONDEMAND programs. So the system must have enough DRAM available to load ALL SHADOW ONDEMAND programs. The “total” amount of DRAM allocated to ONDEMAND programs is tracked.

Programs in FILE and SHADOW ONDEMAND will show a time lag the first time that they are accessed for execution (or any other access). The entire program tree is loaded on the first access. This means that call statements do not take any longer. Also, FILE programs will take longer to load than SHADOW ONDEMAND programs.

When a CMOS program calls a FILE or SHADOW ONDEMAND program there will be a time lag the first time it is called. This is because the call is the first access to that ON DEMAND resource. This is not expected to be a typical use of the ONDEMAND feature.

In addition there are a number of “temporary” states that a program can be in. It is temporary because the system will in some cases move the program back to its permanent state. These states are:

Table 8–12. Temporary Program Storage States

[tbl-205.md](tbl-205.md)

<!-- PDF page 781 -->

Some of the operational modes associated with the new types have some time lags due to loading programs from a file or moving programs to CMOS. The rule of thumb is 1ms/position. However, the time will vary depending on a number of circumstances. There is a section later on devoted timing issues.

Table 8–13. Load/Convert Times for 1,000 Point Program

[tbl-206.md](tbl-206.md)

New settings are provided to show the status of programs in general and specific storage state per program.

### 8.12.2 Maximum Program Size

The largest TP program that can be created is limited by the amount of CMOS. This is because program creation (no matter HOW the program is created) relies on the entire program residing in CMOS.

Table 8–15. Maximum Program Size for Typical CMOS Allocations

[tbl-208.md](tbl-208.md)

<!-- PDF page 784 -->

For other tools there is a similar or same limitation. However, the tool sometimes changes these limits. No enhancements are planned at this time to eliminate this limitation.

The maximum number of programs that can be stored in on the controller is 8,000. With FILE storage types it is possible to reach that 8,000 file limit. If the files are relatively small it can be reached but it is unlikely.

### 8.12.3 KAREL Control of STORAGE

KAREL programs can access and set the permanent storage for TP programs via:

SET_ATTR_PRG(progname, AT_STORAGE, TPSTOR_SHAD, ", status)

KAREL programs can retrieve the current storage state via:

GET_ATTR_PRG(progname, AT_STORAGE, this_storage, ", status)

See the KAREL reference manual for more information on the usage of these built-ins.

### 8.12.4 File Formats

The format of the TP file is unchanged from previous versions. Programs created on V7.50 can be loaded on V7.40 and vise versa.

The format of the LS file is more restrictive. Legacy LS files do not specify STORAGE and can be loaded on V7.50 and later. They will take on the default storage just like a legacy TP file. Storage is explicitly specified in the LS file. So LS files created on V7.50 and later cannot be loaded into V7.40 unless the user edits the LS file to remove the STORAGE specification.

The LS file will only contain the “permanent” storage state. So for example of a file is SHAD(CMOS) at the time that the LS file is output the LS file will contain SHADOW. ASCII to binary conversion will only recognize the “permanent” storage states of CMOS, SHADOW, SHADOW ONDEMAND and FILE.

### 8.12.5 Storage When Loading from a File

On load the controller must make a decision where to put a TP program. In general the storage attribute is stored in the TP file. For legacy TP and LS files this is not the case.

If the storage is not specified because this is a legacy TP file the program will be stored according to the setting of $TPDRAM_CFG.$TPSTORE_DEF (see configuration screen). The default setting for this is SHADOW. So in general legacy programs are loading into SHADOW. The user can set this to be CMOS, SHADOW or SHADOW ONDEMAND.

FILE storage does not behave this way. The file storage attribute is based on the presence of the TP file in the directory specified by $TPDRAM_CFG.$FILE_PATH(see configuration screen). A program will take on the FILE attribute based on the fact that it is loaded via the file mechanism.

<!-- PDF page 785 -->

If FILE programs are saved they are saved as “unspecified” storage. So if they are loaded they will load according to $TPDRAM_CFG.$TPSTORE_DEF

The user also has the option to load all programs into the default storage regardless of what the TP file setting is. Setting $TPDRAM_CFG.$FORCE_DEF(see configf screen) will force all TP pgormas to be laoded into the default storage.

### 8.12.6 Backup and restore

Any SHADOW or SHADOW ON DEMAND programs are treated exactly the way that CMOS programs are with respect to backup and restore. The FROM file components of these programs are hidden and the only TP files that result from these programs types are in the file backup.

All FILE programs are NOT part of backup and restore unless specified $TPDRAM_CFG.$BACK_FILE (see configuration screen). It is up to the user to back these up as files.

TP files that are stored in FILE do not appear on MDB: at all. They do appear on MD: and the corresponding LS files appear on MD:. So the user is expected to copy TP files from MDB:. Any user who deals directly with MD: will get all the TP programs via MD:. This means that the TP files are loaded from the FILE store and then saved to the backup location.

Restore is similar. Any FILE program TP files are put in the $TPDRAM_CFG.$FILE_PATH directory and that’s it. If they are loaded using the standard restore mechanism they wil be retored if TPDRAM_CFG.$FILE_PATH is properly set up.

In general loading a TP program that is a FILE type results in a TP file being created in $TPDRAM_CFG.$FILE_PATH. If the path is invalid then an error will result

### 8.12.7 Issues relating to SHADOW programs

The main issue here is that SHADOW programs take time to load. Therefore they are loaded at the very end of startup. The controller is allowed to complete its general power up sequence and the programs continue to load at a rate of about 1000pts/minute.

If the system is up and ready to go into the standard TPMM menu it will display a status screen Indicating that it is still loading programs. This is the same screen which is available as part of the SELECT menus (under the type screen). The user can force this screen to exit while programs are loading or wait until programs are loaded.

However, at this time program stubs are created and these programs are treated as “ONDEMAND”. So any access to these programs during the load will work. It just may incur unexpected latencies.

The system variable $TPDRAM_CFG.$LOADED can be used to monitor the progress of the load from an application. This will initially have the value 0 but will be 100 when all programs are loaded.

<!-- PDF page 786 -->


<!-- PDF page 787 -->

# TESTING A PROGRAM AND RUNNING PRODUCTION

## Contents

[tbl-209.md](tbl-209.md)

<!-- PDF page 788 -->

## 9.1 OVERVIEW

This section provides an overview of testing a program and running production.

### Testing Operations

During test operations you should

- Run a program by
  - Stepping through each line of the program
  - Continuously running the program for a single cycle
  - Enabling and disabling robot motion and the, spot welding, arc welding, painting, or dispensing process during testing to verify each instruction of the program
- Monitor your program
- Adjust program information without stopping the program or production, if desired.

### Production Operations

During production operations you should

- Run a thoroughly tested program continuously and repeatedly with all production conditions enabled
- Perform maintenance procedures when necessary
- Perform error recovery procedures when necessary
- Execute multiple programs

Note During testing and running production, you must know how to stop the program if there is a safety problem or adjustment to make, and know how to restart the program.

### Verifying the Program with 4D Graphics

With the 4D graphical system (option) you can preview the operation of the robot without actually moving the robot.

#### Warning

4D graphics might not be an accurate representation of the real world, so actual program verification with the robot arm is still required. Otherwise, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

1. Disable motion from the test run menu.
2. Display the 4D graphical program by pressing ⓘ + FCTN, and selecting Node Map.

<!-- PDF page 789 -->

3. Display the 4D graphical program trace by pressing ⓘ + FCTN, and selecting TCP trace.
4. Execute the program with SHIFT+FWD and observe the graphical motion of the robot. Be sure that robot motion was disabled as described in Step 1.

For more details on operating TCP trace and node map see Section 4.8 and Section 4.4.

## 9.2 PROGRAM PAUSE AND RECOVERY

### 9.2.1 Program Pause and Recovery Overview

You can EMERGENCY STOP or HOLD any program running in production using

- The EMERGENCY STOP button on the teach pendant or operator panel
- The HOLD button on the teach pendant

Note If you are using the Error Recovery option, you can perform error recovery procedures if an error occurs while you are running production.

If you have paused a running program, you can jog linear and circular motion instructions using the PATH jog coordinate system. Refer to Chapter 5 JOGGING THE ROBOT.

### 9.2.2 EMERGENCY STOP and Recovery

Press the EMERGENCY STOP button on the operator panel or teach pendant to stop the robot immediately. When you press the EMERGENCY STOP button you

- Stop the running program
- Turn off drive power to the robot servo system
- Apply the brakes to the robot
- Stop the application

Use Procedure 9-2 to perform an EMERGENCY STOP. Use Procedure 9-3 to recover from an EMERGENCY STOP.

### Procedure 9-2 EMERGENCY STOP

#### Step

1. Press the EMERGENCY STOP button on the teach pendant, or operator panel. This causes an EMERGENCY STOP fault.

Note The Original Path Resume feature is used when resuming a stopped motion in a paused program. This feature allows the robot to remember the stop position and return to that position upon resuming, before continuing along the taught path. The motion to return to the stop position will be a linear, FINE termtype motion at 250 mm/sec.

# Caution

The paused program must remain at the same line number as when the emergency stop occurred; otherwise, the original path resume feature will not be used to resume the program.

Note If the position where the robot resumes is outside of the range defined by the resume tolerance feature and you are in AUTO mode, a prompt box message will be displayed. You must either continue or stop and press ENTER.

### 9.2.3 HOLD and Recovery

Press the HOLD button on the teach pendant to pause a running program. Pressing the HOLD button

- Pauses a running program
- Causes the robot to decelerate and come to a controlled stop

Use Procedure 9-4 to recover from a held program.

# Procedure 9-4 HOLD and Recovery

# Steps

1. Press the HOLD button on the teach pendant.

4. Press CYCLE START to resume program execution. The program will resume using the Original Path Resume feature.

Note The Original Path Resume feature is used when resuming a stopped motion in a paused program. This feature allows the robot to remember the stop position and return to that position upon resuming, before continuing along the taught path. The motion to return to the stop position will be a linear, FINE termtype motion at 250 mm/sec.

# Caution

The paused program must remain at the same line number as when the emergency stop occurred; otherwise, the original path resume feature will not be used to resume the program.

Note Hold is released when program execution begins.

### 9.2.4 Setting Tolerance for Resuming a Program

If you resume a program while in AUTO mode, and the distance between the resume position and the stop position is greater than the stop tolerance, a prompt box is displayed. When this occurs, you must perform specific actions to restart the program.

Stop tolerance is the amount of distance allowed between the resume robot position and the robot stop position. You can specify the following stop tolerances:

- Distance tolerance, for the location components of the position (x,y,z)

<!-- PDF page 793 -->

- Orientation tolerance, for the orientation components of the position (w,p,r)
- Axes tolerances for the joint angle (rotary axes) or distance location (translational axes) of any extended axes, if they are used.
- Orientation tolerance, for the orientation components of the position (w,p,r)
- Axes tolerances for the joint angle (rotary axes) or distance location (translational axes) of any extended axes, if they are used.

# Operation

If you have set the tolerance, the following steps occur when the program is resumed. See Figure 9–1.

1. A running program is paused. The position in which the robot stops is called the stop position.
2. The robot is moved to another position prior to resuming the program. This is called the resume position.
3. CYCLE START is issued to resume the program.
4. If the distance between the stop position and the resume position is greater than the stop tolerance

a. A prompt box is displayed and the program is not resumed.

b. You choose the next action:

- Stop the program.

Note In some applications Abort can be used in place of Stop.

- Restart the program in its current position.
- Change the mode to T1 or T2 and move the robot to another position by jogging it. Then, restart the program. The current position will be rechecked for tolerance.

5. If the distance between the stop position and the resume position is less than the stop tolerance, the program is resumed.

<!-- PDF page 794 -->

Figure 9-1. Resume Tolerance Example

> **Image description -- img-494.jpeg:** The image consists of two parts: a diagram on the left and a text block on the right. The diagram shows a robotic arm with three labeled positions: 'resume position,' 'stop position,' and 'stop tolerance.' The 'resume position' is marked as 10 mm away from the 'stop position,' which itself is associated with a 'stop tolerance' of 5 mm. The text block on the right explains that the resume position has exceeded the stop tolerance by 5 mm. It further states that when the program is resumed, a screen will display a message indicating that the robot position is out of stop tolerance and prompts the user to select an action. The options provided are 'STOP' and 'CONTINUE,' with the note that choosing 'CONTINUE' will require a cycle start.

Note In some applications Abort may be used in place of Stop.

### Limitations

You cannot set tolerance for resume in the following cases:

• In line tracking programs
• In programs that use constant joint path (CJP)
