### 14.4 AUTOMATIC ERROR RECOVERY (OPTION)

#### 14.4.1 Overview

A robot program can stop executing during production as a result of various alarms. For example, if a HOLD or EMERGENCY STOP input is detected, the robot stops moving and processing the application such as arc welding, dispensing, or material handling. In arc welding, for example, you might want to clean the torch and cut the wire before you resume the paused welding program. You can use Automatic Error Recovery (J924) to perform these operations automatically and eliminate the time required to jog the robot to and from a manual repair station.

This section is organized as follows:

• Overview - Resume Program, Maintenance Program, and operation
- Features
- Limitations
- I/O interface
- Setup
— Alarm code monitoring
— Digital input alarms
- Programming

<!-- PDF page 1241 -->

- Testing
- Manual function
- I/O timing sequence

### 14.4.2 Features

Table 14–8 summarizes the features available in the Error Recovery option.

Table 14–8. Error Recovery Features

[tbl-278.md](tbl-278.md)

<!-- PDF page 1242 -->

[tbl-279.md](tbl-279.md)

Note Use Error Recovery only when the teach pendant is disabled. When the teach pendant is enabled, Error Recovery programs can be executed only from the Manual Function screen. Refer to Section 14.4.8.

### 14.4.3 Limitations

Error Recovery is DISABLED when any of the following functions are installed:

- Line tracking
- Soft float
- Continuous turn
- MIG EYE

In addition, Error Recovery has the following limitations:

- Maintenance Program style error recovery is not supported for Coordinated Motion, TAST with Multi-Pass/RPM, or AVC.
- Error recovery is automatically disabled during touch sense searching and re-enabled for all other parts of the teach pendant program.
- Single step execution is disabled during Resume Program execution. Single step mode is available only for the execution of the original program. The single step LED on the teach pendant shows the status for the original program execution.
- If the original program is paused after the RESUME_PROG instruction and then the operator moves the cursor to another line, the Resume Program is not executed at the next program execution.
- The status of the Resume Program execution is not displayed at the monitor screen in the program EDIT screen.
- The status line does not indicate when the Resume Program is executing.
- For a multi-tasking system, when the alarm code monitor feature is disabled and the approval DI is not defined, if the HOLD key is pressed, both parent and child task are paused.
- MAINTENANCE PROG (fast fault) error recovery is not supported for TAST and AVC. An error will be posted if this recovery method is enabled and a monitor alarm occurs in a tracking program.

<!-- PDF page 1243 -->

# Caution

When the Remote TCP option is used, a z-offset is applied in the RTCP frame (User Frame), while a z-offset is applied in the Tool Frame for non-RTCP motions. To prevent unexpected motion or damage, do not use circular motion at the transition between RTCP and non-RTCP motion and do not use a z-offset that is large; otherwise, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

— You might not see the z offset item on the Error Recovery screen. This item is displayed only when it is available.

### 14.4.4 I/O Interface

The Error Recovery sequence can be monitored and controlled remotely using digital I/O. The following I/O signals are available for use with Error Recovery.

- Approval DI
- Incomplete End DO
- Reset DI
- Status DO
- Maint DO

These signals can be assigned in the Error Recovery SETUP screen described in Section 14.4.5. Refer Section 14.4.9 for more information on the I/O timing sequence.

### Approval DI

If this input is defined (not zero), it is checked before error recovery is executed.

- If Approval DI is ON, error recovery is approved, and Resume Programs or Maintenance Programs are executed at the appropriate times.
- If Approval DI is OFF, error recovery is not approved and Resume Programs or Maintenance Programs are not executed.

### Incomplete End DO

When an Error Recovery program is aborted before its normal completion, the Incomplete End DO is turned ON. This DO is turned OFF at the next program execution. The Incomplete End DO is not set if the original program is aborted.

Check the status of this digital output signal before you input the START signal. If this signal is ON, confirm the current robot position. If an interference exists between the current robot position and the paused position of the original program, jog the robot to the position near the paused position before you input the START signal.

<!-- PDF page 1244 -->

# Reset DI

When the Incomplete End DO is used as a condition for a start input in the PLC, you need to turn off the Incomplete End DO remotely. When the Reset DI is input, the Incomplete End DO is turned OFF. After the operator performs the appropriate operation (for example, moves the robot to the position near the paused position of the original program), input this DI signal.

# Status DO and Maint DO

The Status DO and Maint DO signals are provided to indicate whether an error recovery program will execute at the next START input signal.

- When the Status DO output signal is ON, it indicates that a Resume Program will execute at the next START input.
- When the Maint DO output signal is ON, it indicates that a Maintenance Program will execute at the next START input.
- When both the Status DO output signal is OFF and the Maint DO input signal is OFF, the original program will execute at the next START input.

# Warning

The Status DO and Maint DO signals are useful; without them, it is difficult to know which program will execute when resuming a paused program. For example, if you have set up Alarm Code Monitoring, only some errors will invoke Error Recovery, not all. As another example, if you have set up the Approval DI, its state dictates which program will execute.

Note You must disable single step mode before you begin error recovery. If single step mode is enabled during error recovery, it is ignored until the recovery sequence is completed.

If you configure error recovery to execute from the operator panel, there is no way to know that RESUME_PROG will be executed at the next start input unless you view the Error Recovery Status screen in the MANUAL FUNCTIONS screen.

# Alarm Code Monitoring

You can set up Error Recovery to execute after either all errors or after a specific set of user-specified errors. Use the ALARM function key (Procedure 14-8) to define a list of specific errors. If you do not define any specific errors, then all PAUSE severity errors will start Error Recovery program execution.

When you have specified alarms to be monitored, and a fault occurs that is not on the alarm code monitor list, the original program will pause and the Resume Program will not be executed.

The default maximum number of alarms that can be monitored is 10. You can change this number by setting the value of $RSMPRG_SV.$num_alarm and turning off the controller and then turning it on. The maximum value is 32.

Note If specific "Monitored alarm code" faults are not defined (they are all zero) and error recovery is enabled (Approval DI is ON), then all PAUSE severity errors will cause resume program execution at a START signal.

Use Procedure 14-8 to set up alarm code monitoring.

#### 14.4.6 Programming

You use the following teach pendant instructions to specify appropriate recovery program names when you use Error Recovery:

• Resume Program instructions
• Maintenance Program instructions

<!-- PDF page 1251 -->

##### Resume Program Instructions

The auto error recovery function executes the resume program defined in the teach pendant program. To define which resume program is used, use the RESUME_PROG instruction. To clear the resume program, use the CLEAR_RESUME_PROG instruction. See Figure 14–10 and Figure 14–11.

Figure 14-10. RESUME_PROGRAM Instruction

RESUME_PROG = resume program name

Figure 14-11. CLEAR_RESUME_PROG Instruction

CLEAR_RESUME_PROG

Figure 14–12 contains an example production program that sets RESUME_PROG to WIRE_CUT, which is shown in Figure 14–13.

Figure 14-12. WELD.TP Example Program

1: J P[1] 40% FINE
2: RESUME_PROG = WIRE_CUT
3: L P[2] 300mm/sec FINE ARC START[1]
4: L P[3] 50cm/min CNT100
5: L P[4] 50cm/min FINE ARC END[2]
6: CLEAR_RESUME_PROG
7: L P[5] 300mm/sec FINE

Figure 14-13. WIRE_CUT.TP (Resume Program) Example Program

1: L P[10] 50mm/sec FINE INC
2: PR[1]=LPOS
3: J P[11] 50% FINE
4: WO[4] = ON pulse 0.5sec Feed wire
5: L P[12] 20mm/sec FINE
6: WAIT 0.8sec Wait for completion
7: L P[11] 20mm/sec FINE of cutting wire
8: RESUME_PROG = WIRE_CUT2
9: J PR[1] 50% FINE

Figure 14–12 shows how to define the resume program. The WIRE_CUT program is defined as the resume program in line 2 using the RESUME_PROG instruction. The WIRE_CUT program is cleared from the resume program in line 6 of WELD.TP using the CLEAR_RESUME_PROG instruction. Therefore, the WIRE_CUT program is available as the resume program only during program lines 3, 4, and 5 in WELD.TP.

When the automatic start feature is enabled and WELD.TP is paused by a monitored alarm and resumed on lines 3, 4, or 5, the WIRE_CUT program is executed as the resume program and the wire is automatically cut using the WIRE_CUT program. In the program WELD.TP, the resume program is not executed after line 6.

<!-- PDF page 1252 -->

Note In the WIRE_CUT.TP program, PR[1] is near the fault position. The INC (incremental) motion option in line 1 puts PR[1] near the fault position by the value of the INC position. In general, the INC position will be a z offset, such as P[10]: 0, 0, 25, 0, 0, 0.

Note In WIRE_CUT.TP, line 8, the RESUME_PROGRAM is redefined to be WIRE_CUT 2 .TP. If another error occurs in WELD.TP after executing the recovery sequence, WIRE_CUT 2 .TP will be executed upon program resume instead of WIRE_CUT.TP.

# Warning

If the wrong program is defined as the resume program, the robot will move toward an unexpected place. Be sure to define the correct resume program. Otherwise, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

# Maintenance Program Instructions

To define which maintenance program is used, use the MAINT_PROG instruction. To disable the ability to use the return path, use the RETURN_PATH_DSBL instruction. See Figure 14–14 and Figure 14–15.

Figure 14–14. MAINT_PROGRAM Instruction

MAINT_PROG = maintenance program name

Figure 14–15. RETURN_PATH_DSBL Instruction

RETURN_PATH_DSBL

Figure 14–16 contains an example production program that sets MAINT_PROG to TORCHCLN, which is shown in Figure 14–13.

Figure 14–16. WELD.TP Example Program

1: J P[1] 40% FINE
2: MAINT_PROG = TORCHCLN
3: L P[2] 300mm/sec FINE ARC START[1]
4: L P[3] 50cm/min CNT100
5: L P[4] 50cm/min FINE ARC END[2]
6: L P[5] 300mm/sec FINE

If the "RESUME_PROG=" or "MAINT_PROG=" instruction is not used in a program but "Fast exit/entry feature" is ENABLED in the error recovery setup, when a monitored alarm occurs, the MAINT_PROG style of error recovery will execute using the "Maintenance program" defined in the error recovery setup.

If you do not want to use either style of error recovery in a given program, you can use the parameter instruction to disable "Fast exit/entry feature," $RSMFST_SV.$FFAST_ENBL=0. To enable the feature, use the parameter instruction $RSMFST_SV.$FFAST_ENBL=1.

See Figure 14–17 for an example program.

#### 14.4.9 I/O Timing Sequence

See Figure 14–18 through Figure 14–22 for error recovery timing diagrams.

<!-- PDF page 1258 -->

Figure 14–18. Normal Operation Auto Start Mode

> **Image description -- img-85.jpeg:** The image is a timing diagram illustrating the operational sequence and signal relationships for a system with error recovery enabled. Key labels and signals include:

1. **Setup Information (Top Section):**
   - Error recovery = ENABLE
   - Approval DI configured, DI = ON
   - Automatic start = ENABLE
   - Monitored alarm codes are defined

2. **Signal Lines and Their States Over Time:**
   - **PROG RUN:** Starts high, drops low during the pause, then returns high at the end.
   - **BUSY:** Follows the PROG RUN signal, indicating system activity.
   - **PAUSE:** Goes high during the pause period, indicating the original program is paused.
   - **STATUS DO:** Goes high during the pause and returns low afterward.
   - **INCOMPLETE:** Goes high briefly during the pause.
   - **END DO:** Goes high briefly at the end of the pause.
   - **FAULT:** Remains low throughout, indicating no fault condition.
   - **START:** Goes high for a minimum of 300 milliseconds at the beginning of the sequence.
   - **APPROVAL DI:** Goes high during the pause period, indicating approval is required before resuming.
   - **RESET DI:** Goes high briefly after the APPROVAL DI signal.
   - **FAULT RESET:** Remains low throughout, indicating no fault reset is needed.

3. **Operational Phases (Bottom Section):**
   - **Execute original program:** The system starts and runs the original program.
   - **Pause signal:** The original program is paused, indicated by the PAUSE signal going high.
   - **Execute resume program:** After approval (APPROVAL DI high), the resume program is executed.
   - **End original program:** The original program resumes and completes after the pause.

4. **Notes:**
   - The PAUSE signal indicates the original program is paused.
   - The FAULT signal does not output at pause because automatic start is enabled.
   - The APPROVAL DI must be turned on before 300 milliseconds when the original program is paused.
   - The APPROVAL DI does not need to be toggled to indicate approval to execute the resume program.
   - The resume executes without a start signal because automatic start is enabled.

### 14.5 AUXILIARY AXIS SERVO OFF (LOCAL STOP) FUNCTION

In the robot system in which an auxiliary axis controls a jig, there is a requirement to cut off the power of auxiliary axis for safety when an operator does a job with that jig. Auxiliary axis servo off (Local stop) is a function for that purpose. This function can turn off motor power supply for each auxiliary axis respectively and prevent axis from unexpected movements.

This function has the following benefits.

- Keep safety for operator who works at jig (auxiliary axis).
- Improve the cycle time of process because it is not necessary to stop the operation of the robot when the operator enters in Load station to replace the work piece.

<!-- PDF page 1263 -->

- Output servo ON/OFF signal by just using macro program or press button.

This function is an option, and dedicated hardware and setup at DCS Local stop menu is required. Refer to the Dual Check Safety Function Operator's Manual for more information.

### 14.5.1 Specifications

- Way to cut off motor power supply

This function cut off power from servo amplifier to motor. Even in the Local stop mode (power supply for motor is cut off), power is supplied to the amplifier.

- Motor for the auxiliary axis

Be sure to use the motor with brake for this function and set the brake number independent of other motion group when you set up auxiliary axis.

- Local stop Hardware

A dedicated hardware is required. In regard to the dedicated hardware, refer to the Local Stop function with STO Maintenance and Order Manual.

- Set up DCS Local stop menu

To use this function, be sure to perform the set up at the DCS Local stop menu. In regard to DCS Local stop menu, refer to the Local Stop function with STO Maintenance and Order Manual and the “AUXILIARY AXIS SERVO OFF (LOCAL STOP) FUNCTION” chapter in the Dual Check Safety Function OPERATOR'S MANUAL.

- Line of Local stop

The unit (group) in which power supply of motors is controlled synchronously is called as Line of Local stop. Line concept corresponds to the software motion group. Motors in the same line must have the same brake number and motors in the different line must have the different brake number. Software supports eight Local stop lines at a maximum.

Figure 14–23. Local Stop Lines

> **Image description -- img-90.jpeg:** The diagram is a flowchart consisting of three rectangular blocks connected by arrows, representing a sequence or process flow. The first block is labeled 'Line of Local stop,' the second block is labeled 'Software motion group,' and the third block is labeled 'Brake number.' The arrows indicate the direction of the process, moving from 'Line of Local stop' to 'Software motion group,' and then from 'Software motion group' to 'Brake number.' The labels suggest a procedural relationship where a local stop line initiates a software-defined motion group, which in turn determines or controls a brake number.

- Number of axes in the Local stop line

If there are multiple axes in the one Local stop line, the power supply for those motors will be controlled synchronously. In this case, there are multiple axes in one motion group. The power supply for those motors cannot be controlled separately. If you want to control separately, please separate a Local stop line.

Note Configuration of Local stop function is determined by the number of lines and the number of axes in one line.

- Example of system configuration

<!-- PDF page 1264 -->

When there are two axes that use Local stop function, possible configurations are as follows.

Figure 14–24. System Configuration Example

> **Image description -- img-91.jpeg:** The image is a diagram illustrating a control system for three groups of robots, each with its own axis and two lines. The diagram is divided into three vertical sections labeled 'Group 1 Robot,' 'Group 2 Local stop 1st line,' and 'Group 3 Local stop 2nd line.' Each section contains two horizontal lines, representing two lines per axis. Below each group, there are labeled components: 'AMP 2' under Group 2 and 'AMP 3' under Group 3, each connected to a red motor symbol. The motors are powered by a separate power supply, as indicated by the text 'Power supply for those motors can be controlled separately.' The diagram visually conveys that each group operates independently with its own local stop and motor control, emphasizing modularity and separate power management for the motors.

> **Image description -- img-92.jpeg:** The image is a block diagram illustrating a control system for two axes of motion, labeled as '1 line / 2 axes'. The diagram is divided into two main groups: Group 1 (Robot) and Group 2 (Local stop 1st line). Group 1 contains a single block labeled 'Robot', while Group 2 contains two blocks labeled 'AMP 2' and 'AMP 3', each connected to a motor symbol (depicted as a red square with an arrow). The motors are positioned below their respective amplifier blocks. A note at the bottom of the diagram states that the power supply for these motors will be controlled synchronously. The overall structure suggests a coordinated control system where the robot's motion is managed alongside local stop functions, with synchronized power supply to the motors.

- Necessary signals for Local stop function

One input signal and one output signal are required for each Local stop line.

1. Input signal #2

Local stop command signal by the user. Local stop software controls power supply for the motor in response to this signal.

— When this signal is ON, supply power to the motor and the axis can move.
— When this signal is OFF, cut off power to the motor and the axis cannot move.

2. Output signal #2

Local stop status feedback signal from a robot controller to a peripheral device such as PLC. This signal shows the state of Local stop software controls power supply for the motor. Use this signal as muting indicator and WAIT condition of wait for transit servo off/on to complete in TP program. Do not operate this signal.

— When this signal is OFF, power is supplied to the motor and the axis can move.
— When this signal is ON, power is not supplied to the motor and the axis cannot move.

Assign general I/O or robot I/O for input signal #2 and output signal #2.

- Basic flow of process

When user inputs the input signal #2, software outputs the internal output signal #1 to the amplifier and power supply for motor will be controlled. Software also outputs the output signal #2 to a peripheral device after checking the state of power supply in amplifier by the internal input signal #1. Please connect a peripheral device such as push button to the input signal #2.

<!-- PDF page 1265 -->

Figure 14–25. Basic Process Flow

> **Image description -- img-93.jpeg:** The diagram is a block diagram illustrating the signal flow between a peripheral device, a robot controller, and a servo amplifier. The peripheral device sends an 'Input signal #2 (Local stop command)' to the robot controller. The robot controller processes this signal and sends an 'Internal output signal #1 (Command to control power supply)' to the servo amplifier. The servo amplifier then sends back an 'Internal input signal #1 (State of power supply)' to the robot controller. Finally, the robot controller outputs an 'Output signal #2 (Local stop state)' back to the peripheral device. The labels indicate the type and direction of signals exchanged between components, highlighting the control and feedback loop for managing the power supply state based on the local stop command.

In case a macro program will input that Local stop command, please output general output signal in that program to the peripheral device such as PLC and control input signal #2 according to that output.

Figure 14–26. Basic Process Flow with Macro Program

> **Image description -- img-94.jpeg:** The diagram illustrates a control system involving a PLC (Programmable Logic Controller), a robot controller, and a servo amplifier. The PLC receives an input signal labeled 'Input signal #2 (Local stop command)' and sends an output signal labeled 'Output signal #2 (Local stop state)' to the robot controller. The robot controller processes a 'Macro Program' and generates an 'Internal output signal #1 (Command to control power supply)' sent to the servo amplifier. The servo amplifier, in turn, provides an 'Internal input signal #1 (State of power supply)' back to the robot controller. The robot controller also outputs a 'General output (Indirect Local stop command)' to an unspecified destination. The labels indicate the flow of control signals and states between the components, highlighting the interaction for managing a local stop command and power supply control within the system.

### 14.5.2 Limitations

- “LSTP-001 Motion grp %d is active” alarm occurs when user command cutting off the power supply (input signal #2 = OFF) while auxiliary axis is moving. Then running program will be paused and robot stops when this alarm occurs. Command power off while axis is not moving.
- “LSTP-011 Motion grp %d is in LSTOP” alarm occurs when user tried to move axis while the power supply is cut off. Then axis does not move. Please turn on power supply for auxiliary axis before you move axis.
- Be sure to specify FINE positioning path for last motion instruction right before command power off (input signal #2 = OFF). If specify CNT positioning path for last motion instruction right before command power off, “LSTP-001 Motion grp %d is active” alarm might occur.
- Be sure to keep time more than 0.2 sec before command power off (input signal #2 = OFF). If command power off right after last motion instruction without waiting 0.2 sec, “LSTP-001 Motion grp %d is active” alarm might occur.

<!-- PDF page 1266 -->

#### 14.5.3 Settings

1. Connect the dedicated hardware. Refer to the Local Stop function with STO Maintenance and Order Manual.
2. Set up the DCS Local stop menu. Refer to the Local Stop function with STO Maintenance and Order Manual and the “AUXILIARY AXIS SERVO OFF (LOCAL STOP) FUNCTION” chapter in the Dual Check Safety Function OPERATOR'S MANUAL.
3. Set system variables. For each Local stop line, setting of motion group number, input signal #2, output signal #2 and internal output signal #1 is necessary. For input signal #2 and output signal #2, specify the port type and port number. For internal output signal #1, please specify the SPO index number. In regard to the SPO index number, refer to the Local Stop function with STO Maintenance and Order Manual and the “AUXILIARY AXIS SERVO OFF (LOCAL STOP) FUNCTION” chapter in the Dual Check Safety Function OPERATOR'S MANUAL.

### 14.6 BRAKE CHECK FUNCTION

#### 14.6.1 Overview

Brake check function (A05B-2500-J951) is a preventive maintenance function. It is used to check that the motor does not move when motor torque is applied while brake is engaged. This allows user to perform early detection of potential brake failure. User is informed of the checking result by warning message or system variables.

#### 14.6.2 Setup

##### 14.6.2.1 Enable/Disable of Brake Check function

For robots that have been tuned for Brake Check function, it is enabled by default once the option is loaded. The system variable that enables/disables brake check function is:

$BCCFG.$BCK_ENABLE TRUE: Enable (default) / FALSE: Disable

Please confirm this variable is TRUE (Enable) before use. If this variable is FALSE (Disable), brake check will not start.

##### 14.6.2.2 Enable/Disable switch for each axis

User can selectively enable/disable brake check for individual axis. To execute brake check on a selected axis, the following system variable needs to be TRUE (Enable):

$BCK_GRP[group].$CHK_AXIS[axis] TRUE: Enable / FALSE: Disable

On robots that are tuned for Brake Check function, the default value is TRUE (Enable). For non-robot axis (such as aux axis, servo gun, ... etc.), the default value is FALSE (Disable).

To execute brake check on dual drive axis, this variable needs to be set TRUE (Enable) for both master and slave axis.

##### 14.6.2.3 Setting Brake Torque

Brake Check function requires brake torque information for each axis in order to determine torque command during brake check. The following system variable needs to be set with the brake torque value [kgf*cm] for each axis.

$BCK_GRP[group].$BRK_TORQUE[axis] brake torque [kgf*cm]

<!-- PDF page 1276 -->

On robots that are tuned for Brake Check function (including robots that use Dual Drive), this variable is set automatically. However, on non-robot axis (such as aux axis, servo gun, or etc.), this variable is not set. Manual setting is required if brake check is needed on non-robot axis. Please refer to AC SERVO MOTOR DESCRIPTIONS “9.1 BRAKE SPECIFICATIONS” on specification value of brake torque. Please note that the unit of this variable is [kgf*cm].

If brake check is required on non-robot Independent Dual Drive axis, please set this variable as follows:

Case-1: Either master or slave motor has one brake.

Set this variable to the brake torque value [kgf*cm] on only the axis that has brake. For the axis that has no brake, please set 0.0 (default).

Case-2: Both master and slave motors have brakes.

Set this variable to the brake torque value [kgf*cm] on both master and slave axes. The brake torque value of both the master and the slave axis must be same. Brake Check function does not support different brake torque value in this case.

### 14.6.3 Start Brake Check

To start brake check, please set the following system variable to TRUE.

$BCCFG.$BCK_START TRUE: Brake check is running / FALSE: Brake check is finished

User can perform brake check by using parameter instruction of Teach Pendant program or by manually setting system variable. This variable will automatically return to FALSE when brake check is completed. Please do not move the robot until checking is completed (this variable automatically returns to FALSE). If brake check function is disabled ($BCCFG.$BCK_ENABLE=FALSE), brake check will not be performed, and $BCCFG.$BCK_START will immediately return to FALSE even if this variable is set to TRUE.

Sample Teach Pendant program that executes brake check:

1: J P[1] 100% FINE
2: L P[2] 2000mm/sec FINE
3: WAIT 1.00 (sec)
4: $BCCFG.$BCK_START=1
5: WAIT $BCCFG.$BCK_START=0
6: L P[3] 2000mm/sec FINE

Brake check cannot be started while the robot is moving, so this program waits for robot to stop completely by WAIT instruction on L3. Then, this program starts brake check at L4 and waits until brake check is completed at L5. As previously described, brake check can only be executed while robot is completely stopped.

Note In case of brake failure, the motor can move during brake check. Therefore, it is important that robot is at a position with sufficient clearance. Total motion command per single check

<!-- PDF page 1277 -->

varies by robot and by axis. However, it is up to 200,000[pulse]. This is about 0.4[rev] in motor revolution and about 1.4[deg] in degree of joint angle assuming a gear ratio of 1/100.

In case power is shut OFF during brake check, the following alarm will be posted at next power ON. This alarm indicates that there was abnormal termination at last check.

BRCH-003 Last check was failed

The following system variable will be also set to TRUE at next power ON.

$BCCFG.$LAST_FAILED TRUE: Last check was failed / FALSE: Last check completed normally

In this case, the results of brake check will not be generated, therefore please execute brake check again at next power ON. If next brake check completes normally, this variable will return to FALSE automatically.

### 14.6.4 Result of Brake Check

$BCCFG.$BCK_START automatically returns to FALSE when brake check completes. The result is also posted as warning message. If all brake passes as “Good” brake, the following message will be posted.

BRCH-001 All brake are normal

By contrast, if brake failure is detected as “Bad” brake, the following message will be posted.

Ex) Brake failure is detected on group1/J2.

BRCH-002 Brake abnormal (G:1,A:2)

The results are also recorded in the following system variable at the same time. The value of this variable is kept until next brake check starts.

$BCK_GRP[group].$CHK_RESULT[axis] TRUE: Brake failure / FALSE: Normal brake (default)

### 14.6.5 Limitations

Brake check function cannot be executed under the following conditions, or alarm will be posted.

- Calibration has not been done.
- Robot is moving.
- Servo is OFF.
- Servo parameter is being updated.
- Dual motor is in adjust mode.

<!-- PDF page 1278 -->

- Even though the axis has brake and $BCK_GRP[group].$CHK_AXIS[axis] is TRUE, brake torque ($BCK_GRP[group].$BRK_TORQUE[axis]) is not set.
- Teach Pendant is enabled.

### 14.6.6 Caution

- It takes about 10 sec for single brake check execution.
- When the motor is heating up, the motor torque can decrease, so it may not be able to detect brake failure. To detect it with high accuracy, please execute brake check preferably when the motor is in low-temperature, e.g. first thing in the morning.

## 14.7 CENTER FINDER

### 14.7.1 Overview

Center Finder is a motion option that allows a user to find the center of a two-dimensional symmetric shape such as a circle, hexagon, or triangle. The found center can be used as a reference point. You can use it for finding the center of a chuck, for example.

Center Finder uses the Torque Observer Sensor (TOS) or I/O method to touch points on the shape. The center is computed based on the contact positions. The same process is repeated until the current center position and the newly computed one are within a pre-defined tolerance. Center Finder then moves the TCP to the center position and records the position to a position register.

Note I/O method is the preferred method for contact detection. If the robot had a very stiff Tool mounted on its faceplate, then TOS can be used for contact detection as well.

Center Finder should not be used during production operation. It can only be used during initial teaching and setup.

Center Finder does not support any robots that have fewer than six axes, and it does not support multi arm configuration.

### Using Center Finder

After you set up Center Finder, it performs the following steps to find the center:

1. Computes the search directions.
2. Moves the robot in the search directions to detect the edge of the opening.
3. Computes the center of the opening, and moves the TCP to the center.
4. Confirms the center by repeating Step 2 until the difference between the currently computed center and the previous center is within the pre-defined tolerance.

<!-- PDF page 1279 -->

5. Updates a position register (defined during setup) to store the center position. The function leaves the robot in the center position. This enables you to verify the acceptability of the position.

Note You can then adjust the chuck jaws and redo the search if desired.

### 14.7.2 Using Center Finder

You must install the Center Finder software option before you can use it. Refer to the *Software Installation Manual* for more information about installing software options.

1. If you are using the TOOL frame, make sure the frame is set up correctly. If you are using the USER frame, make sure the frame is set up correctly.
2. Select the shape's normal (perpendicular) axis. This axis has to align to one of the motion frame's major axes. See Figure 14–33.

Figure 14–33. Shape with a Perpendicular Axis

> **Image description -- img-102.jpeg:** The image depicts a 3D geometric figure resembling a rectangular prism or box with a circular hole or indentation on one of its faces. A normal vector is illustrated as an arrow pointing outward from the center of the circular hole, perpendicular to the plane of the hole. The normal vector is labeled 'Normal Vector' and is represented with a bold arrowhead, indicating its direction away from the surface. The circular hole is centered on one of the rectangular faces of the prism, and the normal vector originates from this circular region. The figure is drawn in a perspective view, showing the three-dimensionality of the object and the orientation of the normal vector relative to the surface.

3. Select the search type.
4. Set up individual motion parameters if required.
5. After you have set it up, you can run the Center Finder program to find the center.

Note In a multiple-group system, the robot is the first group.

### 14.8 COLLISION DETECTION FOR AUXILIARY AXIS

#### 14.8.1 Overview

The Collision Detection Function stops the robot immediately and reduces the damage to the robot, when the robot collides with other objects. Generally, this feature has been applied for the robot axes. But, this feature has not been applied for the auxiliary axis. Because the auxiliary axis is design by the customer, then the parameters for this feature can not be set beforehand. To apply this feature to the auxiliary axis, the parameter tuning is required with tuning procedure shown below.

Caution

The load ratio of auxiliary axis should be less than 5.

Load ratio = (Load Inertia + Motor Inertia) / Motor Inertia

When the auxiliary axis is designed, you must consider the above equation.

If the load ratio of auxiliary axis is more than 5 times, the motion performance and sensitivity for collision detection may deteriorate.

#### 14.8.2 Initial Setting

1. Set up the auxiliary axis (Gear ratio, acceleration time, and etc.) normally.
2. Turn power on.
3. Set the following system variables.

- $SBR[n].$PARAM[112] = 2097152 / ($SBR[n].$PARAM[47])

<!-- PDF page 1287 -->

- \(SBR[n].\)PARAM[119] = 7282
- \(SBR[n].\)PARAM[120] = -7282

n : Hardware axis number of auxiliary axis

n=7~ for aux. Axis / n=1~6 for robot axes

4. Cycle power.

#### 14.8.3 Tuning Procedure

The sensitivity of collision detection will be tuned by below procedure. It should be tuned without mis-detection.

1. Create the program that includes heavy motion like an inverse motion with CNT100 beforehand. If the program for production is already exist, It can be used to tune. In this case, the sensitivity can be optimized for production with this program. (However, if other program was run, the mis-detection might occur. Also, if this program was modified, the re-tuning might be required.)
2. Run the above program. On this occasion, note that this program must not be paused because the disturbance torque displayed in the screen explained below will be cleared at just restarting it.
3. Measure the max. / min. disturbance torque on STATUS/AXIS/ DISTURB screen after running the program.

STATUS Axis
GRP[1]
Disturbance Torque (A)
Curr./ Max. (Allowed) / Min. (Allowed)
J1 : 0.0 20.0(40.0) -19.0( -40.0)
J2 : 0.0 19.0(40.0) -20.0( -40.0)
J3 : 0.0 22.0(40.0) -10.0( -40.0)
J4 : 0.0 12.0(20.0) -5.0( -20.0)
J5 : 0.0 10.0(20.0) -11.0( -20.0)
J6 : 0.0 8.0(20.0) -4.0( -20.0)
J7 : 0.0 24.0(56.0) -30.0( -56.0)
[ TYPE ] MONITOR TRACKING DISTURB [UTIL ] >

As said above, the disturbance torque will be reset at the start of each program. If there are some programs,

- make new program that call all programs for tuning and run this main program.
- record the max. / min. disturbance torque for each programs and find max. / min. value in these recorded value.

4. Move the cursor to allowed value in parentheses for the axis. Change the allowed value to same as measured max. or min. value.

<!-- PDF page 1288 -->

STATUS Axis
GRP[1]
Disturbance Torque (A)
Curr./ Max. (Allowed) / Min. (Allowed)
J1 : 0.0 20.0(40.0) -19.0( -40.0)

# Caution

When the disturbance torque exceeds above allowed value, the following WARNING occurs

SRVO-053 Disturbance excess (G:x,A:x)

Following servo alarm (servo power off) occurs when the disturbance torque exceeds below ALARM LEVELs.

Upper Limit = Max. allowed value + 0.3 x

Max. current of amp. Lower Limit = Min. allowed value - 0.3 x

Max. current of amp. SRVO-050 Collision Detect alarm (G:x,A:x)

Part of  \( 0.3 \times Max. \)  current of amp. is the margin to prevent the miss-detection.

For example in above screen with 40A amplifier,

Upper Limit = 24.0 + 0.3 x 40 = 36 A

Lower Limit = -30.0 - 0.3 x 40 = -42 A

5. Run the programs again with above disturbance allowed setting, and confirm that there is no miss-detection.

### 14.9 COLLISION GUARD

#### 14.9.1 Overview

Collision Guard provides a highly sensitive method to detect that the robot has collided with an object and then stops the robot immediately. This helps to minimize the potential for damage to the end-of-arm tooling and robot. Collision Guard also helps to prevent damage during teaching.

<!-- PDF page 1289 -->

Additionally, you have the ability to change the sensitivity or even disable Collision Guard within a TP program to handle situations in which the disturbance is expected to vary widely from normal operation. Collision Guard is in effect both during jogging motion and programmed motion. There are several ways to configure and adjust Collision Guard:

- The Collision Guard SETUP screen allows you to adjust the sensitivity of collision detection for programmed motion. Collision Guard automatically uses more sensitive limits for jogging motion. These limits cannot be adjusted.
- Within a teach pendant program, you can disable Collision Guard locally through the use of special teach pendant instructions, COL DETECT OFF and COL DETECT ON.
- Within a teach pendant program, you can adjust the sensitivity of Collision Guard locally using the COL GUARD ADJUST teach pendant instruction.

Note In order to decrease the force of collision, Collision Guard allows the robot axes to sag away from the collision for 200 milliseconds after detecting a collision. When this happens, vertical robot axes might fall slightly after detecting a collision, due to the effect of gravity.

# Warning

If you have used the SHIFT + RESET key combination to clear an error condition and you continue to press the SHIFT key without releasing it, subsequent collision alarms will NOT be detected, collision detection alarms will NOT be displayed, and you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

### 14.9.2 Limitations

- Collision Guard cannot be permanently completely disabled.
- Collision Guard cannot be used when the robot brakes are on.

### 14.9.3 Falsely Detected Collisions

Collision Guard might detect a false collision when a collision has not occurred in the following cases:

- Payload information has not been set correctly.
- The ACC motion option has been used, causing jerky robot motion.
- Not enough voltage has been supplied to the controller.
- The payload is larger than the maximum payload for the robot, or the inertia of the payload is too large.
- Very high speed rotations of wrist joints occur with improperly set payload parameters.
- Jerky reverse motion (P[1]->P[2]->P[1]) occurs.
- Linear motion occurs near singularity point where axes revolve in high speed.

<!-- PDF page 1290 -->

### 14.9.4 Setup

Before you can use Collision Guard, you must set it up. Setup includes:

- Setting the Collision Guard Sensitivity
- Specifying a register in which to set and store the sensitivity value for the COL GUARD ADJUST teach pendant instruction, if desired.

Refer to Table 14–17 for information on Collision Guard Setup Items. Use Procedure 14-16 to set up Collision Guard.

Table 14–17. Collision Guard Setup Items

[tbl-294.md](tbl-294.md)

### Procedure 14-16 Setting Up Collision Guard

1. Press MENU.

<!-- PDF page 1291 -->

2. Select SETUP.
3. Press F1, [TYPE].
4. Select Coll Guard. You will see a screen similar to the following.

COL GUARD SETUP G1 JOINT 100%
1/3
Group: 1
Collision Guard status: ENABLED
1 Sensitivity: 100%
2 Sensitivity Macro Reg.: R[0]
3 Collision Guard Error: DO[0]
4 Col. Guard Enabled: DO[0]

5. To select a group, press F3, GROUP, and enter the number of the group you want. If the group you want does not exist, or it includes a robot that has not been tuned for Collision Guard, the group will not be changed and you will see a message similar to the following:

Selected group doesn't support HSCD

6. To display help information, press F2, HELP. When you are finished displaying help, press PREV.
7. Move the cursor to the items you want to set, and set them as desired.

#### 14.9.5 Programmed Motion

You can use the following teach pendant instructions to control Collision Guard during programmed motion:

• COL DETECT ON, COL DETECT OFF
• COL GUARD ADJUST

##### 14.9.5.1 COL DETECT ON, COL DETECT OFF

By default, Collision Guard is enabled.

- To disable Collision Guard, include the COL DETECT OFF instruction in a teach pendant program.
- To enable Collision Guard when it has been disabled previously, include the COL DETECT ON instruction in a teach pendant program. Since Collision Guard is always enabled by

<!-- PDF page 1292 -->

default, you need to use the COL DETECT ON instruction only if you have previously used the COL DETECT OFF instruction in the same teach pendant program.

Note The COL DETECT ON and COL DETECT OFF instructions will only apply to the motion groups that are included in the group mask of the teach pendant program that calls them. For example, if COL DETECT OFF is used in a teach pendant program that contains group 2 only in its group mask, then Collision Guard will only be disabled for group 2; it will remain enabled for all other groups.

Also, if the COL DETECT OFF instruction is used within a teach pendant program, and that program is aborted, then Collision Guard will be automatically turned back on. See the following screen for an example.

10: J P[1] 100% FINE
11: COL DETECT OFF
12: L P[2] 2000mm/sec CNT100
13: L P[3] 2000mm/sec CNT100
14: L P[4] 2000mm/sec CNT100
15: COL DETECT ON
16: J P[5] 50% FINE

#### 14.9.5.2 COL GUARD ADJUST

The COL GUARD ADJUST teach pendant instruction allows you to adjust the sensitivity of Collision Guard within a teach pendant program. The sensitivity value set by this instruction will temporarily override what has been set in the COL GUARD SETUP menu. The instruction can be used in two ways:

- With no arguments. In this case, the new sensitivity value will be obtained from the register whose register number is specified in the COL GUARD SETUP menu.
- With one argument. In this case, the new sensitivity value will be obtained from the argument, which can be either DIRECT (value entered explicitly) or INDIRECT (register number specified).

As with the COL DETECT ON and COL DETECT OFF instructions, the new sensitivity value will apply only to the motion group(s) that are indicated in the group mask of the program that uses COL GUARD ADJUST. For example, if COL GUARD ADJUST is used in a program whose group mask is group 2 only, then the new sensitivity will apply only to group 2; the sensitivity of all other groups will remain unchanged.

If the group mask of the program that uses COL GUARD ADJUST contains a group that does not support Collision Guard, a warning message will be posted as follows:

MOTN-404 Group # does not support HSCD

<!-- PDF page 1293 -->

This message is just a warning to indicate that no action was taken on that group.

To use the COL GUARD ADJUST instruction without arguments in a TP program, the following procedure should be used:

- Set the register(s) specified in the COLL GUARD SETUP menu for the appropriate group(s) to the new sensitivity value(s). NOTE: If the TP program is a multiple group program, the appropriate register for each group needs to be set.
- Insert the COL GUARD ADJUST instruction into the TP program at the desired location.

Note If the register number in the COL GUARD SETUP menu is zero for one of the groups being adjusted, then an error will be posted, as follows:

MOTN-400 No Coll. Guard Reg. Defined

If a valid register number is specified in the setup menu, but the data in that register is not an integer between 1 and 200, then the following error will be posted:

MOTN-401 Coll. Guard Reg. Data Error

See the following screen for an example.

10: J P[1] 100% FINE
11: R[11]=80
12: COL GUARD ADJUST
13: L P[2] 2000mm/sec CNT100
14: L P[3] 2000mm/sec CNT100
15: L P[4] 2000mm/sec CNT100
16: R[11]=100
17: COL GUARD ADJUST
18: J P[5] 50% FINE

This example would apply to a single group program (say, a group 1 only program). In the example, it is assumed that the register number has been set to 11 for group 1 in the COL GUARD SETUP menu.

Alternatively, the COL GUARD ADJUST instruction can be supplied with the new sensitivity value directly. An example of how this could be done is as follows:

<!-- PDF page 1294 -->

10: J P[1] 100% FINE
11: COL GUARD ADJUST 80
12: L P[2] 2000mm/sec CNT100
13: L P[3] 2000mm/sec CNT100
14: L P[4] 2000mm/sec CNT100
15: R[1]=100
15: COL GUARD ADJUST R[1]
16: J P[5] 50% FINE

To use the COL GUARD ADJUST instruction in this way, after inserting the instruction into the program, move the cursor to the right of the instruction. Then, either type in the new sensitivity value directly, or select F3 “INDIRECT” and type in the desired register number.

As stated above, the COL GUARD ADJUST instruction will apply to all groups in the group mask of the TP program that called it. However, if the instruction is used with an argument, the user also has the option to restrict the groups whose sensitivity will be adjusted. This is accomplished by moving the cursor to the argument field and pressing the F1 “GP_MASK” key. Doing so will display the following menu at the top of the Teach Pendant screen:

1 Default
2 [GP:]

Selecting “1” for “Default” means default behavior of the instruction, i.e. all groups in the group mask are adjusted. Selecting “2” inserts a “GP” modifier into the instruction as follows:

COL GUARD ADJUST GP1,2: ##

The cursor will then be on the “##”, which is the field where the sensitivity can be directly entered. The user can then move the cursor to the left to highlight the “GP1,2” field. Once this field is highlighted, the function keys will have labels displayed for each available motion group, i.e. F1 will have “GP1”, F2 will have “GP2”, etc. Pressing the appropriate function key will toggle the appearance of that group number in the “GP1,2” field. Once the “GP1,2” field has been set, only those groups listed in this field will have their sensitivity updated by the instruction.

By default, when a TP program that calls COL GUARD ADJUST is aborted, the sensitivity will be reset to the value specified in the COL GUARD SETUP menu for each group in the program's group mask. This feature can be disabled by setting the following system variable:

$HSCDMNGRP[g].$AUTO_RESET = 0

where “g” refers to the group number.

<!-- PDF page 1295 -->

### 14.10 CONDITION MONITOR FUNCTION

#### 14.10.1 Overview

The Condition Monitor Function monitors the condition of an I/O signal, register value, or alarm status, during teach pendant program execution. As soon as the condition is triggered, the specified teach pendant program is executed and interrupts the current program.

A Condition monitor is defined by two or more teach pendant programs:

- A condition (CH) program specifying one or more sets of conditions, such as a port or register value. Each set of conditions contains the name of an action program to be called when the condition is satisfied.
- One or more action programs specifying what is to be done when a condition is satisfied.

For example, you can use the condition monitor function as follows:

If a robot is handling a workpiece and drops it, an error message is displayed and the robot pauses. See Figure 14–35 and Sample, Condition Handler, and Action Programs.

<!-- PDF page 1296 -->

1: WHEN RI[2] = OFF, CALL ROBOT_PAUSE
[END]
ROBOT_PAUSE.TP (action program)
1: SO[2] = ON ! Notify the peripheral device
2: R[8] = R[8] + 1 ! Count the number of dropped times
3: User alarm[1] ! Display alarm and pause robot
[END]
$UALRM_MSG[1] (system variable)
$UALRM_MSG[1] = 'WORK WAS DROPPED'

#### 14.10.2 Monitors

There are two kinds of monitors:

- The program monitor is started by a program monitor instruction and stops monitoring when the program executes a MONITOR END instruction or is aborted.
- The system monitor is started and ended using the STATUS System Monitor screen.

##### Program Monitor

Program monitor is used to monitor conditions in each teach pendant program. This monitor depends on the status of program execution. The program monitor only monitors while the program is executing. You start the program monitor using the teach pendant instruction MONITOR. You end the program monitor using the teach pendant instruction MONITOR END or by aborting the program. In the example shown in Example of Program Monitor (SAMPLE.TP), the system watches the conditions specified by the CH program.

Example of Program Monitor (SAMPLE.TP)

5: MONITOR <ch program name="">
6: J P[4] 100% CNT100
7: J P[5] 100% CNT100
:
:
19: MONITOR END <ch program name=""></ch></ch>

##### System Monitor

The system monitor does not require a program to be executing for monitoring to take place. When the program is aborted, the program monitor terminates. The system monitor is for monitoring the condition of a system, like a PLC. You can start and end the system monitor from the condition menu. Unlike program monitor, you cannot start and end the system monitor using teach pendant instructions. A MONITOR instruction in the action program of a system monitor can be used to restart the system monitor.

<!-- PDF page 1297 -->

You can use the system variable $TPP_MON.$global_mt to select a mode type at Cold start.

- TYPE1 - If the monitor is executing before the controller is turned off, the system deletes the monitor at Cold start.
- TYPE2 - If the monitor is executing before the controller is turned off, the system starts monitoring at Cold start automatically.

Note You cannot use TYPE1 and TYPE2 together.

Note You can use system monitor and program monitor concurrently.

##### Changing the Monitor Type

You can change the type of monitor as follows:

\(TPP_MON.\)local_mt = 1 - Program monitor TYPE1 (default)
\(TPP_MON.\)local_mt = 2 - Program monitor TYPE2
\(TPP_MON.\)global_mt = 0 - No use system monitor (default)
\(TPP_MON.\)global_mt = 1 - System monitor TYPE1
\(TPP_MON.\)global_mt = 2 - System monitor TYPE2

#### 14.10.3 Monitor State

Table 14–18 shows the state of the monitor for each operation.

@ : Start the monitor

o : Restart the monitor if the monitor was executing at paused

% : Pause the monitor (It can restart)

x : Cancel the monitor (It cannot restart)

- : It does not change the state of the monitor

Table 14–18. State of Condition Monitoring

[tbl-295.md](tbl-295.md)

<!-- PDF page 1298 -->

[tbl-296.md](tbl-296.md)

### 14.10.4 Monitor Instructions

A program monitor is executed using the following two instructions:

- MONITOR <ch program="">Start monitoring the conditions taught in the <ch program="">.
- MONITOR END <ch program="">Stop monitoring the conditions taught in the <ch program="">.</ch></ch></ch></ch>

You can use the system variable $TPP_MON.$local_mt to change monitoring modes while a program is PAUSED.

- TYPE1 - Stop monitoring when the program is PAUSED.
- TYPE2 - Keeps on monitoring even when the program is PAUSED.

Note You cannot use TYPE1 and TYPE2 together.

### 14.10.5 Condition Handler Program

You can teach the condition in a program that has a Cond sub type. When you edit the condition handler program, only the WHEN instruction is available.

WHEN <condition> CALL <program></program></condition>

<!-- PDF page 1299 -->

In a condition handler program, you can teach multiple WHEN instructions as follows.

1: WHEN <cond1> CALL <program1>
2: WHEN <cond2> CALL <program2>
3: WHEN <cond3> CALL <program3></program3></cond3></program2></cond2></cond1>

You can connect the multiple conditions using AND/OR as follows.

1: WHEN <cond1> AND <cond2> CALL <program1>
2: WHEN <cond1> OR <cond2> OR <cond3> CALL <program2></program2></cond3></cond2></cond1></cond1></cond2></cond1>

Note You cannot use both AND and OR in the same WHEN instruction.

#### 14.10.6 Conditions

Figure 14–36 through Figure 14–38 show the conditions that can be monitored.

Figure 14–36. Condition for Register, System Variable, and I/O Parameters

> **Image description -- img-104.jpeg:** The image displays a table with four columns labeled 'WHEN', '[item]', '[operator]', and '[action]'. The table defines conditional logic rules with the following details:

1. **WHEN [item]**: Specifies the type of item to evaluate. Possible items include:
   - R[x]: A register or variable indexed by x.
   - $System variable: A system-defined variable.
   - G[x]: A global variable indexed by x.
   - GO[x]: A global object indexed by x.
   - AO[x]: An application object indexed by x.

2. **[operator]**: Defines the comparison or logical operator to apply. Possible operators include:
   - = (equal to)
   - <> (not equal to)
   - < (less than)
   - <= (less than or equal to)
   - > (greater than)
   - >= (greater than or equal to)

3. **[value]**: The value or expression to compare against the item. This column is empty in the table but implies a placeholder for a specific value or expression.

4. **[action]**: Specifies the action to take based on the condition. Two types of actions are shown:
   - Constant value: Assigns a fixed value.
   - CALL program: Executes a program or subroutine.

The table serves as a reference for constructing conditional statements in a programming or scripting context, where the outcome of the condition determines the subsequent action.

<!-- PDF page 1300 -->

Figure 14–37. Condition2 for I/O

> **Image description -- img-105.jpeg:** The image is a table that outlines a set of conditional logic rules for input/output (I/O) operations. The table has four columns: "WHEN [I/O]", "[operator]", "[value]", and "[action]". 

- The "WHEN [I/O]" column lists different I/O identifiers: DI[x], DO[x], R[x], RO[x], SI[x], SO[x], UI[x], and UO[x].

- The "[operator]" column shows two comparison operators: "=" (equal) and "<>" (not equal).

- The "[value]" column specifies the state or condition to compare against, with possible values being "On" or "Off".

- The "[action]" column describes the resulting action based on the condition met, which is to "CALL program" and lists the same I/O identifiers as in the first column.

The table appears to define a logic where, depending on the state (On or Off) of a specific I/O point, a program is called, and the action may involve interacting with another I/O point. For example, if DI[x] is equal to On, the program calls R[x]; if DO[x] is not equal to Off, the program calls UI[x], and so on.

Figure 14–38. Condition for Error status

WHEN ERR_NUM = [value] [action]
    Constant value    CALL program

##### Error Number

ERR_NUM = aaabbb

aaa : Error facility code (decimal); Refer to Section A.2.2 .

bbb : Error number (decimal)

Example: WHEN ERR_NUM=11006, CALL PROG_A

This refers to the "SRVO-006 Hand broken" error because the SRVO facility code is 11.

If 0 is specified as error number "aaabbb", whenever any error occurs, the condition is satisfied.

You can change the type of system monitors by changing the system variable $TPP_MON.$global_mt as follows. You can only change this system variable in the system variable menu at Controlled start.

- $TPP_MON.$global_mt = 0 - No use system monitor (default)
- $TPP_MON.$global_mt = 1 - System monitor TYPE1 Refer to Section 14.10.3, "Monitor State."
- $TPP_MON.$global_mt = 2 - System monitor TYPE2 Refer to Section 14.10.3, "Monitor State." You can start and end the monitor at the condition menu in the STATUS menu. Refer to Section 14.10.7, "Condition Menu."

<!-- PDF page 1303 -->

#### 14.10.8 Restrictions

The multiple conditions taught in the condition handler program are monitored at the same time.

1: WHEN <cond1> CALL <program1>
2: WHEN <cond2> CALL <program2>
3: WHEN <cond3> CALL <program3></program3></cond3></program2></cond2></cond1>

When the next conditions begin to be monitored before the last conditions are stopped, then both conditions are monitored at the same time.

A program monitor is canceled in the following cases:

• One of the conditions is triggered.
- Execute the "MONITOR END" teach pendant instruction.
• The program is aborted.
- The END function key, on the program monitor screen, is pressed.

Note In the program monitor TYPE1 (\(TPP_MON.\)local_mt=1), when the program is paused, the program monitor is paused. The program monitor is restarted when the program is restarted.

A system monitor is canceled in the following ways:

• One of the conditions is triggered.
- A Cold start is executed and \(TPP_MON.\)global_mt = 1.
- The END function key, on the program monitor screen, is pressed.

A program or system monitor can be restarted after it triggers, by having the action program it calls execute a MONITOR teach pendant instruction.

The maximum number of conditions connected with the AND/OR operator is 5. The total number of monitors is limited to 50.

WHEN <cond1> AND <cond2> ... AND <cond5>
WHEN <cond1> OR <condm> ... OR <condp>
:
:
WHEN <conds> AND <condt> ... AND <condw></condw></condt></condm></cond1></cond2></cond1>

You cannot execute motion instructions in the action program when the robot is moving. You cannot edit the active CH program. The group mask of the action program for a system monitor must be  \( [*,*,*,*,*] \) .

<!-- PDF page 1304 -->

You can specify the group mask of the action program for the program monitor. However, the action program cannot move the robot when the robot is moving.

When the condition is triggered, the monitor state becomes "end." If you want to continue monitoring, you should teach a "MONITOR" instruction in the action program. In this time, the action program should disable the condition. See the following example.
