### 14.16 DISTANCE BEFORE

#### 14.16.1 Overview

The Distance Before (DB) function calls a program or outputs a signal when the Tool Center Point (TCP) goes into a region that is within a specified distance from the destination point. The

<!-- PDF page 1381 -->

program call and signal output are done in parallel with the motion execution of the main program. See Figure 14–62 for an example the execution timing of Distance Before.

Figure 14–62. Execution Timing of Distance Before

1: J P[1] 100% FINE
2: L P[2] 1000mm/sec FINE DB 100mm, CALL A

> **Image description -- img-136.jpeg:** The image depicts a schematic diagram of a motion control system involving a circular motion path. The diagram includes two points, P[1] and P[2], marked on the path. P[1] is located at the start of the motion path, while P[2] is positioned on the circumference of the circle. A label indicates that 'Program A is executed at the same time as motion to P[2]'. The motion path is labeled as 'C FINE DB 100mm, CALL A', suggesting a fine circular interpolation with a diameter of 100mm and a reference to a program named 'CALL A'. The diagram visually represents the relationship between the programmed motion and the execution of Program A, highlighting that the program runs concurrently with the motion toward point P[2].

#### 14.16.2 Specification

Refer to Table 14–33 for the specifications of the Distance Before function.

Table 14–33. Distance Before Specification

[tbl-335.md](tbl-335.md)

<!-- PDF page 1382 -->

#### 14.16.3 Program Instruction

Distance Before is a motion option called DB. You can use Distance Before only as a motion option within a motion instruction. See Figure 14–63 for the motion instruction that includes the Distance Before motion option.

Figure 14–63. Distance Before Motion Option, DB

> **Image description -- img-137.jpeg:** The image is a diagram illustrating the structure of a motion instruction for a database (DB) system. It shows an example of a motion instruction formatted as 'L P[2] 1000mm/sec FINE DB 100mm, CALL A'. The diagram breaks down the instruction into two main components: 'Distance value' and 'Action'. The 'Distance value' is specified as '100mm', indicating the distance parameter for the motion. The 'Action' is labeled as 'CALL A', which represents the command or operation to be executed. The diagram also includes a label at the top stating 'Motion instruction DB distance value, action', providing context for the components below.

#### 14.16.4 Distance Value

Distance Before executes an action when the TCP goes into a spherical region whose center is the destination position. The distance value specifies the radius of this sphere. The distance value is defined in millimeters, with a range of 0 to 999.9 millimeters. The spherical region whose radius is the distance value is called the trigger region. See Figure 14–64.

Figure 14–64. Checking Whether the TCP Goes into the Trigger Region

> **Image description -- img-138.jpeg:** The image is a diagram illustrating a control system operation involving two positions, P[1] and P[2], on a linear path. The system moves from P[1] to P[2] at a speed of 2000 mm/sec with fine control. The distance between P[1] and P[2] is 100 mm. There are internal check points marked along the path between P[1] and P[2]. The diagram highlights a trigger region near P[2], where the controller recognizes that the TCP (Tool Center Point) has entered this region. When the TCP is in the trigger region, a digital output DO[1] is turned ON. The diagram includes labels for the positions (P[1] and P[2]), the speed (2000 mm/sec), the distance (100 mm), and the digital output (DO[1]). The operational meaning is that the system monitors the TCP's position relative to the trigger region and activates DO[1] upon entry into this region.

Internally, the controller calculates the current position to judge whether the TCP is in the trigger region. The action is executed when this calculated position is in the trigger region.

##### Caution

Execution timing of the action is determined by distance (in millimeters). Because the judgement to trigger is done cyclically by calculating the distance between the current position and destination position, the actual execution timing can be different than the distance value.

<!-- PDF page 1383 -->

# Radius of Trigger Region

The radius of the trigger region is defined as shown in Figure 14–65.

Figure 14–65. Size of Trigger Region

> **Image description -- img-139.jpeg:** The image is a technical diagram illustrating the calculation of a radius for a circular region around a point labeled P[1]. The diagram shows three concentric circles: 
1. The innermost solid circle represents the point P[1] at the center.
2. The middle dashed circle represents the minimum radius, denoted as $DB_MIN_DIST, with a default value of 5.0 mm. This circle is labeled with the text "Minimum radius:$DB_MIN_DIST (default value: 5.0mm)".
3. The outermost dashed circle represents the total radius, which is calculated as the sum of the minimum radius ($DB_MIN_DIST) and a margin to trigger ($DB_TOLERANCE). The formula for the radius is given as: Radius = (distance value or $DB_MIN_DIST) + $DB_TOLERANCE. The margin to trigger, $DB_TOLERANCE, has a default value of 0.05 mm and is labeled accordingly.

The diagram also indicates that the distance value can range from 0 to 999.99 mm. The labels and annotations provide a clear explanation of the relationship between these values and how the total radius is determined.

If the distance value is less than $DB_MINDIST, $DB_MINDIST is used as the distance value. For example, suppose the following motion instruction is taught with $DB_MINDIST = 1.0:

L P[1] 2000mm/sec FINE DB 0.0mm DO[1]=ON

In this case, the controller interprets it as DB 5.0 mm. Then, $DB_TOLERANCE (which has a default value of 0.05 mm) is added to determine the radius of the trigger region. In this case, the trigger region radius of the trigger region is 5.0 + 0.05 or 5.05mm when default system variable values are used.

#### 14.16.5 Action

The action specifies what is done when the TCP goes into the trigger region. Distance Before supports the following program instructions for the action:

• CALL program instruction
• Signal output instructions

# Distance Before CALL Program

When a CALL program instruction is the action, the specified program is executed when the condition is triggered. The program to be called cannot use motion groups. You must change the group mask to  \( [*,*,*,*,*] \)  in the program header information screen. You can use parameters when you call a program, as follows:

<!-- PDF page 1384 -->

L P[2] 1000mm/sec FINE DB 100mm, CALL A (1,2)

# Distance Before Signal Output

You can use the signal output instructions listed in Table 14–34 as Distance Before actions. You can use only one signal output for each Distance Before motion option.

Table 14–34. Distance Before Signal Output Instructions

[tbl-336.md](tbl-336.md)

You can also output a signal by calling a program that uses signal output instructions. However, to output only one signal with one Distance Before motion option, it is better to use the direct signal output method for ease of teach pendant program maintenance.

#### 14.16.6 Changing the Trigger Condition

The action of a Distance Before motion option is executed when the controller recognizes that the TCP is in the trigger region. However, in some cases, the controller does not recognize that the TCP is in the trigger region. In these cases, the condition for the action to be executed, called the DB condition, is changed by the system variable $DB_CONDTYP, as shown in Table 14–35.

Table 14–35. $DB_CONDTYP

[tbl-337.md](tbl-337.md)

The going away and penetration cases are described below.

Distance Before executes the action when the DB condition is satisfied. Otherwise, an alarm is posted. There are two alarms for not-triggered Distance Before: INTP-293 and INTP-295. $DBCONDTRIG decides which alarm is posted. Refer to Section 14.16.7 for more information.

<!-- PDF page 1385 -->

Note (*1) When Distance Before is triggered by going away in case of $DB_CONDTYP = 1, you can post an alarm in addition to execution of instruction part. Refer to Going Away Case below for details.

Note (*2) By default configuration, if the motion statement with Distance Before completes and the robot stops before neither region trigger nor going away nor penetration trigger happens, Distance Before executes the instruction part and posts the alarm. Refer to Penetration Case below.

##### Going Away Case

If the termination type is CNT and the distance value is small, the TCP might not go into the trigger region. See Figure 14–66.

Figure 14–66. TCP Does not Go into Trigger Region

> **Image description -- img-140.jpeg:** The diagram illustrates a trajectory path of a TCP (Tool Center Point) in a 2D plane with three labeled points: P[1], P[2], and P[3]. P[1] is the starting point, P[2] is the destination point, and P[3] is a subsequent point along the path. The path from P[1] to P[2] is shown as a series of small circles connected by a line, indicating gradual movement toward the destination. At P[2], the TCP is enclosed in a yellow circle, highlighting it as a critical point. Two distances are marked: L1 (the distance from P[1] to P[2]) and L2 (the distance from P[2] to P[3]). The diagram includes annotations explaining that before reaching P[2], the TCP was gradually approaching the destination point, but at P[2], the controller perceives the TCP as moving away from the destination because L1 is less than L2 (L1 < L2). Additionally, there are small white circles along the path indicating internal checkpoints for a DB (database) trigger condition.

In Figure 14–66, the TCP does not go into the trigger region. The TCP starts to go away from the destination point (P[2]). The controller cyclically judges if the TCP is going away from the destination point in addition to the region trigger. The controller recognizes that the TCP is going away when the calculated distance between the current position and destination position is greater than the previous one by more than $DB_AWAY_TRIG millimeters. This case is referred to as going away.

- To post an alarm in addition to execution of the instruction part only when the DB is triggered by the going away trigger, set $DB_AWAY_ALM to TRUE. DB executes the instruction part and posts the following alarm:

INTP-295 (program name, line number) DB too small (away) (%dmm)

This is a Warning.

##### Penetration Case

This function cyclically checks whether the DB condition is triggered. Because of this cyclical check, CNT motion with high speed might cause the controller to omit cyclical checking in a small trigger region. See Figure 14–67.

<!-- PDF page 1386 -->

Figure 14–67. Penetration

> **Image description -- img-141.jpeg:** The image depicts a linear sequence of five circular nodes connected by a dashed line, representing a path. The nodes are labeled P[1], P[2], and P[3] from left to right. P[1] and P[3] are solid black circles, while P[2] is a yellow circle with a dashed outline. A label above the yellow node states: 'At this point, the controller recognizes that the TCP went through the trigger region.' The dashed line connecting the nodes suggests a trajectory or path of a TCP (Tool Center Point), with the yellow node indicating a specific trigger region where the controller detects the TCP's passage.

In this case, the TCP moves too fast for the controller to check the DB condition in a small trigger region. Because cyclical checking is done outside of the trigger region, the fact that the TCP is in the trigger region is not recognized by the controller. This case is referred to as penetration.

To handle cases like the one shown in Figure 14–67, Distance Before checks whether the TCP went through the trigger region. If the trajectory of the TCP penetrated the trigger region (penetration), the action is executed by the default configuration. However, in this case, the execution of the action is done after the TCP passed the destination point.

Motion with FINE termination type does not cause triggering by penetration. If you do not want to execute the DB action when the case is going away, set $DB_CONDTYP to 2 (the default value is 1).

##### End of Motion

If the motion statement with DB completes and the robot stops before region, going away, and penetration is satisfied, DB executes the instruction part and posts the following alarm.

INTP-297 (program name, line number) DB too small (done) (mm).

This alarm is not posted by FINE motion. If you don't want this trigger, set $DB_MOTNEND to FALSE (default value: TRUE). Distance displayed by this alarm is distance to destination.

##### Caution

1. If you stop your robot by E-stop when motion statement is about to complete, Distance Before may be triggered just after resume of the program.
2. If you halt a program when motion statement with DB is near its completion, DB may not be triggered. In this case, Distance Before executes its instruction part after resume of the program.

<!-- PDF page 1387 -->

### 14.16.7 Alarms Posted When Distance Before is Not Triggered

Distance Before posts an alarm if the condition is not triggered. The alarm posted depends on the value of $DBCONDTRIG, as shown in Table 14–36.

Table 14–36. Distance Before Alarms

[tbl-338.md](tbl-338.md)

By default, INTP-295 is posted. Because the severity of this alarm is WARN, program execution does not stop. If you want to hold the program when a condition is not triggered, set $DBCONDTRIG to 1. INTP-293 will be posted when the condition is not triggered. The program will be held and the robot will decelerate to a stop.

### 14.16.8 Single Step Execution

If the Distance Before CALL program is executed using single step, the program is held at the time the action program is called. The rest of the motion instruction is executed at the next step execution that executes the action program step-by-step.

Single step execution of a motion instruction with a DB signal output action is the same as a motion instruction without DB, except the signal output is executed.

# Caution

If the distance value is small, the program may be halted before completion of motion and before DB conditions are satisfied. In this case, Distance Before is not triggered by step execution of the line it is taught. The DB is triggered by execution of next line.

### 14.16.9 Hold and Resume

When a motion instruction with Distance Before is held and resumed, the execution timing of the next line and action is controlled by $DISBF_TTS. Refer to Table 14–37 for more details.

- Execution timing of the next line - In the default configuration, the execution of the next line waits until the rest of the motion instruction with the DB option completes.
- Execution timing of the action - Execution timing depends on the action, as follows:
  — A signal output action is executed when the DB condition is triggered.

<!-- PDF page 1388 -->

— The execution timing of a CALL program action is decided by DISTBF_TTS. When DISTBF_TTS is set to its default value (1), execution of the action program waits for the completion of the motion instruction.

Table 14–37. DISTBF_TTS for a CALL Program Action

[tbl-339.md](tbl-339.md)

DISTBF_TTS = 0

When DISTBF_TTS = 0, the action program is executed just after it is called. The execution of line 3 does not wait for the completion of the motion in line 2.

Figure 14–68 shows an example of execution when DISTBF_TTS = 0.

Figure 14–68. DISTBF_TTS = 0

> **Image description -- img-142.jpeg:** The image shows a diagram and a snippet of a program code related to a control system or robotics program. The program code (on the left) consists of three lines: 
1. 'L P[1] 2000mm/sec FINE' — This line commands the system to move to position P[1] at a speed of 2000 mm/sec with a fine termination.
2. 'L P[2] 2000mm/sec CNT100 DB 100.0mm CALL TEST' — This line commands the system to move to position P[2] at the same speed, with a continuous path (CNT100) and a distance buffer (DB) of 100.0 mm. It also triggers a subroutine named 'TEST' when the DB condition is met.
3. 'L P[3] 2000mm/sec FINE' — This line commands the system to move to position P[3] at the same speed with a fine termination.

The diagram (on the right) illustrates the spatial relationship between three points: P[1], P[2], and P[3]. P[1] is marked with a black dot, P[2] is marked with a yellow dot, and P[3] is marked with a black dot. A line connects P[1] to P[2], and another line connects P[2] to P[3]. The point P[2] is highlighted with a yellow circle, indicating it is the current target or focus. The text below the diagram explains that the subroutine 'TEST' is executed when the distance buffer (DB) condition is triggered, and the next line of the program is executed as if there were no DB condition.

DISTBF_TTS = 1

Hold before DB condition is triggered - The execution of an action program is done as described in Figure 14–69. The CALL program is executed when the condition is triggered. However, the action program does not progress until P[2], where the motion of line 2 completes. Because the execution of line 3 also waits for the completion of line 2, the motion of line 2 looks like motion with a FINE termination type.

Hold and resume of motion statement with DB changes its radius of the trigger region. After resume, radius of the trigger region is changed to the minimum radius (\$DB_MINDIST +

<!-- PDF page 1389 -->

$DB_TOLERANCE). The purpose of this process is to execute the instruction part after the TCP reaches its destination point. This prevents an earlier trigger because of hold and resume. This means that hold and resume of the program changes the trigger timing of Distance Before.

Figure 14–69. Execution Timing of an Action Program

> **Image description -- img-143.jpeg:** The image is a flowchart or diagram illustrating the execution sequence of a program with three lines of code. The diagram includes the following key elements and annotations: 

1. **Code Lines**: 
   - Line 1: `L P[1] 2000mm/sec FINE`
   - Line 2: `L P[2] 2000mm/sec CNT100 DB 100.0mm CALL TEST`
   - Line 3: `L P[3] 2000mm/sec FINE`

2. **Execution Flow**: 
   - The program starts at Line 1, moving to position P[1] at 2000 mm/sec with a FINE termination.
   - Line 2 moves to position P[2] at 2000 mm/sec with CNT100 (continuous path with 100% blending) and a DB (distance buffer) of 100.0 mm. This line includes a CALL TEST subprogram.
   - Line 3 moves to position P[3] at 2000 mm/sec with a FINE termination.

3. **Annotations and Relationships**: 
   - A note indicates that the subprogram is called at the position of Line 2, but the action is not executed immediately. Instead, it waits for the completion of Line 2.
   - The execution of Line 3 waits for the completion of Line 2.
   - There is a hold point at P[2] where, if there is no hold, DB (distance buffer) executes at this position.
   - The radius of the trigger region for the subprogram is changed to `($DB_MINDIST + $DB_TOLERANCE)`.
   - The subprogram execution starts after the completion of Line 2.

4. **Visual Elements**: 
   - Arrows indicate the flow of execution from Line 1 to Line 2 and then to Line 3.
   - A decision point (diamond shape) at P[2] shows the conditional hold and the trigger for DB execution.
   - A circular node at P[3] marks the start of the subprogram execution after Line 2 completes.

The diagram visually represents the control flow and conditional execution in a robotic or automated programming context, emphasizing the interaction between program lines and subprogram calls.

Hold during the execution of an action program - When a hold occurs during the execution of an action program, the action program is held as well as the motion itself. After resuming, the execution of the rest of the action program does not start until line 2 completes. See Figure 14–70.

Figure 14–70. Hold During the Execution of an Action Program

> **Image description -- img-144.jpeg:** The image is a flowchart or diagram illustrating the execution sequence of a program with three lines of motion commands. The diagram includes the following key elements:

1. **Program Lines**: Three lines of program code are shown:
   - Line 1: `L P[1] 2000mm/sec FINE`
   - Line 2: `L P[2] 2000mm/sec CNT100 DB 100.0mm CALL TEST`
   - Line 3: `L P[3] 2000mm/sec FINE`

2. **Execution Flow**:
   - The execution of line 3 waits for the completion of line 2. This is indicated by an arrow pointing from line 2 to line 3, labeled "Hold."
   - Line 2 includes a `CALL TEST` instruction, which means it calls a subroutine named TEST.
   - The subroutine TEST was already executed, and the action program was running but held at the `CALL TEST` instruction until line 2 completes.
   - After the completion of the motion in line 2, the rest of the subprogram starts at line 3.

3. **Annotations**:
   - A note explains that line 3 waits for line 2 to finish, even though line 2 includes a `CALL` motion, which typically takes time to complete.
   - Another note clarifies that the subprogram resumes execution at line 3 after line 2 is fully completed.

4. **Visual Elements**:
   - The diagram uses arrows and labeled points (P[1], P[2], P[3]) to show the sequence and dependencies between the program lines.
   - The yellow highlighted area emphasizes the interaction between the `CALL TEST` instruction and the hold state during execution.

Holding after the completion of an action program — makes the next instruction wait for the completion of line 2.

Hold after the completion of line 2 but before the trigger of DB condition — In this case, if the DB condition triggers after resuming, execution of the action program is done just after the DB condition is triggered.

For a signal output action - When a HOLD occurs before DB condition is triggered, after resume, signal output occurs at the DB sphere (radius is changed to $DB_MINDIST +

<!-- PDF page 1390 -->

$DB_TOLERANCE). The execution of the next line waits for the completion of the current line (line 2), as it does in the case of a CALL.

DISTBF_TTS = 2.

In Figure 14–71, the TCP is not in the trigger region when the program is held, so the action program is not called yet. In this case, the execution timing of the action program and the next line is the same as DISTBF_TTS = 0.

If the program is held during the execution of the action program, the execution timing of the action program and the next line is the same as when DISTBF_TTS = 1.

Figure 14–71. DISTBF_TTS = 2

> **Image description -- img-145.jpeg:** The image is a diagram illustrating a program execution flow with three labeled points (P[1], P[2], and P[3]) connected by arrows. Each point is associated with a line of code: 
1: L P[1] 2000mm/sec FINE 
2: L P[2] 2000mm/sec CNT100 DB 100.0mm CALL TEST 
3: L P[3] 2000mm/sec FINE 

The diagram shows that when the program reaches P[2], it holds execution at that point. A sub-program is called only if a DB (likely a condition or trigger) is met at P[2]. If the program is held (sub-program not called), the execution timing after resuming is the same as DISTBF_TTS = 0. The next line (P[3]) is executed as if there were no DB condition. The diagram visually emphasizes the conditional execution flow and the role of the DB condition at P[2].

### 14.16.10 Resume After Jogging

If you hold a motion instruction that has the DB motion option, jog the robot, and then resume the program, the execution timing depends on the TCP position at the instant the program is resumed. This is dependant on the setting of $distbf_tts.

$DISTBF_TTS = 1 (default)

After the program is resumed, the radius of the trigger region is changed to the minimum value ($DB_MINDIST+$DB_TOLERENCE). If the TCP is in the new (diminished) trigger region, DB is triggered just after resume of the program. If not, DB is triggered when the DB condition is satisfied.

### Example

Suppose the following program is executed and halted on line two. The DB condition is not triggered yet.

1: L P[1] 2000mm/sec FINE
2: L P[2] 2000mm/sec CNT100 DB 100.0mm DO[1] = ON
3: L P[3] 2000mm/sec CNT100

<!-- PDF page 1391 -->

Figure 14–72. Resume after Jogging

> **Image description -- img-146.jpeg:** The image consists of two diagrams side by side, each illustrating a sequence of operations involving a TCP (Tool Center Point) movement and a program control flow with conditions. 

1. **Left Diagram (Before Program Resume):**
   - Shows a sequence of points labeled P[1], P[2], and P[3] arranged in a triangular formation.
   - The TCP moves from P[1] to P[2] and then to P[3].
   - A 'Hold' state is indicated between P[1] and P[2].
   - A dashed circle highlights the area around P[2], with a label stating: "DB condition is not satisfied here. At point A, DB is triggered."
   - The program is in a 'Hold' state at point A, preventing the TCP from moving further until the condition is met.

2. **Right Diagram (Just After Program Resume):**
   - Shows the same points P[1], P[2], and P[3] in the same triangular formation.
   - The 'Hold' state is still present between P[1] and P[2].
   - The dashed circle around P[2] now has a label stating: "Just after program resume, DB condition is satisfied. DO turns ON."
   - The program resumes from the 'Hold' state, and the condition is now satisfied, allowing the DO (Digital Output) to turn ON.

Both diagrams illustrate the relationship between the program's hold state, the DB (Database) condition, and the subsequent actions (resume and DO turn ON) based on whether the condition is satisfied or not.

##### $DISTBF_TTS=0

Radius of trigger region is not changed. If TCP is in trigger region, DB is triggered just after resume of program. If not, DB is triggered when DB condition is satisfied.

Example)

Suppose following program is executed and halted on line two. DB condition was not satisfied yet.

1: L P[1] 2000mm/sec FINE
2: L P[2] 2000mm/sec CNT100 DB 100.0mm DO[1] = ON
3: L P[3] 2000mm/sec CNT100

If TCP is distant from P[2] enough not to trigger(more than 100mm away), DO[1] turns ON when DB condition is triggered by motion after resume, at point A in left diagram in Figure 14–73. If TCP is in trigger region when you resume program, DO[1] turns ON just after resume (right diagram in Figure 14–73).

Figure 14–73. Resume After Jogging (\$DISTBF_TTS = 0)

Both diagrams include a 'Resume' and 'Hold' state, with a cross marking the transition point between 'Hold' and 'Resume'. The left diagram shows that at program resume, the DB condition is satisfied, causing DO[1] to turn ON at point A. The right diagram shows that the DB condition is satisfied at program resume, with DO turning ON just after the program resumes. Labels and annotations clarify the timing and conditions of the DO turning ON relative to the program's state transitions.

### 14.16.11 Power Failure Recovery

If power is turned off during action program execution and power failure recovery is enabled, resuming after power failure recovery executes the rest of the action program. In this case, the action program is executed from the point where the TCP was at the power failure. Execution timing is different from the usual execution timing.

### 14.16.12 Adding the Distance Before Motion Option (Procedure)

Use Procedure 14-31 to add the Distance Before motion option to a motion instruction.

# Procedure 14-31 Adding the Distance Before Motion Option to a Motion Instruction

# Steps

1. Select the teach pendant program you want to edit.
2. Press EDIT.
3. Insert a motion instruction or move the cursor to an existing motion instruction.
4. Move the cursor to the motion option area of the motion instruction to which you want to add the Distance Before motion option. See the following screen for an example.

PNS0001
1: J P[1] 100% FINE
[END]

5. Press F4, [CHOICE]. You will see a screen similar to the following.

Motion Modify
1 TIME BEFORE 5
2 TIME AFTER 6
3 DISTANCE BEFORE 7
4 8
PNS0001
1: J P[1] 100% FINE
[END]
Select item

6. Select DISTANCE BEFORE.

DB is added to the program. See the following screen for an example.

<!-- PDF page 1393 -->

PNS0001
1: J P[1] 100% FINE
: DB [0.0] mm ...
[END]
Enter Value

7. Type the distance value and press ENTER. You will see a screen similar to the following.

TIME statement
1 CALL program 5 GO[ ]=...
2 CALL program( ) 6 AO[ ]=...
3 DO[ ]=... 7
4 RO[ ]=... 8
PNS0001
1: J P[1] 100% FINE
: DB 100.0mm
[END]
Select item

8. Select the action you want.

- For a CALL program, go to Step 9.
- For signal output, go to Step 10.

9. To insert a CALL Program action:

a. Select CALL program or CALL program (for a program with parameters). You will see a screen similar to the following.

PROGRAM list
1 HANDOPEN 5
2 HANDCLOS 6
3 7
4 8

b. Select the program you want to call.
c. If you want to add parameters to the program call, select the appropriate information to add the parameters to the program call as you would to any program call.

10. To insert a signal output action:

a. Select the output signal you want: DO, RO, GO, or AO.
b. Press the appropriate function keys to enter the output signal number.

11. To find a program or output signal that is used by the DB motion option,

<!-- PDF page 1394 -->

a. Press NEXT, >, until F5, [EDCMD], is displayed.
b. Press F5, [EDCMD].
c. Select Find.
d. Select the appropriate item:

• For a program CALL, select CALL and then select CALL Program.

• For an output signal, select I/O and then select the appropriate signal.

# 12. To replace Distance Before with Time Before/After,

a. NEXT, > until F5, [EDCMD], is displayed.
b. Press F5, [EDCMD].
c. Select Replace.
d. Select the appropriate items to find and replace as desired.

### 14.16.13 Cautions and Limitations

When you use the Distance Before option, be aware of the following cautions and limitations:

• Distance Before cannot be used with TIME BEFORE/AFTER.
• More than ten motion instructions with Distance Before and Time Before/After cannot be processed at the same time.
• Robot TCP path may change during Hold, ESTOP and then resume (i.e. no constant path feature in those cases).

# Caution

In the case of Hold or Estop, then resume around a motion line with the Distance Before statement, the path will deviate. It is important to verify that the path is all right.

• Distance Before calculates the distance between the current position and the destination point cyclically. Because the trigger condition is judged by this cyclical checking, the actual execution of the timing of the action is different from the distance value. The action might be executed inside of the trigger region. This means that the point where the instruction is executed is closer than the distance value. The degree of difference depends on the speed of the robot. The slower the TCP moves, the more accurate the execution timing.
• Distance Before cannot be recovered by power failure recovery if it is attached to a motion instruction with CNT termination type and power turns off when the motion is about to complete.
• Distance Before cannot be used with INC, SKIP, and QSKIP in a motion instruction.

<!-- PDF page 1395 -->

- In the case of a multi-group system, the lowest group is used for the calculation of distance.
- Robots that do not have Cartesian coordination cannot use Distance Before.
- Positional data in matrix form is not supported.
- Integrated axes are not supported.
- Distance Before is not supported on an F-200i.
- Distance Before does not support Line Tracking.
- During deceleration due to the program being held, going away trigger might not work. In this case, DB is triggered after program resume.
- After E-stop, DB doesn't work. If TCP passes by destination point, DB is triggered after program resume.
- After E-stop and program resume, DB might be triggered just after resume.
- Single step execution of DB of small distance value might fail when the program is paused before the motion statement completes, and the DB condition is satisfied. The DB is triggered by execution of next line.
- If the DB condition is satisfied after the program is paused, DB is not triggered by step execution of the line. In this case, the DB is triggered by execution of next line.
- When there is DB/TB that is not yet triggered in the previous line, DB/TB does not trigger even when trigger condition is satisfied. (DB/TB always triggers after previous DB/TB triggered.)

## 14.17 DUAL MOTOR DRIVE

### 14.17.1 Introduction

The Dual Motor Drive (Dual Drive) feature allows single axis control of two motors. One motor is called the master motor and the other motor is called the slave motor.

> **Image description -- img-148.jpeg:** The image depicts a mechanical setup involving two motors labeled as "Master motor" and "Slave motor". Both motors are connected to a rotating shaft or spindle. The master motor is positioned on the left side, while the slave motor is on the right side. The motors appear to be synchronized, as indicated by the label "Synchronous control" and the curved arrow connecting the two motors, suggesting that they operate in unison. The setup likely represents a system where the master motor drives the slave motor to maintain precise coordination in their movements.

- The main function of the Dual Drive feature is to compensate for synchronous error due to servo delay between master and slave axes.

<!-- PDF page 1399 -->

- Dual Drive feature can realize a large size and high-load system which cannot be realized by a single motor.
- Dual Drive feature suppresses the slave motor status on the current position screen, teaching screen, and so on. By jogging or teaching only of the master motor, both motors move in synchronization.

In order to use this function, Dual Drive function option (A05B-2600-J836) is required. Also only Extended axis (A05B-2600-J518), Independent axis (A05B-2600-H895), and Positioner can be used as Dual Drive.

Note The maximum number of axes per group is 9 that includes slave axes of Dual Drives. - Extended axis is supported.

### 14.17.2 Setup

Set up Extended axes or Independent axes or Positioner axes which you plan to assign as a pair of Dual Drive motors.

- The pair of Dual Drive motors must belong to the same motion group.
- In this step, setup both the master motor and the slave motor individually.
- The slave motor must be the last axis in the group. If there exist multiple Dual Drive motor pairs in one group, the order of the slave axes is unconfined while they must be the last axes in the group.

> **Image description -- img-149.jpeg:** The image depicts a schematic representation of a pair of Dual Drive motors, labeled as J1, J2, and J3. J1 is identified as the master motor, while J2 is labeled as the slave motor. The diagram includes annotations indicating that the slave motor (J2) must be the last axis of the group. Additionally, there is a note stating that J3 represents independent additional axes or positioner axes. The motors are shown as black rectangles with white connectors at the top, and the labels and annotations are in black text on a white background.

### Dual Drive motor axes setup

Set the following variables, then cycle the power.

### 14.18 EASY NORMAL UTILITY (formerly known as Auto Normal Utility)

#### 14.18.1 Overview

The Easy Normal utility is a software option that is used to align the end-of-arm tooling of the robot perpendicular, or normal, to a surface, such as a workpiece. This option assumes that a height or range sensor is available on the end of the robot arm.

<!-- PDF page 1401 -->

FANUC America Corporation has successfully used the Easy Normal utility in laser cutting applications in which a laser height sensor is integral with the cutting tool on the end of the robot arm. This cutting tool with the sensor can be purchased from FANUC America Corporation. You can also use this option with your own range or height sensors. Be sure to consider carefully the mounting and usage of the height sensor so you can use the Easy Normal utility effectively. Contact FANUC America Corporation for further assistance.

The Easy Normal utility provides a setup screen in which you can enter various search parameters to tune the utility to your particular application. The search parameters are used with a proprietary algorithm to move the robot in a particular manner relative to the surface, such as the workpiece. At the end of these motions, the robot will re-orient the end of the robot arm to be normal to the surface. The jog frame of the robot is also set up auto so that when you jog the robot in the x and y directions, the end of the robot arm maintains its perpendicular orientation relative to the surface of the workpiece.

Without the Easy Normal utility, it would be time consuming to define an accurate relative position and orientation. However, in applications such as laser cutting of shapes, the tool location and orientation are critical for cut quality.

The Easy Normal utility does the following:

- Simplifies the teaching of robot positions
- Reduces teaching time
- Improves the accuracy of taught positions relative to the work surface

To use the Easy Normal utility option, you do the following:

1. Set up Easy Normal - Section 14.18.3
2. Execute Easy Normal to perform the search and yield the appropriate positions and frames for accurate teaching - Section 14.18.4

### 14.18.2 Using the Easy Normal Utility

This section contains information on the following topics, which you must know in order to use the Easy Normal utility effectively. The descriptions in this section use a laser height sensor as an example. You can use your own height sensor in a similar manner.

- Laser height sensor
- Search motion
- Shape frames

### Laser Height Sensor

The laser cutting tool has an integrated height sensor. The laser height sensor uses an inductive proximity sensor to locate, within a certain degree of accuracy, a surface within the sensor range.

<!-- PDF page 1402 -->

During the searching utility, the height sensor will be locked to its center of travel. The final position will be at a known distance (called the laser cut height) above the workpiece controlled by the laser controller. See Figure 14–74.

Figure 14–74. Laser Height Sensor

> **Image description -- img-150.jpeg:** The image is a schematic diagram illustrating a laser cutting setup with a height sensor. The diagram shows a vertical laser cutting head positioned above a workpiece. The laser cutting head is aligned along the Z axis of travel, which is indicated by a vertical arrow. A height sensor is mounted at the center of travel of the laser cutting head, depicted as a horizontal bar above the cutting head. The diagram includes labels for the 'Taught position' and 'Laser Cut Height'. The 'Taught position' is marked near the bottom of the laser cutting head, indicating the intended or reference height for the cutting process. The 'Laser Cut Height' is shown as a vertical distance from the workpiece to the laser cutting head, representing the actual cutting height during operation. The diagram visually conveys the relationship between the laser cutting head, the height sensor, and the workpiece, emphasizing the importance of maintaining the correct height for precise laser cutting.

# Search Motion

The Easy Normal utility moves the robot, in a specified manner, from a rough position toward an object in the TOOL Z direction. The robot stops searching and moving when the sensor detects an object. A three-point search algorithm is used to locate the object and to determine its orientation and distance relative to the robot. See Figure 14–75.

<!-- PDF page 1403 -->

Figure 14–75. Search Motion

> **Image description -- img-151.jpeg:** The image is a 3D schematic diagram illustrating a search or positioning process involving three labeled positions (Pos 1, Pos 2, and Pos 3) within a coordinate system defined by X, Y, and Z axes. The diagram shows a rectangular object (likely a container or box) with a cylindrical object inside it, positioned at Pos 1. The Z-axis is vertical, the X-axis is horizontal, and the Y-axis is perpendicular to the X-axis, forming a right-handed coordinate system. From Pos 1, there are dashed lines indicating search distances in the X and Y directions, labeled as 'X Search dist.' and 'Y Search dist.' respectively. Pos 2 and Pos 3 are shown as alternative positions along the X and Y search distances. The label 'Rough Pos' is associated with Pos 1, and 'MoveTo Height' indicates a vertical movement along the Z-axis to reach Pos 1. The diagram appears to represent a process of moving or searching within a defined 3D space, likely for robotic or automated systems.

Three search sizes are available: small, medium, and large. A larger search on a flat surface will produce a more accurate normalized position. However, smaller search sizes will allow you to perform a search within a small area where tight teaching tolerances are required.

After a search has been completed, the robot will be located at a new position that is normal (or perpendicular) to the surface where a teach pendant position can be recorded or touched up. The cutting torch will be located at a known distance above the workpiece, determined by the laser controller.

A jog frame is now set, where the X-Y plane is parallel to the surface of the shape frame. This reduces the amount of teaching time by allowing you to jog the robot parallel to the surface and record additional positions located along the same surface. See Figure 14–76. Refer to the next section ("Shape Frames") for more information on shape frames.

<!-- PDF page 1404 -->

Figure 14–76. Positions and Frames Defined After the Search

> **Image description -- img-152.jpeg:** The image depicts a 3D coordinate system diagram used for positioning a tool or sensor relative to a surface. The diagram shows three axes labeled X, Y, and Z, with the X and Y axes forming a plane parallel to the surface, and the Z axis perpendicular (normal) to the surface. The origin of the coordinate system is marked as the 'Jog Frame' with arrows indicating the positive directions of the X, Y, and Z axes. A rectangular object is positioned above the origin, aligned with the Z axis, labeled 'Accurate Position Normal to surface.' Two additional objects resembling tools or sensors are shown to the right of the diagram, oriented in different directions, likely indicating alternative positioning or operational angles relative to the surface.

# Shape Frames

A shape frame is calculated from a shape center position and current uframe:

- The shape frame X-direction is parallel to the object surface where the current UFRAME X-Y plane intersects the object at the shape center position.
- The shape frame Y-direction is also parallel to the object surface but perpendicular to the X-direction.
- The shape frame Z-direction is into the tool along the TOOL Z vector.

When you define the UFRAME (or shape frame), use the six-point method. Also, teach the Z-direction into the tool, as shown in Figure 14–77.

Figure 14–77. Shape Frames

The X-Y Plane is indicated as a reference plane intersecting the Shape Frame. 11 Status register R[100]
12 Contact pos reg: PR[100]

5. Move the cursor to each item and set as desired.

<!-- PDF page 1407 -->

### 14.18.4 Execution

The Easy Normal utility uses a teach pendant macro to call a KAREL routine to execute the search. Use Procedure 14-33 to execute the Easy Normal utility.

The teach pendant macro is named EASY NORMAL. the EASY NORMAL macro executes the teach pendant program named NORMAL.TP. The NORMAL.TP teach pendant program contains one instruction, "CALL FINORM." FINORM is a KAREL program that executes a hidden TP program to run search motions.

# Procedure 14-33 Executing Easy Normal to Perform a Search

# Steps

1. Hold the teach pendant and continuously press the DEADMAN switch on the back of the teach pendant.
2. Turn the teach pendant ON/OFF switch to the ON position.

# Warning

In the next step, the robot will move. To stop the robot immediately any time during jogging, release the DEADMAN switch or press the EMERGENCY STOP button. Otherwise, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

3. Execute NORMAL.TP program.

Note If you release the SHIFT key while the robot is executing the search, the Easy Normal search sequence will be aborted. If this happens, jog the robot or step back to the desired center position and repeat Step 1 through Step 3.

When the Easy Normal utility has completed the search sequence, a jog frame is set to jog the robot with x and y directions parallel to the workpiece along the shape frame.

### 14.19 EASY TEACH SUITE (formerly known as Simple Teach Suite)

### 14.19.1 Overview

The Easy Teach Suite is a set of functions that make it simpler for you to teach a program.

You can touch up points at any time and run the Easy Teach Suite functions again to verify results without affecting production.

<!-- PDF page 1408 -->

### 14.19.2 Auto Path Smoothing

#### 14.19.2.1 Overview

Auto Path Smoothing makes user-taught robot paths smooth while allowing the tool orientation to maintain process-required angles. Auto Path Smoothing also makes position transition smooth. If you want to shift the positions of taught points, Auto Path Smoothing can automatically shift the entire path proportionally.

#### 14.19.2.2 Limitations

Auto Path Smoothing cannot be used with coordinated motion or multi-group systems.

In order to obtain accurate results, you must have an accurate tool center point defined.

Only single-step motion is allowed in the teach pendant program editor “Simple Teach” mode.

### 14.19.2.3 How It Works

#### Auto Path Smoothing – Orientation

Orientation smoothing can be applied to a user-defined range of teach pendant programming instructions. The smoothing algorithm is based on the orientation of start and end points in this range of teach pendant instructions. In other words, the orientation of start and end points will not be changed after conversion. Therefore, these two points need to be taught correctly. Also, you can specify other fixed points between start and end points to avoid an obstacle or fine adjust the smoothing results.

There are two smoothing algorithms from which you can choose: two-angle approach (RS control) and three-angle approach (AES control).

If it is important that the tool stays on one side of the path, the three-angle approach is the better choice. In normal cases, such as corners, the two-angle approach will be sufficient.

#### Auto Path Smoothing – Position (Rubberbanding)

The Auto Path Smoothing – Position (Rubberbanding) function can shift the positions of taught points within user-defined teach pendant programming instructions, but the orientation will remain unchanged unless you enable orientation smoothing at the same time. Unlike orientation smoothing, rubberbanding requires at least one fixed point other than start and end points. You must then define the new location of the fixed point(s) by touching up the program using the Easy Teach Suite interface. The difference between the old and new location will then be used and re-organized for all the points within the selected range.

<!-- PDF page 1409 -->

### Guidelines for Using Path Smoothing

When the motion line is selected with circular motion type as the start or end line, only one of the positions can be used. For example, if the via position is selected as a start line, the destination position with the same motion line number cannot be selected as fixed-points or end line. However, both positions with the same motion line number can be selected as fixed-points.

Note If for any reason the smoothing results are not ideal for the specific application, the F1 UNDO key is available after the conversion has been successfully applied. However, UNDO will not be available if you enter Easy Teach Suite in another teach pendant program or after a Cold start occurs. Verify the smoothing results as soon as possible.

#### Caution

Do not use the Path Smoothing function with the 3-angle smoothing method selected for the range of the teach pendant program in which taught points have a zig-zag pattern. If it is needed the small range of the teach pendant program can be selected.

### 14.20 ENHANCED MIRROR IMAGE (OPTION)

The enhanced mirror image option allows you to translate an entire teach pendant program or portion of a teach pendant program to mirror-image the original programmed points. This option can be used to teach symmetrical parts easily. The enhanced mirror image option provides additional functionality so that existing frames such as user frames can be used directly with any specified XY, YZ, or XZ plane. Also, additional orientation shifting is provided for different application requirements.

Mirror imaging of a program can be accomplished either as:

- mirror image using existing frames such as World frame or user frames. No teaching required.
- mirror image using flexible mirror planes such as X-Y, Y-Z, or X-Z from existing frames for better selection
- parallel mirror image with mirrored orientation
- parallel and rotational mirror image with mirrored orientation
- mirror image orientation shifting can be selected based on application requirements.

Refer to Table 14–43 for descriptions of the Mirror Image Shift screen items.

<!-- PDF page 1417 -->

Table 14-43. ENHANCED MIRROR IMAGE Screen Items

### Parallel Mirror Image

A parallel mirror image mirrors the program about a mirror plane without an offset or a rotation. See Figure 14–78 and Figure 14–79.

Figure 14–78. Parallel Mirror Image with Mirror Plane in Center of Robot

> **Image description -- img-154.jpeg:** The image is a schematic diagram illustrating the principle of equal distance in a periscope system. The diagram shows two parallel lines labeled 'D' at the top and bottom, representing equal distances. A vertical line in the center represents a mirror plane, which reflects light from an object on one side to an observer on the other side. The object is labeled 'P1' on the left side, and the observer's position is labeled 'Q1' on the right side. The mirror plane is positioned between points labeled 'B' and 'B'', with corresponding points 'A' and 'A'', and 'C' and 'C''. The labels 'A', 'B', 'C', and 'D' on the left side correspond to 'A'', 'B'', 'C'', and 'D' on the right side, indicating symmetry around the mirror plane. The diagram demonstrates that the distance from P1 to the mirror plane is equal to the distance from Q1 to the mirror plane, ensuring that the observer sees the object at the same apparent distance.

Figure 14–79. Parallel Mirror Image with Mirror Plane Offset from Center of Robot

> **Image description -- img-155.jpeg:** The image depicts a schematic diagram of an optical setup involving a mirror plane and a light path. Key components and labels include: a light source at point P1, which emits a beam that passes through points A, B, C, and then reflects off a mirror plane. After reflection, the beam continues through points C', B', and A', reaching point Q1. The diagram indicates that the distances from P1 to the mirror plane and from the mirror plane to Q1 are equal (denoted as D). The mirror plane is centrally located, and the light path is symmetric about this plane. The labels A, B, C, and their primed counterparts A', B', C' represent sequential points along the light path before and after reflection. The operational meaning of the diagram is to illustrate the principle of reflection symmetry in optics, where the path of light from P1 to Q1 via the mirror plane is symmetric, ensuring equal distances on both sides of the mirror.

<!-- PDF page 1419 -->

# Caution

To be sure the parallel mirror image works correctly, you must have an exact TCP. If you do not, the resulting mirror image program will contain an offset value. See Figure 14–80.

Figure 14–80. Parallel Mirror Image with Offset

> **Image description -- img-156.jpeg:** The image depicts a diagram illustrating the concept of reflection and equal distance in a mirror plane. The diagram shows two points, P1 and Q1, positioned on opposite sides of a vertical mirror plane. From P1, lines are drawn to points A, B, C, and D on the mirror plane, and these lines are reflected to corresponding points A', B', C', and D' on the opposite side of the mirror plane, forming a symmetric pattern. The labels indicate that the distance from P1 to the mirror plane at point B is equal to the distance from Q1 to the mirror plane at point B', as denoted by the label 'D - Equal Distance'. The mirror plane is clearly marked, and the reflected points (A', B', C', D') are aligned symmetrically with the original points (A, B, C, D) relative to the mirror plane. The diagram visually demonstrates the principle that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the distances from the object to the mirror and from the mirror to the image are equal.

# Mirror Image Example

Figure 14–81 displays a mirror image of A, B, and C to A', B', and C' when P1 and Q1 are taught positions. Figure 14–81 also displays a mirror image with an offset when P1 and Q1 are taught but Q1 is taught at an offset of 200mm. In this case, the result is A", B", and C".

Figure 14–81. Positional Mirror Image

> **Image description -- img-157.jpeg:** The diagram illustrates the concept of mirror images in robotics, comparing two scenarios: "Mirror Image Without Offset" (top) and "Mirror Image With Offset" (bottom). Both scenarios show a robot positioned at the origin (0,0) with coordinate axes labeled +X and +Y. In the top scenario, the mirror image of a shape (comprising points A, B, C, C', and A') is reflected across the y=0 line without any offset, resulting in points A', B', C', and Q1. The diagram includes labels for key points, the offset distance, and the y-coordinate values, demonstrating how the mirror image changes with the introduction of an offset.

# Rotational Mirror Image

A parallel mirror image mirrors the program about a mirror plane first, and then the mirrored program is rotated about a center of rotation. Orientation of the part to be imaged is rotated about one or more of its axes relative to the mirror plane. See Figure 14–82.

Figure 14–82. Rotational Mirror Image

> **Image description -- img-158.jpeg:** The diagram illustrates a system involving source positions, a mirror pane, and destination positions. On the left side, there are three labeled source positions: P1, P2, and P3, arranged in a triangular formation. These sources emit rays that are directed toward a central mirror pane positioned in the middle of the diagram. The mirror pane reflects the rays to the right side of the diagram, where three destination positions labeled Q1, Q2, and Q3 are arranged in a triangular formation similar to the source positions. The rays from each source position are reflected by the mirror pane and directed toward specific destination positions, indicating a one-to-one mapping between source and destination positions. The operational meaning of the diagram is to show how light or signals from different source points are redirected by a mirror to corresponding destination points, maintaining spatial relationships.

In Figure 14–83 the positions, P1, P2 and P3 are mirrored about the mirror plane as Q1, Q2 and Q3. These positions are then rotated  \( 45^{\circ} \)  about Q1 and stored as Q1', Q2' and Q3'.

# Mirror Image of Extended Axes

Extended (Ext) axes determines how the mirror image function will translate the program when you are using extended axes. Figure 14–86 displays a key for use with Figure 14–87 through Figure 14–89.

Figure 14–86. Mirror Image Key

> **Image description -- img-162.jpeg:** The image is a simple diagram illustrating the relationship between a robot base position and an extended axis in the context of a T.C.P. (Tool Center Point). The diagram consists of a horizontal line with a vertical line intersecting it at the center. The vertical line is labeled 'T.C.P.' and the horizontal line is labeled 'Extended Axis.' Below the intersection point of the two lines, there is a label 'Robot base position.' The diagram visually represents that the robot's base position is the origin point from which the extended axis and the T.C.P. are measured or aligned.

Possible extended axes configurations are:

- Robot axes only - allows you to mirror the axes of the robot without mirroring any non-integrated extended axes such as a positioning table. The shift is calculated using the change in the robot tool center point (TCP).

<!-- PDF page 1423 -->

Figure 14–87. Example of Robot Axes Only Mirror Image

> **Image description -- img-163.jpeg:** The image is a schematic diagram illustrating a signal path with two distinct transmission control points (T.C.P.). The diagram shows a horizontal line labeled 'Original' at the top, which represents the original signal path. Midway along this line, there is a vertical line with an arrow pointing downward, labeled 'Destination,' indicating a point where the signal is directed. To the right of this, there is a second horizontal line labeled 'T.C.P.' at both ends, representing a controlled or modified signal path. This line has a vertical dashed line connecting it to the original signal path, with arrows indicating the direction of signal flow. Below the second horizontal line, there is another vertical line with an arrow pointing downward, also labeled 'T.C.P.' and 'Destination,' suggesting another controlled signal path leading to a destination. The diagram visually represents the concept of signal control or modification at two distinct points, labeled as T.C.P., with the original signal being directed to a destination either directly or through these control points.

- Ext integrated - allows you to mirror the axes of the robot and any integrated axes. The amount of mirror image for the robot and the extended axes is calculated using the change in the TCP. See Figure 14–88.

Figure 14–88. Example of Extended Axes Integrated Mirror Image

> **Image description -- img-164.jpeg:** The image is a schematic diagram illustrating a transformation process involving a robot base and a target point labeled 'X'. The diagram shows three labeled positions: 'Original', 'New T.C.P.', and 'T.C.P.' along with the 'ROBOT BASE' and 'Destination'. The 'Original' position is connected to the 'Destination' by a vertical arrow, indicating a direct path. The 'New T.C.P.' and 'T.C.P.' positions are marked with crosses and are connected to the 'ROBOT BASE' by lines, showing their spatial relationship to the robot base. The 'New T.C.P.' is positioned above the 'T.C.P.', and both are aligned horizontally with the 'ROBOT BASE'. The diagram appears to represent a change in the Tool Center Point (T.C.P.) of a robot, where the original path is adjusted to a new T.C.P. position, likely for precision or alignment purposes in robotic movement or operation.

- With ext axes - allows you to mirror positions for robot axes and any extended axes in your system. The amount of mirror image for the robot is calculated by using the change in the TCP. The amount of shift for the extended axes is calculated using the center of the difference between an original position (P1) and a new position (Q1) as the point where the mirror image occurs. ### 14.21 EXECUTING MULTIPLE PROGRAMS (MULTI-TASKING)

#### 14.21.1 Overview

Multi-tasking allows more than one program to run on the controller on a time-sharing basis, so that multiple programs appear to run simultaneously. The maximum number of user programs, or tasks, that can be executed simultaneously is four. The default number of simultaneous tasks is one.

To increase the number of user programs that can be executed simultaneously, perform a Controlled start and select the PROGRAM SETUP option from the Controlled start menus.

Refer to Section B.1.5 for information on performing a Controlled start.

You can execute multiple programs in the following ways:

- SOP cycle start, Section 14.21.5
- Program number select (PNS), Section 14.21.6 This item is only for Arctool, DispenseTool, HandlingTool, and KAREL applications
- RUN program instruction, Section 14.21.7
- Single step, Section 14.21.8

#### 14.21.2 Guidelines

Use the guidelines in this section when you write a program for multi-tasking and when you execute multiple programs.

##### Writing a Program for Multi-Tasking

- Make sure all of the programs involved in the multi-tasking (up to four) each use a different motion group. Programs that are executed at the same time cannot use the same motion group.

You specify the motion group for a program in the program header information. Refer to Section 8.5.

- Use the ignore pause program attribute for programs you do not want to be paused by an error, by a command (such as the HOLD or EMERGENCY STOP button), or by enabling the teach pendant. Programs that use the ignore pause attribute cannot have a motion group specified. This means that these programs cannot contain any motion instructions.

For example, if you have a program that monitors I/O signals, which must execute continuously regardless of external events, you must specify the ignore pause attribute.

Ignore pause behaves differently during single step execution. Refer to Section 14.21.8 for more information.

<!-- PDF page 1435 -->

You specify whether to use ignore pause for a program in the program header information. Refer to Section 8.5.11.

# Executing Multiple Programs

The following restrictions apply to executing multiple programs:

- Up to four programs can be run at a time.
- You cannot execute a program if that program is currently running or paused.
- The programs you run using multi-tasking cannot use the same motion group.
- If you run a program continuously using a PLC, you must enter enough delay in the execution loop. If you do not use any delay, this program can lock other program execution.

#### 14.21.3 Synchronizing the Execution of Multiple Programs

To synchronize the execution of two programs, use register instructions within the two programs. Figure 14–92 shows an example of register instructions used to synchronize the execution of two programs.

Figure 14–92. Using Register Instructions to Synchronize Program Execution

> **Image description -- img-168.jpeg:** The diagram illustrates the interaction between two programs, Program A and Program B, through shared registers. It shows two registers labeled [1] and [2]. Program A contains two instructions: "WAIT R[1] = 1" and "R[2] = 1". Program B also contains two instructions: "R[1] = 1" and "WAIT R[2] = 1". The arrows indicate the flow of data or control between the programs and the registers. Specifically, Program A's instruction "R[2] = 1" writes to register [2], which is read by Program B's "WAIT R[2] = 1". Conversely, Program B's instruction "R[1] = 1" writes to register [1], which is read by Program A's "WAIT R[1] = 1". This setup suggests a synchronization mechanism where each program waits for a specific register value to be set by the other program before proceeding.

#### 14.21.4 Effect of Multi-Tasking on Dedicated I/O Signals

During multi-tasking program execution, keep in mind the following effects on dedicated I/O signals:

- *IMS TP input (instantaneous stop) is enabled for all motion groups.
- The operability of CMDENBL output (input acceptable) is checked for all motion groups.
- SYS RDY output (system ready) is checked whether servo power for all groups is supplied.

<!-- PDF page 1436 -->

### 14.21.5 Standard Operator Panel (SOP) Cycle Start Execution

You can start the execution of multiple programs using the standard operator panel (SOP) CYCLE START button. Use Procedure 14-38 to execute multiple programs using the SOP CYCLE START button.

# Procedure 14-38 Executing Multiple Programs Using the Standard Operator Panel (SOP) CYCLE START Button

# Conditions

- The programs you will execute at the same time do not use the same motion group.
- You are executing no more than four programs at a time.
- All other conditions related to executing a program using SOP CYCLE START are satisfied.
- You are not executing the same program more than once simultaneously.
- The MODE SELECT switch is set to AUTO.

# Steps

1. Select the first program you want to execute using the SELECT menu on the teach pendant.

# Warning

This procedure starts production run. Make sure all safety barriers are in place, all personnel are outside of the workcell, all equipment is in place, and all production conditions have been met before you continue; otherwise, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

2. Press the CYCLE START button on the operator panel.

> **Image description -- img-169.jpeg:** The image is a black-and-white line drawing depicting a sequence of steps or components related to a mechanical or electronic assembly process. From left to right, the sequence includes: 1) A rectangular component with a small square inside it, possibly representing a circuit board or a chip. 2) A set of three circular objects arranged in a triangular formation, which could be buttons, dials, or sensors. 3) A rectangular object with a smaller square inside it, similar to the first component but possibly a different part. 4) A circular object with a smaller circle inside it, resembling a gear or a wheel. 5) A hand holding a tool, such as a screwdriver or a pen, indicating an action being performed on the assembly. The hand and tool suggest the final step involves manual intervention or adjustment.

3. Select the next program you want to execute using the SELECT menu on the teach pendant.
4. Press the CYCLE START button on the operator panel.
5. Repeat Step 3 and Step 4 for each program you want to execute.

<!-- PDF page 1437 -->

### 14.21.6 Program Number Select (PNS) Execution

You can start the execution of multiple programs using program number select (PNS). Use Procedure 14-39 to execute multiple programs using PNS.

### Procedure 14-39 Running Multiple Programs Using Program Number Select (PNS)

#### Conditions

- The programs you will execute at the same time do not use the same motion group such as, the group mask is different for each program.
- You are executing no more than four programs at a time and $SCR.$MAXNUMTASK > 2.
- All other conditions related to executing a program using PNS are satisfied. (Refer to Chapter 9 TESTING A PROGRAM AND RUNNING PRODUCTION)
- You are not executing the same program more than once simultaneously.
- The MODE SELECT switch is set to AUTO.
- The REMOTE/LOCAL setup item in the System Configuration Menu is set to REMOTE. Refer to Section 10.12.

#### Warning

This procedure starts production run. Make sure all safety barriers are in place, all personnel are outside of the workcell, all equipment is in place, and all production conditions have been met before you continue; otherwise, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

#### Warning

If you do not follow this procedure, temporary memory in the controller will be filled. This causes the process CPU to be locked into a busy and running condition. Make sure your PLC logic is correct and does not contain a high rate of production start calls; otherwise, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

#### Steps

1. Set the 8 bit PNS input to the number that when added to the base number will determine which program is selected.
2. Strobe the PNSTROBE input. When the controller receives the input signal, the selected program will be displayed on the teach pendant screen. The ACK UOP signal indicates what binary input is being received. This stays ON until a new program is selected.
3. Press the production start button on the user operator panel to start production operation or, if your system uses a PLC, production operations will begin as soon as the PROD_START input is received.
4. Repeat Step 1 through Step 3 for each program you want to execute.

<!-- PDF page 1438 -->

#### 14.21.7 RUN Program Instruction Execution

Use the RUN program within the main program to execute a second, third, or fourth program simultaneously. When you execute a program in which you have added RUN program instructions, the program you specify will execute, and execution of the main program that contains the RUN program instruction will continue at the same time.

Figure 14–93 shows an example of using a RUN program instruction to execute multiple programs.

Figure 14–93. Multi-Tasking Using the RUN Program Instruction

Main Program
PROC0001
1: J P[1] 100% CNT100
2: J P[2] 100% CNT100
3: RUN PROC0002
4: L P[4] 500mm/sec CNT100
5: RUN PROC0003
6: L P[5] 500mm/sec CNT100 SE

Note In line three the second program will begin executing and in line five the third program will begin executing.

After you have included the RUN program instructions within your main program, execute the program using one of the execution methods available.

#### 14.21.8 Single Step Program Execution

When the main task is executed in single step mode, the subtask is also executed in single step mode. A task in which a RUN instruction is issued is called a main task. A task activated by a RUN instruction within the main task is called a subtask. See Figure 14–94.

<!-- PDF page 1439 -->

Figure 14–94. Single Step Execution Example

> **Image description -- img-170.jpeg:** The image shows a structured programming example with two labeled code blocks: MAIN.MN and SUB.MN. MAIN.MN (group mask ['1','.','*','*']) contains three lines of instructions: 1) RUN SUB, which activates the subroutine SUB.MN; 2) J P[1] 100% FINE, a jump command to position P[1] at 100% speed with fine positioning; 3) L P[2] 500mm/sec CNT 100, a linear move command to position P[2] at 500 millimeters per second with a count of 100. SUB.MN (group mask ['1','.','1','*']) also contains three lines: 1) J P[1] 100% FINE, a jump to position P[1] at 100% speed with fine positioning; 2) J P[2] 100% FINE, a jump to position P[2] at 100% speed with fine positioning; 3) L P[3] 100mm/sec FINE, a linear move command to position P[3] at 100 millimeters per second with fine positioning. The diagram illustrates the flow of control from the main program to the subroutine and the specific movement commands executed in each block.

Figure 14–94, the program MAIN.MN is the main task(motion group 1), and SUB.MN is the subtask (motion group 2), which is activated by a RUN program instruction within MAIN.MN.

When MAIN.MN is executed in single step mode, SUB.MN, activated by a RUN instruction in MAIN.MN, is also executed in single step mode.

Special considerations for single step execution of multi-tasking programs must also be made in the following areas:

- Backward execution
- Backward execution of the RUN instruction

##### Backward Execution

When the main task is restarted in backward execution mode, the subtask is activated also in backward execution mode. See Figure 14–95.

Figure 14–95. Single Step Backward Execution

> **Image description -- img-171.jpeg:** The diagram is a flowchart illustrating the relationship between a 'Main task' and a 'Subtask'. The 'Main task' and 'Subtask' are represented as two separate boxes. An arrow labeled 'RUN instruction' points from the 'Main task' to the 'Subtask', indicating that the subtask is executed as part of the main task. Both the 'Main task' and 'Subtask' have a 'Pause' symbol (an 'X' inside a circle) beneath them, with annotations stating 'Activated in backward execution mode'. This suggests that pausing can occur in both tasks specifically during backward execution. The diagram visually conveys that the subtask is initiated by the main task and that pausing functionality is applicable to both in the context of backward execution.

##### Backward Execution of a RUN Instruction

If a RUN instruction is encountered during backward execution, it is executed in that mode. After backward execution of the RUN instruction, the cursor moves to the instruction next to the RUN

<!-- PDF page 1440 -->

instruction. If you want to continue backward execution after the RUN instruction, move the cursor to the instruction before the RUN instruction manually, then specify the backward mode again.

In Figure 14–96, using backward execution can easily return both main task and subtask to the states they were in immediately after the RUN instruction was executed.

Figure 14–96. Backward Execution of a RUN Instruction Example

> **Image description -- img-172.jpeg:** The diagram illustrates two scenarios of task execution involving a main task and a subtask. On the left side, labeled 'Pause during multitask execution,' the diagram shows a vertical timeline where the main task is paused at a specific point, indicated by an 'X Pause' symbol, while the subtask continues. The RUN instruction is shown as a horizontal line intersecting the timeline. On the right side, labeled 'Restart,' the diagram depicts the continuation of backward execution from the subtask to the main task. The main task and subtask are again represented on a timeline with a RUN instruction line. The subtask's backward execution continues up to the first line of the main task, where it restarts, indicated by an 'X Restart' symbol. The diagram highlights the interaction between pausing and restarting tasks during execution, emphasizing how backward execution in the subtask affects the main task's restart point.

In this example, a subtask is first activated by the RUN instruction in the main task. Both tasks are then caused to pause for any reason during multi-tasking execution.

When the program is restarted from a pause during backward execution, the main task is executed to the line next to the RUN instruction in backward mode. Backward execution will not continue any further. However, the subtask is executed to the first line in backward mode. As a result:

- The main task returns to the line next to the RUN instruction.
- The subtask returns to the first line.

This is equivalent to the state immediately after the RUN instruction is executed.

### 14.22 GRAVITY COMPENSATION

Gravity compensation calculates the bending of the robot arm caused by the tool/work on the flange, the equipment on the arm, and the self weight of the arm. Then it compensates the motor position depending on the calculation of the bending, and it improves the absolute position accuracy.

Gravity Compensation option is necessary to use this function. This function can not be used with Soft float (A05B-2600-J612).

### 14.22.1 System Variables

$PARAM_GROUP[group].$SV_DMY_LNK[8]

[Name] Gravity Compensation Enable/Disable

<!-- PDF page 1441 -->

# [Meaning]

• TRUE: Gravity Compensation is Enabled.
• FALSE: Gravity Compensation is Disabled.

Except for some specific system configurations, Gravity Compensation is disabled by default when the robot is shipped. To enable Gravity Compensation, set this variable to TRUE and cycle power. To disabled the Gravity Compensation, set this variable to FALSE, and cycle power.

# $PARAM_GROUP[group].$MOUNT_ANGLE

[Name] Mount Angle of Robot (Unit: deg) [Meaning] Set 0deg for floor mount type, 180deg for upside down type, or the mount angle for wall mount or angle mount type. Cycle power after setting.
