#### 14.22.3 Mastering

Note Mastering is executed when Gravity Compensation is ENABLED. Because the procedure has been changed from R-30iA Controllers, please read and understand this section before mastering

##### 14.22.3.1 Normal Mastering and GC Mastering

There are two methods for mastering:

1. Normal Mastering: Mastering with Gravity Compensation DISABLED.
2. GC Mastering : Mastering with Gravity Compensation ENABLED.

- You should try to select the same method as the one that was used at the previous mastering. This is because the result of (1) and (2) are different from each other.
- Gravity Compensation works with either mastering result. But you can achieve better absolute position accuracy with GC Mastering.
- If you switch from Normal Mastering to GC Mastering, the TCP position will shift slightly. Therefore, confirm in advance that the TCP shift will cause no problem.

<!-- PDF page 1443 -->

# Mastering Method at the Shipment of the Robot

For some specific system configurations, GC Mastering has been done at the shipment of the robot. Please find this information in the Data Sheet which is attached to the robot controller.

Table 14–44. Mastering Methods

[tbl-353.md](tbl-353.md)

### 14.22.3.2 How to Choose Mastering Method

Table 14–45. Mastering Method Selection

[tbl-354.md](tbl-354.md)

### 14.22.3.3 Mastering Procedure

# Mastering procedure for Normal Mastering

1. If Gravity Compensation is ENABLED, disable it.
2. Perform Mastering.
3. If you have disabled Gravity Compensation in step 1, enable it again.

# Mastering procedure for GC Mastering

1. Perform Mastering with Gravity Compensation ENABLED.

<!-- PDF page 1444 -->

After mastering execution, record (write down) the value of $DMR_GRP[group].$GRAV_MAST together with mastering counts ($DMR_GRP[group].$MASTER_COUN[ ]).

Note When you use the Gravity Compensation function, you must treat $DMR_GRP.$GRAV_MAST as a part of the mastering data. Write down the value of this system variable together with the mastering counts. You will need this value if you need to manually enter the mastering data into the system variables.

Figure 14–97. Mastering Data

> **Image description -- img-173.jpeg:** The image displays a snippet of mastering data, specifically from a dataset labeled as "$OMR_GRP[1]". The data includes several variables and their corresponding values: "$MASTER_COUNT[1] = 137859", "$MASTER_COUNT[2] = 22309853", "$MASTER_COUNT[3] = 30596", "$MASTER_COUNT[4] = 810348", "$MASTER_COUNT[5] = 87291", and "$MASTER_COUNT[6] = 23124". Additionally, the variable "$GRAV_MAST" is shown with a value of "1" and is explicitly noted as part of the mastering data. The relationships depicted indicate that both "$MASTER_COUNT[]" and "$GRAV_MAST" are components of the mastering data under the group "$OMR_GRP[1]". The operational meaning suggests that these variables are used for tracking or processing within a larger system, with "$MASTER_COUNT[]" likely representing counts of different categories or items, and "$GRAV_MAST" serving as a flag or indicator.

##### 14.22.3.4 GC Mastering

Consider the following in GC Mastering:

1. Before performing the GC mastering, set the correct payload parameters via the MOTION screen.
2. When determining the joint angles of a reference position which will later be used for mastering, collect them under the following conditions:

• Gravity Compensation is ENABLED.
- Calibration is completed.
- Correct payload parameters are set.

3. When you perform Single Axis Mastering, keep the following in mind:

- As a precaution, document the Mastering Data ($DMR_GRP[group].$MASTER_COUN[axis]) of all the axes before you perform mastering.
- If there are more than one axis which need to be mastered, you must select and master them all at the same time.

Example) Single Axis Master after J2, J4, and J5 motor replacement: You must master J2, J4, and J5 all at the same time. You cannot master just J2 while J4 and J5 are still not mastered.

If you have no way to master multiple axes simultaneously, use the following method as a work around: (NOTE: Master in ascending order; from the base of the robot to the end-effector.)

<!-- PDF page 1445 -->

1. Master J2, J4, and J5 all at once. You need to master J2 accurately, but you do not need to master J4 and J5 accurately. At this stage, a temporary master for J4 and J5 which is moderately correct is sufficient.
2. Master J4 accurately.
3. Master J5 accurately.

- If you need to move an axis that does not need mastering, but you have already documented its reference position, move it after performing temporary mastering of the axis that requires mastering.

Example) Single Axis Master using reference angles of J1, J2, J4, J5, and J6 after J3 motor replacement:

4. Perform a temporary mastering for J3 which is moderately accurate, then do CALIBRATE.
5. Move the axes which do not require mastering (J1, J2, J4, J5, and J6) to the joint angles which have been documented as a reference position.
6. Master J3 accurately.

- If you perform “mastering after temporary mastering” as described above, master count of the axes which have an interaction with the recently mastered axis will change. This causes unexpected position change. Therefore, after performing mastering, verify that master count of the axes that did not require mastering stayed the same as the original. If this value has changed, enter the original value which was documented before.

### 14.23 GROUP MASK EXCHANGE

#### 14.23.1 Overview

Group Mask Exchange is used to copy a teach pendant program into a new program with a different group mask than an original program. The position data from the original teach pendant program will be copied into another group in the new teach pendant program. You can copy multiple group programs from a single robot or dual robots.

Note This feature does not validate the logic of the output program, its positional data, or the program header (except group mask information). The resulting program might also require some position touchup.

<!-- PDF page 1446 -->

Table 14-46. Group Mask Exchange Screen Items

[tbl-355.md](tbl-355.md)

#### 14.23.2 Setting Up Group Mask Exchange

# Procedure 14-40 Copying a Program Using Group Mask Exchange

1. Press MENU.
2. Select UTILITIES.
3. Press F1, [TYPE].
4. Select Group Exchg and press ENTER. You will see a screen similar to the following.

Group Exchange G1 JOINT 10 %
Program Selection 1/8
1 Orig Prog : (*,*,*,*,*) [SIDE_A ]
2 New Prog : (*,*,*,*,*) [SIDE_A ]
Group Selection New Prog Group
3 Copy Orig Grp[1] to New Grp[0]
4 Copy Orig Grp[2] to New Grp[0]
5 Copy Orig Grp[3] to New Grp[0]
6 Copy Orig Grp[4] to New Grp[0]
7 Copy Orig Grp[5] to New Grp[0]

Note If a program is currently selected, it is used as the default for the original and new program displayed in lines 1 and 2 above.

5. To select a different original program, press F3, [CHOICE].
6. To rename the new program, move the cursor to line 2 and press ENTER. You can then choose a method to rename the program and type the new program name. You must then identify the new group for the copy to take place.
7. To select a motion group in the original program to copy to the new program motion groups:

a. Move the cursor to the first New group [#] to copy.

b. Type a group number, and press ENTER.

Note If any of the entries for New Group [#] are left at 0, this group will be deleted from the new program.

<!-- PDF page 1447 -->

8. To clear a single entry, press NEXT, > and then press F1, CLEAR.
9. To clear all entries, press NEXT, > and then press SHIFT and F1, CLEAR.

Note If lines 1 and 2 are changed, the New Grp column in lines 3 through 7 are cleared.

10. When you have finished identifying the groups to be copied, press F2, EXEC.

Note If the new program exists when you press F2, EXEC, you must confirm the overwrite operation before the execute takes place.

### 14.24 HIGH SPEED INPUT FUNCTIONS

#### 14.24.1 Overview

The following High Speed Input Functions are available:

- Frequency Interface
- High Speed Scanning (for Line Tracking Part Detect)
- Position Snap and Map

<!-- PDF page 1449 -->

### 14.24.2 Frequency Interface

Outputs are supplied as system variables that are accessible by the FANUC America Corporation Software.

The following outputs are supplied:

- Frequency Reading (x1000 Hz)
- Total Pulse Count
- Standard Operator Panel Input (SOPIN)

Refer to the High Speed Digital Input Module (HSI) Option Manual for more information.

### 14.24.3 High Speed Scanning (for Line Tracking Part Detect).

The High Speed Scanning feature ensures an accurate part detection process when the conveyor operates at very fast speeds. R30/B Plus supports up to 5 High Speed Digital Input (HSDI) #1–#5, located on the JRL5 connector of the controller, in place of the standard digital input normally used for part detection. Two inputs can be supported with a standard cable. More than two inputs, however, require a special interface cable. Contact your FANUC America Corporation technical representative if you need more than two ports.

To use High Speed Scanning, you must

- Enable the High Speed Scanning system variable
- Modify your line tracking program

Refer to the Linetracking Setup and Operations Manual for more information.

### 14.25 HIGH SPEED POSITION OUTPUT

This function enables the robot to stream its current Tool Center Point (TCP) or joint angle position at high speed through Ethernet. The data can be output in binary or XML, and KAREL variables can also be output. The maximum output cycle can be set to 2 msec.

To use this function, R891 must be ordered. This function uses one of the controller's regular Ethernet communication ports (port 1 or port 2) or the vision communication port (port 3).

Note The software that runs on the receiving PC used to receive the packets must be provided by the system designer.

Note For high-speed communication such as a 2 msec cycle, it is necessary to use the vision communication port (port 3), and only binary data format can be used. If this feature does not use port 3, it will usually display a warning and will not enable the feature if it is set faster than 8

<!-- PDF page 1450 -->

msec. If your have a system configuration such as multi-group, it may be necessary to set a cycle longer than 8 msec.

### 14.25.1 DATA FORMATS

Multiple data types can be selected, and the positions of multiple motion groups can be output. The output data format can be selected from binary or XML. The unit of the output position data is millimeter for X-Y-Z, degree for W-P-R, and each Joint angle.

Caution

For a fast data rate of 2 msec, please select one data type only to minimize CPU loading. For a slower data rate, more than one data type can be output.

### 14.25.1.1 Binary

The following information is added to the front part of the packet output in binary format.

Table 14–48. Data in the front part of the packet

[tbl-358.md](tbl-358.md)

#### 14.25.1.1.1 TCP Cartesian Position with Binary

When using this data format, the following data is output.

- Version (long - 4 bytes)
- Index (long - 4 bytes)
- Clock (long - 4 bytes)
- Type (short - 2 bytes)
- Motion Group (short - 2 bytes)
- Position [x, y, z, w, p, r] (six floats - 24 bytes total)

<!-- PDF page 1451 -->

• Status (long - 4 bytes)
• I/O (long - 4 bytes)]

###### 14.25.1.1.2 Joint Angles with Binary

When using this data format, the following data is output.

• Version (long - 4 bytes)
- Index (long - 4 bytes)
- Clock (long - 4 bytes)
- Type (short - 2 bytes)
- Motion Group (short - 2 bytes)
- Position [J1, J2, J3, J4, J5, J6, J7, J8, J9] (nine floats - 36bytes total)
• Status (long - 4 bytes)
• I/O (long - 4 bytes)]

###### 14.25.1.1.3 Variables with Binary

When using this data format, the following data is output.

• Version (long - 4 bytes)
- Index (long - 4 bytes)
- Clock (long - 4 bytes)
- Type (short - 2 bytes)
• Data [1 -10] (ten long/float - 40 bytes total)

##### 14.25.1.2 XML

###### 14.25.1.2.1 1.1.2.1 TCP Cartesian Position with XML

If the TCP Cartesian position is selected to be output with XML, the following packet will be output. “*” are the time, TCP cartesian position, program execution status, and I/O value.

<POS><usec>*</usec><G1><X>*</X><Y>*</Y><Z>*</Z><W>*</W><P>*</P>
<R>*</R></G1></POS><CYCLE>*</CYCLE><IO>*</IO>

###### 14.25.1.2.2 1.1.2.2 Joint Angles with XML

If the joint angles is selected to be output with XML, the following packet will be output. “*” are the time, joint angles, program execution status, and I/O value.

<!-- PDF page 1452 -->

<ANG><usec>*</usec><G1><J1>*</J1><J2>*</J2><J3>*</J3><J4>*</J4>
<J5>*</J5><J6>*</J6><J7>*</J7><J8>*</J8><J9>*</J9></G1></ANG>
<CYCLE>*</CYCLE><IO>*</IO>

###### 14.25.1.2.3 Variables with XML

If the Variables is selected to be output with XML, the following packet will be output. * are the time and selected variables.

<VAR><usec>*</usec><V1>*</V1><V2>*</V2><V3>*</V3><V4>*</V4>
<V5>*</V5><V6>*</V6><V7>*</V7><V8>*</V8><V9>*</V9><V10>*</V10></VAR>

# Conditions to press button

Condition to press button can be setup for each button. The condition is set up in the operation condition setup screen. By default, the following conditions have to be satisfied to press a button. Refer to Section 14.26.10 for detail of operation condition and its setup screen.

(A) Enable switch of Interface panel is ON
(B) Shift key is pressed.

By default, the operation condition of a momentary button is checked only when it is pressed. The lamp does not have an operation condition setup screen because it cannot be pressed.

When you set up a button, you have to decide where to place it by selecting the position number. Then the type of the button on the position must be set. After the button is set up by the detail screen, the button is displayed on panel on the position. For setup, refer to Section 14.26.3 through Section 14.26.5.

# Error button

If setup is wrong, the button is displayed as an error button. They are similar to the following figure.

<!-- PDF page 1460 -->

> **Image description -- img-182.jpeg:** The image shows a table with three columns, each labeled as 'Error' at the top. The first column is labeled 'Pos 7' with 'DO 0' below it. The second column is labeled 'Pos 8' with 'DI 0' below it. The third column is labeled 'Pos 9' with 'Op.Cond' below it. The table appears to represent error positions or states, with 'Pos 7', 'Pos 8', and 'Pos 9' likely indicating specific positions or points of reference, and 'DO 0', 'DI 0', and 'Op.Cond' representing associated values or conditions for each position.

- The button displays the position number and I/O that can not be read.
- If the button has 2 signals and both cannot be read, both signals are displayed. Button type 3(2 contact points switch) displays only the 1st signal if index of the 2nd signal is 0.
- Button type 6 and 7 (digital switch and digital lamp) display only the 1st found signal that cannot be read.
- If signal is specified and enabled as operation condition, and if the signal cannot be read, an error button is displayed. Signal for actual operation (output signal for example) is also wrong, it has priority.
- Press of the button displays the detail setup screen.

# F3 SETUP

Pressing the function key displays the button type setup screen of the same page. For button type setup screen, refer to Section 14.26.5

##### "Toggle ON/OFF" button

The button exists in detail screen of buttons that have ON/OFF status. They have colors for ON and OFF state. The button toggles “ON” state and “OFF” state of button without changing the actual signal the button refers to. The button works only when “Display based on I/O value” button status is OFF.

##### "Display based on I/O value" button

When the button is ON, preview is displayed based on current status of I/O specified. When this button is pressed, status of “Toggle ON/OFF” button does not affect to preview. Based on the setup in the figure above, we explain how the button works. DO  \( [11] \)  is specified for output signal. When panel is actually displayed, button is displayed based on DO  \( [11] \) . The following table shows how “Toggle ON/OFF” and “Display based on I/O value” button changes preview.

# Color for disabled button

A few types of buttons have a setup item, “Color for disabled button”. If the item is set to “Enable”, the button color is changed according to whether the condition to press the button (operation condition) is satisfied or not. You can compare the two looks by preview. In preview, panel enable switch is treated as if it is always ON in operation condition check.

By default setting of operation condition, the button is displayed in color of “Button enabled” column when shift key is pressed.

When a setup item is changed successfully, the error message is cleared. In the above figure, any color change would clear error message on error line. However, the preview still shows error button.

When the operation condition signal cannot be read, the preview displays the error button. If the signal for actual operation (output signal for example) is also wrong, it has priority.

### 14.26.8 Type of Button

This function can use the following buttons and lamps.

- Push button (type 1)
- Push button lamp (type 2)
- 2 contact points button (type 3)
- Lamp (type 5)
- Digital switch (type 6)
- Digital lamp (type7)

Overview of properties that is common to some button types is explained in the next section.

### 14.26.9 Common Properties

#### Label

This is the string shown on the button. The number of labels depends on the type of button. They are shown as Label1,..., Label4 in button detail setup screen. Label n is displayed at the nth row of the button. When the panel has 7 columns, each label should have less than 10 characters. If the number of columns is 8, each label should have less than 8 characters.

Foreground color and background color

<!-- PDF page 1473 -->

Following type of buttons have two sets of colors. “Button enabled” and “Button disabled” column of button detail setup screen.

- Push button (type 1)
- Push button lamp (type 2)
- 2 contact points switch (type 3)
- Digital switch (type 6)

The following figure is extract of button detail setup screen of type 1, 2 and 3.

[tbl-368.md](tbl-368.md)

The digital switch doesn't have ON/OFF status. There are only Foreground, Background and color for disabled button. Colors of “Button enabled” column are for when button can be pressed. The “Button disabled” column is for when the button can NOT be pressed. Refer to Section 14.26.10 for conditions to press a button.

Note If the “Color for disabled button” is disabled, colors of “Button enabled” column are always used.

#### Turn Off Signal at Screen Change

If this item is enabled, specified output is turned off at following event

- When panel is displayed
- When screen is changed to another screen (This includes page change between panels)
- Any operation that re-displays panel (Refresh pane of FCTN menu, Zoom for example)

#### Supported Signal Type

Buttons of this function supports digital type I/O only. I/O that has integer value are not supported. For example, analog I/O and group I/O are not supported. Digital switch and lamp treat a series of digital signal as a group and treat them as numeric value. The following I/O types are supported by output signal of push button (type 1), output signal of push button lamp (type 2), both signal of 2 points contact switch (type 3) and output of digital switch (type 6).

• DO
• RO
• F (Flag)

Status signal of push button lamp (type 2), signal of lamp (type 5) and digital lamp (type 7) support following I/O types.

• DI
• DO
• RI
• RO
• SI

# Operation condition

This item exists in detail screen of button type that can be pressed. You can display operation condition setup screen by pressing detail button on the row of operation condition. Refer to Section 14.26.10 for more information.

### 14.26.10 Operation Condition

### 14.26.10.1 Overview

The Interface panel function can specify condition to press buttons on the panel. -

- Conditions are specified by combining following keys and I/O.

- Panel enable switch
- Shift key
- TP enable switch
- DEADMAN switch
- Signal specified by user is ON or OFF

- Conditions are specified for each button.

- If a button is pressed when its operation condition is not satisfied, warning is posted. Some button may look the button was successfully pressed, but the function of the button does not work. Output signal is not turned on for example.

Signal specified by operation condition setup screen is referred as operation condition signal.

### 14.26.10.2 Button Types Supported

Operation condition is supported by following button types.

- Push button lamp (type 1)
- Push button lamp (type 2)

<!-- PDF page 1476 -->

• 2 contact point switch (type 3)
• Digital switch (type 6)

Lamp (type 5) and Digital lamp (type 7) don't support operation condition. They are lamp and cannot be pressed.

#### 14.26.19 Backup and Restore

Files for backup and restore are classified into two groups.

- IFP0**.XML (** is 2 characters that are language suffix). For example, it is “eg” for English and “kn” for Japanese.
- IFP_VARS.SV

IFP0**.XML - This file contains setup of panel. Position number, type and parameters for buttons are saved into these files.

- Contents of panels are saved into file for each language

<!-- PDF page 1496 -->

- IFP**.XML can be restored at cold start.

Note Don't load the XML file when panel or setup screens are displayed. 2

Setup of type setup screen and button detail setup screens are saved at exit from screen. Backup after exiting from the screens.

IFP_VARS.SV contains following setup.

- Signal number of external Interface panel selection
- Items of miscellaneous setting screen.
- IFP_VARS.SV should be read in controlled start mode.

### 14.26.20 Limitations

1. The iPendant with USB and touch panel is required. This function has nothing to do with USB. However it is required for faster communication and processors than iPendant of older types.
2. Buttons and lamp of this function only support digital type signal. Digital type signal means signals that have ON/OFF value, DIO and RIO for example. This function does not support I/O type that has integer value, GIO and AIO for example. The other data of robot such as register and system variable cannot be handled by buttons of this function.
3. You cannot use "<" and ">" in string of label.
4. After pressing a button, release it after confirming change of color and pressed/released status of button.
5. After pressing a button, release your finger at the same button. If you drag your finger and release it on another button or empty place, button doesn't work properly. Especially, momentary button doesn't turn off specified signal. Press and release the button again, properly.
6. Display panel and all setup screens in single pane mode. Otherwise, whole screen cannot be displayed. Cursor may be displayed outside of screen. You cannot change focus by touching panel and type setup screen. Use window key.
7. Setup of type setup screen and button detail setup screens are saved at exit from screen. Exit from the screens before display panel, power off or backup.
8. Zoom function does not zoom text and image of button.

## 14.27 JOG RETRACT & RETURN

### 14.27.1 Overview

Jog Retract & Return (R786) provides a simple way to recover from an error. During production operation, a program can be paused by a fault (or by the HOLD button). At that time, the operator

<!-- PDF page 1497 -->

can manually jog the robot to perform necessary operations to fix any problems that caused the fault. This feature enables the arm to trace the jogged path backward, and thus safely brings the robot arm back to the position where the program was paused.

Note This feature is currently supported on a single-arm systems only.

#### 14.27.2 Sequence of Operations

The operation of the Jog Retract & Return feature is as follows:

1. A program has been paused due to a fault or by the HOLD operation
2. The operator initiates the Retract operation by pressing the "Jog Retract" button.
3. The operator jogs the robot away to a safe location.
4. When the operator finishes the manual (repair) operation, he/she initiates the Return operation by pressing the Robot Return button. At this time, the robot will return to the position where the program was paused, moving backward along the jogged path.
5. After the robot finishes the Return motion, the paused program can be resumed.

Figure 14-114. Jog Retract & Return

> **Image description -- img-238.jpeg:** The image depicts a robot path programming diagram with a list of commands and a visual representation of the robot's movement. The command list (JOB TP) includes nine steps with specific movements and parameters: 1) J P[1] 100% FINE, 2) L P[2] 500mm/sec FINE, 3) Weave Start, 4) L P[3] 50mm/min FINE, 5) L P[4] 50mm/min FINE, 6) L P[5] 50mm/min FINE, 7) Weave End, 8) L P[6] 500mm/sec FINE, 9) J P[1:HOME] 50% FINE. The visual diagram shows the robot's path with labeled points P[1] through P[6], where P[1] is marked as the HOME position. The path includes a weaving motion between P[3] and P[5], with an error point indicated between P[3] and P[4]. The robot's movement directions are labeled as 'Jog Away' and 'Robot Return'. The diagram illustrates the sequence of movements and transitions between points, with solid lines representing the programmed path and dashed lines indicating the robot's return path.

<!-- PDF page 1498 -->

#### 14.27.4 Operation

There are two major steps in recovery from an error.

- Jog Retract operation (Section 14.27.4.1)
- Robot Return operation (Section 14.27.4.2)

You can also abort the recovery operation using the Abort jog retract operation procedure (Section 14.27.4.3).

##### 14.27.4.1 Jog Retract Procedure

The jog retract operation is performed as follows.

# Procedure 14-47 Jog Retract

# Conditions

• A TP program is paused or running.

<!-- PDF page 1500 -->

1. • A pulse (>200msec; typically, a push of a button) is sent to the Jog Retract digital input port to request the Jog Retract operation.

• If a program is running, the running program will be held (decelerate-stop and pause)
• The Jog Retract in progress digital output port will turn ON, indicating that the Jog Retract operation is active.
• At this point, Cycle Start UOP input is disabled, and Robot Return input becomes active.

2. The operator can now put the robot control into T1 or T2 mode, and enable the teach pendant to jog the robot.

3. Every time a jog button is pressed, the system will record the current robot position and motion (motype, speed) information. The maximum number of jog motions remembered is 50 (by default), and can be configured in the setup menu.

# Note

• While Jog Retract in progress output is ON, running/resuming a TP program by the UOP input (PLC) is prohibited.
• If Jog Retract is requested while no program is running or paused, a warning JOG-052 No program is running or paused will be posted, and the request will be ignored.
• After the program has been paused, the system starts recording the arm jogging information from the first jog operation. Therefore, the Robot Return operation will bring the robot back to the place where the program was paused even if Jog Retract was requested some time after the arm was jogged.
• If Auto launch item is ENABLED in the setup menu, the Jog Retract operation will automatically start as soon as the arm is jogged after a program has been paused.
• After the number of recorded positions reaches its maximum, a warning message JOG-056 Jog Retract recorded Max Num positions will be posted, and no more jogging operation will be allowed until Abort Jog Retract is requested (by asserting the abort retract digital input port).

### 14.27.4.2 Robot Return Procedure

To return the robot back to the point where the Jog Retract started at, do the following.

# Procedure 14-48 Robot Return Procedure

# Conditions

• The Jog Retract in progress output is ON.
1. Put the robot controller into Auto mode.
2. Reset any outstanding error (using fault reset operation).
3. Send a pulse (>200msec; typically, a push of a button) to the Robot Return digital input port, to request the Robot Return operation

<!-- PDF page 1501 -->

- The Robot Return in progress digital output port will turn ON, indicating that the Robot Return operation is active.
- The robot will start moving to the previously stored positions, one by one, in the reverse order, until it reaches the position where the robot was first jogged after the TP program was paused.
- The robot will move back to a stored position with the same motype and speed as when the robot was jogged away from it, thus following the jog motion as close as possible.
- The robot will stop momentarily (FINE termtype, or G09) at each recorded position, and then will proceed to one previous recorded position.

4. When all return moves have been completed, both the Jog Retract in progress and the Robot Return in progress digital output ports will turn OFF, and Robot Return Complete digital output will turn ON.

5. At this point, the operator (or PLC) may request a Cycle Start to resume the paused program.

# Note

- If Robot Return is requested without setting Auto mode, a warning message Auto mode is required will be posted, and the request will be ignored.
- If Robot Return operation is requested while Jog Retract in progress output is OFF, a warning JOG-054 Jog Retract NOT in progress is posted.
- If Robot Return operation is interrupted by an error, or hold button, etc., the operation can be resumed by requesting Robot Return again.
- If the operator start jogging of the robot again after the Robot Return motion has been interrupted, the system will re-start recording the jogged position. The information will be appended to the remaining information so that the robot will safely return to the initial stopped position.
- Robot Return motions are such that TCP (Tool Center Point) follows the same trajectory. Therefore, robot joint angles may be different if the uframe or tool_frame is modified during Jog Retract & Return operation.
- During return motion, the system modifies the following system variables to the value as recorded during jogging. After all Return motions are finished, and the robot has returned to its stopped positions, the following system variables will be restored to the value before the Jog Retract was initiated.

- $rmt_master
- $group[].$rotspeed
- $mcr.$genoverride
- $mnuframenum
- $mnutoolnum
- $mcr_grp[].$prgoverride

<!-- PDF page 1502 -->

### 14.27.4.3 Abort Jog Retract Operation

The Abort Jog Retract input will abort the Jog Retract & Return operation.

### Procedure 14-49 Abort Jog Retract Operation

#### Conditions

- The jog Retract in progress output is ON.

1. Send a pulse (>200msec; typically, a push of a button) to the Abort Jog Retract digital input port, to abort the Jog Retract & Return operation. The system will do the following.

- If the robot is moving for Robot Return operation, it will decelerate and stop.
- The Jog Retract in progress digital output and the Robot Return in progress digital output ports will turn OFF
- After Abort request, no more jog positions will be recorded. All recorded jog motion information thus far will be kept in the memory.
- If so wished, the operator can press Jog Retract button. The system will re-start recording of the jogged positions (as long as the number of recorded position has not reached the maximum).
- Pressing Robot Return button at this time will cause the robot to start the return motion. The robot will move back all the way to the initial stopped position, based on the recorded positions in the memory.

2. The paused TP program will not be aborted.

Note If Abort Jog Retract operation is requested while Jog Retract in progress output is OFF, a warning JOG-054 Jog Retract NOT in progress will be posted.

### 14.28 LIMIT SET

The limit set function allows you to determine the software axis limits for a robot automatically, and to determine the mechanical stopper locations. If you want to set the axis limits without the limit set function, you must run all programs step-by-step, record the maximum value for each angle, and then set the axis joint limits manually.

The limit set function reads all of the programmed positions on the robot automatically and determines the maximum and minimum taught joint angles used in all programs. It then takes this information and sets the specified joint limits automatically, while taking into account a limit buffer you specify. The limit set function also reports the appropriate angles for the mechanical stoppers.

By default, software axis limits will be set only for axes 1, 2, and 3. You can specify that they be set for more axes, if desired.

A limits buffer is added to the detected limits to allow tolerance for motion between positions when you run a program. When the robot moves from one position to another, the motion of the robot between the positions might be outside of the axis limits. The limits buffer is applied to the

<!-- PDF page 1503 -->

detected maximum and minimum taught points to ease the axis limits so that a joint limit error does not occur on the motion between the taught points.

You can set a limits buffer of from 0 to 50 degrees. The limits buffer is set to 10 degrees, by default. A limits buffer of 10 degrees provides adequate ease in many cases. After using the limit set function, if you encounter many joint limit errors while running programs, increase the limits buffer and try again.

Before you set limits, you select the axes for which you want to set limits and change the value of the limits buffer, if desired. You can reset the limits to factory settings if you do not want to use the new ones.

Limit set uses position registers for limit calculations. Position registers in Cartesian representation do not have an associated UFrame or UTool. When calculating joint limits from these position registers, limit set will convert them into joint representation relative to world frame with the center of the faceplate as the TCP.

#### Procedure 14-50 Using the Limit Set Function to Set Software Axis Limits

##### Steps

1. Press MENU.
2. Select UTILITIES.
3. Press F1, [TYPE].
4. Select Limit Set and press ENTER. You will see a screen similar to the following.

[tbl-391.md](tbl-391.md)

5. To view the currently active settings, press PREV. To return to this menu, press PREV again.

6. To select a motion group for limit setting, press F2, GROUP, type the desired group number, and press ENTER.

7. To select an axis for limit setting

a. Move the cursor to the number of the axis you want to select.
b. Press F4, YES, to select the axis to set. If you press F5, NO, the limit will not be set for that axis.

8. To set the limits buffer, move the cursor to Limits Buffer, type the number of degrees, and press ENTER.

#### 14.29.2 Prompt Box Message Menu

A prompt box message menu is used to make sure the operator is aware of something. When a prompt box message screen is displayed, the teach pendant program pauses until the operator presses ENTER. In addition, when the prompt box is displayed, the operator cannot access any other menus. See Figure 14–116 for an example of a prompt box message menu.

The text reads: 'Robot is not at PERCH position' in the top section, and 'OK' in the bottom section. The top text indicates that the robot is not currently in the designated 'PERCH' position, while the bottom text suggests that this status is acceptable or normal.

##### Macro: Prompt Box Msg (menu)

A prompt box message menu uses the Prompt Box Msg(menu) macro.

Parameter 1: menu - This is the menu number or menu name. The menu can be chosen by number or name.

##### Errors

The following errors are possible:

<!-- PDF page 1507 -->

- If the Prompt Box Msg(menu) macro was used in the teach pendant program without a parameter, an alarm is given and the program is aborted.
- If the selected prompt box message menu does not exist when it is called from a teach pendant program, a prompt box similar to the one shown in Figure 14–117 will be displayed. To abort the program, select OK.

Figure 14–117. Prompt Box Message Menu Does not Exist Screen

> **Image description -- img-241.jpeg:** A rectangular error message dialog box is displayed. The dialog box contains the following elements:

2. A message area in the center displaying the text 'Selected menu OK'.
3. A single button at the bottom labeled 'OK', which is presumably used to close the dialog box. The dialog box appears to be a standard system alert or notification window.

##### Menu File Name

Each prompt box message menu is stored in its own variable file that begins with the prefix "MENU1." The next two characters of the filename are the menu number. For example, the prompt box message menu 1 is stored in the variable file named "MENU1 01 .VR."

b. Move the cursor to the lines you want to change, press ENTER, and press the appropriate function keys to type the text. When you are finished with each line, press ENTER.

## 9. To save (back up) a menu to the default device:

a. Set the default device. Refer to Section 12.1.3.
b. Move the cursor to the name of the menu you want to save.
c. Press NEXT, >, and press F1, SAVE. The menu will be saved to the default device.

Note If the file already exists on the default device, you will be prompted whether to replace the existing file with the one you are backing up. To replace the file, select YES. To cancel, select NO.

Note You can also back up a menu using FILE, BACKUP APPLICATION. Refer to Chapter 12 PROGRAM AND FILE MANIPULATION for more information.

Note Each prompt box message menu is stored in its own variable file that begins with the prefix "MENU1." The next two characters of the filename are the menu number. For example, the prompt box message menu 1 is stored in the variable file named "MENU1 01 .VR."

<!-- PDF page 1511 -->

10. To load (restore) a menu:

a. Move the cursor to the name of the menu you want to load.
b. Press NEXT, >, and press F2, LOAD. The menu will be loaded from the default device.

Note If the file already exists on the controller, you will be prompted whether to replace the existing file with the one you are loading. To replace the file, select YES. To cancel, select NO.

Note You can also load a menu using FILE, LOAD, *.VR. Refer to Chapter 12 PROGRAM AND FILE MANIPULATION for more information.

11. To clear a menu:

a. Move the cursor to the name of the menu you want to clear.
b. Press NEXT, >, and press F3, CLEAR.
c. Confirm the clear:

- To clear the menu, select YES and press ENTER.
- To cancel the clear, select NO and press ENTER.

12. To copy a menu:

a. Move the cursor to the name of the menu you want to copy.
b. Press NEXT, >, and press F4, COPY.
c. Type the menu number to which you want to copy the menu and press ENTER.

Note If the new menu already exists, you will be prompted whether to replace the existing menu with the one you are copying. To replace the old menu with the new menu, select YES. To cancel the operation, select NO.

#### 14.29.3 Prompt Box Yes/No Menu

A prompt box yes/no menu asks the operator a question that can be answered YES or NO. When a prompt box yes/no screen is displayed, the teach pendant program pauses until the operator selects YES or NO and presses ENTER. In addition, when the prompt box yes/no screen is displayed, the operator cannot access any other menus. See Figure 14–118 for an example of a prompt box yes/no menu.

Figure 14–118. Prompt Box Yes/No Menu

Send the robot home?
YES NO

<!-- PDF page 1512 -->

# Macro: Prompt Box YN(menu, answer_reg)

A prompt box yes/no menu uses the Prompt Box YN(menu, answer_reg) macro.

Parameter 1: menu - This is the menu number or menu name. The menu can be chosen by number or name.

Parameter 2: answer_reg - This is the register that will contain the answer from the operator.

- R[answer_reg] = 0 if operator selected NO
- R[answer_reg] = 1 if operator selected YES

# Errors

The following errors are possible:

- If the Prompt Box YN(menu, answer_reg) macro was used in the teach pendant program without two parameters, an alarm is given and the program is aborted.
- If the selected prompt box yes/no menu does not exist when it is called from a teach pendant program, a prompt box similar to the one shown in Figure 14–119 will be displayed. To abort the program, select OK.

Figure 14–119. Prompt Box Yes/No Menu Does not Exist Screen

Error:
Selected menu
does not exist.
OK

- If the register answer_reg does not exist, then an alarm is given and the program is aborted.

# Menu File Name

Each prompt box yes/no menu is stored in its own variable file that begins with the prefix "MENU2." The next two characters of the filename are the menu number. For example, the prompt box yes/no menu 1 is stored in the variable file named "MENU2 01 .VR."

# Examples

See Prompt Box YN(menu, answer_reg) Macro Example 1 and Prompt Box YN(menu, answer_reg) Macro Example 2 for examples of how to use the Prompt Box YN(menu, answer_reg) instruction in a teach pendant program.

# Prompt Box YN(menu, answer_reg) Macro Example 1

PROG TEST1

<!-- PDF page 1513 -->

1: Prompt Box YN(1,2)
2: IF R[2] = 0, CALL ABORTIT

#### Prompt Box YN(menu, answer_reg) Macro Example 2

PROG TEST2

1: Prompt Box YN('NotAtPerch', 6)
2: IF R[6] = 1, JMP LBL[5]

#### 14.29.4 List Menu

A list menu asks the operator to select an item from a list of items. When a list menu is displayed, the teach pendant program pauses until the operator selects an item from the list. See Figure 14–120 for an example of a list menu.

Figure 14-120. List Menu

USER
Move Menu
1 Ignore
2 Move to Maint. Pos.
3 Move to Perch Pos.

# Macro:List Menu(menu, answer_reg)

A list menu uses the List Menu(menu, answer_reg) macro.

Parameter 1: menu - This is the menu number or menu name. The menu can be chosen by number of name.

Parameter 2: answer_reg - This is the register that will contain the answer from the operator.

- R[answer_reg] = item number the operator selected

# Display

To display a list menu you create, use the List Menu macro. The menu will be displayed automatically on the USER screen. If the operator changes the teach pendant display to another

<!-- PDF page 1518 -->

screen during teach pendant execution of this menu but before making the selection, he can return to this screen by pressing MENU and selecting USER.

##### Setup

In a list menu, you can specify

- Up to eight list items from which to choose
- A macro program to execute when the item is selected, if desired; this is called the ActionTP program.

Note The ActionTP program is a teach pendant program that is executed when the corresponding item number is selected. Do not use ActionTP teach pendant programs that use menu macros.

##### Errors

The following errors are possible:

- If the List Menu(menu, answer_reg) macro was used in a teach pendant program without two parameters, an alarm is given and the program is aborted.
- If the selected list menu does not exist when it is called from a teach pendant program, a prompt box similar to the one shown in Figure 14–121 will be displayed. To abort the program, select OK.

Figure 14-121. List Menu Does not Exist Screen

Error:
Selected menu
does not exist.
OK

- If the register answer_reg does not exist, then an alarm is given and the program is aborted.

##### Menu File Name

Each list menu is stored in its own variable file that begins with the prefix "MENU3." The next two characters of the filename are the menu number. For example, the list menu 1 is stored in the variable file named "MENU3 01 .VR."

##### Examples

See List Menu(menu, answer_reg) Macro Example 1 and List Menu(menu, answer_reg) Macro Example 2 for examples of how to use the List Menu(menu, answer_reg) macro instruction in a teach pendant program.

<!-- PDF page 1519 -->

List Menu(menu, answer_reg) Macro Example 1

PROG TEST1
1: List Menu(2, 21)
2: SELECT R[21]=1,CALL TOOL1
3: =2,CALL TOOL2
4: =3,JMP LBL[2]
5: ELSE,CALL ABORTIT

List Menu(menu, answer_reg) Macro Example 2

PROG TEST2
1: List Menu('ErrorRecov', 2)
2: SELECT R[2]=1, JMP LBL[2]
3: =2, CALL MOVEMANT
4: =3, CALL MOVEPRCH
5: ELSE, CALL ABORTIT

#### 14.29.5 Status Menu

A status menu displays status information to the teach pendant screen. When a status menu is executed, the teach pendant displays the status menu and then continues executing. The values that are displayed are refreshed at least once every second. This is a read-only menu.

See Figure 14-122 for an example of a status menu.

Figure 14-122. Status Menu

STATUS Menu
Production Status
Program: TESTIII
Routine: TESTIII
Status: RUNNING
PART Count 101
Part on Conv1 ON
Pallet Count 15

##### Macro: Status Menu(menu)

A status menu uses the Status Menu(menu) macro.

Parameter 1: menu - This is the menu number or menu name. The menu can be chosen by number or name.

##### Display

When a status menu is executed, the teach pendant displays the status menu and then continues executing. The values that are displayed are refreshed.

A status menu can also be displayed as follows:

1. Press MENU.
2. Select STATUS
3. Press F1, [TYPE].
4. Select Prod. Status.

<!-- PDF page 1525 -->

Several status menus can be displayed. If the status menu you want to see is not the one displayed, either press F2, MENU, and then select the number of the status menu you want to display, or press F4, [CHOICE], and select the menu by name.

##### Errors

The following errors are possible:

- If the Status Menu macro was used in a teach pendant program without a parameter, an alarm is displayed. However, the program is not aborted and the teach pendant screen is not changed.
- If a menu that was selected by name does not exist, or the menu is the wrong kind of menu, an alarm is given. However, the program is not aborted and the teach pendant screen is not changed.
- If the selected status menu does not exist when it is called for in a teach pendant program by number, an alarm is given and the teach pendant screen is changed to the default status menu, shown in Figure 14–123.

Figure 14-123. Default Status Menu

STATUS Menu
ProductionStatus
Current Program TESTIV
Current Routine
Current Line 0
Status ABORTED
Time 20-JAN-XX 12:27

##### Menu File Name

Each status menu is stored in its own variable file that begins with the prefix "MENU4." The next two characters of the filename are the menu number. For example, the status menu 1 is stored in the variable file named "MENU4 01 .VR."

##### Setup

In a status menu, you can specify

- Up to nine status items
- The names of the variables that correspond to the status items, and detailed variable information

Table 14–75 lists and describes the variable detail information.

#### 14.29.6 Operator Entry Menu

An operator entry menu requires the operator to enter INTEGER, REAL, BOOLEAN, or text values. When an operator entry menu is executed, the program pauses until the operator types the information and then presses F3, DONE.

See Figure 14–124 for an example of an operator entry menu.

Figure 14-124. Operator Entry Menu

USER
Select Tool
1 Tool number to use: 2
2 Number to pickup: 1
Press DONE to continue.

The operator uses the:

• Numeric keys to type numbers
• Function keys to select YES or NO
• ENTER key and function keys to type letters

# Macro: Op. Entry Menu(menu)

An operator entry menu uses the Op. Entry Menu(menu) macro.

<!-- PDF page 1535 -->

Parameter 1: menu - This is the menu number or menu name. The menu can be chosen by number or name.

##### Display

To display an operator entry menu you create, use the Op. Entry Menu(menu) macro. The menu will be displayed automatically on the USER screen. If the operator changes the teach pendant display to another screen during teach pendant execution of this menu but before pressing DONE, the operator can press MENU and select USER to display this screen again.

##### Error

The following errors are possible:

- If the Op. Entry Menu(men) macro was used in a teach pendant program without a parameter, an alarm is given and the program is aborted.
- If the selected operator entry menu does not exist or the menu is the wrong kind of menu when it is called from a teach pendant program, a prompt box similar to the one shown in Figure 14–125 will be displayed. To abort the program, select OK and press ENTER.

Figure 14–125. Operator Entry Menu Does Not Exist Screen

Error:
Selected menu
does not exist
OK

##### Menu File Name

Each operator entry menu is stored in its own variable file that begins with the prefix "MENU5." The next two characters of the filename are the menu number. For example, the operator entry menu 1 is stored in the variable file named "MENU5 01 .VR."

##### Setup

In an operator entry menu, you specify

- Up to ten prompt items
- The names of the variables that correspond to the prompt items, and detailed variable information

Table 14–79 lists and describes the variable detail information.

## 10. To load (restore) a menu:

a. Move the cursor to the name of the menu you want to load.

### 14.29.7 Using Your Teach Pendant Menus

After you have set up a menu, you can use the menu macro instruction to display it.

When you edit a teach pendant program to use a teach pendant menu, you select the name of the menu from a sub-window. In the sub-window, you will see a list of all menus that were created using the Menu Utility SETUP screens. This list is updated at Cold start and when menus are added and deleted on the SETUP screen. Because there are five kinds of menus and each kind of menu can be used only with its own specific macro, you must choose the appropriate menu from the list.

A maximum of 20 menu names will be listed. If the menu you need is not listed, you can type its name or number manually with the teach pendant number and letter keys.

Use Procedure 14-56 to use your teach pendant menus.

### 14.30 MIRROR IMAGE UTILITY

The mirror image utility allows you to translate an entire teach pendant program or portion of a teach pendant program to mirror image the original programmed points. This option can be used to teach symmetrical parts easily.

Mirror imaging of a program can be accomplished either as a

- Parallel mirror image
- Parallel and rotational mirror image

Refer to Table 14–83 for information on Mirror Image Shift screen items.

Table 14–83. MIRROR IMAGE SHIFT Screen Items

[tbl-410.md](tbl-410.md)

<!-- PDF page 1545 -->

[tbl-411.md](tbl-411.md)

### Parallel Mirror Image

A parallel mirror image mirrors the program about a mirror plane without an offset or a rotation. See Figure 14–126 and Figure 14–127.

Figure 14–126. Parallel Mirror Image with Mirror Plane in Center of Robot

> **Image description -- img-242.jpeg:** The image is a schematic diagram illustrating the principle of a Michelson interferometer. Key components and labels are as follows: 

1. **P1 and Q1**: These are two points on a light source or detector plane, separated by a distance D.
2. **Mirror Plane**: Positioned centrally in the diagram, this plane contains two mirrors (one labeled A and the other A') that are perpendicular to each other and form a right angle. The mirrors are positioned such that they are equidistant from the central beam splitter.
3. **Beam Splitter**: Located at the intersection of the paths from P1 and Q1, this component splits the incoming light beam into two perpendicular paths, directing one part towards mirror A and the other towards mirror A'.
4. **Paths A-B and A'-B'**: These paths represent the distances traveled by the split beams of light to the respective mirrors (A and A') and back to the beam splitter.
5. **Compensator Plate (C and C')**: Positioned in the paths of the split beams, these plates ensure that both beams travel through the same thickness of glass, compensating for any dispersion effects.
6. **D**: This label indicates equal distances between the beam splitter and the mirrors (A and A'), as well as between the beam splitter and the points P1 and Q1 on the light source or detector plane.

The diagram visually demonstrates how light from a single source is split into two paths, reflected by mirrors, and then recombined to produce interference patterns, which are used to measure precise distances or other physical properties.

<!-- PDF page 1546 -->

Figure 14–127. Parallel Mirror Image with Mirror Plane Offset from Center of Robot

> **Image description -- img-243.jpeg:** The image depicts a schematic diagram of an optical setup involving a light source, a mirror plane, and a detection system. Key components and their relationships are as follows: 1) A light source labeled 'A' emits a beam that passes through a lens system (labeled 'B' and 'B'') and is directed toward a mirror plane labeled 'C' and 'C''. 2) The mirror plane is positioned vertically in the center of the diagram, reflecting the incoming light. 3) The reflected light is then directed toward a detection screen or sensor labeled 'D' and 'D'', positioned symmetrically on either side of the mirror plane. 4) The labels 'P1' and 'Q1' appear to denote specific points or paths of the light beam before and after reflection. 5) The entire setup is aligned along a horizontal optical axis, with the mirror plane acting as the central reflective element. The diagram illustrates the principle of reflection, where the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and demonstrates how light paths are traced through the system.

D - Equal Distance

# Caution

To be sure the parallel mirror image works correctly, you must have an exact TCP. If you do not, the resulting mirror image program will contain an offset value. See Figure 14–128.

Figure 14–128. Parallel Mirror Image with Offset

> **Image description -- img-244.jpeg:** The image depicts a schematic diagram of an optical setup involving a mirror plane and a light path. The top part of the diagram shows a horizontal line labeled P1 on the left and Q1 on the right, with points A, B, D, and C marked along this line. A vertical line intersects the horizontal line at point D, representing the mirror plane. Points A', B', C', and D' are the reflections of points A, B, C, and D, respectively, across the mirror plane. The reflected points are connected by dashed lines, indicating the path of light rays reflecting off the mirror plane. The bottom part of the diagram shows a physical setup with a light source directed upwards through a series of optical components, including lenses and a vertical structure, which likely represents the mirror plane. The light path is aligned with the vertical line in the top diagram, suggesting that the physical setup corresponds to the schematic representation above it.

D - Equal Distance

<!-- PDF page 1547 -->

#### Mirror Image Example

Figure 14–129 displays a mirror image of A, B, and C to A', B', and C' when P1 and Q1 are taught positions. Figure 14–129 also displays a mirror image with an offset when P1 and Q1 are taught but Q1 is taught at an offset of 200mm. In this case, the result is A", B", and C".

Figure 14–129. Positional Mirror Image

> **Image description -- img-245.jpeg:** The image consists of two diagrams labeled 'Mirror Image Without Offset' (top) and 'Mirror Image With Offset' (bottom), illustrating the effect of an offset on a mirrored image relative to a robot's coordinate system. Both diagrams show a robot positioned at the origin (0,0) with its +X and +Y axes labeled. In the 'Without Offset' diagram, points A, B, C, A', B', and C' are mirrored across the y=0 line, with P1 at (0, -1000) and Q1 at (0, 1000). In the 'With Offset' diagram, the same points are mirrored but shifted horizontally by 200 mm, resulting in new positions P1' at (200, -1000) and Q1' at (200, 1000). The y-coordinates of all points are labeled, showing their vertical positions relative to the robot's coordinate system. The offset is indicated by a horizontal arrow labeled 'Offset 200 mm' between the two sets of mirrored points.

#### Rotational Mirror Image

A parallel mirror image mirrors the program about a mirror plane first, and then the mirrored program is rotated about a center of rotation. Orientation of the part to be imaged is rotated about one or more of its axes relative to the mirror plane. See Figure 14–130.

<!-- PDF page 1548 -->

Figure 14–130. Rotational Mirror Image

> **Image description -- img-246.jpeg:** The diagram illustrates a system involving the reflection of light or signals from source positions to destination positions using a mirror pane. On the left side, there are three labeled source positions: P1, P2, and P3, arranged in a triangular formation. A light or signal path is shown originating from P1 and reflecting off the mirror pane in the center. The mirror pane is depicted as a vertical rectangular surface. On the right side, three destination positions labeled Q1, Q2, and Q3 are arranged in a triangular formation, mirroring the source positions. The reflected path from the mirror pane reaches Q1. The diagram visually represents the concept of reflection, showing how a signal or light originating from a source position (P1) is redirected by the mirror pane to a corresponding destination position (Q1). The labels and arrows indicate the direction and path of the signal or light, emphasizing the relationship between the source and destination positions through the reflection process.

In Figure 14–131 the positions, P1, P2 and P3 are mirrored about the mirror plane as Q1, Q2 and Q3. These positions are then rotated 45° about Q1 and stored as Q1', Q2' and Q3'.

Figure 14–131. Rotational Mirror Image

> **Image description -- img-247.jpeg:** The image is a diagram illustrating the positioning and transformation of points in a 2D coordinate system (x-y plane) related to a robot and its mirror plane. Key elements include: 1) A robot positioned at the origin (0,0) with axes labeled +x and +y. 2) Four points labeled Q1, Q2, Q3, and Q4 with their respective coordinates: Q1 (800, 800), Q2 (1365.7, -800), Q3 (1200, -800), and Q4 (1200, -1200). 3) A mirrored point Q1' (800, 800) corresponding to Q1, with a 45-degree angle and a distance of 565.7 units indicated between Q1 and Q1'. 4) A mirror plane represented by a vertical dashed line at x = 1200. 5) Three points labeled P1 (800, 800), P2 (1200, 1200), and P3 (1200, 800) on the right side of the mirror plane, forming a right triangle with P1 at the vertex. 6) A point Q3' (1082.8, -517.2) near the mirror plane, connected to Q3 with a dashed line. The diagram shows spatial relationships and transformations between these points, likely for purposes such as robot motion planning or coordinate system reflection.

### Mirror Image of Extended Axes

Extended (Ext) axes determines how the mirror image function will translate the program when you are using extended axes. Figure 14–132 displays a key for use with Figure 14–133 through Figure 14–135.

<!-- PDF page 1549 -->

Figure 14–132. Mirror Image Key

> **Image description -- img-248.jpeg:** The image is a simple diagram illustrating the relationship between a robot's base position and an extended axis. The diagram consists of a horizontal line with a label 'Robot base position' at the left end. From this point, a shorter line extends upward at an angle, labeled 'Extended Axis.' At the intersection of the horizontal and angled lines, there is a label 'T. C. P.' (Tool Center Point). The diagram visually represents the spatial relationship between the robot's base, its extended axis, and the tool center point.

Possible extended axes configurations are:

- Robot axes only - allows you to mirror the axes of the robot without mirroring any non-integrated extended axes such as a positioning table. The shift is calculated using the change in the robot tool center point (TCP).

Figure 14–133. Example of Robot Axes Only Mirror Image

> **Image description -- img-249.jpeg:** The image is a schematic diagram illustrating a signal transmission process involving a destination and two TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) points. The diagram shows a horizontal line labeled 'Original' at the top and another horizontal line labeled 'Destination' at the bottom. A vertical line connects the 'Original' line to the 'Destination' line, with a black dot at the 'Original' line indicating the starting point of the signal. The signal then travels downward along the vertical line to the 'Destination' line, where it is marked by another black dot. Two additional vertical lines extend from the 'Destination' line, each labeled 'T.C.P.' with an 'X' marking a point on these lines. The first 'T.C.P.' line is connected to the 'Original' line, and the second 'T.C.P.' line is connected to the 'Destination' line. The diagram visually represents the concept of signal transmission and the involvement of TCP points in the process.

- Ext integrated - allows you to mirror the axes of the robot and any integrated axes. The amount of mirror image for the robot and the extended axes is calculated using the change in the TCP. See Figure 14–134.

Figure 14–134. Example of Extended Axes Integrated Mirror Image

> **Image description -- img-250.jpeg:** The image is a schematic diagram illustrating the movement or adjustment of a robot base relative to a target or destination. The diagram shows three labeled points marked with 'X' symbols: the 'Original' position, the 'New T.C.P.' (Tool Center Point) position, and the 'T.C.P.' position. The 'Original' position is connected to the 'Destination' by a vertical arrow labeled 'Original'. The 'New T.C.P.' is positioned above the 'T.C.P.' and is connected to it by a vertical arrow labeled 'New T.C.P.' The 'T.C.P.' is connected to the 'ROBOT BASE' by a vertical arrow labeled 'T.C.P.'. The diagram visually represents the shift in the robot's tool center point from the original position to a new position, indicating a change in the robot's operational reference point or tool alignment.

<!-- PDF page 1550 -->

- With ext axes - allows you to mirror positions for robot axes and any extended axes in your system. The amount of mirror image for the robot is calculated by using the change in the TCP. The amount of shift for the extended axes is calculated using the center of the difference between an original position (P1) and a new position (Q1) as the point where the mirror image occurs. See Figure 14–135.

Figure 14–135. Example of With Extended Axes Mirror Image

> **Image description -- img-251.jpeg:** The image is a diagram illustrating a network communication scenario involving two Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) connections. The diagram shows a path from an 'Original' point to a 'Destination' point. Along this path, there are two TCP connections labeled 'TCP' and 'TCP' (repeated). Two points, E1 of P1 and E1 of Q1, are marked with 'X' symbols and are connected by a bidirectional arrow indicating a distance or delay between them. Another bidirectional arrow is shown between the two TCP connections, also marked with 'X' symbols, indicating another distance or delay. The diagram appears to represent the concept of TCP connection paths and the delays or distances between specific points in the network.

- Ext axes only - Ext axes only is not available for a mirror shift.
- Replace Ext axes - Replace Ext axes is not available for a mirror shift.

Use Procedure 14-57 to perform a mirror image of a program.

HINTS: P1 and Q1 should not be part of the program to be mirrored. They should be new positions that are located at an equal distance from the mirror plane. (See Figure 14–126.) Use the following guidelines to teach these positions:

a. Jog the robot to zero degrees by matching up the witness marks on the robot (if they are available), or by displaying the POSITION screen.
b. Jog the robot:

- Set the jog coordinate system to WORLD.

- Jog the robot in +Y by a known distance, 200 mm for example.

##### OR

- Set the jog coordinate system to JOINT.
- Jog the robot a known angle, \(20^{\circ}\), for example.

c. Record this position as P1.
d. Jog the robot back to zero.
e. Jog the robot in the opposite direction by the exact same distance from the mirror plane as you jogged the robot in Step 10b.
f. Record this position as Q1. See Figure 14-126.

### 14.32 MOTION GROUP DO OUTPUT FUNCTION (MULTIPLE MOTION GROUP OPTION)

#### 14.32.1 Overview

This section contains information about the Motion DO feature. Motion groups can be robots, positioners, index devices, or robots. Basic systems include a single motion group, the robot, so the busy indicator (when running a program) or the TP enable output (when jogging the robot) are sufficient for a PLC to monitor motion group use. When a system has more than one motion group, motion group usage can only be monitored by viewing the teach pendant. This information can not be known externally without using the teach pendant.

Motion DO is a status mechanism that uses digital or robot I/O to indicate:

- A motion group is selected /locked for use by a motion control program
- A motion group is being jogged via the Teach Pendant
- A motion group is not in use.

Two signals are provided for each group configured in the multi-group system. In this way, it is possible to recognize the currently "in use" motion groups without using the teach pendant, providing control information to the PLC, thus enhancing safety.

Note The motion group DO output function is available only when the multiple motion group option is used.

#### 14.32.2 Restrictions

Be aware of the following restrictions when using the motion group DO output function:

- The same signal cannot be defined for different motion groups.
- When a program is running or paused, the type of signal (DO/RO) or signal number cannot be changed.

#### 14.32.3 Operations

The motion group DO output function can assign two types of digital output signals to one motion group: jog signals and programmed signals. Any digital output signal the robot has or a robot output signal can be used as the Motion DO signal.

Each specified digital output signal can be turned on and off under the following conditions:

- Jog signals are turned on when the teach pendant is enabled for the selected jog group.

<!-- PDF page 1561 -->

- Program signals are turned on when a motion group is locked by a paused or running motion program.

The same digital output can be assigned to the program signal and the jog signal of the same motion group. In this case, the two signals are logically OR-ed. This means that if either signal is ON, the OR-ed signal is also ON. The output signal is OFF only when both signals are OFF.

# Jog Signals

All jog signals are turned OFF when the teach pendant is disabled. If the teach pendant is enabled, only the signals corresponding to the motion group selected by the teach pendant are turned ON; the other signals are turned OFF.

# Programmed Signals

Regardless of whether the teach pendant is enabled, programmed signals might be turned on depending on whether the motion group specified by the program that is running or paused; the signals will not be turned on merely by selecting a program. If a program running or paused in multi-tasking mode has a motion group, the programmed signals for that motion group are also turned on.

Note For coordinate motion jogging, only the leader group DO[ ] will be turned ON.

#### 14.32.4 Setup

You can set up jog and programmed digital output signals from the Motion group DO screen.

The Motion group DO screen displays the items in Table 14–84.

Use Procedure 14-59 to set up jog and programmed digital output signals.

Table 14–84. Motion group DO Screen Items

#### 14.32.5 Subprogram and Multi-tasking Execution

This section explains how the motion group DO output function works when a subprogram is called or when multi-tasking mode is used.

# Example 1

If a program A with no motion group CALLs a subprogram B that has a motion group or groups, the signals for the subprogram B motion group(s) is (are) kept ON only when the subprogram is being executed.

# Example 2

If a motion program A CALLs a subprogram B that has a motion group, if the subprogram has the same group mask as the CALLing program, the Motion DO outputs will not appear to change. In the case where the subprogram contains a different motion group than the CALLing program A, the output associated to the different motion group will turn ON only while the subprogram is running.

# Example 3

If program A with no motion group RUNs program B with motion groups, the digital outputs associated to the motion groups in program B will be turned ON only while program B is executing.

# Example 4

If motion program A RUNs program B with motion groups, the digital outputs associated to the motion groups in program A will be ON while program A executes, the DO's for motion groups

<!-- PDF page 1563 -->

in program B will be turned ON only while program B is executing. In this multi-tasking case, program B can only use groups that are not used in program A.

# Example 5

Program "mainpro" does not have a motion group. It issues a RUN instruction to activate "progA" and "progB," which both have motion groups. "progA" operates motion group 1, and "progB," motion group 2.

Merely selecting program "mainpro" does not turn on programmed signals of any group.

When line 1 of "mainpro" is executed, "progA" is activated, resulting in the program signal of motion group 1 being turned ON.

When line 2 of "mainpro" is executed, "progB" is activated, resulting in the program signal of motion group 2 being turned ON.

When "progA" ends, the program signal of motion group 1 is turned OFF. When "progB" ends, the program signal of motion group 2 is turned OFF.

### 14.33 MOTION START DELAY DETECTION FUNCTION

#### 14.33.1 Overview

When a robot must repeat motions within a short time (for example, because of short travel distance or high motion speed), the motions might be decelerated or oscillate even if the termination type of the corresponding motion instruction is "CNT 100." This is because the robot might not be ready for the next motion when one short motion ends, and cannot start immediately.

The motion start delay detection function detects and displays this kind of a delay in motion start. If deceleration or oscillation occurs, it is possible to determine the program line to be corrected according to the information detected by this function.

The motion start delay detection function is always enabled. The detected information is available at any time.

#### 14.33.2 Restrictions

Keep in mind the following restrictions when you use the motion start delay detection function.

- If there is a non-motion instruction (such as a register, I/O, or wait instruction) between motion instructions, it might prevent an immediate start of motion even if the motion instructions use a termination type of CNT100, possibly causing a motion start delay to be detected.
- A CNT termination type setting is ignored when the tool shifts from joint motion to linear or circular motion, or vice versa. The robot always decelerates at such points. Therefore, a motion start delay is detected if the CNT termination type has been specified.

<!-- PDF page 1564 -->

- No motion start delay is detected during single-step execution.

### 14.33.3 Detection Information and System Variables

The motion start delay detection function detects a motion start delay if the following condition is satisfied:

Condition: When a motion instruction that uses CNT 100 ends, the next motion cannot be started immediately.

If a delay is detected, the related information is recorded in a system variable.

All information related to a motion start delay is recorded in system variable $PODATA_GRP[group] . This system variable is provided for individual motion groups. The contents of the system variable are all cleared at cold start. The fields of this system variable are described in the following sections.

$PODATA_GRP[ ].$OVERRUN_CNT

This system variable indicates the number of times motion start delays are detected.

$PODATA_GRP[ ].$CUR_INDEX

This system variable indicates the index of the latest motion start delay data. The information about motion start delays are recorded in 50 memory locations (called buffers) in the order of indexes (sequence number).

Each buffer has a ring structure. When it becomes full of 50 (fixed) pieces of data, the latest data is overwritten to the oldest data. See Figure 14–138 .

This system variable holds the index of the information about the motion start delay that occurred most recently. First check this index, then the contents (program ID, program line number, and amount of delay, described later) of the buffer that corresponds to this index.

$PODATA_GRP[ ].$PROGRAM_ID[50]

This is a program ID memory buffer for a detected motion start delay. It indicates the internal ID of a program encountered with the motion start delay.

$PODATA_GRP[ ].$LINE_NO[50]

This is a program line number memory buffer for a detected motion start delay. It indicates the program line where the motion start delay was detected.

Keep in mind that the line number indicated here only correspond to the line where a motion start delay was detected. The line that caused the delay has a number lower than this line.

<!-- PDF page 1565 -->

# $PODATA_GRP[ ].$OVERRUN_ITP[50]

This is a motion start delay memory buffer. It indicates the amount of a detected delay. The larger the value, the larger the delay.

If you reference these buffers with the same index (in $PODATA_GRP[ ].$cur_index). you can identify the following information:

- Which program ($PROGRAM_ID[i])
- Which motion, or program line ($LINE_NO[i])
- How much delay ($OVERRUN_ITP[i])

where "i" is an index.

Each memory area consists of 50 buffer locations. It is always possible to check up to 50 pieces of the latest information about motion start delays.

The memory buffers are shown in Figure 14–138.

Figure 14–138. Motion Start Delay Memory Buffers

> **Image description -- img-254.jpeg:** The image depicts a tabular data structure with three columns labeled $PROGRAM_ID, $LINE_NO, and $OVERRUN_ITP. Each column contains a vertical list of entries arranged in a grid format. The rows are indexed from [1] at the top to [50] at the bottom. The middle section of the table is divided into three parts: the top part labeled 'Second latest information,' the middle part labeled 'Latest information,' and the bottom part labeled 'Oldest information.' An arrow labeled $CUR_INDEX->[+1] points from the 'Latest information' row to the 'Second latest information' row, indicating a directional relationship or data flow. The table appears to represent a data structure where each column holds sequential or historical data entries, with the arrow suggesting a reference or pointer to the next most recent data entry.

#### 14.33.4 Motion Start Delay Detection Function Example

The following sequence describes an example of how to use the motion start delay detection function.

1. Test run a program given to the robot to assure safety.
2. Reset the following system variables. The function can be used without being reset. However, if you reset it, the data will be more readable.

\(PODATA_GRP[ ].\)OVERRUN_CNT = 0
\(PODATA_GRP[ ].\)CUR_INDEX = 0

<!-- PDF page 1566 -->

3. Run the program with the override for actual operation applied. Consider the following example program.

Example: Program (internal ID: 1290)
1: J P[1] 100% Cnt 100
2: L P[2] 1000mm/sec Cnt 100
3: L P[3] 1000mm/sec Cnt 100
4: L P[4] 1000mm/sec Cnt 100
5: L P[5] 1000mm/sec Cnt 100
[END]

4. Check the results of the detection. Display the SYSTEM Variables screen, move the cursor to $PODATA_GRP[ ], and press ENTER to view the contents of the system variables.

Assume the following conditions:

Example: Conditions immediately after the above program is
executed $OVERRUN_CNT 1
$CUR_INDEX 1
$PROGRAM_ID[1] 1290
$LINE_NO[1] 4
$OVERRUN_ITP[1] 1

This example means that a motion start delay occurred when line 4 in a program with internal ID 1290 was executed.

5. Correct the program. According to the detected result, it is likely that motions before line 4 (P[4]) might be too close to each other. Check the positional data and correct the position or speed as required.
6. Repeat 1 through 5 until deceleration or oscillation does not occur any more.

### 14.34 OPERATION LOG BOOK [OPTION]

#### 14.34.1 Overview

Operation Log Book automatically records teach pendant operations and alarms in a buffer that can be displayed in the Log Book menu of the teach pendant or saved as a text file. Some operations can include a screen image to help in analyzing the event.

A system can have multiple Log Books and you can specify which events are recorded in each Log Book. In this way, frequent and infrequent events can be recorded to separate Log Books.

<!-- PDF page 1567 -->

When a Log Book buffer is full and a new record is added, the oldest record is deleted. The number of events that can be stored in a Log Book buffer varies based on the type of events saved because not all events are the same size. You can change the size of the buffer by setting a system variable.

Note This function is independent of the password log function.
