#### General Limitations

Note the following general limitations for Log Book:

- Log Book does not support certain /Pendant operations such as selecting a link on a web page.
- Operations are not recorded in controlled start just after initial start. Cold start must be performed to begin logging events.
- Operations in the configuration menu are not recorded
- If you change the size of a log book, all data in the log book are lost.
- Some events are cyclically monitored for logging. Some of the following operations may not be recorded if they occur faster than the monitoring cycle:

— Override ("Override x%")
— Coordination (JOINT coordinate, User Coordinate etc.)
— Single step (Single step ON/OFF)
— Motion group (“Motion group x”)
— Sub group (“Sub group ROBOT/EXT”)
— User frame number (“User frame x”)
— Tool frame number (“Tool frame x”)

- If you change the dictionary, some entries in the LOG BOOK screen cannot be read. To read such log, you must use the language that was used when the log was recorded.
- If passwords are enabled and $LOGBOOK.$LOG_ENT is a valid book number when you log in, your password input is recorded as “‘x’ is entered”. Passwords for other functions are also recorded. To prevent passwords from being recorded, you can use screen filtering to filter out the screens that contain passwords.
- If you press a function key that has no label, the key number followed by empty parentheses will be recorded.

Example If the function key line is as follows:

[TYPE]

ON OFF

F3 has no label. If you press F3 and $LOGBOOK $LOG_FNKEY is a valid value, "F3() is pressed" is recorded.

- If you change the remote TCP number in remote TCP jog mode, this is recorded as a change of user frame.

<!-- PDF page 1569 -->

- If you changed current JOG coordination by parameter instruction, the change is recorded when the group is selected.
- For KAREL read instructions, screen image is recorded just after input.
- KCL is not supported
- If the TP and CRT are used at the same time, log book records the operations of both of them. It might be difficult to distinguish between TP and CRT operations in a log.
- Screen changes caused by the automatic backup function are not recorded.

Refer to Filtering Alarms and Screens.

### 14.35 OPERATIONS WITHOUT A TEACH PENDANT

This chapter describes operations when the system does not have a Teach Pendant.

For the R-30iB Compact Plus controller, the Teach Pendant is optional. A PC or tablet device can be used to teach robot programs instead of a Teach Pendant.

### 14.35.1 OVERVIEW

To operate the robot controller on a PC or tablet device, iRProgrammer or the Remote iPendant function should be used.

For R-30iB Compact Plus, these functions are provided by default. iRProgrammer is supported only on R-30iB Compact Plus and cannot be used on any other type of controller. A Software option (R843) is needed to use the Remote iPendant function on other types of controllers.

<!-- PDF page 1579 -->

iRProgrammer has the following features.

- This function is available for use on common external devices like a PC or tablet device.
- The program text editor is provided to create robot programs on a PC or tablet device.
- Robot movement operations, such as Jogging and TP program execution, is allowed.
- One-touch Tree menu is provided on the PC or tablet device.

iRProgrammer is supported on the R-30iB Compact Plus controller.

Remote iPendant has the following features.

- This function is available for use on common external devices like a PC or tablet device.
- The following modes of the Remote iPendant can be used for teaching and operation of the robot system.

Jogging iPendant (JITP)

- An iPendant-like screen is provided on the PC or tablet device.
- Robot movement operation such as Jogging and TP program execution is allowed.

Navigate iPendant (JCGTP)

- An iPendant-like screen is provided on the PC or tablet device.
- Robot movement operation such as Jogging and TP program execution is not permitted.

These functions work on a web browser. Installing any additional software is not required.

The following browsers are supported.

- Google Chrome (after version 31)
- Internet Explorer (version 11 or greater). Verify it is not using Compatibility View.

# Warning

When the Robot controller does not have a Teach Pendant, the robot must be operated from outside of the safeguarded zone in AUTO mode. Otherwise, serious personal injury could result.

# Warning

When the robot is moved by a PC or tablet device, an emergency stop button must be connected and located near the operator for use at any time.

<!-- PDF page 1580 -->

### 14.35.2 SETUP

To connect to your PC using the iRProgrammer and the Remote iPendant function, you must set the TCP/IP setting on the robot controller.

The IP address of the controller is set by default for the R30/B Compact Plus as follows.

- Port#1 IP address: 192.168.1.100
- Subnet Mask: 255.255.255.0
- Router IP address: 192.168.1.1
- PC JOG IP address: *

You will need to set the IP address of your PC to access the controller.

For Example:

- IP address: 192.168.1.200
- Subnet Mask: 255.255.255.0

Note In the IP address, 192.168.1.200, 200 is an example. It can be any address other than 100. If there are other robots connected to the network, you will have to choose a new address to avoid IP address conflicts.

When Ethernet port1 of the robot controller is connected to the PC directly by means of an Ethernet cable, iRProgrammer and the Remote iPendant function can be used without changing any controller settings.

If the PC JOG IP address is set, the PC or tablet device which can access the controller is restricted by iRProgrammer and Jogging i Pendant. Only the device that has the same IP address as “PC JOG IP address” can access the controller. For the R-30/B Compact Plus, the default value of the “PC JOG IP Address” is *. This means that any device can connect to the controller using iRProgrammer and Jogging iPendant.

To change a network setting without an i Pendant, refer to Section 14.35.3.5.3.

To find out more about TCP/IP settings, please refer to chapter “2 SETTING UP TCP/IP” in the “Internet Options Setup and Operations Manual.”

For the R-30/B Compact Plus, when the controller is powering up, the CYCLE START LED on the controller panel blinks.

When the blinking stops, the start up process is complete. The PC or tablet device can then connect to the controller using iRProgrammer or Remote iPendant.

### Procedure 14-61 Connection to iRProgrammer and Remote iPendant

#### Conditions

- The controller is an R-30iB Compact Plus Controller.

Ethernet port 1 of the controller is connected directly to the PC by an Ethernet cable.

The network setting of the controller is the default setting.

The IP address of your PC is set to access the controller.

- The PC or tablet device, and the robot controller are connected to a network.

Their IP addresses are set to conform to the network.

Refer to Section 14.35.3.5.3 for information on setting up the network without an iPendant.

1. Activate your browser on your PC or tablet device.

2. In the Address field of the browser, input “http://<Robot IP Address> ” to open the robot Homepage (Example: “http://192.168.1.100” for the default system). If the connection is successfully made, you will briefly see the robot homepage, similar to that shown in Figure 14–140 , displayed on the PC or tablet device.

Note When in controlled start, you cannot connect via the IP address.

3. Select the link you want to use from the HMI iPendant section.

For iRProgrammer and Jogging iPendant, if an actual iPendant is connected, the following operations are needed before the functions are started.

- Turn off the TP enable switch

- Select AUTO mode

When iRProgrammer or Jogging iPendant is opened, any actual iPendant will be disconnected automatically and you will see an iPendant screen as shown below.

<!-- PDF page 1584 -->

> **Image description -- img-257.jpeg:** The image shows a small handheld device with a screen displaying a message. The screen reads: 'iPendat is inactive. Press MENU to reconnect. Browse Robot Home Page.' Below the text, there is a graphical interface with several icons, including a house icon, a settings gear, and a few other symbols. The device has a black body with a red circular button on the top right corner. The screen appears to be a monochrome LCD display, and the device is connected via a coiled cable, likely for data or power transmission.

Note The Navigate iPendant (JCGTP) function uses the standard port No.80. Jogging iPendant (JITP) and iRProgrammer use special ports 3080 and 4080.

Note Web page cache should be cleared if a new robot is connected or a full load/auto update was performed.

Note When the system is repowered, the web page will remain up. This page needs to be closed and the link will need to be selected again, once system is fully powered.

# Procedure 14-62 Disconnection from iRProgrammer and Remote iPendant

1. To disconnect the iRProgrammer and Remote iPendant function, press the "Logout" key at the top or the bottom of the screen before closing the window of the browser. Some devices do not close the network connections properly if you close the window without logging out.

##### 14.35.3.2 iRProgrammer

iRProgrammer is used to create and edit programs.

iRProgrammer provides the following features.

- Programming Editor
1. Text-based editor to edit programs
2. A tabular form to edit position data
3. Jog operation using a Jog Panel
4. Ability to run programs from the PC or Tablet
- Setting screens
1. Setting and monitor screens (Frames, Payload, I/O, etc.)

# Warning

- Robot operation must be executed from outside of the safeguarded space.
- You must check to ensure that no one is inside of the safety fence.
- The Emergency stop button must be connected and located near the operator for use at any time.
- Robot operation must be executed with the robot in sight.

### 14.35.3.2.6 Limitations of iRProgrammer

The following limitations apply to the iRProgrammer function

- iRProgrammer connection is refused when the robot mode is T1 or T2.
- Multiple iRProgrammer connections are not supported.
- The Teaching Pendant cannot be operated when iRProgrammer is connected.
- The iRProgrammer connection is refused when the Teaching Pendant connects.
- To be used with iRProgrammer, the screen size of the device is recommended to be more than 9 inches.
- The Teaching Pendant might have some functions that are not displayed on the tree menu.
- There are unsupported instructions in the programming editor.
- Supported languages are English, Japanese, and Chinese. The screen displays as English when no other language is selected.
- Prior to 9.10P/19, the program cannot be run from an arbitrary line. The program starts from the first line, or the program restarts from the paused line.
- A program started by iRProgrammer stops when iRProgrammer is disconnected.

### 14.35.3.3 Jogging iPendant (JITP)

The Jogging iPendant function allows you to display an iPendant-like screen using a browser on a PC or tablet device. This function provides the following functions.

- Robot movement operations such as Jogging and TP program execution.
- Foreground TP editing.
- Change coordinates.

<!-- PDF page 1598 -->

- Change override.
- Change TP Enable/Disable.
- Applying DCS parameter.
- Clearing DCS alarms.

# Warning

The Jogging iPendant function enables you to move the robot using a PC or tablet device. Extreme caution must be exercised when using this function. When you jog using the Jogging iPendant function, you must strictly adhere to the following precautions.

- Set the Mode Switch to AUTO mode.
- Jog operation must be executed from outside of the safety fence.
- You must check that no one is inside the safety fence.
- An Emergency stop button must be connected and located near the operator for use at any time.
- Jog operation must be executed with the robot in sight.

###### 14.35.3.3.3 Jog Operation

This subsection provides the sequence to jog the robot from the Jogging iPendant screen. All steps described in Procedure 14-63 can be performed on a PC or tablet device.

# Procedure 14-63 Robot Jog Operation

1. Show the Jog Panel by pressing the "Pos/Jog Panel", "4D/Jog Panel" or "Jog Panel" keys.
2. Press the TP enable/disable switch located in the upper right of the screen, to turn it ON.
3. Press the RESET key to clear the "SYST-045 TP enabled in AUTO mode" alarm.
4. Press the SHIFT key. When you press the SHIFT key, the color of the key is changed from blue to aqua. This means that the SHIFT key is pressed and in a hold state (latched state). When you press the SHIFT key again, the color turns to blue. This means the SHIFT key is released. Refer to Table 14–97 for details.

<!-- PDF page 1604 -->

Table 14–97. SHIFT Key State

[tbl-1.md](tbl-1.md)

5. When you press and hold a jog key with a latching SHIFT key, the robot moves.

# Warning

When you jog, you must strictly adhere to the following precautions.

- Jogging must be executed from outside of the safeguarded space.
- You must check no one is inside of the safety fence.
- An Emergency stop button must be connected and located near the operator for use at any time.
- Jog operation must be executed with the robot in sight.

### 14.35.3.4 Navigate iPendant (JCGTP)

The Navigate iPendant function allows you to display an iPendant-like screen on a browser on your HMI device. Navigate iPendant provides iPendant screens independent of the actual iPendant. So the PC or tablet device user can display screens, navigate menus, and enter data independent from an actual iPendant.

# Caution

Remote Operation is completely independent from the operation of the actual iPendant, therefore it can affect the operation the robot controller. Extreme caution must be exercised when using this feature.

### 14.35.3.5 Special Operation

The R-30/B Compact Plus controller can perform the following operations by means of the XML file, that is saved on the UD1: device, when power is turned on.

- Select start mode
- Configure Ethernet
- Set PC Jog IP address
- Image backup/Image restore
- Full Load

<!-- PDF page 1606 -->

# 14.35.3.5.1 Operation

In order to perform any of the above operations, you have to write the tag in STARTUPCONFIG.XML that is saved on the UD1: device. Also, you have to get the key that allows execution of the XML in advance. Then write the key in STARTUPCONFIG.XML.

Whether you perform any operation, the following tag is always required. However, you have to change the key in the CONTROLLER tag to what was generated in BOOTKEY.DAT.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<ROOT>
</CONTROLLER>
</ROOT>

If STARTUPCONFIG.XML exists in UD1:, BOOTKEY.DAT will be created in UD1:.

In BOOTKEY.DAT, a new key will be generated. The expiration date of the key is one hour from the generation of the key.

If the key that written in STARTUPCONFIG.XML is incorrect or it is expired, the operation of XML will not execute.

When executing the operation, you have to write the operation tag between <CONTROLLER> and </CONTROLLER>. Usable tags are as follows.

Table 14–98. Tag

[tbl-2.md](tbl-2.md)

<!-- PDF page 1607 -->

Note If the XML command is incorrect, unintended operation may occur. Please check the XML command thoroughly before execution.

If XML command was successfully executed, STARTUPCONFIG.XML is renamed to OLDSTARTUPCONFIG.XML. If you want to run XML command again, you need recreate STARTUPCONFIG.XML.

Note When you rename OLDSTARTUPCONFIG.XML to STARTUPCONFIG.XML, the XML command is executed if the key is within the expiration date. If you change the file name, please check the XML command before turning on the power.

# Procedure 14-64 Operation By XML

1. Create STARTUPCONFIG.XML in the USB memory device and plug it into UD1:.
2. Boot the controller. BOOTKEY.DAT, EXAMPLE.XML, and STARTUPCONFIG.LOG are generated in the UD1: device.

In BOOTKEY.DAT, the key that allows execution of XML and CONTROLLER tags are generated.

In EXAMPLE.XML, a description example of STARTUPCONFIG.XML is generated.

In STARTUPCONFIG.LOG, the log used during execution of the XML is written. Error information (if execution fails) is also written here.

3. Describe the contents of STARTUPCONFIG.XML. The following is a description example when executing an image backup. In the CONTROLLER tag, you have to write the key that is generated in BOOTKEY.DAT.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<ROOT>
    <CONFIG image = "UD1:\IMG\" startmod = "backup"/>
</CONTROLLER>
</ROOT>

4. Plug in the USB memory device, to which STARTUPCONFIG.XML has been saved, into UD1:. Then boot the controller.
5. The operation written in XML will be executed. If execution fails, error information is written in STARTUPCONFIG.LOG. Please check the cause by referring to STARTUPCONFIG.LOG.
6. If the XML command was successfully executed, STARTUPCONFIG.XML is renamed to OLDSTARTUPCONFIG.XML.

### 14.36 OPERATIONS WITHOUT A MODE SWITCH

This section describes operations when the system does not have a Mode switch. For the R-30/B Compact Plus controller, the Operator Panel and mode switch are provided as optional hardware.

Contents of this section:

- Overview
- Setup

#### 14.36.1 Overview

Note When the Robot controller does not have a Teach Pendant, the robot should be operated in AUTO mode. The mode does not need to change from AUTO and mode select functions should not be used.

When the robot system has a Teach Pendant, the mode select function has to be selected depending on the system configuration and requirements for the system.

<!-- PDF page 1612 -->

To change the mode, the following functions can be used.

- TP Mode Select function
- External mode Select function
- Operator panel (optional hardware for R-30/B Compact Plus)

To use a Teach Pendant on an R-30/B Compact Plus controller which does not have an operator panel, you must change the mode switch function setting using the TP Mode Select function. Please refer to Section 14.36.3.2 to set up the TP Mode Select function.

To use the TP Mode Select function or the External Mode Select function on R-30/B Plus and R-30/B Mate Plus, the appropriate software option is needed. And the operator panel must be the “No mode switch” type. If the option is loaded and the operator panel has the mode switch, the alarm occurs.

### 14.36.2 Setup

The function to select the mode can be changed by the “Mode Select Func.” item in DCS screen.

### Procedure 14-65 Change mode select function for R-30iB Compact Plus

1. Press the [MENU] key.
2. Select 0, NEXT then move the cursor to SYSTEM.
3. Select DCS, then select ‘Mode Select’. The Mode Select screen is displayed.
4. Move cursor to the item “Mode Select Func.
5. "Do you want to change setting?" is displayed. Press F4, YES.

<!-- PDF page 1614 -->

6. Press F4,[CHOICE] and choose used modes select function.
7. Press PREV to display the DCS screen. Then, press F2, [APPLY].
8. Then the message "Code number (Master):" is displayed, please enter the DCS master code number.
9. Re-power the controller.

# Warning

If a robot is used with an incorrect setting, the safety function does not work correctly and serious personal injury could result. When the setting of the mode select function is changed, the setting must be verified and the function must be tested again.

### 14.36.3 TP MODE SELECT Function

Teach Pendant mode select function can select the mode, AUTO, T1 or T2, in Teach Pendant Screen.

The mode is selected in the Teach Pendant screen. Input of a single purpose password for this function is needed to change the mode. The Mode is changed immediately by operations in the screen.

When AUTO is selected using the Teach Pendant, the servo power is turned off with “SRVO-483 Input AUTO confirmation signal.” It is not reset until the confirmation signal is changed from OFF to ON.

Any digital input can be used as the confirmation signal. The confirmation signal is defined as “Confirmation input for AUTO” in the “System Config” menu.

# Warning

The system integrator is responsible for designing the robot system such that it complies with the following requirements.

- To use this function, a switch to be used as the AUTO confirmation signal is needed. The AUTO confirmation signals shall be connected to a switch located outside of the safeguarded space, but in the vicinity of the space.
- Install an interlocking device, a safety plug, and so forth in the safety gate so that the robot is stopped as the safety gate is opened.

Operators shall lock the safety gate in the open position with a padlock when they enter the safeguarded space, depending on a risk assessment.

<!-- PDF page 1615 -->

# Warning

The AUTO Confirmation Switch shall only be pushed after it is confirmed that nobody is in the safeguarded space.

The mode is selected when the controller starts up as follows.

- When the controller powers down in T1, the mode is kept T1 at start-up.
- When the controller powers down in T2, the mode is set to T1 at start-up.
- When the controller powers down in AUTO, the mode is kept as AUTO at start-up. Input of the confirmation signal is needed to reset the SRVO alarm and to start moving the robots.

When the Teach Pendant is disconnected, the controller retains the selected mode. Connecting to the Teach Pendant is needed to change the mode.

The safe I/O SSI7, SSI8, and SSI9 is used to choose the current selected mode when the Teach Pendant mode select function is used. These safe I/O are safety signals rated as Cat.4, PL e.

Note You do not have access to these signals if the Safe I/O Connect option is installed.

To use this option on R-30/B Plus and R-30/B Mate Plus, the operator panel must be set to “No mode switch” type. If the option is loaded and the operator panel has the mode switch, the alarm External mode select is not available” occurs.

To use this option on R-30/B Compact Plus, disconnect the optional mode switch and connect a special short connector. If the option is enabled and the hardware is not matched, the alarm occurs.

The mode cannot be changed from the PC screen (by the Remote iPendant function). This pop-up screen does not appear even if TP Enable switch on the PC screen is changed.

### 14.36.3.1 Operation

The pop-up screen to change the mode appears when the TP Enable switch is changed.

The pop-up screen is displayed in the following cases.

- The selected Mode is AUTO and the TP Enable switch is changed to ON.
- The selected Mode is T1 or T2 and the TP Enable switch is changed to OFF.

The mode is changed when another mode button is pressed, or if the cursor is moved and the ENTER key is pressed.

When CANCEL is selected or the PREV key is pushed, the pop-up screen disappears and the selected mode is not changed.

#### 14.36.4 External Mode Select Function

Safe I/O SSO[6] and SSO[7] are used to select the AUTO/T1/T2 operation mode in place of a mode switch on the operator panel.

When the “External mode select” option is used (AUTO/T1/T2 operational mode is selected by SSO[6] and SSO[7]), a risk assessment for the whole robot system is necessary, including the means to select the operational mode. If a robot is used with an incorrect operational mode, the safety function does not work correctly and serious personal injury may result. The means to select the operational mode must fulfill the following requirement.

Operational modes shall be selectable with a mode selector which can be locked in each position (e.g. a key operated switch which can be inserted and extracted in each position). ### 14.37 ORIGINAL PATH RESUME

Original Path Resume is a feature that, after Hold or Emergency Stop, allows the robot to return to its stop position before resuming the program, even if the robot has moved since the hold occurred. The stop position is the last program commanded position when the Hold or Emergency Stop occurred. The move from the current position to the stop position is called the “Restart Move”.

For example, if a Stop severity alarm occurs, the robot will decelerate to a stop and pause the TP program. The user might then jog the robot to another position to correct the cause of the alarm.

<!-- PDF page 1622 -->

When the TP program is resumed with Original Path Resume, the robot will first execute a Restart move to the Stop position, and then resume the program.

Figure 14–156. Hold Without Original Path Resume — Path Resumes from Current Position

> **Image description -- img-7.jpeg:** The image is a diagram illustrating a motion control concept involving a path with labeled points P[1], P[2], P[3], and P[4]. The path starts at P[1] and moves to P[2], then to P[3], and finally to P[4]. The diagram shows a 'Hold' position between P[2] and P[3], where the motion temporarily stops. From this stop position, the path can either resume following the original path (dotted line labeled 'Original Path') or take an alternate route (dashed line labeled 'Resume') to continue the motion. The labels 'Hold without Original Path' and 'Resume from Current Position' indicate that the system can either hold the position without returning to the original path or resume movement from the current position along a new path. The diagram visually represents the decision point and the two possible resumption strategies after a hold.

Figure 14–157. Hold With Original Path Resume — Path Resumes from Stop Position

> **Image description -- img-8.jpeg:** The image is a diagram illustrating a motion control concept involving a path with labeled points and actions. The diagram shows four points labeled P[1], P[2], P[3], and P[4], connected by a dashed line representing the "Original Path." At point P[1], the path branches into a curved segment labeled "Jog" that leads to a "Stop Position." From the stop position, the path continues with a segment labeled "Hold" and then "Restart," before reconnecting to the original path at a point labeled "Resume." The diagram includes annotations indicating that the path resumes from the stop position after being held. The overall concept demonstrates a process where motion along the original path is temporarily interrupted (stopped and held), then restarted, and finally resumed to continue along the original path.

When an Emergency Stop occurs, servo power is removed and the brakes are applied. Depending on the payload mass, speed, and direction of gravity, the robot will typically depart from the normal path. When the TP program is resumed with Original Path Resume, the robot will first execute a Restart move to the Stop position, and then resume the program.

<!-- PDF page 1623 -->

Figure 14–158. Emergency Stop With Original Path Resume — Path Resumes from Stop Position

> **Image description -- img-9.jpeg:** The image is a diagram illustrating the concept of an 'Emergency Stop With Original Path Resume'. It shows a curved path with four labeled points: P[1], P[2], P[3], and P[4]. The path starts at P[1] and moves through P[2] and P[3] before reaching P[4]. A section of the path between P[2] and P[3] is highlighted as the 'Original Path'. An 'Emergency stop' occurs at a point labeled 'Stop Position' along this original path, where 'Brakes applied' are indicated. After the stop, the path resumes from the stop position, as shown by the 'Resume' label, and continues along the original path toward P[4]. The diagram visually represents the process of stopping and then resuming movement along the same path without deviation.

# System Variables

Original Path Resume is enabled using $SCR.$ORG_PTH_RSM:
$SCR.$ORG_PTH_RSM = TRUE (Original Path Resume Enabled)
$SCR.$ORG_PTH_RSM = FALSE (Original Path Resume Disabled)

Motion type of the restart move is set by $MCR_GRP[].$RSM_MOTYPE

1. Joint
2. Linear
3. Program (Joint when hold segment Joint, Linear when hold segment Linear, Circular, or Arc)

Speed of the restart move is set by $MCR_GRP[].$RSM_SPEED, in mm/s or % as appropriate to motion type.

Orient type of the restart move is set by $MCR_GRP[].$RSM_ORIENT

1. ORNT
2. WJNT

# Limitations of Original Path Resume

- Without the Constant Path Option, the resumed path may not exactly match the position and orientation of the original path. The stop position orientation may be close to, but not exactly, on the original path.
- With the Constant Path Option, the resumed path will match the position and orientation of the original path.

<!-- PDF page 1624 -->

- The Restart move is subject to the same limitations as any other move. It is possible for the robot to get to a position in which the Restart move may cause alarms such as “Axis Limit” or “In Singularity”, in which case operator intervention will be necessary to resume the program.
- Because the Restart move starts from the current position, it is possible for the robot to hit something if the path is not clear between the current position and the stop position. For example, the robot can be jogged to a position that will cause a collision with a fixture when the Restart move executes.

### 14.38 PATH SWITCHING FUNCTION

The Path switching function, (J693), executes the assignment statements at several points in a motion path.

When the Path Switching (hereinafter called PS) instruction is specified in the DB calling program as follows, PS statements define the trigger point and the assignment statement to be executed.

DB CALL statement

1: L P[1] 200mm/sec FINE DB 100mm, CALL A

Contents of sub-program A

1: PS -100mm +0.2sec, DO[1]=(ON)
2: PS -150mm -0.2sec, IF(DI[1]), DO[2]=(DI[2] AND !DI[3])

The distance specified just after the DB statement does not affect to the each trigger timing of the PS commands in the sub-program. The PS statements in the sub program start their execution when the motion starts. You can mix another normal logical statement with the PS statement in the sub program.

Figure 14–159. Path Switch Application

> **Image description -- img-10.jpeg:** The image depicts a timing diagram with labeled axes and directional arrows. The horizontal axis represents time, with specific intervals marked as -0.2 seconds (corresponding to -40 mm) and +0.2 seconds (corresponding to +40 mm). The vertical axis is not explicitly labeled but appears to represent a positional or operational state. The diagram shows two main directional arrows: one pointing to the right labeled as 100 mm, and another pointing to the left labeled as -150 mm. Below the diagram, there is a conditional statement written in pseudocode: 'IF (DI[1]), DO[2] := (DI[2] AND !DI[3]) DO[1] := (ON) P[1]'. This suggests a logical operation where the output DO[2] is set based on the inputs DI[1], DI[2], and the negation of DI[3], and DO[1] is set to ON, with P[1] likely representing a process or state.

The PS instruction is composed of two parts, a trigger point and an assignment statement.

PS -100mm +0.2sec, DO[1] = (ON)
Trigger point Assignment statement

<!-- PDF page 1625 -->

The trigger point specifies the trigger distance (mm) from the destination position and the offset time (sec).

When you enter a negative value, you can specify the trigger point before the motion is completed (distance-before type). When you enter a positive value, you can specify the trigger point after the motion is completed. (distance-after type)

The offset time is converted to the distance according to the specified speed, in the above case, 0.2sec is converted to 40mm (= 200mm/sec * 0.2sec). This conversion is not accurate in the acceleration and deceleration period.

The adjustment of trigger point by the offset time is affected by override value.

For R-30/B/R-30/B Mate, according to the sign of the trigger distance value, its behavior is treated as distance-before or distance-after type. When the trigger distance value is a minus value, the PS instruction is regarded as distance-before type. Therefore, even if the plus value is set as offset time and the trigger point is calculated as plus value, the actual trigger point will be clamped to -0.0mm. And when the trigger distance value is plus value, the PS instruction is regarded as distance-after type. Therefore, even if a minus value is set as an offset time and the trigger point is calculated as a minus value, the actual trigger point will be clamped to +0.0mm.

For R-30/B Plus/R-30/B Mate Plus, the trigger point is not clamped by plus/minus of the trigger distance.

The assignment statement part specifies the statement to be executed at the trigger point.

The assignment statement can have an IF condition.

PS -150mm -0.2sec, IF (DI[1]), DO[1] = (ON)

In this case, when DI[1] is ON, DO[1] is turned on, when DI[1] is OFF, DO[1] is not changed.

The assignment statement can use the following items and operators.

Table 14–107. Assignment Statement Items and Operators

[tbl-13.md](tbl-13.md)

<!-- PDF page 1626 -->

[tbl-14.md](tbl-14.md)

The marker assignment and TC_ONLINE can be specified in the PS statement.

The AR[] (calling parameter) can not be specified in the PS statement.

Up to 20 operations can be specified in one motion line as total of right side formula and IF condition.

One motion statement can have up to 20 PS statements.

#### If the trigger point is negative and it is farther than the start position (distance-before type)

If the trigger point is negative and it is farther than the start position, this is triggered immediately.

1: L P[1] 200mm/sec FINE
2: L P[2] 200mm/sec FINE DB 100mm, CALL A

##### If the trigger point is passed by jog while the program is paused

When original path resume is disabled (\(SCR.\)ORG_PTH_RSM=FALSE), if the program is paused during the motion with PS, and jogged by TP, and the trigger point is passed by jog, then the PS condition is triggered immediately when the program is resumed.

When original path resume is enabled (\(SCR.\)ORG_PTH_RSM=TRUE), once back to the paused position on the original motion path and re-start the program. In this case, the PS condition is triggered when the trigger point is passed after resume and re-start.

You can choose to cause error at this situation by above parameter setting.

($PS_CONFIG.$DB_IMMTRIG,$DA_IMMTRIG)

1: L P[1] 200mm/sec FINE
2: L P[2] 200mm/sec FINE DB 100mm, CALL A

##### About multi group configuration

In case of multi group configuration, the PS statement is implicitly executed for the first motion group in the group mask of the TP program. For example, if the motion mask is  \( [*,1,1,*,*,*,*,*] \) , then the PS statement is executed for group 2.

##### Limitations

The PS statement is not available for the following motion type.

<!-- PDF page 1630 -->

- Weaving motion
- Tracking motion which can not define actual destination point beforehand, as line-tracking, MIG-EYE, Robot-Link.

# Caution

- PS statement is interpreted in a flash only at the start of the new motion line. When the motion including PS statement is paused, if you edit and change the PS statement in the sub program during this pause status, modified PS commands do not take effect until the motion line is newly executed. After pausing program, to take effect of the modified PS statement immediately, you can BWD the motion line and re-start. Then the modified PS statements will take effect.
- PS command for joint motion is not prohibited. But it must be used carefully. Regardless of the motion type Linear, Circular, or Joint, PS command is checking the linear distance between TCP and destination point as trigger threshold.

Note In cases of PS command's Distance-Before type usage, if TCP once goes into the defined sphere around the destination point, the PS command will be triggered regardless how long the rest of path. Please note the distance which is being checked in PS motion is not the total remaining path length to the destination point. Please see the following figure for example.

### 14.39 PAYLOAD CONFIRM

#### 14.39.1 Overview

Payload confirm consists of two functions:

- Payload Setting Confirm
- Payload Over Confirm

Payload setting confirm evaluates payload setting accuracy with little robot motion. When this function is used, the robot has to be in the position where where J5 and J6 have maximum moment loading. Only axes J5 and J6 have to be at the maximum moment position for the current payload. The other axes have no limitation.

When using Payload Confirm, J5 and J6 axes move between the current position +1[degree] and the current position -1[degree] when F4, PLSET and F3, YES are selected. The payload setting error will be shown after robot moved. Payload setting error of payload [1]-[10] is stored.

Payload over confirm disables the overload warning when the motor is able to move in actual program with the payload that is over specification.

The program to be evaluated must be executed beforehand. When F5, OVLD is selected, this function evaluates the last executed program. The maximum torque of the last executed program and rated torque is compared. The overload warning is disabled when the maximum torque of the checked program is lower than the rated torque. Note that the overload warning is not shown even if the maximum torque of the other program is higher than the rated torque.

6. The result shown in the screen that is displayed when the program running is not correct. Display the screen again after the program to evaluate has ended.

### 14.40 POSITION BUMPBOX (formerly known as Bump Box)

#### 14.40.1 Overview

Position BumpBox is an optional feature that allows you to offset a programmed robot path or the shape center when used in conjunction with the Shape Generation option. The offsets can be applied from the teach pendant or by setting the digital inputs. The offsets can be applied only in x, y, or z directions. You have the option to remove the offsets applied by Position BumpBox at any time.

All the information needed to apply offsets (bump) is contained in a Position BumpBox schedule which must be set up before using Position BumpBox. In order to apply the offsets by setting digital inputs, Position BumpBox I/O must be set up properly.

<!-- PDF page 1637 -->

Position BumpBox applies offsets to a path in the following ways:

- You set up the Position BumpBox schedules that contain the information such as the program name and the line numbers needed to apply the offsets.
- You set up the Position BumpBox I/O which includes the digital inputs required for applying the offsets and a group input required for selecting the Position BumpBox schedule.
- When you apply the offsets from the teach pendant or set a digital input, based on the information contained in the schedule, the position data in the teach pendant program is modified. The robot will move along the bumped positions.
- When you remove the offsets, the original positions in the teach pendant program are restored.

### 14.40.2 Setting Up Position BumpBox Schedules

You need to set up the Position BumpBox schedules and I/O before you can apply offsets to a path. You set up the schedules from the Position BumpBox schedules screen. You can define up to 255 Position BumpBox schedules. By default, 15 Position BumpBox schedules are available. You can change the number of schedules by modifying the system variable $BB_TOT_SCH. Use Procedure 14-71 to change the number of bump schedules. Use Procedure 14-72 to set up a Position BumpBox schedule.

#### Position BumpBox Schedule Screen

The Position BumpBox schedule screen allows you to view limited information for several schedules at once. DETAIL allows you to view and set the complete information for a single schedule. See Table 14–110 for a description of the items on the Position BumpBox DETAIL screen.

### 14.40.3 Setting Up Position BumpBox I/O

In order to apply offsets using the digital inputs, the Position BumpBox I/O must be set properly. You must set up one group input and several digital inputs and outputs. The group input specifies the Position BumpBox schedule number. Six consecutive digital inputs are used to apply offsets in positive and negative (BUMP_UP and BUMP_DN) x, y and z directions. Two digital outputs are used. One acknowledges the offsets and another indicates a limit error.

The group input and digital inputs and outputs must be properly configured before you can use them. Refer to Chapter 13 INPUT/OUTPUT (I/O) SETUP for information on configuring digital I/O. The number of points in the group input determines the number of schedules that can be bumped using I/O. For example, if there are three points in the group input only schedules 1 through 7 can be bumped. If there are four points then schedules 1 through 15 can be bumped. If there are n schedules, schedules 1 through (2^n - 1) can be bumped.

When Position BumpBox I/O is enabled, Position BumpBox monitors the six digital inputs selected as Bump inputs. When any one of the six inputs turn from OFF to ON, Position BumpBox applies the offsets in the direction corresponding to the input according to the schedule given by the group input value. If the requested bump exceeds the limits specified in the schedule, the limit error digital output is set to ON for the duration specified by the pulse width. After successfully applying the offsets, the acknowledge offset digital output is set to ON for the duration specified by the pulse width.

If Position BumpBox I/O is disabled, then Position BumpBox stops monitoring the digital inputs and changing the state of the digital inputs has no effect. When Position BumpBox I/O is enabled, offsets are applied using digital inputs and cannot be applied from the teach pendant.

Use Procedure 14-73 for setting up the Position BumpBox I/O. Refer to Table 14–111 for descriptions of Position BumpBox I/O items.

Table 14–111. Position BumpBox I/O Items

### 14.40.4 Position BumpBox with Coordinated Motion - Overview

Position BumpBox will work with programs using Coordinated Motion instructions within the weld path. You can “bump” coordinated motion instructions in multi-group programs. The bump has the expected results for WELD, WELD & TOOL, and WORLD/UFRAME bump frames, but it is done with respect to the coordinated motion frame or the coordinated motion leader frame. This can be used to “bump” part paths in the coordinated leader frame defined on the part, and also to offset the weld position along the axis of rotation, as shown in the figure below:

##### 14.40.4.1 Position BumpBox with Coordinated Motion Supported Configurations

- CD BumpBox code is loaded only if your robot system has Coordinated Motion option (J619) installed
- A “CD Bump” is applied when coordinated motion instructions are used in a multi-group program. The software uses CD bump by detecting that at least one Coord or Coord [#] or Coord[R[#]] motion instruction is included in the “Bump lines” of the selected Bump Schedule.
- The program must have a leader group and follower group that belong to the same CD_PAIR (meaning coordinated motion calibration has been done between the leader and the follower motion group.) The “Motion group” setting in the Bump Schedule refers to the follower group of the cd_pair
- “CD bump” allows the follower robot path points, defined in the “Bump lines” of the Bump Schedule, to be offset with respect to the coordinated motion frame of the CD leader.
- Multiple leader and follower group devices may be contained in the same program, but offsets will be generated with respect to only one leader. The motion instruction must use COORD [ldr] or COORD [R[#]] to indicate which of the leader groups is used with the follower motion group defined in the “Motion group” setting in the Bump Schedule. The CD motion of the additional leader group(s) is not guaranteed to perform to the user’s expectation. Motion of the additional follower group(s) is not guaranteed to perform to the user’s expectation. The user must validate the operation of Position BumpBox in these complicated programs.
- Changing the leader group within the “bump lines” will cause an alarm to be posted and the operation will abort prior to changing any position data.

<!-- PDF page 1648 -->

- The leader and follower frames do not have to be aligned for CD bump calculations to be performed, but the user may have to train a CD leader frame to align a bump direction to a part manipulated by the leader group. Uframe, Utool, and leader frame are supported on follower robots.
- Robot-to-Robot coordinated motions are not supported in the “bump lines” of the selected schedule; an alarm will be posted and the operation will abort prior to changing any position data.
- Non-CD Shape motion lines can be bumped. Shape generation programs using CD motion in the bump lines are not supported; an alarm will be posted and the operation will abort prior to changing any position data.
- The first line of the “Bump lines” cannot be the VIA point of a circular motion ( C P[ ].) An alarm will be posted and the operation will abort prior to changing any position data.

### Leader Group Devices

Two Types of positioner devices are used for leader groups in CD pairs:

- Most Basic positioner leader groups are single axis devices, either a headstock or a tabletop positioner. They can also have multiple axes if the axes are either parallel or perpendicular to each other.
- General positioner type can be used interchangeable with basic positioner type and it is typically used in multi-axis leader devices. General positioner type must be used in cases where two or more axes are not perpendicular or parallel to each other.

Coordinated motion calibration assigns the leader group “world frame” which is analogous to the robot world frame.

### Multi-group or Multi-Arm Systems

- Systems including one positioner leader with one robot follower. (The leader device is generally a single axis headstock, or a tabletop positioner, but positioner leaders can be composed of up to 3 axes and also include linear or rotary extended axes.)
- Systems including one positioner leader and multiple follower robots simultaneously coordinate with the leader.
- Two positioner leaders and 2 robot followers where each robot is permanently paired to one of one of the leader groups; each pair of robot and headstock executes independently.
- Systems including multiple positioner leaders with multiple robot followers. One headstock is being loaded while the other is being welded; they rotate when the loading and welding complete. For programs including multiple follower robots, only one follower will be exactly coordinated during CD motion. The other robot will run slower unless the follower paths move the same distance on a point-by-point basis.

### Bump Offsets Supported Paths

CD ‘bump’ operations can to be applied to coordinated motion paths that are:

- Linear or circular paths with positions taught in a user frame of the follower
- Concentric circular paths to an axis of rotation of headstock or tabletop leaders.

<!-- PDF page 1649 -->

- Linear or circular paths on, or parallel to, the faceplate or table-top
- Linear or circular paths contained in a CD leader frame plane with respect to the leader world frame.
- CD leader frames for the leader frame can be used to align bump directions to “bump” axis inputs.

# Position Types Supported and Motion Modifier Qualifications

The following interpolation types and motion modifiers can are supported by CD BumpBox operations in coordinated motion programs:

- CD, CD[LDR], and CD[R[ n]] instructions in the same bump path; the reference to leader must be consistent for all bump lines.

Note Coordinated leader device cannot be changed in the path points in the bump schedule “lines” parameter.

Supported Motion Types are

- “C P[ ] .. CD” and “L P[ ] .. CD” motions are supported in the bump “lines.”
- “A P[ ].. CD” motion is supported; resume to path feature and restart location are different than for C P[ ] motions.
- J P[ ] motions will be supported within a CD Bump “Lines”

Note CD does not apply to J P[] motion.

- “PR[ ].. CD” is not supported. This position type will be bypassed in the Bump operation, and an alarm will be posted. The bump program will not be aborted, and all other normal positions will be bumped.
- The results of adding additional “frame” and “tool” offsets will not be guaranteed to have the expected results when “bumped” as non-CD motion positions using the same motion offset modifiers.
- Unsupported motion options for CD are unsupported motion options for CD BumpBox operations.
- Scratch motion and overlap distance are not guaranteed to be on the motion path.

The “CD” bump frames are internal to the software and not displayed to the user in the bump schedules. In the coordinated motion bump cases, the alignment of the reference frames is not always consistent with the Bump direction “Along/X” and “Across/Y”, or “ on the part. This can be corrected by using the a CD Leader frame aligned so that the bump direction corresponds to the “bump offset”.

### Leader Group Frames

There are two frames that determine how coordinated motion “bumps” executed, These are the leader world frame and the CD leader frame. The leader world frame defines the origin and axis alignment of the leader motion group. A CD leader frame is analogous to a Jog frame with respect to the leader world frame. The CD leader frame moves when the leader group moves. These are transparent to most uses of coordinated motion, but they play an important and function in setting up the Bump directions relative to the part path.

The following figure of a tabletop positioner shows the leader world frame and also a CD leader frame. The CD leader frame defines the plane in which the path P[1] .. P[3] executes in this example. When this frame is defined, the bump offsets are calculated with respect to the X, Y, and Z-axes of this frame. In addition, the user can select to jog in this frame by pressing the COORD hardkey on the teach pendant when a follower motion group is selected. The relationship of the frames is covered in more detail below. Please refer to the “Coordinated Motion Setup and Operations Manual” section “Calibration” regarding details of that operation.

<!-- PDF page 1652 -->

Figure 14–172. BBox with Table

The diagram shows three primary axes: the leader group world X-axis (horizontal), Y-axis (vertical), and Z-axis (depth), forming a right-handed coordinate system. The leader group world origin is marked, and several points labeled P[1] through P[3] are shown, representing positions that have been "bumped" along the X, Y, and Z axes to accommodate batch variance. The "bump along" direction is indicated along the X-axis, while the "bump across" direction is along the Y-axis. ### Leader Group World Frame (Unknown Kinematics Type)

When a positioner group is added to the system, the installer is prompted to select a kinematics type. “Unknown kinematics “ indicates that a user will define the calibration by point teaching methods in the Coordinated Motion Setup menu. “Known kinematics “ indicates that the user knows the exact alignment of the positioner axes and also the exact location of the positioner with respect to the follower robot origin. This type requires information to be added immediately upon installation of axes in the positioner group.

When an axis is added to the “Unknown kinematics “group, the axis assignment and axis direction are entered. For multiple axes, the Cartesian offset of the subsequent axes is entered. These assignments are overridden when Coordinated Motion calibration is performed. Calibration consists of recording thee points for each rotary axis of the leader group in the Coordinated Motion calibration screen

The CD motion calibration normally assigns the leader world Z-axis perpendicular to the tabletop or headstock faceplate axis of rotation. The positive direction of the axis is determined by the right hand rule for current based on the direction the axis turns when its positive rotation key is pressed. The X and Z are defined normal to the Z-axis.

<!-- PDF page 1653 -->

For basic and general positioner leaders with multiple axes, the calibration software determines the offset between axes and makes the direction assignment using the right hand rule for. The last axis, the tabletop or faceplate, is assigned as the Z-axis. The axis immediately preceding the last axis is defined as the X-axis, and Y is applied to the next preceding axis when three axes are present. For basic positioners, the X axis and Y-axis are assigned normal to the Z-axis assignment and parallel to the other axes “axis of rotation”. In the case of general positioner the DH parameters of axes is determined, and a world frame is assigned. If multiple axes have parallel axis of rotation, the same direction is assigned to all such axes.

The calibration data ($CD_PAIR[n].$CD_XF) defines the position of the leader group world origin with respect to the follower robot origin. Seldom is the origin located in the faceplate plane of the positioner device, or at the intersection point of the axes of rotation in the case of multiple axes. Please refer to the “Coordinated Motion Setup and Operations Manual” section “Calibration” regarding details of that operation.

### Leader Group World Frame (Known Kinematics Type)

For the “Known Kinematics” case, the world frame of the leader is determined before the calibration data is entered. When “Known kinematics “ is selected at the time a positioner group in created, the axis assignment of +/-X, +/-Y, or +/-Z to each axis of the basic or general positioner is entered.

In addition, the Cartesian offsets between axes of multi-axis positioners are manually entered. The Coord Motion calibration consists of manually installing values for X, Y, Z, W, P, and R, based on a known alignment of the origin of the leader device with respect to the origin of the follower robot. Please refer to the “Coordinated Motion Setup and Operations Manual” section “Calibration” regarding details of that operation.

### Leader Group “CD Leader Frame”

The CD leader frame is a component of the Coordinated Motion software option. It is a jogging frame for the follower robot that is taught with respect to the leader world frame. The CD leader frame is a dynamic frame, so LDR jogging the direction of the X, Y, and Z axes of the CD leader frame will appear to change as the leader axis (axes) position change.

The CD leader frame is setup in the Coordinated Motion setup screen. There are six CD leader frames that can be taught for each cd_pair that is defined, and they are taught by using a three-point teaching method:

You select to use the CD leader frame for jogging pressing the COORD key on the teach pendant until “LDR #” is shown as the jogging frame for the robot. To switch between CD leader frames, you need to change the CD leader frame index in the Coordinated Motion setup screen (see figure 1.3.) These frames may be aligned to the workpiece, the leader world frame, or some arbitrary frame that is suitable for jogging the robot. When leader frame is zero, and the leader device is at it zero position, LDR jogging shows the leader world frame. Please refer to the “Coordinated Motion Setup and Operations Manual” section “Calibration” regarding details of teaching the CD leader frame.

CD BumpBox uses the CD leader frame and leader world frame for bump calculations. When the current CD leader frame value is zero, the leader world frame is used for the CD World/Uframe bump frame. When the CD leader frame has a non-zero value, the CD leader frame is used for the “World/ UF” reference. The CD_LDRFR_UF bump frame uses, the X, Y, and Z values. The CD_WELD Bump frame uses the Y and Z components.

### Using “CD Leader Frame” to Align the Bump Frames

When the current CD leader frame value is zero, the leader world frame is used for the X, Y, and Z of the CD World/Uframe bump frame and uses the Y, Z for CD_WELD Bump frame.

If the bump frames do not have the proper alignment to the workpiece, “X, Y, Z” bump (CD_LDRFR_UF) are not aligned to the part, or the “Across” (CD_WELD), then a CD leader frame that defines these directions can be taught to correct the alignment. This is more likely to be necessary in multiple axis positioner leaders, or when the plane of motion for the robot process path is not parallel the tabletop or faceplate axis.

Note When a non-zero CD leader frame is used to correct for misalignment of bump directions, this frame must always be set to be the default CD leader frame when a bump operation is performed, otherwise the bump calculation will be incorrect. When this bump operation is

<!-- PDF page 1656 -->

completed, the CD leader frame must be set to a zero value CD leader frame so that it is not applied to other bump operations.

##### Controlling the Default CD Leader Frame

There are two ways to control the Default CD leader Frame

1. To switch between CD leader frames, you need to change the CD leader frame index in the Coordinated Motion setup screen.
2. The CD leader frame can be controlled in the program that is using BumpBox. By inserting a “Parameter” instruction into the program, you can force a default CD leader frame to be assigned. In the program below, CD leader frame 6 of cd_pair[3] is used (see Figure 14–174 above) when line 3 is executed. CD leader frame 1 of cd_pair[3], a zero value, removes the CD leader frame line 8 is executed. Line 7 is the end of the bump lines.

Figure 14–176. CD Leader Frame Example

1: UFRAME_NUM=1;
2: UTOOL_NUM=1;
3: $CD_PAIR[3].$LDR_FRM_NUM=6;
4: ;
5:L P[1] 500mm/sec FINE ;
6:L P[2] 1.5sec CNT100 COORD
: Arc Start E1[1] ;
7:C P[3]
: P[4] 60.0inch/min FINE COORD
: Arc End E1[2] ;
8: $CD_PAIR[3].$LDR_FRM_NUM=1;
9:L P[5] 500mm/sec FINE ;
10:L P[6] 500mm/sec FINE ;

### 14.41 POSITION REGISTER LOOK-AHEAD EXECUTION FUNCTION

#### 14.41.1 Overview

While the robot is executing a program, it reads the lines ahead of the line currently being executed (look-ahead execution). The position register look-ahead execution function enables look-ahead execution for position registers. To understand fully the features of the position register look-ahead function, it is helpful to understand some of the details of program execution.

<!-- PDF page 1657 -->

### Program Execution without the Position Register Look-Ahead Function

Conventionally, look-ahead execution is performed for motion instructions that have normal positional data (do not use position registers). Look-ahead execution can not be performed for motion instructions that use position registers for their positional data.

Motion instructions that use position registers cannot be read in advance because the values in the position registers could be changed by the program, data transfer function, and so forth.

If the robot reads a motion instruction that uses a position register prior to its execution, the value of the position register might yet be changed by a program or another function (such as data transfer). Such a change is not reflected in the motion instruction that has already been read by the robot. Consequently, the robot's operation might be unpredictable.

Motion instructions that use position registers can be classified into two types:

- Motion instructions with the target position specified by a position register
- Motion instructions with an offset instruction where an offset is given by a position register

Even when a target position or offset is calculated during program execution, and a position register holding this calculation result is used with a motion instruction, look-ahead execution is not performed for the instruction, for the reason explained above.

### Program Execution with the Position Register Look-Ahead Function

The position register look-ahead execution function enables look-ahead execution for position registers. For this purpose, an instruction to lock position registers and an instruction to unlock position registers are provided. Using these instructions, you can explicitly specify a program portion. Then, for the specified program portion, even when it contains motion instructions that use position registers, look-ahead execution can be performed.

The position registers can be locked to prevent their contents from being changed after they are read. When an attempt is made to execute an instruction to change a locked position register (for example, an assign instruction for the position register, or an application instruction to set data in the position register), the following error message is issued:

INTP-128 Pos reg is locked

When a function other than the program (such as the data transfer function) attempts to change the value of a locked position register, the following error message is issued, and the attempt fails:

VARS-037 Position register is locked

Position registers are generally locked and unlocked with instructions taught in a program. When a program that has locked the position registers terminates, the position registers are unlocked automatically.

<!-- PDF page 1658 -->

All position registers are locked simultaneously. While the position registers are locked, access to any position register is disabled, even in a different motion group.

### 14.41.2 Program Instructions

The following program instructions have been added for the position register look-ahead function:

- LOCK PREG
- UNLOCK PREG

#### LOCK PREG

Locks all position registers. This instruction prevents any change being made to any position register.

#### UNLOCK PREG

Unlocks the position registers.

These are control instructions, not motion instructions. They can be taught in the same way as other control instructions.

### 14.41.3 Program Example

Position Register Look-Ahead Program Example shows how to use the LOCK PREG and UNLOCK PREG instructions in a program.

Position Register Look-Ahead Program Example

1: J P[1] 100% FINE
2:    PR[1]=PR[2]
3:    PR[2]=PR[3]
4: LOCK PREG
5: L P[2] 100mm/sec Cnt100
6: L P[3] 100mm/sec Cnt100
7: L PR[1] 100mm/sec Cnt100
8: L P[4] 100mm/sec Cnt100 offset, PR[2]
9: L P[5] 100mm/sec FINE
10: UNLOCK PREG

When line 4 of this sample program has been executed, the position registers are locked. They are unlocked when line 10 has been executed. Therefore, the motion instructions with position registers in lines 7 and 8, which are executed with the position registers locked, are subject to look-ahead execution.

<!-- PDF page 1659 -->

If the program is terminated between lines 4 and 10, the locked position registers are unlocked automatically. If the program is paused between lines 4 and 10, the cursor is moved manually, then the program is restarted, the locked position registers are unlocked. In this case, look-ahead execution is not performed for the instructions in lines 7 and 8.

When backward execution is performed, then normal execution is restarted, the position registers are unlocked. For example, suppose that program execution is paused during the execution of line 6, backward program execution is performed up to line 5, then forward program execution is restarted. In this case, the position registers are unlocked. So, look-ahead execution is not performed for lines 7 and 8.

When program execution is started from a line located after line 4, the position registers are not locked. So, look-ahead execution is not performed for lines 7 and 8.

A LOCK PREG instruction can be executed even when the position registers are already locked. Nothing occurs, however, when the LOCK PREG instruction is executed for a second time. Similarly, the UNLOCK PREG instruction can be executed even when the position registers are not locked. Nothing occurs, however, when the UNLOCK PREG instruction is executed for a second time.

### 14.41.4 Execution

When executing position register look-ahead program instructions, be aware of the following:

- The LOCK PREG and UNLOCK PREG instructions are not executed in backward program execution mode.
- Look-a head execution is not performed for the LOCK PREG and UNLOCK PREG instructions. This means that when one of these instructions is encountered, look-ahead execution is stopped temporarily; after the instruction is executed, look-ahead execution is again enabled.

## 14.42 PROCESS AXES

### 14.42.1 BASIC PROCESS AXES (R689)

#### 14.42.1.1 Overview

The Basic Process Axes software option (R689) provides the user with the capability of configuring and operating a motor or motors independent of any motion group. A “Process Axis” has the following characteristics:

- The axis accepts only speed commands; its position cannot be commanded directly
- The axis does not belong to any motion group

<!-- PDF page 1660 -->

Process axes are intended to be used to drive devices for which position control is not needed, e.g. a pump or a drill bit.

Process axes are also used by other software options, which integrate the operation of the process axes directly into the application tool itself. Since these options access the process axes directly, they cannot be loaded on the controller with the Basic Process Axes option. That is, Basic Process Axes is mutually exclusive with these options.

The software options that are mutually exclusive with Basic Process Axes are as follows:

- Integral Pump Control (R554)
- FRA Waterborne (R556)
- ISD Gear Meter (R563)
- ISD Dual Meter (R562)
- ISD Single Acting (R564)
- ISD Double Acting (R561)
- Pneumatic Servo (R595)
- Servo Torch (J691, J982)
- Pump Only Motion (J801)

Accordingly, the Basic Process Axes option should be loaded and used in simple, generic cases when the use of a process axis is desired but it does not fit one of the above options. With this option, the process axes can be controlled by TP instructions or by group inputs.

The Basic Process Axes option provides the following functions:

- The ability to setup and configure process axes, up to a maximum of 8.
- TP instructions to send a speed command to the axes, and to stop the axes.
- A torque monitoring function to post an alarm and stop program execution and robot motion when the process axes encounter excessive torque.
- A setup menu to specify a scale factor for speed commands, torque limit values, group outputs for speed data, and group inputs for speed commands.
- A status screen to display speed and torque data for the process axes.

### 14.42.1.2 Setup

The Basic Process Axes option has a setup menu available to configure its features. The setup menu covers the following items:

- Torque Monitoring function
- Scale factor for the speed value in the TP instruction
- Group Input for speed command
- Group Output for speed display

<!-- PDF page 1661 -->

Refer to Table 14–113 for further details on the items included in the setup menu. Use procedure Procedure 14-75 to setup the Basic Process Axes option.

Table 14–113. Basic Process Axes setup menu items

[tbl-26.md](tbl-26.md)

### Procedure 14-75 Setting up Basic Process Axes

1. Press MENU.
2. Select SETUP.
3. Press F1, [TYPE].
4. Select Process Axes. You will see a screen similar to the following

<!-- PDF page 1662 -->

SETUP ISDT
1/5
Process Axis Number: 1
Current Limit: 0.0 amps
Curr Lim fault after 0 msec
Scale factor for TP Inst: 1.0
Note: Scale factor is applied in addition to gear ratio!!
(Current gear ratio is 10:1)
Speed Command Group Input: 0
Actual Speed Group Output: 0

5. To change the process axis number being setup, press F3, AXIS, and enter the desired process axis number. If the number entered does not correspond to a valid, properly setup process axis, the following message will be displayed:

Invalid Axis Number!

6. To display help information, press F2, HELP. When you are finished displaying help, press PREV.
7. Move the cursor to the item you wish to change, and enter the new value for that item.

If a nonzero value is set for “Speed Command Group Input” in this setup menu, then the resulting behavior of that process axis will be as follows:

- The group input will be monitored continuously, so that the value of the input will be the instantaneous speed command to the process axis motor.
- The value stored in the group input will be treated as a 16-bit integer, converted to RPM at the motor shaft as follows:

— The most significant bit will be treated as the sign bit, where 0 means positive and 1 means negative. (i.e. for a negative speed value add 32768).
— The value designated by the remaining 15 bits will be multiplied by 10 to obtain the RPM to be commanded to the motor.

- The process axis that uses this group input number will be in motion as long as the following conditions are met:

— The axis' servo amplifier is enabled
— The axis' brake is released
— The group input has a nonzero value

For example, if a value of “11” were entered for “Speed Command Group Input” for process axis #1 in the setup menu, then in order to drive the process axis #1 motor at 1000 RPM (at the motor shaft), the group input #11 must be set to a value of 10000. If instead a speed of —1000 RPM were desired, then group input #11 should have the value 42768, which is  \( 10000 + 32768 \)

<!-- PDF page 1663 -->

Note If a group input is setup to be used as the speed command for any process axes, then the TP instructions are automatically disabled. That is, TP instructions and Group Inputs cannot be simultaneously used to control the process axes.

If a nonzero value is set for “Actual Speed Group Output” in the setup menu, then the actual RPM at the motor shaft of the process axis will be copied in real time to that group output, as a 16-bit integer value, with the most significant bit representing the sign bit. As with the speed command group input, when the most significant bit is 1, then the group output is indicating a negative speed value.

For example, if a value of “12” were entered for “Actual Speed Group Output” for process axis #1 in the setup menu, then if group output 11 displays a value of 1000, it means that process axis #1 has a speed of 1000 RPM at the motor shaft. If group output 11 displays 33768, then the speed of process axis #1 is —1000 at the motor shaft.

##### 14.42.1.3 TP Instructions

The Basic Process Axes option includes two teach pendant instructions for setting process axes speeds:

- SET ISDT SPEED
- STOP ALL ISDT

##### SET ISDT SPEED Instruction

The SET ISDT SPEED instruction is used to send speed commands directly to the process axes and can include speed data for up to 8 axes. The instruction allows two fields for each axis, one for axis number and one for the speed value. The following screen is an example of the usage of this instruction:

TEST
1:J P[1] 100% FINE
2: SET ISDT SPEED A1=100
3:J P[2] 100% FINE
[End]
Enter Value
ADD AX

In this example, the cursor is on the field corresponding to the axis number (“1” in the example). To the right of this field, following the “=” is the speed value that will be sent to process axis #1, which in this example is 100 user speed units. (See section Section 14.42.1.2 for more details on the relationship between user speed units and motor RPM). If this instruction needs to set speeds

<!-- PDF page 1664 -->

for additional process axis, pressing F1 (labled “ADD AX”) will add an additional set of fields to the instruction as shown in the following screen:

TEST
2/3
1:J P[1] 100% FINE
2: SET ISDT SPEED A1=100, A...=...
3:J P[2] 100% FINE
[End]
Enter Value
ADD AX DIRECT INDIRECT

The cursor can then be moved to the “...” fields to enter a new axis number and speed value. Note also in the above screen that the cursor is on the speed field, which means that function keys F2 and F3 are available to allow the speed value to be specified as a direct integer value or indirectly via numeric register.

There is no error checking performed on the fields of the SET ISDT SPEED instruction at the time the instruction is added to, or edited in, a TP program. However, error checking is performed at the time the instruction is actually executed. For each field in the instruction, first the axis number will be checked to verify that it is a properly setup process axis. If that process axis has not been setup, then the following alarm will be posted:

ISDT-012 Invalid Axis # in L:# Instr

The error text will indicate the process axis number in the instruction that is invalid, as well as the line number in the TP program containing the offending instruction. If the same process axis number is used in multiple fields in the instruction, then the following alarm will be posted:

ISDT-013 Duplicate Ax:# in L:# Instr

The alarm text will indicate which axis number was repeated, and also the line number from the TP program. If the speed value specified exceeds the speed limit of that process axis (as specified in the process axis setup routine at controlled start), then the following alarm will be posted:

ISDT-001 Joint speed limit (G:0 A:#)

If the speed value specified results in a motor RPM that exceeds the maximum RPM for this motor, then the following alarm is posted:

ISDT-002 Motor speed limit (G:0 A:#)

<!-- PDF page 1665 -->

Finally, if there is a process axis that has been properly setup at controlled start but that does not have a corresponding field in the SET ISDT SPEED instruction, then when the instruction is executed that process axis will remain unaffected: it will continue moving at its current speed, or remain stopped if it was stopped.

##### STOP ALL ISDT Instruction

The STOP ALL ISDT instruction is used to immediately send a zero speed to all properly setup process axis. It does not have any arguments. An example of the usage of this instruction appears in the screen shot below:

TEST
2/3
1:J P[1] 100% FINE
2: SET ISDT SPEED A1=100, A2=200
3:J P[2] 100% FINE
4: SET ISDT SPEED A2=0
5:J P[3] 100% FINE
6: SET ISDT SPEED A1=50
7:J P[4] 100% FINE
8: SET ISDT SPEED A1=100, A2=50
9:J P[5] 100% FINE
10: STOP ALL ISDT
[End]

In this example program, once the robot has moved to P[1], process axis #1 will begin moving at speed 100 while process axis #2 will begin moving at speed 200. Then the robot will move to P[2], after which process axis #2 will stop (i.e. speed will change to 0), but process axis #1 will continue moving at speed 100. Next, after the robot moves to P[3], process axis #1 will change its speed from 100 to 50, while process axis #2 will remain stopped. Then the robot will move to P[4], after which both process axes will change speed, process axis #1 from 50 to 100 and process axis #2 from 0 to 50. Then the robot will move to P[5], and finally on the last line of the program both process axis #1 and #2 will stop.

The Process Axes Status screen displays speed and torque data for all process axes defined on the controller. This screen is only available when the Basic Process Axes option is loaded on the controller. See figure Figure 14–177 for an example screen and Table 14–114 for a description of the items on this screen.
