### 14.42.1.5 Torque Monitor Function

The Basic Process Axes option includes a torque monitor function, which allows the user to specify a level of torque (more specifically, of commanded motor current) and a corresponding length of time beyond which a stop error will be posted. This is useful for protecting equipment connected to the process axis in such a case as the torque capacity of the motor exceeds that of the hardware being driven.

The torque monitor function is setup and enabled by the first two items in the process axis setup screen (see section for further details). These items are the current limit and the fault time. The current limit is specified in amps and represents an absolute value of the commanded current from the servo amplifier. The fault time is specified in milliseconds and represents the amount

<!-- PDF page 1667 -->

of time for which the absolute value of the commanded motor current must exceed the specified current limit for the alarm to be posted.

When the commanded motor current has exceed the “Current limit” value from the Process Axis Setup menu for at least the number of milliseconds defined by “Curr Lim fault after” in the setup menu, then the following alarm will be posted:

ISDT-014 Torque Limit on Ax:#

This alarm will stop program execution and robot motion, in addition to stopping the process axes.

If the commanded motor current exceeds the current limit for only a brief period of time, specifically a period of time that is less than “Curr Lim fault after” in the setup menu, and then returns to a value below the limit, then no alarm will occur.

If a value of zero is specified under “Curr Lim fault after” in the setup menu, then the alarm will be posted immediately when the commanded current exceeds the limit.

If a value of zero is specified for the current limit in the setup menu, then the torque monitor function is disabled and motor current will not be checked.

### 14.42.2 EXTERNAL PROCESS AXES CONTROL (R824)

#### 14.42.2.1 Overview

External Process Axes Control (R824) is a software option that allows an External Device (such as a PLC) to control the speed of FANUC Process Axes (Motors). It is NOT for position control.

The External Device sends speed command and control signals to, and receives status outputs from the FANUC controller using Group Inputs / Outputs, and Digital Inputs / Outputs.

External Process Axes Control option (R824) is based on the Basic Process Axes software option (R689). All the restrictions and software options that are mutually excluded from the Basic Process Axes option also applies to the External Process Axes Control (R824).

Refer to Section 14.42.1 as a reference.

External Process Axes Control (R824) is an enhancement that provides the following key functions:

- External Device (such as PLC) commands process axes speed (in user defined units) using Group Inputs
- FANUC controller outputs actual process axes speed (in user defined units) using Group Outputs.
- FANUC controller outputs process axes torque (converted from Amperes to user defined units)

<!-- PDF page 1668 -->

- FANUC controller outputs a Process Usage accumulated value in Group Output in user defined units.

Note The units cc/min, cc/rev are only example units for illustration purposes.

The relationship between motor speed and process speed is:

process speed [cc/min] = (motor speed [rpm]/gear_ratio) * usr_scale [cc/rev]

or

motor speed [rpm] = process speed [cc/min] / usr_scale [cc/rev] * gear_ratio

If

IS_GI_SCALE[a] = gear_ratio / usr_scale

then

motor speed [rpm] = process speed [cc/min] * IS_GI_SCALE[a] [rev/cc]

Figure 14–178. External Process Axes Control

> **Image description -- img-31.jpeg:** The diagram illustrates a control system for fluid flow regulation using a gear pump. Key components include a Digital Signal Processor (DSP) generating pulses (pulse/msec), a gear mechanism with an input speed W_in (rpm) and output speed W_o (rpm), and process equipment receiving fluid flow. The DSP outputs pulses to control the gear's input speed. The gear ratio relates W_in to W_o. The output speed W_o drives the gear pump, which delivers fluid to the process equipment. The fluid flow rate (Gf) is measured in cubic centimeters per minute (cc/min) and is controlled by the gear pump's output speed. The diagram also includes a user-scalable parameter (usr_scale) in cubic centimeters per revolution (cc/rev), indicating the pump's displacement per revolution. The relationship between the gear's output speed and the fluid flow rate is governed by this displacement parameter.

Note Process axes cannot share a brake with a robot. If the process motors have brakes you must use brake 2 or 3 and a brake module.

### 14.43 PROGRAM SHIFT UTILITY

The program shift utility allows you to offset the positions of an entire teach pendant program or a portion of a teach pendant program. This is an easy way to adjust a teach pendant program after a fixture or the physical location of a robot has been changed.

<!-- PDF page 1671 -->

Note PaintTool and line tracking applications commonly use the program adjust function. Use of this utility is not recommended for PaintTool and line tracking applications.

Shifting a program can be accomplished either as a

- Parallel shift
- Parallel and rotational shift

You can shift the positions of an entire program or a portion of a program from within a program or from one program to another. In this way, robot paths can be transferred from one program to another or one robot to another in order to perform backups. See Figure 14–181 and Figure 14–182.

# Parallel Shift

A parallel shift of a program is accomplished by reteaching the location of one point from the original (source) program, to the destination program. See Figure 14–183.

Figure 14–183. Parallel Shift

# Parallel and Rotational Shift

A parallel and rotational shift is accomplished by reteaching the location of three points from the original (source) program (P1, P2 and P3) to the destination program (Q1, Q2 and Q3). See Figure 14–184.

Figure 14–184. Parallel and Rotational Shift

The points P1, P2, and P3 are connected to Q1, Q2, and Q3 respectively by dashed lines, indicating a shift or transformation from the original program to the shifted program. The diagram also includes labels for 'Source position' near P1 and 'Destination position' near Q1, suggesting that the shift involves moving from the source position in the original program to the destination position in the shifted program. The overall concept conveyed is the spatial or positional shift between two programs, with specific reference points illustrating the transformation.

# Extended Axes

Extended (Ext) axes determines how the program shift function will translate the program when you are using extended axes. Figure 14–185 displays a key for use with Figure 14–186 through Figure 14–188

The diagram visually represents the concept of the robot's Tool Center Point (T.C.P.) being positioned relative to the robot's base along the extended axes.

### 14.44 REFERENCE POSITION UTILITY

A reference position defines position limits within which an output signal will turn on. To use the reference position utility you specify a joint position for each axis of your robot, assign an output signal to the position, and, optionally, specify tolerance ranges for each axis joint position.

When the robot moves to within the tolerance range of the specified reference position joint axis locations, the assigned digital output (DO) or robot output (RO) signal turns on. When the robot moves out of the tolerance range, the DO or RO signal turns off. If a tolerance range is not specified, every axis of the robot must be at the EXACT reference position joint axis location for the signal to turn on.

To use a reference position, your program must contain a taught joint position whose axes locations match those of the reference position.

In a multiple motion group system, independent reference positions are available for each group, as follows:

- For group 1, 10 independent reference positions are available, and a digital output is available for each of these reference positions.
- For groups 2–8, one reference position and one digital output is available for each group.

Note You can increase the number of reference positions for each motion group by setting the system variable $REFPOSMAXNUM[n], where "n" is the number of the motion group. The maximum number of reference positions is 64. If you want to change the number of reference positions, change the value of $REFPOSMAXNUM[n] for the motion group you want to change. Turn off and then turn on the controller for the change to take effect. The maximum number of enabled reference positions at any one time is 10.

The Reference Position Output operates in all modes - T1, T2, and Auto.

Two screens are associated with the reference position utility: the LISTING screen and the DETAIL screen. The listing screen allows you to view limited information for all reference positions. The detail screen allows you to view all information for a single reference position.

Table 14–121 lists and describes each item on the LISTING screen. Table 14–122 lists and describes each item on the DETAIL screen.

### 14.45 RESUME OFFSET

Resume Offset allows the Restart move to go to a previous position of the path, “offset” from the normal stop position. Processes that are continuous along the path, such as cutting, welding, or dispensing, use this feature. For example, sealant dispensing applications are sensitive to the TCP speed, so resume offset is used to allow time to accelerate to speed along the path before reaching the original stop position and resuming sealant flow.

### 14.45.1 Limitations of Resume Offset

- Resume Offset requires Original Path Resume. Resume Offset is subject to the limitations of Original Path Resume.
- Resume Offset uses the same Restart move as Original Path Resume. The Restart move goes directly to the Resume Offset stop position, not backward along the original path.
- The actual Resume Offset position will be close to the desired offset, but usually not exact.

### 14.45.2 Constant Path Resume Offset

Constant Path Resume Offset works in conjunction with the Constant Path Option to maintain a “memory” of the TCP path, so that at the end of Hold the stop position can be offset to any

<!-- PDF page 1686 -->

position in recent memory. The Resume move will accelerate from the offset stop position, follow the identical path to the original stop position, and then continue execution normally.

Figure 14–192. Hold With Constant Path Resume Offset — Path Resumes from Offset Stop Position

> **Image description -- img-45.jpeg:** The diagram illustrates a path control mechanism with a 'Hold With Constant Path Resume Offset' feature. It shows a curved path with five labeled points: P[1], P[2], P[3], and P[4]. The path starts at P[1], moves through P[2], and continues to P[3] and P[4]. A section of the path between P[2] and P[3] is highlighted as the 'Hold Stop Position,' where the path temporarily stops. From this hold position, a dashed line labeled 'Hold With Constant Path Resume Offset' indicates that the path resumes from an offset stop position, bypassing the hold stop point. The 'Original Path' is shown as a solid line continuing from P[3] to P[4], while the 'Restart' direction is indicated by an arrow pointing from the hold stop position back toward the path. The operational meaning is that the path can be paused at a specific point and resumed from an offset position, maintaining continuity without retracing the exact hold stop point.

### 14.45.3 Limitations of Constant Path Resume Offset

- Constant Path Resume Offset requires the Constant Path option. Constant Path Resume Offset is subject to the limitations of the Constant Path option.
- Constant Path Resume Offset requires the offset distance to be set before the robot has stopped due to Hold. Changing the offset distance after Hold but before Resume has no effect.
- Constant Path Resume Offset can't offset past the beginning of recent memory. Attempting to do so will only move to the earliest position in recent memory. The recent memory size can be increased using the Setup->Resume Offset menu.

### 14.45.4 Non-Constant Path Resume Offset

Non-Constant Path Resume Offset computes the offset on the current segment, not on the path. It is used in situations where Constant Path Resume Offset is not supported. The resumed path is generally not on the original path, but will be close for applications with slow program speeds or limited corner blending.

<!-- PDF page 1687 -->

With Non-Constant Path Resume Offset, the offset distance can be changed any time until resume.
There is no need to set the offset distance before Hold is complete.

Figure 14–193. Hold with non-Constant Path Resume Offset — Path Resumes from Offset Stop Position

> **Image description -- img-46.jpeg:** The image is a diagram illustrating a path with a non-constant path resume offset. It shows a curved path starting at point P[1] and ending at point P[4], passing through intermediate points P[2] and P[3]. The path is divided into segments with labels indicating key positions and actions. The 'Offset Step Position' is marked near P[1], indicating where the path deviates from the original trajectory. The 'Hold Stop Position' is marked near P[3], indicating where the path pauses. The 'Resume' action is shown as a dashed line starting from the 'Hold Stop Position' and reconnecting to the original path near P[4]. The 'Original Path' is depicted as a dashed curve that the path attempts to follow after resuming. The diagram visually explains the concept of pausing a path at a specific point and then resuming it from that position, potentially deviating from the original path before reconnecting.

### 14.45.5 Limitations of non-Constant Path Resume Offset

- Non-Constant Path Resume Offset records a stop position on the taught segment, not necessarily on the path. This can lead to path deviation at resume.
- Non-Constant Path Resume Offset can't offset past the start position of the current segment. Attempting to do so will only move to the start position of the current segment.

### 14.45.6 Selecting Resume Offset Type

Table 14–123 describes how the style of Resume Offset is selected:

<!-- PDF page 1688 -->

When Constant Path option is loaded and Constant Path Resume is used, the value of $CPCFG.$RESUME_OFST.$RO_ENABLE determines whether or not Resume Offset is applied.

When Constant Path option is not loaded, non-Constant Path Resume Offset is used.

Some options do not support Constant Path Resume. When these options are used, Non-Constant Path Resume is used. These options include:

- Touch Sensing
- Line Tracking

#### 14.45.7 Resume Offset Setup Menu

The Resume Offset Setup Menu is used to configure the recent memory for Constant Path Resume Offset. This configuration has a direct effect on system memory usage. Changes to the configuration require a power cycle to take effect.

### 14.46 ROBOT-PC COMMUNICATIONS MACROS

### 14.46.1 Overview

A teach pendant program can coordinate with a program running on a PC using the macros described in this section. These macros "wake up" the PC application by raising an Event and optionally Send Data that can be used immediately by the PC program.

The robot to PC communication macros require you to have the PC communication option loaded, and requires that you have a program developed under PCDK running on a host PC. Refer to the PC Developer's Kit Help file for details on writing this program.

The five communication macros are listed below.

- Send Event( )
- Send Data( )
- Send SysVar( )
- Get Data( )
- Request Menu( )

<!-- PDF page 1690 -->

The following sections describe the syntax and parameters for the communication macros.

### 14.46.2 Send Event ( )

The Send Event macro is used to send (or signal) an Event to the PC. To receive this Event, the PC must be running an application based on the FANUC Robot Server and have an FRCPacketEvent Event Handling active, waiting for this request code.

Table 14–125 lists and describes the Send Event macro. Send Event Sample Teach Pendant Program shows a sample teach pendant program that uses the Send Event macro.

Table 14–125. Send Event Macro Description

[tbl-41.md](tbl-41.md)

### Send Event Sample Teach Pendant Program

PROG TEST1
1: ! Send Event 5
2: ! No answer from PC
3: Send Event (5)
PROG TEST2
1: ! Send Event 7
2: ! Wait for PC answer
3: ! Answer in Reg 5
4: Send Event (7,1,5)
5: If R[5]<9999,JMP LBL[10]
6: ! Error in macro

<!-- PDF page 1691 -->

7: !
8: LBL[10]

#### 14.46.3 Send Data()

The Send Data macro is used to send up to seven values to a PC application that is waiting for the event. The request code tells the PC application what data is being sent and what the PC is supposed to do with it.

Table 14–126 lists and describes the Send Data macro. Send Data Sample Teach Pendant Program shows a sample teach pendant program that uses the Send Data macro.

Table 14–126. Send Data Macro Description

[tbl-42.md](tbl-42.md)

# Send Data Sample Teach Pendant Program

PROG TEST1

1: ! Send Event 42 and Data
2: ! No answer from PC
3: Send Data(42,0,0,'PARTS_ITEM3',R[1],5,6,7.1,8,

<!-- PDF page 1692 -->

'TOOL_ITEM1')
PROG TEST2
1: ! Send Event 9 and data
2: ! Wait for PC answer
3: ! Answer in REG 3
4: Send data (9,1,3,'TOOLING',R[1],5,'TEST')
5: IF R[3]<9999,JMP LBL[10]
6: ! Error in macro
7: !
8: LBL[10]

### 14.47 RSI INTERFACE

Remote Sensor Interface (RSI) is a function that facilitates communication with an RSI device. This function sends position data, etc., to the device, which supports RSI in real time.

The order number of this function is “RSI Interface” (J802).

Sending time is better with this function if one of the following Main boards, with a fast communication processor (COMM CPU), is ordered.

- Main board C (Force sensor I/F, fast communication processor) A05B-2600-H003
- Main board F (Force sensor I/F, fast communication processor, I/O Link i slave compliant) A05B-2600-H006

Data is sent by the robot controller through the Ethernet port UDP communication to the external device every communication interval of this function regardless of the selected COMM CPU. The current communication interval is set by means of the system variable $RSI.$INTERVAL.

There are 2 types of Cartesian positional data that this option sends: Measured and Forward. Both are represented in XYZWPR format.

The Measured Position is the actual position to which the robot moved. The Measured Position is abbreviated as M_*, where * are each of the XYZWPR positional elements.

The Forward Position is the robot pre-planned position; by default, three interpolation times ahead of the actual (or Measured) position. Forward Position is abbreviated as F_*, where * are each of the XYZWPR positional elements.

<!-- PDF page 1696 -->

Figure 14–194 depicts the relationship between the Forward Position and the Measured Position

Figure 14–194. Relationship Between Forward and Measured Position

> **Image description -- img-47.jpeg:** The diagram illustrates a timeline-based comparison between forward predictions and measured values over past, current, and future time points. The timeline is divided into three segments: past (t0-3, t0-2, t0-1), current time (t0), and future (t0+1, t0+2). Two rows are shown: the top row labeled 'Forward' (F*) and the bottom row labeled 'Measured' (M*). Each row contains labeled ovals representing predicted or measured values at specific time points (e.g., Ft0, Ft0+1, M t0-3, M t0-2). The forward predictions (F*) are shown as a sequence of future states extending from the past into the future, with arrows indicating the progression of time. The measured values (M*) are similarly arranged but represent actual observed data. The diagram highlights two key annotations: 'Ft0 will be reached at t0' and 'Ft0+2 will be reached at t0+2,' indicating the alignment between forward predictions and actual measurements at specific times. The overall concept conveyed is the comparison and alignment of predicted future states with actual measured states over time.

When the target position is planned in the robot controller, the target position data is immediately sent to the external device via RSI, but the actual move is delayed by the delay time contained in a variable (\(AVC_GRP[1].\)AVC_MODE[2]). Therefore, there may be a delay when this function is enabled and the delay time is set. The cycle time may become slightly longer; the communication interval time is set in \(RSI\).\(INTERVAL\) (units in milliseconds).

Time Before and Distance Before functions would consequently shift by the same amount.

When this option is not ordered, the robot will move just after the target position is internally planned by the robot controller.

    <f_y>1931.863</f_y>
    <f_z>1295.158</f_z>
    <f_w>-91.728728</f_w>
    <f_p>17.543543/F_p>
    <f_r>177.519519</f_r>
    <iPOSTat>0</iPOSTat>
    <bMode>3</bMode>
    <trg>0</trg>

<myRob>0</myRob>
<IPOC>27189883</IPOC>
</Rob>

### 14.47.2 Setting

Set the robot controller IP address and subnet mask etc. in the screen displayed by pressing the following key sequence; MENU -> 6 SETUP -> Host Comm. -> TCP/IP.

Set the following system variables. To enable the change in settings, perform a COLD START or HOT START.

$AVC_GRP[1].$AVC_MODE[1] Default : 1

0: Disable this function (no robot data will be streamed to device)

1: Enable this function

$AVC_GRP[1].$AVC_MODE[2] Default : 0 (Max value is 20)

Delay time

F_* is 3 communication interval faster than M_* when this variable is set to 0.

When you set n to this variable, F_* becomes (n+3) communication interval faster than M_*.

$RSI.$INT_PORT Default:2

1: Using Main board Ethernet port 1 (CD38A)

2: Using Main board Ethernet port 2 (CD38B)

<!-- PDF page 1699 -->

# $RSI.$INTERVAL

Communication interval is showed to this variable with ms unit. Value is set at power-on time.

This system variable can't be changed.

# $RSI.$PRIORITY Default:16

Priority of communication task in COMM CPU.

If jitter performance is not enough, change this system variable to lower value.

1 is highest priority.

255 is lowest priority. (Not running.)

# $RSI.$PORT_NUM Default:31439

Source port number of the robot in UDP communication.

##### 14.47.2.1 Configuration of the Data Connection

On a PC, using any text editor, create the following configuration XML file and copy it manually to the controller at the main root of FR:

Its file name can be selected by using RSI_CREATE, which is a KAREL program used to set the communication setting (Section 14.47.3).

e.g. abc.xml

<CONFIG>
<IP_NUMBER>136.230.168.112</IP_NUMBER>
<PORT>6008</PORT>
<SENTYPE>IPFO</SENTYPE>
<ONLYSEND>TRUE</ONLYSEND>
</CONFIG>

# Remarks:

Start tag and end tag should be exactly same case sensitive.

IP_NUMBER = IP address of the RSI device

PORT = Port number of the RSI device.

SENTYPE = Any name describing external device.

ONLYSEND = Unidirectional (TRUE) or bidirectional (FALSE) data connection. Only Unidirectional (TRUE) is supported. If ONLYSEND is set other than to TRUE, STOP global alarm “HOST-390 RSI: ONLYSEND in RSI configuration XML should be TRUE” will occur.

## 14.48 SAFETY SPACE (OPTION)

### 14.48.1 Overview

Safety Space allows you to specify strict limits for detecting robot collisions. You can determine the parts of the motion path where collisions are more likely to occur and increase the Collision Guard sensitivity to collisions for those particular areas. The Safety Space settings do not affect Collision Guard global settings.

### 14.48.2 Requirements

The Collision Guard option must be installed and active for the Safety Space function to work properly. Refer to the Software Installation Manual for more information.

Note Accurate specifications of the payload characteristics are required to maximize the accuracy of this function and to avoid false detections.

In the sample program shown in Sample Safety Space Program, the path defined by points P[1], P[2], and P[3] is considered the safety space.

### Sample Safety Space Program

1: J P[1] 100% FINE
2: CALL SFSPC
3: L P[2] 200mm/sec CNT100
4: L P[3] 200m/sec FINE
5: CALL SFSPCEND

<!-- PDF page 1705 -->

6: L P[4] 2000mm/sec FINE

### 14.48.3 Operation

Use Procedure 14-78 to call the Safety Space function.

In the SFSPC macro program, the lines that assign values to $SBR system variables should set the values to the default settings for the first run. After running the program, the actual values for maximum and minimum disturbance torque are obtained from $MOR_GRP system variables in Step 7 and Step 8. When the actual disturbance is known, the SFSPC macro program can be changed according to the formulas in Step 7 and Step 8.

### Procedure 14-78 Calling the Safety Space Function

#### Conditions

- The Collision Guard option is installed and active. Refer to the Software Installation Manual for more information.

#### Steps

1. Insert the CALL SFSPC instruction where you want the safety space function to begin.
2. Insert the CALL SFSPCEND instruction where you want the safety space function to end.
3. Delete any unnecessary groups and joints within the SFSPC and SFSPCEND macro programs.

Note Step 4 through Step 8 assume that you want to detect collisions that affect axis 1 the most. If you want to monitor axes in motion groups other than motion group 1, change the index in the system variable to the appropriate number. For example, to monitor axis 1 of the second group, refer to $SCR_GRP[2].$axisorder[1]. The value of this variable should be used as the index for $SBR. Assuming that $SCR_GRP[2].$axisorder[1] = 7, SFSPC can be changed to reference $SBR[7].$param[119].

4. Set the value of the system variable $SBR[1].$param[119] to a default value (for example, $SBR[1].$param[119] = 30000).
5. Set the value of the system variable $SBR[1].$param[120] to a default value (for example, $SBR[1].$param[120] = -30000).
6. Execute the Safety Space portion of the program to determine the values for SFSPC.
7. Replace the value 30000 with ($MOR_GRP[1].$MAX_DIS_TRQ[1] + 728)
8. Replace the value -30000 with ($MOR_GRP[1].$MIN_DIS_TRQ[1] - 728)

<!-- PDF page 1706 -->

### 14.49 SERVO TOOL (Option)

Servo Tool is an option that simplifies and improves programming for servo grippers or other servo-driven axes.

This option provides a schedule-based user interface that allows the user to specify torque limits for specified auxiliary or robot axes. The Servo Tool TP instruction allows the user to call a particular servo tool schedule during TP program execution.

Also, this option provides high sensitive part detecting function that can be used in any section of regular program flow or in jogging conditions.

Warning

Enabling Servo Tool on robot axes could cause damage to equipment or personnel due to low motor torque and reduced error checking.

### 14.49.1 Benefits

ServoTool provides the following benefits:

- Gives the user a way to program the amount of torque needed without any slowdown, hesitation, or faulty position reporting.
- Automatically adjusts the error checking level to be suitable with the system when torque is low and the specified axis is not responsive.
- Automatically updates the program position to the contact position when Servo Tool is used. No extra programming logic is required.
- Provides a schedule-based user interface to allow users to assign torque limits for a specified auxiliary or robot axis.
- Provides a special TP instruction to call a particular servo tool schedule during TP program execution.
- Allows the robot to maintain the position where contact is made and increase actual torque to overcome the motion dynamics limitation without crushing the part.
- Provides high sensitive part detecting functions with various detecting methods including disturbance torque, torque, and position.

Warning

Regular error checking will be reduced or disabled when Servo Tool is enabled. Verify the path with extra caution.

<!-- PDF page 1707 -->

### 14.49.2 Limitations

Servo Tool has the following limitations:

- When used in Single Step mode or when the program is paused, the ServoTool [ ] TP instruction will only activate the torque limit servo setting. No position update or offset will be applied. Longer execution time for motion instructions can be expected.
- When a program aborts, all torque limits will be reset to 100% value and error checking limits will be reset to their default values.
- As with other TP instructions, if the program resumes or skips to the motion instructions between ServoTool [] and ServoTool End, no ServoTool schedule will be used.
- Multi-arm multi-tasking application is not supported.
- If DCS includes Servo Tool enabled axes, a DCS FB_CMP alarm may occur when or after Servo Tool is used. If needed, this can be resolved by setting $DCS_CFG.$EXCLUDE to -1. However, please refer to DCS manual for details.

Note If $DCS_CFG.$EXCLUDE[motion group] is set to -1, Position/Speed Check function cannot be used in this motion group.

# Warning

Motor torque is low and regular error checking is disabled when a program is paused while Servo Tool is enabled.

### 14.49.3 Program Instruction

The SERVOTOOL[ ], SERVOTOOL END, and SERVOTOOL END[ ] TP instructions can be used in TP programs whenever needed.

# SERVOTOOL[schedule number]

When the robot executes this TP instruction, the following occurs:

- A special set of servo parameters is updated in real time to make sure the specified torque limit is used.
- Error checking is open.
- Quick stop is used at the moment when contact is made (for example, at gripper contact with the part). This prevents hesitation that could affect cycle time.
- If Auto Position Update is enabled, the controller remembers the contact position for the specific axis, and applies it to the next moves until SERVOTOOL END is executed.

Torque limits and position offsets can be kept in the subsequent motion lines until SERVOTOOL END is reached.

<!-- PDF page 1708 -->

#### SERVOTOOL END/SERVOTOOL END[schedule number]

When the program reaches the SERVOTOOL END command, there is no delay or hesitation before the next motion. The following occurs:

- Torque limit is reset to its default value.
- Error checking is reset to normal.
- The internal position is updated.

Note SERVOTOOL END[schedule number] can be used to disable Servo Tool per the schedule. However, if multiple Servo Tool enabled axes are configured in the same group, even though SERVOTOOL END[schedule number] may be disabled independently, all motion in the same group needs to be stopped at the same time; therefore all axes in the same group may still be affected.

#### Example Program Fragment

:
4: ServoTool [1]
5: L P[3] 1500mm/s FINE
6: J P[4] 100% CNT100
7: ServoTool End

Figure 14–197. Servo Tool

> **Image description -- img-49.jpeg:** The image depicts a robotic arm system with two grippers, each shown in two different states: programmed position and actual stopped position. The left side of the image shows a close-up of the grippers with labeled positions. The top left shows a gripper in the programmed position labeled 'P[4]' with a red arrow pointing downward, and the actual stopped position labeled 'P'[4]' with a red arrow pointing upward. Skip standard TP instruction can be used to monitor $SV_DETECT[group].$DETECTED system
variable to switch program flow when collision detected.

### 14.49.5 Detection

You can set up Servo Tool for high sensitive detecting function in many different conditions. $SV_DETECT[group].$DETECTED can be used to monitor detecting condition after $SV_DETECT[group].$TRIGGER has been set any number greater 0. For example, High Speed Skip standard TP instruction can be used to monitor $SV_DETECT[group].$DETECTED system variable to switch program flow when collision detected.

### System Variables

All detecting required system variables are in group based $SV_DETECT system variable.

- $SV_DETECT[].$ENABLE[]: These axis based variables are used to determine which axes will be used to detect.
- $SV_DETECT[].$TOL[]: These axis based variables are used to determine the detecting tolerance for each enabled axis. The default value is 5% of max torque (if torque is used to detect) or standard disturbance torque margin value (if disturbance torque is used to detect).
- $SV_DETECT[].$DET_TYPE: This variable determines the detecting type. 0 is disturbance torque (default) and 1 is motor torque.
- $SV_DETECT[].$ALGO: This variable determines the detecting algorithm.0: the upper and lower limits in $SV_DETECT[].$DET_LIMIT[1].$UPLIM[axis] and in $SV_DETECT[].$DET_LIMIT[1].$LOWLIM[axis] will be used to determine detection occurred or not. 1: only positive value of $SV_DETECT[].$DET_TYPE will be used to set detection flag. 2:: only negative value of $SV_DETECT[].$DET_TYPE will be used to set detection flag. 4: absolute value of $SV_DETECT[].$DET_TYPE over $SV_DETECT[].$DET_LIMIT[1].$UPLIM[axis] will be used to set detection flag.
- $SV_DETECT[].$DET_LIMIT[1].UPLIM[]: These axis based variables are upper limits for detection when $SV_DETECT[].$ALGO is 0 or 4.
- $SV_DETECT[].$DET_LIMIT[1].LOWLIM[]: These axis based variables are lower limits for detection when $SV_DETECT[].$ALGO is 0.
- $SV_DETECT[].$LEARN: This variable is used for automatically learning the upper and lower limits when $SV_DETECT[].$ALGO is 0. Please set $SV_DETECT[].$DET_LIMIT[1].UPLIM[] to large negative values, for example, -10000

<!-- PDF page 1711 -->

and \(SV_DETECT[].\)DET_LIMIT[1].LOWLIM[] to large positive values, for example, 10000, to make this learning works.

- \(SV_DETECT[].\)TRIGGER: This variable is used for start detecting or learning (if \(LEARN\) is 1). To bypass the region which easy to cause mis-detection, this variable can be set to any value greater than 1 to start counting down. The recommended value is 20.
- \(SV_DETECT[].\)DETECTED: This variable is used for start detecting or learning (if \(LEARN\) is 1). To bypass the region which easy to cause mis-detection, this variable can be set to any value greater than 1 to start counting down. The recommended value is 20. This variable will be set when trigger starts (also \(LEARN\) is 0) and the detection criterion met.

#### Program Example (with high speed skip)

For example, the original program is:

1: J P[1] 100% FINE
2: L P[2] 2000mm/s CNTO
3: L P[3] 800mm/s CNT100
4: L P[4] 2000mm/s CNT100
5: J P[5] 100% FINE

If extra protection is required for line 3. \(SV_DETECT[].\)DETECTED can be used combined with High Speed Skip

1: J P[1] 100% FINE
2: SKIP CONDITION $SV_DETECT[1].$DETECTED = 1
2: L P[2] 2000mm/s CNTO
3: $SV_DETECT[1].$TRIGGER = 20
3: L P[3] 800mm/s CNT100, SKIP LBL[1], PR[1] = LPOS
4: L P[6] 2000mm/s CNT100
5: LBL[1]
6: $SV_DETECT[1].$TRIGGER = 0
7: L P[4] 2000mm/s CNT100
8: J P[5] 100% FINE

#### Operation

1. Modify the program to turn on $SV_DETECT[].$ENABLE[] for the desired axes.
2. Set \(SV_DETECT[].\)DET_LIMIT[1].UPLIM[] to large negative values and \(SV_DETECT[].\)DET_LIMIT[1].LOWLIM[] to large positive values.
3. Execute the modified program with \(SV_DETECT[].\)LEARN = 1. Please be careful to only set \(SV_DETECT[].\)LEARN = 1 when the program is ready to be played back completely from start to end and no more program logic or position changes are required.
4. Verify that \(SV_DETECT[].\)DET_LIMIT[1].UPLIM[] and \(SV_DETECT[].\)DET_LIMIT[1].LOWLIM[] have been set automatically with proper values.
5. Turn off $SV_DETECT[].$LEARN and start normal program execution.

<!-- PDF page 1712 -->

6. If mis-detection happens, $SV_DETECT[].$TOL[] can be used to fine tune sensitivity.

### 14.50 SHAPE GENERATION 3 (OPTION)

#### 14.50.1 Overview

The Shape Generation 3 option simplifies cutting two dimensional shapes. The software also reduces online programming time by reducing the number of required taught robot positions and providing features such as shape cut interface.

The following shapes can be cut using the Shape Generation 3 option:

- Circles
- Hexagons
- Rectangles
- Slots
- Key slots
- Pommels
- Custom

To use the Shape Generation 3 option, you must do the following:

1. Set up default shape information - Section 14.50.3
2. Generate shape programs for the shapes you want to cut - Section 14.50.7
3. Include process instructions within the generated shape program - Procedure 14-83

# Warning

Make sure your program stops the process (such as laser or water jet cutting) when an error occurs. The Shape Generation 3 option does not automatically turn off the process equipment when an error occurs. For example, if you are cutting shapes using a laser or water jet, you must write the program so that the process shuts off if an error occurs. If you do not, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

4. Create a production program that calls the generated shape programs - Step 9

# Caution

Shape Gen will only generate programs for a single group. Multi-Group motion is not supported.

<!-- PDF page 1713 -->

### 14.50.2 Quick Start Hints

# **Setup**

Under SETUP, you will find “Shapes”. This is where you can change the default data for “Step to center” as well as the data for each shape. This is the default data and all items can be changed at the time of shape creation.

Note “Step to center” is programmable, so setting it here is not critical. Setting or clearing FLAG 101 in the main or calling program, will dictate this behavior when running a shape program.

# **Shape Gen**

Shape Generation 3 creates complete independent programs; it does not create these shapes “on the fly” like the original Shape Generation. All shapes must be completed before any “production” start is initiated.

# **Create or Edit**

Under UTILITIES, you will find ” Shape Gen”. This is where you will choose which shape to work with. Most of these parameters are taken from the original Shape Generation Feature, so they will function the same way.

# **Edit**

If you have created a program with this utility already, simply go to the type of shape created and press DETAIL; then from the second item (Program Name) press F4 (CHOICE) to select the program to modify

### 14.50.3 Shape Setup

You can set up detailed information before you use the Shape Generation 3 option. You will specify this information in the SETUP Shapes DETAIL screens. The information you specify in these screens will become the default information that applies to all shapes you generate using the Shape Generation 3 option.

You can set up data to define how you want to generate the following shapes:

- Circle
- Hexagon
- Rectangle
- Slot
- Keyhole
- Pommel
- Custom

# Procedure 14-81 Using the SETUP Shape and DETAIL Screens

# Steps

1. Press MENU.
2. Select SETUP.
3. Press F1, [TYPE] and select Shapes.

7. To display help information, press F5, HELP.

# Procedure 14-82 Setting Up a Custom Shape

# Steps

1. Define the path: Create a template teach pendant program that will define a special shape with the x, y and z coordinates of the shape to be cut from a reference point. The data must include the reference point, Cut Start Point (with lead in if desired), End Point (with overlap or runoff if required) and all intermediate points.

The custom shape template program is flexible and can have any TP instruction that is needed for the shape. These templates will be duplicated and the points updated for the TCP location at the time of shape creation. The following screen shows an example template program.

TRIANG60.TP
1: !Template for 60deg triangle ;
2:L P[1] 2000mm/sec FINE ;
3:L P[2] 100mm/sec CNT100 ;
4: CALL PROC_ON1 ;
5:L P[3] 100mm/sec CNT100 ;
6:L P[4] 100mm/sec CNT100 ;
7: DO[1]=OFF ;
8:L P[5] 100mm/sec CNT100 ;
9: WAIT .50(sec) ;

<!-- PDF page 1730 -->

## 2. Create the custom shape template program.

# Caution

You must take precautions when selecting the TERM type. Otherwise, the shapes will not be accurate.

Note Only L (Linear) and C (Circular) type motions can be used. Use only x, y and z for entering point data. W, P, and R are always 0.

Note You can add up to 64 motion lines to the custom ShapeGen3 template program.

# Warning

You must not perform SHIFT TOUCHUP on any of the points because it is not intended to be executed as a stand-alone teach pendant program.

## 3. Set up Custom Shape Detail data : After you create the teach pendant program, set up the Custom Shape detail data.

a. Press MENU.
b. Select SETUP.
c. Press F1, TYPE and select Shapes.
d. Select Custom and press DETAIL. You will see a screen similar to the following.

[tbl-75.md](tbl-75.md)

e. Set custom shape details as desired. Refer to Table 14–146 for information on custom shape details.

#### 14.50.7 Generating a Shape Program from UTILITIES Shape Gen

Using Shape Generation 3 requires a minimum of two teach pendant programs:

- Generated Shape Programs. One or more TP programs created by the Shape Generation 3 option, using information you enter in the UTILITIES Shape Gen DETAIL screens. These

<!-- PDF page 1731 -->

programs define the paths to generate the shapes; they automatically include process-on and process-off instructions but they do not include additional motion statements.

- Production Program. A production TP program that you create to call the generated programs. This includes all other logic and motion statements required by your application.

# Warning

In your production program, you must be aware of the calling sequence of the shape programs for the proper execution of your application program. Otherwise, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

Make sure the production program stops the process (such as laser or water jet cutting) when an error occurs. The Shape Generation 3 option does not automatically turn the process equipment off when an error occurs. For example, if you are cutting shapes using a laser or water jet, you must write the production program so that the process shuts off if an error occurs. If you do not, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

# Generated Shape Programs

Instructions and information you provide are used by the Shape Generation 3 feature to generate the shapes you specify.

You will use the UTILITIES Shape Gen DETAIL screens to enter data for the particular shape you are defining; this data will override the default data you previously set up in the SETUP Shapes DETAIL screens.

In addition to the data you enter in the UTILITIES Shape Gen DETAIL screens, the system will use the following information to generate a shape program:

- Currently selected jog GROUP (for multi group systems)
- Current TOOL frame of the selected group
- Current USER frame of the selected group
- The location of the TCP of the GROUP that is selected. This will be the center point.
- PROC_ONx (where x is the GROUP number)
- PROC_OFx (where x is the GROUP number)

Note The generated shape programs will automatically include a process-on and a process-off CALL statement during the creation process. If these programs do not already exist, they will be created automatically. Once they are created, they will not be touched again by the system and you can add instructions for the process requirements.

# UTILITIES Shape Gen DETAIL Information

The UTILITIES Shape Gen DETAIL screens include the same information as the SETUP Shape DETAILS screens, with the addition of three items.

<!-- PDF page 1732 -->

Changing the data on these screens will affect only the current shape you are working on. When you press CREATE, the shape will be created with that data and you can immediately start using that program.

- Table 14–148 provides information about the items that appear only on the UTILITIES Shape Gen DETAIL screens.
- Refer to Table 14–139 for information about the items on the UTILITIES Shape Gen DETAILS screen that are common to all shapes.

#### Procedure 14-83 Generating or Modifying a Shape Program

##### Steps

1. Press MENU.
2. Select UTILITIES.
3. Press F1, TYPE.
4. Select Shape Gen and press ENTER. You will see a screen similar to the following:

Figure 14-212. UTILITIES Shape Gen Screen

UTILITIES Shape
Shape select:
1 Circle:
2 Slot:
3 Hexagon:
4 Rectangle
5 Keyhole:
6 Pommel:
7 Custom:

5. Select the shape you want to create or modify and press DETAIL.
6. Start a new program, select an existing program to edit, or copy an existing program:

• To start a new program,

1. Move the cursor to Create or Edit Program and press ENTER.
2. Type a name for the shape program that will be generated and press ENTER. The name of the new program will move to Program Name.

If all the default shape data is correct for the new program, go to Step 8 to generate the program.

If you want to modify the default data for the new program, go to Step 7.

If the original default data is not correct for your normal operation, you can modify it at the SETUP Shapes DETAIL screens. Refer to Section 14.50.4.

• To edit an existing program,

3. Move the cursor to Create or Edit Program and press F4, [CHOICE].

<!-- PDF page 1734 -->

4. Select the name of the program you want to modify and press ENTER.

- To copy an existing program if a generated shape program that you want to use for another shape of the same type already exists,
5. Move the cursor to Program Name and press CHOICE.
6. Select the name of the program you want to copy and press ENTER.
7. Move the cursor to Create or Edit Program and enter the new program name. The new program data will be copied from the existing one.

You can now go to Step 7 to modify data or go directly to Step 8 to generate the new program.

7. Modify shape data as desired. The modifications you make here will affect only the current shape. The default shape data will not change.

# Caution

If you leave the DETAIL screen before pressing CREATE to generate the program, when you return it will be re-populated from the default data. Any changes you made to data will be lost.

- For information about DETAIL screen items that are common to all shapes, refer to Table 14–139.
For information about DETAIL screen items that appear only on the UTILITIES DETAIL screen, refer to Table 14–148.
- For information about Circle-specific DETAIL screen items, refer to Table 14–140.
- For information about Slot-specific DETAIL screen items, refer to Table 14–143.
- For information about Hexagon-specific DETAIL screen items, refer to Table 14–141.
- For information about Rectangle-specific DETAIL screen items, refer to Table 14–142.
- For information about Keyhole-specific DETAIL screen items, refer to Table 14–144.
- For information about Pommel-specific DETAIL screen items, refer to Table 14–145.
- For information about Custom-specific DETAIL screen items, refer to Table 14–146.

8. To generate the program when all the information is correct, press CREATE. This will create the new shape program or re-create the existing program you edited.

Note When you press CREATE to generate a new program, the system will always use the current location of the group that is selected. However, if you are editing an existing program, the TCP that was recorded in the existing program will always be used. Changes you make to the TCP while editing the existing program will not take effect. If you want to move the center point, you must move the TCP to the new location and use TOUCHUP to re-record the TCP.

<!-- PDF page 1735 -->

9. Add your application and process-specific instructions to the PROC_ON and PROC_OFF instructions.

Note The instructions you enter in the PROC_ON and PROC_OFF instructions are never changed by the Shape Generation 3 option. Any other modifications made to the program logic will be lost when you press CREATE.

10. To run the program

a. Enable the Teach Pendant.
b. Press and hold the deadman switch.
c. Press and hold SHIFT.
d. Press TEST.

Note Single step is not supported from the TEST key. If you need to single step the program, go to the SELECT program screen and run it from there.

This will leave the TCP at the last point in the program. If you want to move back to the center point, move the cursor to Center position (located near the bottom of the screen). Press F4, TOUCHUP or F5, MOVETO to re-teach the center position or move to the center position.

If the shape is not exactly the way you want it to be, you can change the data in the UTILITIES Shape Gen DETAIL screen, then press CREATE again to re-create that shape. You will see a screen similar to the following:

This will DELETE the program
file and all of the
information that it contains.
Are you sure you want to
continue?

Caution

Pressing CREATE again will completely erase the current program and re-create it with the same name, using the data you set at the UTILITIES Shape Gen DETAIL screen. The instructions you enter in the PROC_ON and PROC_OFF instructions are never changed by the Shape Generation 3 option. Any other modifications made to the program logic will be lost when you press CREATE.

Examples of shape programs generated by the Shape Generation 3 option are shown in Figure 14–213 and Figure 14–214.

<!-- PDF page 1736 -->

Figure 14-213. Shape Generated Program Example ACIR1

/PROG ACIR1
/ATTR
OWNER = KAREL;
COMMENT = "Cut Circle GP1";
PROG_SIZE = 1169;
CREATE = DATE 07-04-16 TIME 14:33:56;
MODIFIED = DATE 07-04-16 TIME 14:33:56;
FILE_NAME = ;
VERSION = 0;
LINE_COUNT = 17;
MEMORY_SIZE = 1593;
PROTECT = READ;
TCD: STACK_SIZE = 0,
TASK_PRIORITY = 50,
TIME_SLICE = 0,
BUSY_LAMP_OFF = 0,
ABORT_REQUEST = 0,
PAUSE_REQUEST = 0;
DEFAULT_GROUP = 1, *, *, *, *, *;
CONTROL_CODE = 00000000 00000000;
/APPL
/MN
1: !SHAPE GENERATED CIRCLE ;
2: UTOOL_NUM=1 ;
3: UFRAME_NUM=0 ;
4: IF (F[101]=OFF), JMP LBL[1] ;
5:L P[1] 60mm/sec FINE ;
6: LBL[1] ;

# Production Program

Shape Generation 3 only creates shape programs. You must write a production application program that does cell operations, required startup checks, and calls the generated shapes for the specific operation.

<!-- PDF page 1738 -->

##### Warning

In your production program, you must be aware of the calling sequence of the shape programs for the proper execution of your application program. Otherwise, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

Make sure the production program stops the process (such as laser or water jet cutting) when an error occurs. The Shape Generation 3 option does not automatically turn the process equipment off when an error occurs. For example, if you are cutting shapes using a laser or water jet, you must write the production program so that the process shuts off if an error occurs. If you do not, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

Figure 14–215 shows a simple example of a production program.

Figure 14–215. Production Program Example

1: !Move robot to home ;

5: CALL ACIR1 ;
6: !Move above second circ point ;

9: !Move away for next part ;
10: ;

#### 14.50.8 Servo Schedules

Up to 20 servo schedules are available, if the Small Circle Accuracy (J644) option is loaded along with the Shape Generation 3 option. Schedule selection is included as part of the shape definition if Small Circle Accuracy is loaded.

The servo schedule feature can also be used without the Shape Generation 3 cut programs. In this case, a system macro is provided to manually access the servo schedules from a teach pendant program: SET_SRVO.TP.

##### Warning

When using the servo adjust macro to manually change the values of the servo gains, it is very important to reset the servo gains to their default values after the cut is performed. This ensures that the custom values that have been tuned for a specific cut are not used throughout the rest of the programmed motion. Otherwise, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

<!-- PDF page 1739 -->

Refer to Section 14.54 for more information.

### 14.51 SIMULATED INPUT SKIP

#### 14.51.1 Overview

Simulated Input Skip provides a way for TP programs that are WAITing on simulated inputs to continue after a specified time if the input condition is not satisfied. You can define a Simulated Input Wait Delay Time, that will apply to all programs, and to designate specific inputs as Skip When Simulated inputs.

With Simulated Input Skip enabled, if a running program executes a WAIT for an input that is simulated and designated as Skip When Simulated, the program will either continue when the input condition is satisfied or it will continue after the specified delay time.

#### 14.51.2 Setup

Two setup procedures are required to configure the system to use this feature.

You must:

- enable the feature
- designate any input points that are to be used with the feature as Skip When Simulated.

# Enabling Simulated Input Skip

1. Press MENU.
2. Select SYSTEM.
3. Press TYPE.
4. Select CONFIG. You should see a screen similar to the following:

System/Config
31 Signal to set in AUTO mode DO[ 0]
32 Signal to set in T1 mode DO[ 0]
33 Signal to set in T2 mode DO[ 0]
34 Signal to set if E-STOP DO[ 0]
35 Set if INPUT SIMULATED DO[ 0]
36 Sim. Input Wait Delay: 0.00 sec
37 Set if Sim. Skip Enabled DO[ 0]
38 Hand broken : <*GROUPS*>
39 Remote/Local setup: Remote
40 External I/O (ON:Remote) :DI[ 0]
41 UOP auto assignment: Full

<!-- PDF page 1740 -->

5. Move the cursor to Sim. Input Wait Delay and enter a value from 0 to 99.99. This setting is the time in seconds that a WAIT instruction will delay before continuing.
6. Move the cursor to Set if Sim. Skip Enabled and enter the index of a valid digital output that will be turned on to indicate that Simulated Input Skip is enabled. Valid numbers for this item are 0 through 32766.
7. Turn the controller off, then on again to recognize the change.

# Designating the Inputs to Time Out when Simulated

1. Press MENU.
2. Select I/O.
3. Press TYPE.
4. Select Digital or Robot and use the IN/OUT function key to select inputs. You will see a screen similar to the following:

7. Move the cursor to Skip when simulated and press

• TRUE to set the timeout designation, or
- FALSE to clear the timeout designation.

8. Press PRV-PT or NXT-PT to do the same setting for other input points.
