On this screen, any points that have been designated as Skip When Simulated will have parenthesis ‘( )’ in the Sim column. If you have an iPendant, if the point is simulated, the Sim entry will be highlighted in green.

#### 14.51.3 Operation

After you set up Simulated Input Skip and designate input points as simulated and Skip when simulated, you can use these inputs in a WAIT instruction in any teach pendant program. The WAIT statement will time out if the wait condition is not satisfied. The WAIT statement does not need any additional clauses.

The following are examples of this type of WAIT instruction:

WAIT DI[1] = ON
WAIT DI[2] = OFF-
WAIT RI[1] <> DO[5]

##### Limitations

There are two restrictions on the use of Simulated Input Skip in a WAIT instruction.

- If the WAIT instruction contains a TIMEOUT clause, the instruction will time out based on the clause rather than the Simulated Input Skip, even if Simulated Input Skip is enabled and a Skip when simulated input is used in the instruction. After time out, program execution will continue at the label specified in the TIMEOUT clause.

<!-- PDF page 1742 -->

- The WAIT instruction must contain only one condition, and not several ANDed or ORed together. For example, the following instructions will not time out even if Simulated Input Skip is enabled and if they contain 'Skip when simulated' inputs.

WAIT DI[1] = ON AND DI[2] = ON
WAIT DI[1] = ON OR RI[2] = ON OR RI[3] = ON

##### Program Example

The following is an example of a program that can use Simulated Input Skip. If all of the inputs to the left of the operators are designated as Skip When Simulated and if they are all simulated, when each instruction is executed, the WAIT will time out in the time specified in Sim. Input Wait Delay if the condition is not satisfied.

Note DI[3] on the right side of the operator in line 3 does not need to be designated as Skip When Simulated.

1: WAIT DI[1]=ON
2: WAIT RI[1]=ON
3: WAIT DI[2]<>DI[3]
4: WAIT RI[5]=OFF-
[End]

When a program is started from the teach pendant using SHIFT FWD or SHIFT BWD, if the feature is enabled (that is, 'Sim. Input Wait Delay' is greater than zero and at least one input point is defined to timeout) a pop-up window will be displayed indicating that the program is being run in Simulated Input Skip mode.

The Simulated Input Skip feature is enabled.
WAIT instructions may time out automatically.
[OK]

This is to alert an operator running a program in test mode that WAIT instructions may time out.

When this message is displayed, you must press ENTER on the Teach Pendant to begin program execution. This warning will not be displayed if a program is started from a source other than the pendant, such as the SOP, UOP or from KCL.

##### Error Messages

Two error messages are used by Simulated Input Skip. They are:

• PRIO-188 PAUSE Sim. Skip output not defined

PRIO-188 will be posted to indicate that the 'Set if Sim. Skip Enabled' configuration item is not set properly. IE it is set to zero or to an invalid digital output index. This error is posted at run time when a WAIT instruction is executed if Simulated Input Skip is enabled and

<!-- PDF page 1743 -->

the WAIT contains a 'Skip when simulated' input. The program will pause on the WAIT instruction. A user can continue program execution by first unsimulating the input used in the instruction or by setting the Skip When Simulated mode of the input to FALSE and then restarting the program.

- PRIO-189 WARN (%s^4, %d^5) WAIT will time out

PRIO-189 will be posted whenever a WAIT instruction that will time out due to Simulated Input Skip is executed. This error will not stop execution. It will contain the program name and line number being executed and the text "WAIT will time out". The purpose of this error is to provide additional warning that WAIT will time out.

### 14.52 SINGULARITY AVOIDANCE (formerly known as Auto Singularity Avoidance)

#### 14.52.1 Overview

Robot singularity causes regional structure degeneracy or wrist degeneracy depending on the structure of a robot. For most six-axis robots, the singularity that occurs at the elbow (at the boundary between "up" and "down" configurations) or at the boundary between "front" and "back" configurations causes regional structure degeneracy. This kind of singularity easily can be avoided by restricting the workspace of a robot. However, the wrist singularity might happen virtually any place inside the workspace. When a robot travels through or near a wrist singular position, motion performance becomes undesirable because:

- Wrist axis 4 and axis 6 will rotate a large angle often within a short time period.
- The TCP speed of the robot will slow down as a result of limiting the wrist axes joint speed.
- The path might deviate from the programmed path if motor speed limit is exceeded.

Without the Singularity Avoidance option, the system uses the system variables $param_group[].$auto_sngstp and $param_group[].$t1t2_sngstp to control the robot behavior when singularity is encountered in the following way:

- Auto Mode

- If $param_group[].$auto_sngstp = FALSE (default), the robot is allowed to move through singularity but with undesirable motion performance.
- If $param_group[].$auto_sngstp = TRUE, the robot will stop when singularity occurs.

- T1/T2 Mode

- If $param_group[].$t1t2_sngstp = TRUE (default for HandlingTool), the robot will stop when singularity occurs.
- If $param_group[].$t1t2_sngstp = FALSE (default for P-Series robots), the robot is allowed to move through singularity but with undesirable motion performance.

<!-- PDF page 1744 -->

Singularity Avoidance provides a real-time solution to wrist singularity. With the Singularity Avoidance option, the system will:

- Move the robot through wrist singularity smoothly without excessive wrist rotation. As a result, the TCP speed can be maintained.
- Support both teach pendant program motions and jogging motions with the singularity avoidance features.

When this function is active, the system variables $param_group[].$auto_sngstp and $param_group[].$t1t2_sngstp will be ignored and the system will allow the robot to move through singularity smoothly.

When this function is not active, the system behaves the same way as before as if Singularity Avoidance option is not loaded.

In order to use Singularity Avoidance, you must have a 6-axis robot with a wrist, or a P-500 robot, and a FANUC robot controller.

### 14.52.2 How it Works

For Linear motion with the Singularity Avoidance function enabled, the system will:

- Predict singularity based on one segment when given the start and destination positions.
- Treat motion in the conventional way if singularity is not predicted.

If singularity is predicted at any point along the segment, the following motion control method will be used:

1. Determine the best wrist configuration (flip or nonflip) of the destination position.

Note The taught wrist configuration might not be used. Hence the actual wrist configuration might be different from the taught one, as shown in Figure 14–216.

2. Directly control movement of axis 4 from the start point to the destination point.
3. Maintain TCP positions during the motion.
4. Minimize orientation errors during the motion.

By default, singularity avoidance feature for linear jogging is enabled with a default singularity zone. With singularity avoidance feature enabled, Linear jogging of the robot will result in the following behavior:

- Away from the singularity zone, conventional jogging is used.
- Inside the singularity zone, the singularity avoidance control method takes effect. Therefore, the robot can move through singularity smoothly without high wrist axes speed.

<!-- PDF page 1745 -->

Figure 14–216 shows an example of how the Singularity Avoidance works with linear motion.

Figure 14–216. Taught Configuration vs. Actual Configuration

Singular Point

> **Image description -- img-57.jpeg:** The image is a simple diagram illustrating a configuration state transition. It consists of a horizontal arrow pointing from left to right. On the left side, labeled 'Taught: start point config.flip=True', there is a vertical line with a filled black circle above it. On the right side, labeled 'Dest. Point: config.flip=True', there is another vertical line with a filled black circle above it. Below the arrow, there is a label 'Actual: Config.flip=True' at the left end and 'Config.flip=False' at the right end. The diagram indicates that the taught starting point and destination point both have the configuration 'config.flip=True', but the actual observed configuration at the destination point is 'Config.flip=False'.

Note that when this function is enabled, the system will ignore flip/nonflip configuration of the taught positions you specified and will determine automatically the new configuration for you.

#### 14.52.3 Compatibility

Singularity Avoidance works with:

- Baseline system
- Extended Axis option
- Multi group motion option
- Accupath option

#### 14.52.4 Limitations

The following limitations apply to Singularity Avoidance.

1. The function only supports LINEAR motion type. That is, Circular motion type is not supported.
2. Singularity Avoidance does not support:

• Line Tracking, Circular Tracking, or Rail Tracking

• Coordinated Motion option

- Remote TCP option

- Continuous Turn

3. In the case where Accupath option is used, when singularity is encountered, constant path may not be maintained around the singularity.

<!-- PDF page 1746 -->

4. In a multi-application system (such as SpotTool+), Singularity Avoidance is only supported for programs with “Handling” selected as the application in the program header. Refer to Section 8.5.15 for further details.
5. The Singularity Avoidance Jog feature can be enabled only when HandlingTool is the only application loaded.

#### 14.52.5 Cautions

Keep the following important information in mind when you set up and use Singularity Avoidance.

1. With the Singularity Avoidance function, actual wrist configuration (flip/nonflip) might be different from the taught destination positions.

The function might change configuration internally not only for the destination position in the motion line where singularity is detected but also for the subsequent destination positions in the following motions inside the special teach pendant program.

For example, suppose that the taught points all have "F" (flip) configuration.

20 L P[16] 1000 mm/s CNT100 --- singularity is predicted
21 L P[17] 500mm/s CNT50 --- no singularity
22 L P[18] 200mm/s FINE --- no singularity

If singularity is detected for line 20 during the execution of the special teach pendant program, the function will internally use “N” (non-flip) the configuration of the destination position in the following way:

20 L P[16] 1000 mm/s CNT100 --- change config to "N"
21 L P[17] 500mm/s CNT50 --- change config to "N"
22 L P[18] 200mm/s FINE --- change config to "N"

The system will use internally a different configuration type at points P[16], P[17], and P[18]. Note that the Cartesian position is reached but with different wrist joint angles.

2. Since the function will change configuration internally, single step forward and backward might produce different behavior. See Figure 14–217 for an example.

<!-- PDF page 1747 -->

Figure 14–217. Single Step Forward (FWD) vs. Backward (BWD)

> **Image description -- img-58.jpeg:** The image is a schematic diagram illustrating a sequence of positions and configurations in a mechanical or robotic system, likely related to a linear actuator or a similar mechanism. The diagram is divided into two main directions: Forward (FWD) and Backward (BWD). 

Key elements and their relationships:

1. **Positions (P[1] to P[4])**: Four distinct positions are marked along a horizontal axis, labeled as P[1], P[2], P[3], and P[4]. These positions are aligned sequentially from left to right.

2. **Configurations (F, L, J)**: Each position is associated with a specific configuration indicated by letters: F, L, or J. For example, P[1] is associated with F, P[2] with L, P[3] with J, and P[4] with F.

3. **Directional Arrows**: Arrows indicate the direction of movement between positions. Forward (FWD) movement proceeds from P[1] to P[4], while Backward (BWD) movement proceeds from P[4] to P[1].

4. **Singular Position**: A specific position, labeled as "Singular position," is marked between P[1] and P[2]. This position is highlighted with a black dot and is associated with the configuration L.

5. **Taught Configuration**: The sequence of configurations is labeled as "Taught config" and follows the pattern F, L, F, L, F, J, F, corresponding to the positions P[1] through P[4].

6. **State Labels (F, N)**: Each position is annotated with a state label, either F or N. For example, P[1] in the forward direction is labeled F, while in the backward direction, it is labeled N. Similarly, P[2] is labeled N in the forward direction and F in the backward direction.

The diagram visually represents the transitions and configurations of the system as it moves forward and backward through the defined positions, highlighting a critical singular position and the taught sequence of configurations.

The following rules will be applied:

- JOINT motion will reach the taught configuration and LINEAR motion should keep the same configuration as the one at the previously reached position unless singularity occurs.
- In Figure 14–217, suppose that the taught configurations at all the points are "flip" (F). When moving single step forward from P[1] to P[4], since the first segment is LINEAR motion from P[1] to P[2] and there is singularity, the configuration at P[2] is changed to "non-flip" (N) to avoid the singularity. The second linear motion from P[2] to P[3] does not have any singularity and should keep the same configuration as the one at P[2]. Therefore, the configuration at P[3] is "non-flip". The last motion is JOINT and will reach the taught configuration—"flip".
- When moving single step backward from P[4] to P[1], the first motion is JOINT from P[4] to P[3] and will reach the taught configuration –"flip" (F) at P[3]. The second motion is LINEAR from P[3] to P[2] and has no singularity. Hence the configuration at P[2] is kept the same as the one at P[3]. The last motion is LINEAR from P[2] to P[1] and there is singularity. The actual configuration at P[1] is changed to "non-flip" (N) to avoid the singularity. As shown Figure 14–217, the single step forward and backward produce different behavior in the example.

To prevent the above from happening, during single step forward motion, the system will post a warning message "MOTN-208 Config Not Reached (L:%d)" at the point where the actual configuration is different from the taught one. By observing the message, the user should re-touch up the taught point at the specific line shown in the warning message this will update the taught configuration to the actual configuration. As a result, when stepping backward, the motion will behave the same way as stepping forward.

3. Jogging and program motion might be different when the robot moves near singularity.

<!-- PDF page 1748 -->

Figure 14–218. Program Motion vs. Jogging: Behavior Might Be Different Near Singularity

Singularity Zone

> **Image description -- img-59.jpeg:** The image depicts a schematic representation of a coin-flipping experiment or process. It shows two labeled regions, A and B, separated by a vertical dashed line. Region A is on the left and contains a series of small, evenly spaced vertical lines, with a label 'P[1]: Nonflip' above it. Region B is on the right and contains a single vertical line labeled 'X' followed by a series of small, evenly spaced vertical lines, with a label 'P[2]: Flip' above it. The vertical dashed line separating A and B is labeled 'X' at the boundary. The labels 'Nonflip' and 'Flip' suggest that the process involves two possible outcomes: one where the coin does not flip (Nonflip) and one where it does flip (Flip). The vertical lines likely represent discrete steps or states in the process, with the transition at 'X' indicating a point of decision or change between the two outcomes.

The behavior of LINEAR jogging through a singularity zone:

As shown in Figure 14–218, the jogging motion from P[1] to P[2] can be partitioned into three regions: (1) from P[1] to A; (2) from A to B and (3) from B to P[2]. The regions (1) and (3) are outside of a pre-defined singularity zone, whereas region (2) is inside the zone. With Singularity Avoidance Jogging function enabled, when you jog linearly from P[1] to A, the jogging has the conventional jogging behavior and axis 4 may rotate gradually in one direction. From A to B, linear jogging will use new orientation control method, moving smoothly through singularity, and the configuration at B is different from the one at A. From B to P[2], the jogging yields the conventional jogging behavior again and axis 4 gradually rotates in the same direction as you jog from P[1] to A. In summary, when linearly jogging a robot from P[1] to P[2] in the above example, you might notice that:

• Axis 4 gradually rotates back and forth
• The configuration changes from P[1] to P[2]

The behavior of LINEAR program motion through a singularity zone:

As shown in Figure 14–218, during the program motion from P[1] to P[2], the system will predict the singularity and use new orientation control method for the entire motion. As a result, you might notice that:

• The robot moves smoothly through the singularity
• Axis 4 gradually rotates in one direction only
• The configuration changes from P[1] to P[2]

4. The destination position is inside the singularity zone. By default, the system will change the taught position in the following way:

- Keep location intact
- Use the same joint angle of Axis 4 as the previous point
- Minimize the orientation error between the modified orientation and the taught orientation

This results in a more intuitive motion behavior. But if the exact taught position required, you can overwrite this default system behavior by setting $ra_paramgrp[].$use_strt_j4 = FALSE.

When the system internally modifies the taught orientation to control the rotation of axis 4, it will post a warning message "MOTN-209 Modify Singular Dest(L:%d)" to indicate the taught

<!-- PDF page 1749 -->

point at the specific line is singular and is modified internally (minimal orientation error is expected and the location of the modified destination point is the same as the taught one).

5. The function might not help for the singularity at the corner path.

For example, you might teach three points as shown in the following figure. Singularity might not be detected on either of the two segments. However, singularity might occur on the corner path (blending of the two segments). Since in planning it is impossible to know the blending with one segment information, the function does not help in this situation.

Figure 14–219. Unforeseeable Singularity at a Corner Path

> **Image description -- img-60.jpeg:** The image is a schematic diagram featuring a curved, irregularly shaped boundary that separates two regions labeled P[1] and P[2]. The boundary is marked with a dashed line, indicating a 'Singularity zone' within this region. To the right of the singularity zone, the boundary continues as a solid line, leading to a point labeled P[3]. The labels P[1], P[2], and P[3] are positioned near the respective regions or points they denote. The diagram visually represents a transition or boundary between different states or phases, with the singularity zone highlighting an area of particular interest or anomaly.

### 14.52.6 How to Use Singularity Avoidance

To use Singularity Avoidance with program motion, refer to Procedure 14-86.

To use Singularity Avoidance with jogging, refer to Procedure 14-87. This procedure describes how singularity avoidance can be enabled or disabled for jogging. By default, singularity avoidance is enabled during jogging.

### Procedure 14-86 Using Singularity Avoidance with Program Motion

# Warning

When you execute a program with the Singularity Avoidance function, you are changing the configuration of taught points. This affects the motion behavior of the robot. When you execute the program, make sure the program is running at safety speed to verify that it is working correctly; otherwise, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

Note The Singularity Avoidance feature under program motion can be enabled or disabled in the teach pendant program header field called "Enable Singularity Avoidance".

# Conditions

- The teach pendant program contains the motion group that has a 6-axis robot with a wrist or a P-500 robot.

<!-- PDF page 1750 -->

- The system uses a controller with Singularity Avoidance software loaded.
- Singularity Avoidance is enabled for the appropriate motion group (\(ra\_paramgrp[].\)enable = TRUE by default).

# Steps

1. Press Select.
2. Move the cursor to select the program you want to modify.
3. Press F2, DETAIL. You will see a screen similar to the following.

Program detail JOINT 10 %
1/6
Creation Date: 29-Jul-xxxx
Modification Date: 29-Jul-xxxx
Copy Source: [ ]
Positions: FALSE Size: 135 Byte
1 Program name: [TESTMAIN]
2 Sub Type: [None ]
3 Comment: [ ]
4 Group Mask: [1, *, *, *, *]
5 Write protect: [OFF ]

4. Press F3, NEXT. You will see a screen similar to the following.

TESTMAIN LINE 0 T2
JOINT 10 %
Singularity Avoidance Func 1/1
Program Header
1 Enable Singularity Avoidance: TRUE

5. Press F4, TRUE, to set Enable Singularity Avoidance to TRUE.

The system will try to maintain the consistency between the singularity avoidance header flag of program motion and the singularity avoidance jog mode.

By default, the system uses the following rules to set the "Enable Singularity Avoidance" program header field.

- When a new program is created, the status is set based on the jog mode.

<!-- PDF page 1751 -->

— If singularity avoidance jog mode is enabled (this is the default), "Enable Singularity Avoidance" is set to TRUE. Refer to Procedure 14-87.
— If singularity avoidance jog mode is disabled, "Enable Singularity Avoidance" is set to FALSE. Refer to Procedure 14-87.

- Since you can manually change the "Enable Singularity Avoidance" program header field, you can overwrite the default system behavior by manually enabling or disabling singularity avoidance function for a teach pendant program.
- By default, for **old** programs, a new program header field "Enable Singularity Avoidance" is created and set to FALSE by the system. Hence, by default, **old** programs will behave the same as the old way.

**Note** If you are using singularity avoidance jogging to touch up a point in the teach pendant program that is a disabled singularity avoidance function, then the program might NOT run through because the taught configuration might be different.

6. Run the teach pendant program. Refer to Chapter 9 TESTING A PROGRAM AND RUNNING PRODUCTION for more information about testing a program.

Under T1/T2 mode, during the execution of a teach pendant program with Singularity Avoidance function enabled, the system may display the following warning messages on the top of teach pendant:

- MOTN-205 (program name, xx) Singularity
- MOTN-208 Config Not Reached (L: xx)
- MOTN-209 Modify Singular Dest(L: xx)

where xx indicates the line number in the program. Under Auto mode, no such message will be displayed.

**MOTN-205 (program name, xx) Singularity:** This warning message shows that the system predicts a singularity for the motion line xx in the named program. Most likely, the system will use different configuration for the motion line and the subsequent motion line(s) to avoid the singularity.

**MOTN-208 Config Not Reached (L:xx):** This warning message is displayed only when the program is executed with single step forward. It shows that the actual configuration is different from the taught one at the specific motion line. It is recommended that the user re-touch up the point at the particular line to make the single step forward and back behave the same way.

**MOTN-209 Modify Singularity Dest(L:xx):** This warning message is displayed only when $ra_paramgrp[].$use_strt_j4 = TRUE and the taught point is in a pre-defined singularity zone (the absolute angle value of axis 5 is less than $ra_paramgrp[].$sngrlty_tol). It indicates that the destination point at the specific line is singular and its orientation is modified to control the motion of axis 4. To reach exactly the taught point even if it is singular, set $ra_paramgrp[].$use_strt_j4 = FALSE.

<!-- PDF page 1752 -->

# Warning

The behavior of teach pendant program motion with singularity avoidance function enabled might NOT reach the taught configuration. When you execute the program, make sure the program is running at a safe speed to verify that it is working correctly; otherwise, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

# Warning

The behavior of teach pendant program motion with singularity avoidance function enabled or disabled might be very different. The flip/non-flip configuration will be different if there is singularity. When you execute the program, make sure the program is running at a safe speed to verify that it is working correctly. Pay close attention to wrist axes motion; otherwise, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

# Warning

With singularity avoidance function enabled, and a robot is traveling through or near a singular position, an orientation error is expected. When you execute the program, make sure the program is running at safety speed to verify that it is working correctly; otherwise, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

# Warning

With singularity avoidance function enabled, single step forward and backward might result in a different configuration. When you execute the program, make sure the program is running at safety speed to verify that it is working correctly; otherwise, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

# Procedure 14-87 Using Singularity Avoidance with Jogging

# Warning

When you execute a program with the Singularity Avoidance function, you are changing the configuration of taught points. This affects the motion behavior of the robot. When you execute the program, make sure the program is running at safety speed to verify that it is working correctly; otherwise, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

# Conditions

- The motion group you want to jog has a 6-axis robot with a wrist or a P-500 robot.
- The system uses a controller with Singularity Avoidance software loaded.

<!-- PDF page 1753 -->

- Singularity Avoidance is enabled for the appropriate motion group (\(ra_paramgrp[].\)enable=TRUE by default).

##### Steps

1. Select the motion group you want to jog if your system is configured as multiple motion groups:

Note The group should contain a 6-axis robot with a wrist or a P-500 robot.

a. Press and hold the SHIFT key and press COORD to display the JOG menu.
b. Move the cursor to GROUP and press the appropriate numeric key.

2. Select a coordinate system among the frames WORLD, TOOL, USER, JGFRM, by pressing COORD.

By default, the system enables singularity avoidance jogging. From the status line indicator, if singularity avoidance jogging function is enabled, the jog mode will be displayed in the upper right hand corner of the teach pendant screen similar to the following:

Program name

G1

S/WORLD

10%

If you see "S/" followed by a coordinate system on the teach pendant, skip Step 3 for singularity avoidance jogging.

The system will try to maintain the consistency between the singularity avoidance header flag of program motion and the singularity avoidance jog mode.

By default, the system uses the following rules to enable/disable singularity avoidance for jogging.

- By default, when the system comes up without any program selected, singularity avoidance jog mode is enabled.
- When a teach pendant program is being selected or edited, the jog mode status is set based on the "Enable Singularity Avoidance" header of the program.
— If the header field "Enable Singularity Avoidance" of the program is TRUE, singularity avoidance JOG mode is enabled.
— If the header field " Enable Singularity Avoidance" of the program is FALSE, singularity avoidance JOG mode is disabled.

This is an attempt to make the robot jog in the same way as it would move with program motion.

However, you can overwrite this default system behavior by manually enabling/disabling singularity avoidance JOG mode as follows.

<!-- PDF page 1754 -->

3. Enable singularity avoidance jogging function.

a. Press FCTN
b. Move the cursor to "T/SINGULARITY JOG" and press ENTER. The status line indicator for singularity avoidance jog is displayed in the upper right hand corner of the teach pendant screen similar to the following.

Program name

G1

S/WORLD

10%

c. To deselect singularity avoidance jogging function:

a. Press FCTN.
b. Move the cursor to "T/SINGULARITY JOG" and press ENTER. The status line indicator should be similar to the following:

Program name

G1

WORLD

10%

Note Singularity avoidance jogging function is NOT available or applicable in the following jog modes:

- JOINT (joint jogging)
- WRIST JOINT JOG (wrist joint jogging)
- RTCP JOG (remote TCP jogging)
- COORD JOG (coordinate jogging)

4. Turn the teach pendant ON.
5. Choose jog speed by pressing and releasing the appropriate jog speed key.

# Warning

In the next step, the robot will move. To stop the robot immediately at any time during jogging, release the DEADMAN switch or press the EMERGENCY STOP button.

6. To jog, press and hold the SHIFT key and continuously press the jog key that corresponds to the direction in which you want to move the robot. To stop jogging, release the jog key.
7. When you are finished jogging, turn the teach pendant OFF and release the DEADMAN switch.

<!-- PDF page 1755 -->

# Warning

When using singularity avoidance jog mode, if the robot travels through or near a singular position, an orientation error is expected. Make sure that the motion is all right. Otherwise, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

### 14.53 SINGULARITY CHECK FUNCTION

When positional data is used in Cartesian coordinates to perform motion instruction teaching or position modification, the robot position might be close to a singularity point. In such a case, when the taught motion instruction is executed, the robot can operate at an attitude other than that with which the instruction was taught.

To prevent this, the singularity check function is provided. When a position is taught, this function checks whether the taught position is at a singularity position. The function can record the position in joint coordinate format, if so specified by the user.

#### Function

To enable the singularity check function, set the system variable $MNSING_CHK to TRUE.

If a motion instruction is taught using the SHIFT and POINT keys, or if a position is modified using the SHIFT and TOUCHUP keys, while the robot is at a singularity point, this function checks whether the taught position is at a singularity point.

This check is performed when all of the following conditions are satisfied:

- The position is recorded in Cartesian coordinates.
- An additional instruction with INC or offset is not specified.
- The UF (user frame number) of the position data is 0.

If the check finds that the taught position is at a singularity point, the following warning message appears in the upper two lines on the teach pendant:

[Can't record on Cartesian (G:i)]
[In singularity]

where, "i" is the number of the motion group at the singularity point.

At the same time, the following prompt appears at the bottom on the teach pendant:[Record current position on joint?]

The [YES] and [NO] function keys are displayed. Select the appropriate key.

- [YES]: The position data is recorded in joint coordinate format.
- [NO]: The position is not taught or modified.

<!-- PDF page 1758 -->

For position data in a program that has multiple motion groups, the singularity check is performed in ascending order of group number. When more than one group is at a singular point, the warning message and prompt message appear repeatedly for each group.

You cannot use this function to teach BOTTOM POINTS for the palletizing function or to teach the ROUTE POINTS.

### 14.55 SOFT FLOAT (OPTION)

#### 14.55.1 Overview

Soft Float is a feature that is used to compensate for variances in workpiece precision in applications where the robot is used to mount workpieces on a machine tool.

In most applications, the robot moves accurately to the taught points. When the robot is used to mount workpieces on a machine tool, variances in workpiece precision can cause the workpiece position to shift relative to the tool. This shifting could result in interference between the workpiece and the tool. The Soft Float function can compensate for these variances.

There are several robots that do not support all Soft Float types. The following Soft Float types are available:

- Joint Soft Float — Softness around the robot joint can be specified.
- Cartesian Soft Float — Softness along and around Cartesian coordinates can be specified. It is good at contouring and face matching with robot motion.

<!-- PDF page 1763 -->

- Pushout Soft Float — (High Performance Soft Float only) Force and moment necessary become smaller than the current Cartesian Soft Float. Pushout Soft Float does not work where J5 = 3.5 ~ +3.5. It is good at following the pushout.

The Soft Float function is enabled and disabled using an instruction in a teach pendant program. Its conditions are also specified using the instruction.

To use the Soft Float function, you must do the following:

- Set payload information. Accurate payload information is crucial in getting the desired result with the Soft Float function. Refer to Section 10.10.
- Set up Soft Float schedules. Setting up schedules involves choosing between Cartesian and Joint mode for each schedule, as well as specifying the flexibility. Refer to Section 14.55.3 for details on setting up Soft Float schedules.
- Add Soft Float instructions to your teach pendant program. For a description of Soft Float teach pendant instructions, refer to Section 14.55.6.

### 14.55.2 Restrictions

When you use the Soft Float function, keep in mind the following restrictions:

Warning

When the Soft Float function is enabled,

- The robot might not always follow the taught path
- The taught path changes according to the override
- Execution time might be increased

Be aware of these effects before you enable the Soft Float function. Otherwise, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

Warning

When the Soft Float function is enabled, robot brakes are affected as follows:

- If an attempt is made to enable Soft Float with a brake enabled, the brake is released automatically before the function is enabled.
- When the Soft Float function is enabled, brake control is ineffective.

Be aware of these effects before you use the Soft Float function. Otherwise, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

<!-- PDF page 1764 -->

- The Soft Float function is **disabled automatically** when

Program execution starts.
Program execution ends.
The program stops due to an alarm that turns off the servomotors.
Jogging is performed with the program paused.
The program is restarted after the cursor is moved manually with the program paused.
Backward execution is performed.
Power is turned on.

- If the **program is paused and then restarted**, the states of the Soft Float function (such as enabled/disabled and the exec start ratio) are set to the conditions that existed before the program was paused, except for the cases listed in the previous item that cause the Soft Float function to be disabled automatically.
- The Soft Float function **cannot be enabled** by any method other than by using the Soft Float instruction.
- When the **Soft Float function is enabled**, the robot moves using the termination type CNT0 (no position check is made), even if FINE has been specified as motion instruction termination type.
- When the **Soft Float function is enabled**, if an external force causes the robot to move beyond a certain distance, the following servo error messages are displayed:

If the robot is at rest: [SRVO-023 Stop error excess(G:i A:j)]

If the robot is operating: [SRVO-024 Move error excess(G:i A:j)]

- If an attempt is made to **enable the Soft Float function with a brake applied**, the brake is released automatically before the function is enabled.
- When the **Soft Float function is enabled**, brake control is ineffective.
- If the **motion group mask in a program is [*,*,*,*,*,*,*,*] (there is no motion group), when the program issues instructions with the Soft Float function, the following error message is displayed:[INTP-216 (program name, line number) Invalid value for group number]
- Minimize the **range of motion** used with the Soft Float function enabled.

Load distribution on the robot's axes varies with the position and speed of the robot. When the robot is moved away from the nominal position (at which the Soft Float function was enabled), these variations can cause the robot to move in a direction other than the direction of the applied external force. Since gravity is the most dominant load, this motion is often along the z direction. As a result of this behavior, you should try to keep the range and speed of robot motion to a minimum when the Soft Float function is enabled.

<!-- PDF page 1765 -->

### 14.55.6 Program Instructions

The following Soft Float instructions can be used:

- Soft Float[n]
- Soft Float END
- FOLLOW UP

### Soft Float[n]

Soft Float[n] enables the Soft Float function from the next instruction in your teach pendant program until a Soft Float END instruction is executed. The Soft Float function enabled will use Soft Float schedule "n."

Refer to Section 14.55.3 to define Soft Float schedules.

Note You must set up payload information properly and specify the correct payload schedule in the program to use the Soft Float function. Accurate payload information is crucial in getting the desired result with the Soft Float function. Refer to Section 10.10.

You can use Soft Float[n] in two forms within your teach pendant program. The form you use determines when during program execution the Soft Float function will be active. The Soft Float[n] instruction can be specified:

<!-- PDF page 1772 -->

- As an independent instruction, on its own line within the program.
- As a motion option within a motion instruction.

# Independent Instruction

# Soft Float[n]

When specified as an independent instruction on its own line within the program, the Soft Float function is enabled after the end of the motion specified on the line preceding the independent Soft Float[n] instruction.

In Figure 14–227, the Soft Float function is enabled after the motion specified on line 1 completes, and disabled using Soft Float END on line 5. In this example, the FINE termination type in lines 4 and 5 has the same effect as CNT0.

Figure 14–227. Soft Float[n] Independent Instruction Example

> **Image description -- img-66.jpeg:** The image depicts a programming code snippet and a corresponding motion diagram for a robotic or CNC system. The code snippet, written in a structured format, includes the following lines: 
1. PAYLOAD[GP1:1]
2. J P[1] 100% FINE
3. SOFTFLOAT[1]
4. L P[2] 100mm/sec FINE
5. L P[3] 100mm/sec FINE
6. SOFTFLOAT END

The motion diagram below the code shows three points labeled P[1], P[2], and P[3], connected by arrows indicating movement from P[1] to P[2] and then to P[3]. The text 'The soft float function is enabled.' is written beneath the diagram. The code indicates that the system is configured to handle a payload labeled GP1:1, followed by a joint move (J) to point P[1] at 100% speed with a FINE termination. The SOFTFLOAT[1] function is then enabled, allowing for smooth motion. Two linear moves (L) are executed: first to P[2] at 100 mm/sec with FINE termination, and then to P[3] at the same speed and termination. The SOFTFLOAT function is subsequently disabled. The diagram visually represents the movement path between these points, emphasizing the enabled soft float function during the motion.

# Motion Option

# L P[i] 100mm/sec FINE Soft Float[n]

When specified as a motion option within a motion instruction, the Soft Float function becomes enabled during the execution of the motion statement that contains the Soft Float[n] motion option.

The point at which the Soft Float function becomes enabled is determined by a Soft Float schedule item, Exec Start Ratio. This is available only for JOINT Soft Float schedules.

The exec start ratio is specified as the percentage (from 0% to 100% in 1% steps) of a distance to be traveled before the robot reaches the taught point that corresponds to the motion instruction that contains the Soft Float[n] motion option.

In Figure 14–228, the Soft Float function is effective between P[1] taught using the motion instruction on line 1, and P[2] taught using the motion instruction on line 2 that contains the Soft Float[n] motion option. In this example, the FINE termination type in line 3 has the same effect as CNT0.

- Exec Start Ratio 100% - The robot has completed 100% of the move to P[2] when Soft Float is enabled. This means that the robot is at P[2].

<!-- PDF page 1773 -->

- Exec Start Ratio 50% - The robot has completed 50% of the move to P[2] when Soft Float is enabled. This means that the robot is halfway between P[1] and P[2].

Figure 14–228. Soft Float[n] Motion Option Example

> **Image description -- img-67.jpeg:** The image depicts a programming or control sequence diagram for a motion system, likely related to a robotic or CNC (Computer Numerical Control) setup. It includes four labeled lines of code (1 to 4) and a corresponding graphical representation of the motion path and speed control. 

1. **Code Lines**: 
   - Line 1: `J P[1] 100% FINE` – This indicates a joint move to position P[1] at 100% speed with a FINE termination.
   - Line 2: `L P[2] 100mm/sec FINE SOFTFLOAT[1]` – This indicates a linear move to position P[2] at 100 mm/sec speed with a FINE termination and soft float function enabled (index 1).
   - Line 3: `L P[3] 100mm/sec FINE` – This indicates a linear move to position P[3] at 100 mm/sec speed with a FINE termination.
   - Line 4: `SOFTFLOAT END` – This indicates the end of the soft float function.

2. **Graphical Representation**: 
   - Three circular nodes labeled P[1], P[2], and P[3] are connected by arrows indicating the direction of movement from P[1] to P[2] to P[3].
   - The speed of movement between P[1] and P[2] is shown as 100%, while the speed between P[2] and P[3] is shown as 50% and 0% (indicating deceleration or controlled stop).
   - The soft float function is visually represented by a dashed line connecting P[2] and P[3], with a note stating 'The soft float function is enabled.'

3. **Operational Meaning**: 
   - The diagram illustrates a motion sequence where the system moves to P[1] in a joint move, then transitions to a linear move to P[2] at a controlled speed with soft float enabled, and finally moves to P[3] with a controlled deceleration or stop. The soft float function likely provides smooth motion control or compliance during the transition between positions.

# Soft Float END

Soft Float END disables the Soft Float function. Add this instruction within your teach pendant program at the location where you want to stop using the Soft Float function.

# FOLLOW UP

When an external force is removed from a robot, the robot usually tries to go back to the taught point. However, the FOLLOW UP instruction causes the robot to assume that the current position is the taught point, and prevents it from going back to the taught point. Use this instruction to override the robot's usual behavior when an external force is removed.

### 14.55.7 General Soft Float Guidelines

#### 14.55.7.1 Overview

This function is NOT intended to be used when the tooling is flexible, the fixture is not fixed, or the part is fragile (breakable). Also, CSF can be used when the space between part and fixture is around couple of millimeters. CSF is NOT intended to use for mating parts in tight tolerance.

When Soft float is enabled, no external force can be applied to the robot. When Soft float is enabled, the servos will observe gravity by recording the motor torque at the instance and then change the rigidity of robot. If the external force is present at the moment when Soft Float is enabled, the servos will not be able to distinguish this external force from the gravity effect. This means that SRVO-023 Stop/Move Error Excess or SRVO-112 or SRVO-111 Soft Float Time Out might occur. For example in a pushout handling application, you should make a program in which the Soft Float starts before the hand is closed. See the following for an example.

- Bad example

<!-- PDF page 1774 -->

4:
5:
6:
7: CALL HNDCLOSE
8:
9: SOFTFLOAT[10]
10:
11: WAIT 10.00(sec)
12: SOFTFLOAT END
[END]
Force from outside will be added if softfloat starts after the hand is closed.

- Good example

4:
5: SOFTFLOAT[10]
6:
7: CALL HNDCLOSE
8:
9:
10:
11: WAIT 10.00(sec)
12: SOFTFLOAT END
[END]
Force from outside will not be added if softfloat starts before the hand is closed.

##### 14.55.7.2 Improving Softness

Even with the same Soft Float schedule settings, the softness of Soft Float differs depending on the direction of the motion just before Soft Float starts. This is because Soft Float is more soft to move in the same direction to the motion just before and less soft to move in the opposite direction to the motion just before.

Therefore, make the program as that just before Soft Float starts and move the robot a little in the direction opposite to the direction the robot should move using Soft Float, then move the robot back to the position to start Soft Float. The distance necessary is 1–2mm or longer. For example, when you want to start Soft Float to move in +X direction in P[1], you should add the following motion instruction between the motion instruction to P[1] and the Soft Float instruction. See Figure 14–229.

<!-- PDF page 1775 -->

Figure 14–229. Improving Softness Example

2: Z50
3: L P[2] 100mm/s CNT0 INC
4: L P[3] 100mm/s CNT0 INC

By this method, the robot will become more soft to move in the +X direction and less soft to move in the -X direction. This is effective for use in Joint, Cartesian, and Pushout Soft Float.

### 14.55.8 Cartesian Soft Float Guidelines

#### 14.55.8.1 Overview

Cartesian Soft Float is supported both in the current Soft Float and in High Performance Soft Float. Softness along and around Cartesian coordinates can be specified.

<!-- PDF page 1776 -->

### 14.55.8.2 General Cartesian Soft Float Guidelines

# **Layout and Tool Selection**

The area of 10% – 20% inside from the outside border of mechanical unit operation area is recommended. Select the shortest tool possible.

# **TCP Settings**

Use the actual tool frame setting.

# **Installation of robot and peripheral equipment/tooling selection**

CSF has better performance if CSF is used within 10%~20% of the robot work envelope. Take this into account when you decide the robot installation and tooling selection.

Also, try to use short tooling if possible. The longer the tool, the more difficult it is to make it soft in XYZ directions.

The moment is needed for this re-orientation motion. select the correct tooling and set the proper softness in CSF orientation directions (WPR).

See Figure 14–231 .

Figure 14–231. Layout and Tool Selection

The diagram visually emphasizes this portion of the work envelope by highlighting it with the green arrow, suggesting its significance or proportion relative to the whole.

# **Schedule Setup**

Set 100% in soft ratio of the direction or rotation that you want to make soft. Adjust Soft Tolerance in the pushing direction to limit the force and to avoid pushing with too large a force.

# **Velocity Teaching**

In Soft Float with robot motion, the robot might not move if a small velocity is taught. Teach the velocity more than about 100 mm/sec.

### 14.55.9 Other Guidelines

#### 14.55.9.1 Soft Float Setup Variables

When the Soft Float function is enabled, if follow-up processing requires more time than specified in the system variable $SFLT_FUPTIM, the servo alarm or program pause alarm occurs. The system variable $SFLT_ERRTYP specifies which alarm will occur.

# $SFLT_FUPTIM

Default value: 1000 (ms)This value varies from one system to another. The large value that does not cause an alarm during normal operation should be used.

# $SFLT_ERRTYP

Default value: 0-If 0, servo alarm "SRVO-111 Soft Float time out" occurs.-If 1, Program pause alarm "SRVO-112 Soft Float time out" occurs. (The alarm number is different between the alarms.)The default value should be used unless turning the servo off invites any inconvenience in the system.

Refer to the FOLLOW UP teach pendant instruction in Section 14.55.6 for more information on follow-up processing.

When the Soft Float function is enabled, follow-up processing is normally performed for individual motion instructions.This processing is enabled or disabled according to the system variable $SFLT_DISFUP.

<!-- PDF page 1781 -->

# $SFLT_DISFUP

Default value: FALSE

- If FALSE, follow-up is performed at the start of each motion instruction in the program.
- If TRUE, follow-up is not performed for individual motion instructions in the program.

### 14.55.9.2 True Position Variables

When Soft Float is enabled, the positional data that is displayed is the commanded robot position. The true robot position might be very different due to forces being applied to the robot. The following set of variables allows you to see the actual, machine pulse position of the robot. The machine pulse position is the current robot position (not the commanded position) based on the mechanical unit location, which is determined using encoder (machine) pulses. These variables will display a variety of useful values and are described below. See $SCR_GRP[n].$DPOS_DST Example for an example of how you can examine one of the variables to determine whether the robot TCP is within a given tolerance.

# $SCR_GRP[ ].$m_pos_enb

This switch enables the current position function from machine pulse.

True = Enable

False = Disable

When it is enabled, Joint angle and x, y, z data of the TCP position are copied to $mch_ang [ ] and $mch_pos.

Note This variable must be set to true to make use of any of the other variables.

Note When $SCR_GRP[].$m_pos_enb = TRUE, Axis Limits will be enforced while in Soft Float mode. Refer to Section 14.55.9.3 .

# $SCR_GRP[ ].$mch_ang[ ]

This variable displays the current joint position from machine pulse. When $M_POS_ENB = T, $mch_ang[ ] will be update continuously.

# $SCR_GRP[ ]$mch_pos

This variable displays the current TCP x, y, z, w, p, and r position from machine pulse. When $m_pos_enb = T and program motion executes, it sets the current TCP position.

# $SCR_GRP[ ].$dpos_dst

This variable displays the distance to destination position. When $m_pos_enb = T, the distance between the machine pulse position and the destination position of the program is set during programmed motion. Under normal conditions, this number will approach zero as it approaches

<!-- PDF page 1782 -->

the taught point. With Soft Float, this value might never reach zero and can be used to determine how close the TCP actually is to the taught position.

$SCR_GRP[n].$DPOS_DST Example

1: LBL[1]
2: L PR[1] 400 mm/sec FINE Soft Float[1]
3: WAIT 1(sec)
4: ! Allow for any settling
5: IF $SCR_GRP[1].$DPOS_DST >= 100, JMP LBL[2]
6: ! Compare distance with tolerance
7: L P[8] 400mm/sec FINE
8: Soft Float END
9: J P[5] 100% FINE
10: JMP LB[1]
11: LBL[2]
12: ! TCP is out of tolerance
13: UALM[1]

##### 14.55.9.3 Axis Limit Checking in Soft Float

While in Soft Float mode, the robot can move or be moved past the axis software limits by default. Program motion beyond axis limits is never allowed.

By setting $SCR_GRP[].$m_pos_enb = TRUE, the robot limits will be checked while in Soft Float mode. When the robot exceeds the software limits, the following alarm will be posted:

SRVO-116 Axis Limit Exceeded (G:x, A:y)

When this alarm occurs, the robot will have to be jogged back within axis limits prior to resuming.

### 14.56 SOFT OPERATOR PANEL

#### 14.56.1 Overview

Using Soft Operator Panel you can start production from a PC screen instead of the hardware operator panel on the controller. To use this function, iRProgrammer option (J767) or Remote iPendant option (r843) is needed. For R-30iB Compact Plus, this option is provided by default.

The Soft Operator Panel is used to start the execution of robot programs from a PC. When the Soft Operator Panel is enabled, production cannot be started using any other method.

<!-- PDF page 1783 -->

The Soft Operator Panel can open from only one PC. The IP address of the PC which uses Soft Operator Panel has to be defined in the controller. Pleases refer to Section 14.56.2 for more information on setup.

The Soft Operator Panel provides the following functions.

- Cycle start by soft key
- Hold and Abort All by soft keys
- Reset alarm by soft key
- Display program status
- Change Remote/Local setting

Please refer to Section 14.56.3 for more detail.

These functions work on a web browser. Installing any additional software is not required. The following browsers are supported.

- Google Chrome (after version 31)
- Internet Explorer 11

### 14.57 SPACE CHECK FUNCTION (OPTION)

The space check function, incorporated into a robot, monitors a predetermined interference area (space). When another robot or a peripheral unit is located within that space, the function stops robot operation if it is being commanded to move into that space. See Figure 14–242. The space check function releases the stop state and allows robot operation to continue only after checking that the other robot or peripheral unit has moved out of the area. See Figure 14–243.

Figure 14–242. Space Check - Single Robot Controller

> **Image description -- img-81.jpeg:** The diagram illustrates a safety control system involving two robots, Robot A and Robot B, operating within a shared workspace labeled as the 'Common Space.' Robot B is shown locking the Common Space, indicated by a dashed circle around it and the label 'Robot B (or other Peripheral Device) LOCKS the Common Space.' Robot A is positioned outside the Common Space and is labeled 'Robot A is NOT CLEAR TO ENTER and is being HELD at Common Space boundary.' Both robots have associated control signals: Robot B has 'DI[#] = ON' and 'DO[#] = OFF,' while Robot A has 'DI[#] = OFF' and 'DO[#] = ON.' The diagram includes visual indicators such as 'GO' and 'STOP' signals, with Robot B displaying 'GO' signals and Robot A displaying 'STOP' signals. The operational meaning conveyed is that Robot B has exclusive access to the Common Space, preventing Robot A from entering, as indicated by the control signals and the physical positioning of the robots.

> **Image description -- img-82.jpeg:** The diagram illustrates a coordinated interaction between two robots, Robot A and Robot B, within a shared workspace labeled 'Common Space.' The key components include Robot A on the right, Robot B on the left, and the central Common Space. Robot A is depicted with a green 'GO' signal and a red 'STOP' signal, while Robot B has a red 'STOP' signal and a green 'GO' signal. The operational meaning conveyed is a hand-off protocol ensuring mutual exclusion in accessing the shared workspace.

Two interlock signals are assigned to a single interference area: one input and one output. These interlock signals are used for communication between the robot and another robot or a peripheral device.

#### Interlock Input Signal

When an attempt is made to move the robot into the interference area while the interlock input signal is OFF, the robot enters a hold state. If the robot is under program control, the program is still running, and the Busy Running lamp on the teach pendant remains ON. When the input signal goes ON, the hold state is released and the robot resumes automatic operation.

#### Warning

Since the robot starts decelerating as soon as the tool center point enters the interference area, the robot can stop at a point within the area. The faster the robot speed, the further within the area is the point where the robot stops. Taking this fact and the size of the tool into consideration, specify a larger interference area than what actually exists. Otherwise, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

#### Override Interlock Input Signal Function

This function allows you to override the interlock input signal for a specified common space. After this function is enabled, the robot will never enter into a hold state even it moves into a common

<!-- PDF page 1792 -->

space while the interlock input signal is OFF or the interlock input is not specified. This function does not change the behavior of the interlock output signal.

You can enable or disable this function by setting a system variable $RSPACEg[n].$NO_USE_DI = TRUE or FALSE for each common space. You can also enable or disable this function On The Fly.

# Warning

If you change $RSPACEg[n].$NO_USE_DI from TRUE to FALSE you must specify the interlock input. Otherwise, you could injure personnel or damage equipment.

# Interlock Output Signal

When the tool center point enters the interference area, the interlock output signal goes OFF. When the tool center point is not located within the area, the signal is ON. Refer to Table 14–159.

### 14.57.2 Limitations

Space Check currently does not support any tracking functions, any functions involving moving frames, Continuous Turn, and programs with multiple robot groups. Therefore, it is not compatible with:

- Line/Rail/Circular Tracking
- Robot Link
- Any other sensor tracking functions
- Coordinated Motion
- Dynamic remote Tool Center Point
- Simultaneous motion programs with more than one robot group

Therefore, do not load these functions with Space Check. If loaded, the common space defined will need to be disabled when the above functions are used. Otherwise, the SSPC-004 alarm CTV option not allowed, or other Space Check alarms could occur due to mis-detection. Common

<!-- PDF page 1801 -->

space could be disabled from either the user interface or by setting $RSPACEg[n].$ENABLED to FALSE, where g is the motion group number and n is the common space number for that group.

### 14.58 STREAM MOTION

#### 14.58.1 Overview

This Stream Motion function allows an external device to control the robot's motion by sending UDP packets through the Ethernet connection between the external device and the robot controller. The external device sends position command data in a fixed interval and the robot moves to the commanded position after a very short delay. The following option provides this new functionality: J519 Stream Motion.

Note For software versions V8.30P/57, V9.10P/31, V9.30P/11, and V9.40P/03 or later see Section 14.59

The Stream Motion function provides two new TP instructions:

**IBGN start[*]**

Allowable range for *: 1 to 16

When the new instruction is executed, the controller waits at this line for the external device to send a motion command. During the stream motion session, the cursor stays at this instruction until the external device signals the end of the session.

Note Please make sure the first position commanded by the external device is very close to the current robot position. Otherwise, a servo alarm will occur. The external device can get the robot's current position by reading the Robot Status Packet sent from the controller to the external device.

**IBGN end[*]**

Allowable range for *: 1 to 16. This number should be the same as the number specified in its corresponding IBGN start[*] instruction.

When the external device completes the stream motion session, it sends a Motion Command Packet with its Last Data byte set to 1 (see Table 14–164), At this point, the TP program completes the IBGN start[*] instruction, jumps to the IBGN end[*] line, and continues its execution from here.

Note Any TP Instructions that are between IBGN start[*] and IBGN end[*] are ignored.

<!-- PDF page 1802 -->

# Warning

When executing the stream motion, the robot just follows motion commands sent from the external device. Therefore, the motion commands should be very carefully checked by the external device's path generation algorithm so the command path will not damage the robot or cause serious personal injury.

To verify the path, you can put the robot in dry run mode and use the DCS POSITION/SPEED CHECK function to check the position and speed of your command path. To put the robot in dry run mode, go to the TEST CYCLE Setup menu and change the Group Motion from ENABLE to DISABLE. The robot does not move when it is in dry run mode.

Note The TEST CYCLE is not supported on software versions prior to V9.10P/10.

Note The stream motion function requires the external device to send a Motion Command Packet within an 8 ms window starting from when the robot sends the Robot Status Packet. If the external device is a PC running Windows or Ubuntu Linux (without real-time kernel), the PC may not be able to meet this requirement. FANUC recommends using a real-time operating system to avoid this issue.

### 14.58.1.1 Ethernet Cable Requirement

The Stream Motion option uses UDP packets to transmit data between the external device and the robot controller. In order to maintain data integrity, it is important that the Ethernet cable used between the robot controller and the external device is shielded and is grounded properly. Please Strip a portion of the shielded Category 5 twisted-pair cable (STP cable) to expose its metal shield and push the shield against the grounding plate with the clamping hardware as described in FANUC Robot series R-30iB/R-30iB Plus CONTROLLER MAINTENANCE MANUAL, section 4.10.2.

### 14.58.1.2 Motion Stream Setup Procedure

1. Set $STMO.$PHYS_PORT = 1 if CD38A (Ethernet port 1, default) is used to connect the external device to the robot controller.
2. Set $STMO.$PHYS_PORT = 2 if CD38B (port 2) is used to connect the external device to the robot controller.
3. Teach a TP program and add "IBGN start[*]" / "IBGN end[*]" (* should be same number) instructions to the TP Program to allow the external device to control the robot's motion. You can insert the IBGN start[*]/end[*] instruction by pressing [ INST ] -> "ASCII INTERFACE".

<!-- PDF page 1803 -->

##### 14.58.1.3 Protocol

Stream Motion uses UDP packets to transfer data between the external device and the robot controller. The UDP packet uses big endian byte order.

Stream Motion uses port address 60015 as its UDP port for stream motion communication. Users have to make sure their application running on the external device is connected to this port.

Stream Motion software supports four different types of UDP packets. Three are from the external device to the robot controller, and one is from the robot controller to the external device.

1. Start Packet: Table 14–162. The external device sends this packet to the robot controller to indicate the external device is ready to communicate with the controller. This packet can be sent anytime after the controller is powered up. When the robot controller receives this packet, it starts to send the Robot Status Packet to the external device.
2. Robot Status Packet: Table 14–163. The robot controller sends this packet to the external device to notify the external device of information about the robot's current status, such as:

- Robot current position
• I/O status
- Robot status
- Other handshaking information

This packet is sent at a fixed interval defined by $STMO.$COM_INT (default is 8); the unit used is ms. FANUC requires, at this time, that $STMO.$COM_INT not be changed from its default value. The UDP data is sent through the same stream motion port address (60015).

3. Motion Command Packet: Table 14–164. The external device uses this packet to send the commanded positions to the controller. The external device must send this packet immediately after the robot has notified the external device that it is ready to receive motion commands (the robot does this by setting the Active Status flag bit in the Robot Status Packet to 1). The external device continues to send one of these packets after each Robot Status Packet it receives from the robot until the external device is done streaming the whole path.

4. Stop Packet: Table 14–165. The external device sends this packet to the robot controller to indicate that it would like to stop communication with the robot controller. The robot controller should stop sending Robot Status Packets to the external device at this time.

Data formats for each of these packets are defined in the following table.

### 14.58.1.4 Cartesian position data (X,Y,Z,W,P,R)

The position is the TCP position in robot's World coordinate system.

### 14.58.1.5 Stream Motion Handshaking Sequence

1. After the controller powers up, the external device can send the Start Packet to notify the controller that the external device is ready for handshaking.
2. When the controller receives the Start Packet, the robot controller will send the Robot Status Packet back to the external device to notify it of the robot's current status and position at every $STMO.$COM_INT ms interval.
3. The external device can use an HMI to start a TP program that has the IBGN START[*]/IBGN END[*] instructions in it.
4. When the controller executes the IBGN start[*] instruction, the controller will send a Robot Status Packet with its status flag bit 0 set to 1. This indicates that the robot controller is ready to receive the Motion Command Packet from the external device.
5. The external device will send a Motion Command every time it receives a Robot Status Packet and copy the Robot Status Packet's sequence number as its Motion Command Packet's sequence number. NOTE: The robot controller expects a Motion Command Packet within the $STMO.$COM_INT ms interval between when it sends the current Robot Status Packet, and when it sends the next Robot Status Packet. If the robot controller does not receive a motion command within the interval, MOTN-603 ST: Receiving interval over" [PAUSE] alarm occurs.
6. When the external device completes its motion trajectory, the external device sends a Motion Command Packet with the Last data byte set to 1. When the robot controller receives this packet, the TP program will terminate the IBGN start[*] and move the cursor to the IBGN end[*] instruction and continue the TP program execution. Note that all the TP instructions between the IBNG start[*] and IBGN end[*] are ignored.
7. If the external device no longer requires status information from the robot, it can send the Stop Packet to the controller so the controller will stop sending the Robot Status Packet to the external device. Otherwise, the external device can go back to step 3 and run another stream motion session.

<!-- PDF page 1809 -->

### 14.58.2 Execution of Stream motion

1. During stream motion, the override should be set to 100%. If the override is changed during the stream motion, The stream motion software posts an alarm and pauses the execution of the TP program.
2. The robot controller's Ethernet Port 1 and Port 2 can support up to 1000 packet read/write operations per second. If the communication rate exceeds this limit, packets may get discarded and an alarm will occur during stream motion.
3. The robot controller has to be in AUTO mode when the TP program with IBGN start[*] is executed. You can start the TP program using the UOP START button or through the HMI.
4. During Stream Motion, the commanded positions sent from the external device should be in the same configuration (e.g. NUT or FUT), especially when streaming points in Cartesian coordinates. If configuration is changed during Stream motion, a "MOTN-156 PM: Config changed(L:%d)" alarm or "MOTN-605: Infeasible Command (Sq. %d)" alarm is posted and the TP program is paused.

### 14.58.4 Stream Motion Acceleration and Jerk Limits

To protect the robot mechanism, the streaming motion option limits velocity, acceleration, and jerk of each robot axis. For controllers with V9.10P/14 or earlier software, the threshold of each axis is defined in the following system variables: $STMO_GRP[1].$JNT_VEL_LIM[1-9] (joint velocity limit), $STMO_GRP[1].$JNT_ACC_LIM[1-9] (joint acceleration limit), and $STMO_GRP[1].$JNT_JRK_LIM[1-9](joint jerk limit). For controllers with V9.10P/15 or newer software, you need to send a UDP packet to the controller to get this information, since the $STMO_GRP[1].$JNT_XXX_LIM system variables are no longer valid.

#### 14.58.5 Stream Motion Packet Stack

The stream motion requires very tight interaction between the controller and the external device within an 8 millisecond window. If there is any delay and the external device misses the 8 millisecond time window, the stream motion faults out. To prevent this from happening, stream motion implements a first-in-first-out buffer to store packets sent from the external device. When a command packet is delayed and there are still packets in the buffer, the stream motion can use the reminding packets in the buffer for its next motion, and therefore, avoid an unexpected stop.

The first-in-first-out buffer is called Packet Stack and it has a size of 10. The external device can store up to 10 command packets into the buffer before stream motion starts. You can use the system variable $STMO.$START_MOVE (default 1, maximum 10) to control when the stream motion will start. For example, if the $STMO.$START_MOVE = 3, the stream motion will start after there are 3 command packets in the buffer.

Modifying the $STMO.$START_MOVE value will increase the latency of the response time for the first motion. Therefore, it is recommended to keep the $STMO.$START_MOVE to a small value if latency is a concern.

#### 14.58.6 Restrictions

- During stream motion execution, if the controller is paused for any reason, you cannot resume/continue the TP program. You have to abort the TP program and start the stream motion again.

<!-- PDF page 1814 -->

- Stream motion only supports single group motion streaming. If your system has multiple groups, the stream motion will work for group 1 only. That is, your TP program that runs IBGN start[*]/IBGN end[*] instructions should be a single group program and only group 1 is enabled.
- The stream motion software monitors the instantaneous velocity, acceleration and jerk of the input motion command. If the command exceeds the threshold defined in $STMO_GRP[1].$JNT_VEL_LIM[1-6], $STMO_GRP[1].$JNT_ACC_LIM[1-6], or $STMO_GRP[1].$JNT_JERK_LIM[1-6], an error message "MOTN-605 ST: Infeasible command" will be posted.

Note The unit for the $JNT_VEL_LIM[] is degree/seconds for rotary axis or mm/seconds for linear axis. The unit for $JNT_ACC_LIM[] is degree/seconds² for a rotary axis or mm/seconds² for a linear axis.

- If an IBGN end[*] instruction is executed before an IBGN start[*] instruction, the controller will post an alarm.
- The Stream Motion option can't be ordered with External Path Optimization (J829).
- For a TP program with IBGN start[*]/IBGN end[*] instructions, the jump label cannot exceed 30000.
- The Stream Motion option can't be used with the options listed in the table below. (But you can load these options in the controller as long as, during the stream motion, these options are not active/enabled.)

Table 14–169. Options that can not be used with Stream Motion

### 14.59 STREAM MOTION V8.30P/57, V9.10P/31, V9.30P/11 AND V9.40P/03 OR Later

Stream motion is a feature that controls the robot according to the path planned by an arbitrary external device by transmitting the desired position data in real-time (usually 8 ms interval) via Ethernet. This feature is used for directly specifying the path, that is difficult to be formed with ordinary motion instructions such as LINEAR or JOINT move, from an external device, or for applications which require online path generation based on items such as sensor data. To use this feature, the stream motion (A05B-2600-J519) option is necessary. In addition, the customer is required to develop software that can generate a path in consideration of robot-specific constraints such as the upper limit of speed, acceleration, and jerk. (For more details, please refer to Section 14.59.5)

### 14.59.1 Setup Procedure

#### Cable Connection

Connect the shielded Category 5 or more twisted-pair cable (STP cable) to a physical port (CD38A or CD38B), according to “CABLE CONNECTION” in the Ethernet Function OPERATOR’S MANUAL (B-82974EN) or in the “Internet Options Setup and Operations Manual” (MAROUIN9010171E). To expose the metal shield, push the shield against the grounding plate, and then clamp with the bracket. Since this feature sends data using the UDP protocol, noise suppression is very important.

#### Communication settings

Set the system variable $STMO.$PHYS_PORT according to the physical port number used. (1: CD38A, 2:CD38B) For details of communication settings in the robot controller, please refer to “2.1 OVERVIEW”, “2.2 HARDWARE REQUIREMENTS AND INSTALLATION”, and “2.4 SETTING UP TCP/IP” in the “Ethernet function OPERATOR’S MANUAL” (B82974EN) or the “Internet Options Setup and Operations Manual” (MAROUIN9010171E).

#### Program Creation

To start the robot control with this feature, the robot controller needs to be running a program including a specific instruction. In the program edit screen, select the control instruction “ASCII interface”, and specify the following instructions (IBGN start [*], IBGN end [*]) included in that item. For the general procedure for creating and editing a program, please refer to “5 PROGRAMMING” in the “OPERATOR’S MANUAL (Basic Function)” (B-83284EN) or the “CREATING A PROGRAM” chapter in this manual.

<!-- PDF page 1816 -->

IBGN start[*] * :

Set an arbitrary integer of from 1 to 16.

While executing this instruction, the robot moves based on the desired position data sent from external device.

IBGN end[*] * :

Set the same value as the integer set in IBGN start[*].

When the control from the external device is finished, execution moves to this instruction and continues.

The following is an example of creating a program.

1: OVERRIDE=100%
2: P#[1] 100% FINE
3: IDGM start[]
4: IDGM end[]
5: exit
The top-right corner shows '0/5', indicating the current progress or selection state.

Note 1 IBGN start [*] must be specified in the line before the paired IBGN end [*].

2 If there are instructions between IBGN start [*] and IBGN end [*], they will not be executed.

#### 14.59.2 Execution of Stream motion

Execute the program created in Section 14.59.1 in AUTO mode with 100% OVERRIDE. When the program lines are executed from the top and the cursor moves to the IBGN Start [*] instruction, the robot is ready to receive the desired position data sent from external device. After that, start communication according to Section 14.59.3.

If you need to start the program via Ethernet, please refer to “55 HMI DEVICE COMMUNICATION” in the “OPERATOR'S MANUAL (Optional Function) GUIDES” chapter in this manual.

<!-- PDF page 1817 -->

# Warning

1 This feature may cause unintended motion if there is an error in the command from the external device, and can cause severe personal injury.
2 Use simulation software such as ROBOGUIDE and check the operation sufficiently in advance.
3 Consider using it in combination with other safety software such as “DCS position / speed check”.

### 14.59.3 Communication Protocol

Communicate between the external device and the robot controller (hereafter referred to as the robot) is according to the following protocol.

The UDP packet in big endian byte order is used to transfer data, and the robot side uses 60015 for the port address. The communication interval depends on the robot model and is 8ms or 4ms. (For 4ms models, refer to “support models”)

# Status Packet

Send a packet such as shown in Table 14–170 from the external device to the robot. After that, a packet of Table 14–171 is sent from the robot to the external device using the same socket every communication interval (usually 8ms). The status packets have information about the current robot position, motor current value, etc.

To stop the output of the status packets, send the packet of Table 14–173 from the external device to the robot. The communication of status packet described above can be started/ended at any time without executing the IBGN start [*] instruction.

# Command packet

After starting execution of the IBGN start [*] instruction, confirm that bit 0 (LSB) of the “status” data contained in the status packet has changed from 0 to 1. Then, set the desired position of the robot to the packet according to Table 14–172. Send it to the robot to start controlling the robot.

After receiving the first command packet, the robot continues to be controlled by continuously reading the desired position from the subsequent command packet for each communication interval. As a guide, each time the external device receives one status packet from the robot, immediately send the next command packet to the robot. The figure below shows communication started from the sequence number k.

<!-- PDF page 1818 -->
