The timeline is divided into discrete steps labeled Sq-k, k+1, k+2, k+3, and so on. At each step, two types of packets are exchanged: Command Pkt (dashed arrows) and Status Pkt (solid arrows). The External Device sends a Command Pkt to the Robot at Sq-k, and the Robot responds with a Status Pkt. This pattern repeats at each subsequent step: the External Device sends a Command Pkt at k+1, k+2, k+3, etc., and the Robot replies with a Status Pkt at the same time points. The diagram visually represents the bidirectional, synchronized exchange of command and status information between the External Device and the Robot, indicating a structured and periodic communication protocol.

To terminate this communication, set the value of “Last data” included in the command packet to 1 and send it to the robot. When the robot processes this command packet, this communication ends normally.

Note 1 An alarm will be posted if the robot cannot receive the second and subsequent command packets within the communication interval.
2 An alarm may occur if the status packet communication is terminated before the command packet communication is terminated.
3 It is highly recommended to use a real-time OS for accurate response within the communication interval.
4 If the total communication rate of Ethernet Port 1-2 exceeds 1 packet/ms, a communication error may occur

### 14.59.4 Buffering command packets

In this feature, if the second and subsequent command packets from an external device arrive at the robot earlier than the communication interval, the packets can be stored in the packet buffer without being processed (Enabled by default). The robot moves by reading the command packets in the buffer in order from the one that arrived first. The packet can be stored up to $STMO. $PKT_STACK-1 and an alarm will not be posted even if the robot does not receive a new command packet from the external device as long as there are unprocessed packets inside the buffer.

By using this packet buffer, it is possible to prevent an alarm that occurs when a packet does not arrive within the communication interval due to communication delay. The figure below is an example of controlling the robot while keeping two packets in the buffer at all times by sending two command packets in advance. If a command packet with the last data set to 1 is sent when using the buffer, there will be a time delay until all command packets inside the buffer are processed first.

> **Image description -- img-94.jpeg:** The image is a timeline diagram illustrating the communication sequence between an External Device and a Robot over time. The timeline is marked with discrete time steps labeled k, k+1, k+2, k+3, k+4, and k+5. The External Device sends Command Packets (Cmd Pkt) to the Robot at time steps k, k+2, and k+4, indicated by dashed arrows. The Robot sends Status Packets (Status Pkt) back to the External Device at time steps k+1, k+3, and k+5, indicated by solid arrows. The diagram shows a clear alternating pattern where the External Device sends a command, followed by the Robot sending a status update in the subsequent time step. The labels 'Sq=k' and 'Sq=k+1' near the first command and status packets suggest sequence numbers or identifiers for the packets. The diagram visually represents a request-response communication protocol between the two entities.

Also, by changing the value of the system variable ($STMO.$START_MOVE), it is possible to configure the robot to start moving after a certain number of unprocessed command packets have accumulated in the packet buffer.

(Available in software versions 7DC3/55 (V8.30P/55), 7DF1/26 (V9.10P/26), 7DF3/05 (V9.30P/05), or later.)

Note 1 Only command packets are stored in the buffer. Status output stop packets are processed immediately after they are received.

2 Do not send the status output stop packet while the command packet remains in the buffer.

### 14.59.5 Conditions for executable motion commands

#### Reachable Positions

The desired position specified in the command packet must be reachable by the robot. If a command packet to an unreachable position is received, the robot will stop with an alarm.

The reachable desired position must mainly meet the following conditions.

- Joint position of the robot corresponding to the desired position must exist uniquely. (In case of Cartesian format)

<!-- PDF page 1825 -->

- The configuration(*1) of the desired position matches that at the starting of IBGN start [*]. (In case of Cartesian format)
- The desired position satisfies the upper and the lower limit for each robot axis.
- The desired position must not cause the self collision of the robot.

In order to perform a strict check on the above on the external device side, software such as forward kinematics, inverse kinematics, and self-collision checker would be required. FANUC cannot provide the mathematical formulas and know-how regarding these matters.

Therefore, it is necessary for the customer to consider and develop it based on the public information such as the operating space diagram described in the operator's manual of mechanical unit.

The diagram is annotated with various measurements and labels to provide a clear understanding of the robotic arm's operational limits and potential interference zones.

*1 refer to "4 Program Configuration" in the "OPERATOR'S MANUAL (Basic Function)" (B-83284EN) or the "MOTION INSTRUCTION" section of this manual.

### Definition of J3 axis

In generating the motion command, it is necessary to consider the definition of the J3 axis peculiar to the FANUC robot.

<!-- PDF page 1826 -->

The J3 axis definition of the FANUC robot is based on the angle between the horizontal plane as seen by the robot and the J3 arm, not the angle between the J2 arm. Therefore, even if you send a command packet to displace the J2 axis only, the J3 arm will also move in tandem. Please take this specification into consideration and be careful not to take an unintended posture resulting in an accident. There is no way to change this specification.

## Restrictions on speed, acceleration, and jerk

While controlling the robot by sending a command packet, it is necessary to control so that the allowable upper limits of speed, acceleration, and jerk set for each axis of the robot are not exceeded. If a command packet that will violate the upper limit is detected, the robot may stop with an alarm. The purpose of this constraint is to prevent premature damage to the reducer and mechanical parts by continuing to execute excessive motion commands. (Extended axes are not included in the target of this constraint.)

For details on the upper limit, refer to the following system variables that exist under the system variable $STMO_GRP.

They do not depend on the format of the position data. For the lower limit value, add a negative sign to the upper limit values.

- $JNT_VEL_LIM[*]: Allowable upper limit value for speed for each axis [deg/s]
- $JNT_ACC_LIM[*]: Allowable upper limit value for acceleration for each axis [deg/s^2]
- $JNT_JRK_LIM[*]: Allowable upper limit of jerk for each axis [deg/s^3]
- $MAX_SPD: Maximum speed of the robot to which the above allowable upper limit is applied [mm/s]

The above system variables are Read-Only and cannot be used by changing their values. In addition, since the values are reference values, depending on the conditions, larger acceleration/jerk upper limit values may be set internally (see Section 14.59.10 “). The alarm may not occur even if a command packet that violates the reference values above is received. On the other hand, if the robot is moving at a speed exceeding $MAX_SPD [mm/s], the robot may stop with an alarm even if the acceleration/jerk of the motion does not exceed the reference values above.

Note 1 This restriction cannot be deactivated or relaxed even for special reasons such as experimental purposes.

2 For the calculation of velocity, acceleration, and jerk (instantaneous), communication interval (usually 8ms) is used as a fixed time length.

3 For J3 axis, the speed, acceleration, and jerk of the J3 axis alone based on the above definition are limited.

## Difference between Command position and Servo position

There is a distinction between the command position and the servo feedback position (hereinafter referred to as the servo position) in the current position of the robot. The servo position is controlled to follow the command position as much as possible, but there is a certain error between the two positions. Please note that the current position that can be read in the status packet is the servo position.

<!-- PDF page 1827 -->

The desired position in the command packet needs to be set so that the motion can be started smoothly from the command position of the robot. If a path is generated starting from the servo position or current servo position is set as the desired position of the command packet and transmitted, Acceleration/Jerk may become excessive due to the above-mentioned error, and an unexpected alarm may occur.

As shown in the program example described in Section 14.59.1, if a Joint move is executed before the IBGN start[*] instruction, the robot can be moved to the taught command position.

# Reducer load

If the load level applied to the reducer unit of the robot exceeds a certain threshold, the robot may be stopped with an alarm. This is because drive system components such as the reducer unit and gears may be damaged early.

It rarely occurs under conditions that satisfy the constraints of speed, acceleration, and jerk, but please consider measures such as making the robot motion more conservative so that the load on the reducer is reduced. The method of calculating the load level on the reducer unit is confidential and not disclosed.

### 14.59.7 Restrictions

# **Precautions when creating a program**

- Programs that includes the IBGN start[*]/end[*] instruction cannot use numbers higher than 30,000 as the index for jump/label instructions.
- This feature can be used only with robots in motion group 1. When using in a system with two or more groups, disable the motion of the second and subsequent groups in the detailed program information settings.

# **Precautions when executing the program**

- If you try to read or write I/O that contains an index that has not been assigned, an alarm will occur.
- When specifying a desired position in Cartesian format, specify the position of the flange center point in the world coordinate system. Neither the tool coordinate system or user coordinate system can be used with this feature.
- If the correct payload is not set according to the weight of the work piece, an alarm may occur due to problems such as false collision detection.
- HOLD stop is not supported during execution of the IBGN start [*] instruction. It is necessary to generate a deceleration path equivalent to HOLD stop by an external device and execute it via command packets.

# **Option software constraints**

- This feature cannot be installed at the same time as the ascii interface function (J829).
- This feature cannot be used at the same time as the following option software. (It is possible to be installed at the same time.)

#### 14.59.10 Calculation method of acceleration / jerk upper limit

In this feature, the allowable upper limit of acceleration and jerk set for each axis is calculated as follows based on the Cartesian speed [mm/s] at the center of the flange and the payload [kg]. (Only when $STMO_GRP[].$LMT_MODE is 0).

The calculation result is used only for internal judgment and is not reflected in the system variables.

##### Change of allowable upper limits according to the Cartesian speed at the center of flange

Each allowable upper limit has a table of 20 stages according to the Cartesian speed [mm/s] at the center of the flange.

We define the maximum speed of the center of flange as Vmax(=\(STMO_GRP[].\(MAX_SPD\)), at this time, each speed obtained by dividing Vmax into 20 stages corresponds to each index of that table.

In general, the lower the speed at the center of the flange, the higher the allowable upper limit, and the higher the speed, the lower the allowable upper limit. This is illustrated as follows.

<!-- PDF page 1834 -->

Allowable upper limit [deg/s^2 or deg/s^3]

> **Image description -- img-96.jpeg:** The image shows a line graph plotting the speed of the center of a flange (in millimeters per second) on the horizontal axis against an unspecified variable on the vertical axis. The horizontal axis is labeled 'Speed of the center of the flange [mm/s]' and ranges from 0 to V_max. The vertical axis is labeled with a value of V_max/20 at the top. The graph displays a series of data points connected by a line, showing a decreasing trend from left to right. The data points start near the top left and gradually decline toward the bottom right, indicating that as the speed of the flange's center increases, the unspecified variable on the vertical axis decreases. The graph suggests an inverse relationship between the two variables.

- The limit value at arbitrary speed is calculated by linearly interpolating the values at two adjacent indexes.
- For speeds less than Vmax/20, the limit value at Vmax/20 is applied as it is.
- The limit value at the speed higher than Vmax is calculated by linearly extrapolating the limit values at Vmax and the adjacent.

In addition, the allowable upper limit is not updated every communication interval. In the entire time domain until the flange center speed exceeds Vmax/20 and falls below it again, the allowable upper limit value according to the maximum observed speed Vpeak is applied.

Since Vpeak is identified at the end of the above time domain, the calculation of the allowable upper limit value and the excess judgment are also performed at this time.

> **Image description -- img-97.jpeg:** The image is a graph depicting the speed of the center of a flange over time. The vertical axis represents the speed in millimeters per second (mm/s), with two key speed values marked: V_peak (the peak speed) and V_max/20 (a lower threshold speed). The horizontal axis represents time in seconds (s). The graph shows a speed profile that rises to a peak value (V_peak) and then gradually decreases, crossing the V_max/20 threshold before returning to zero. Two time intervals are highlighted: the "Time domain to apply the upper limit according to V_peak" spans the duration from the start of the speed increase until the speed falls back below V_max/20 after the peak. The "Timing to judge excess with the allowable upper limit according to V_peak" marks the specific time interval during which the speed exceeds the V_max/20 threshold, indicating the period used to evaluate if the speed remains within allowable limits relative to V_peak.

After the flange center speed falls below Vmax/20, the Vpeak value is reset to 0 and the allowable upper limit value at Vmax/20 is applied. When the flange center velocity exceeds Vmax/20, Vpeak observation is restarted and the same process is repeated.

<!-- PDF page 1835 -->

> **Image description -- img-98.jpeg:** The image is a graph depicting the speed of the center of a flange over time, measured in millimeters per second (mm/s) on the vertical axis, and time in seconds (s) on the horizontal axis. The graph shows two distinct peaks in speed, labeled V_peak1 and V_peak2, with V_peak1 being higher than V_peak2. The graph is divided into two main sections by vertical dashed lines, each representing the time domain during which the upper limit according to V_peak1 and V_peak2 is applied. The first section, on the left, shows the speed rising to V_peak1 and then falling, with a corresponding time domain marked for applying the upper limit according to V_peak1. The second section, on the right, shows the speed rising to V_peak2 and then falling, with a corresponding time domain marked for applying the upper limit according to V_peak2. Additionally, a horizontal dashed line labeled V_max/20 is shown, indicating a lower speed threshold. The graph illustrates the relationship between the speed peaks and the time intervals during which specific upper limits are enforced.

Note 1 Due to this specification, there may be a time lag between the excess and the alarm occurrence.

2 Whenever the limit value at Vmax/20 is exceeded, the robot will stop immediately with an alarm.
3 If more than one allowable upper limit is exceeded, the alarm will be raised only for the largest excess.

As an exceptional situation, if the speed at the center of the flange exceeds Vmax/20 and does not fall below it again after a certain period of time, a tentative check will be made based on the limit value according to Vpeak at that time. If no excess is detected, the robot motion continues as it is, and after that, the tentative judgment is made again every time a certain period of time elapses. The time for this tentative judgment (intermediate check time) depends on the robot model, but is usually set to about 5 [sec].

### Change of allowable upper limit value according to the payload

There are two types of twenty-staged table that is according to the speed at the center of flange, one for a payload of 0 [kg] and the other for a maximum payload [kg], which are used by linear interpolation according to the actual payload.

In general, the smaller the payload, the larger the allowable upper limit value, and the larger the payload, the smaller the allowable upper limit value. The figure is as follows.

<!-- PDF page 1836 -->

> **Image description -- img-99.jpeg:** The image is a graph plotting rotational speed limits of a flange's center against angular acceleration or jerk (units: deg/s^2 or deg/s^3). The vertical axis represents the upper limit for angular acceleration or jerk, while the horizontal axis represents the speed of the center of the flange in millimeters per second (mm/s). Two curves are shown: a blue curve labeled 'The upper limit for no payload' and a red curve labeled 'The upper limit for maximum payload.' The blue curve is positioned above the red curve, indicating that the flange can tolerate higher angular acceleration or jerk when no payload is attached compared to when it carries the maximum payload. The graph visually demonstrates the relationship between speed and allowable angular acceleration or jerk under different payload conditions.

Note 1 It is necessary to set the payload information according to the actual weight of the work piece.

Refer to “3.17 PAYLOAD SETTING” in the “OPERATOR’S MANUAL (Basic Function) (B-83284EN)” or “ROBOT PAYLOAD SETTING” in this manual.

2 If the payload information has never been set, the setting is based on the maximum payload [kg].
3 If the payload is significantly incorrect, vibration may increase or a collision may be falsely detected.

# Periodic update mode of allowable upper limit ($LMT_MODE=1)

For some robot models, the mode with $LMT_MODE=1 that updates the allowable upper limit of acceleration and jerk for each communication interval based on another algorithm is enabled by default. It may allow greater acceleration and jerk than the conventional. To disable this mode, set the system variable $STMO_GRP[].$LMT_MODE to 0 and cycle power.

If you encounter a problem and wish to make an inquiry, please obtain the diagnostic log by using the following procedure.

Warning

If you execute the diagnostic log function, confirm that the status of robot is STOP.

Note 1 Do the following operation just after the problem occurs and BEFORE POWER OFF.

If you turn off the power, the useful log for investigation will be cleared.

2 Do it only one time just after the problem occurs. The saved log data will be deleted from the robot controller if the same operation is done twice.

### 14.60 SYMMETRIC PART

When a work piece is symmetric, the robot may reach the work piece in different orientations. One of the orientations will use the shortest time. If system automatically chooses this shortest time, it will reduce the total cycle time for the application.

This function provides a method for you to specify the parts symmetric property.

- An irregular shaped object has a symmetric angle of 360 degrees.
- A rectangular part or an oval has a symmetric angle of 180 degrees.
- A square part has a symmetric angle of 90 degrees.
- A hexagonal part has a symmetric angle of 60 degrees.
- A round part has a symmetric angle of 0 degrees.

When a vision process is used to locate a part, vision may be able to know the symmetry of the parts. However, the vision system does not know where the robot is and its orientation. So it may provide a location that causes the robot to rotate more than necessary. This may cause the robot to reach its axes limit or waste valuable production time.

For a non-vision process, the same condition would also happen. However, because the starting position is known, you may be able to avoid it by programming the shortest move.

For a palletizing application, the pallet size and pattern may vary. The pallet program can not predict the robot location, so the program may cause robot to rotate unnecessarily and cause production time delay. Unnecessary tool rotation may also shorten the life span of the dress-out cable.

<!-- PDF page 1844 -->

When this function is enabled, the robot will only rotate the minimum angle based on part symmetry. When this function is enabled, the robot will not rotate more than half of the part's symmetric angle when this function is used. As shown in the figure below:

Figure 14–250. Symmetric Part Orientation

> **Image description -- img-103.jpeg:** The image is a circular diagram illustrating the relationship between a robot's current orientation and its original destination orientation under different symmetry angles (sym_ang). The diagram includes the following key elements: 1) A central point representing the robot's current orientation, marked in red. 2) A vertical line labeled 'Original destination orientation' extending upward from the center, indicating the target direction. 3) Three colored arrows originating from the center and pointing in different directions: - A black arrow labeled 'With sym_ang=360' pointing directly upward, aligned with the original destination orientation. - A green arrow labeled 'With sym_ang=90' pointing to the left, forming a 90-degree angle with the original destination orientation. - A magenta arrow labeled 'With sym_ang=180' pointing downward, forming a 180-degree angle with the original destination orientation. 4) A label 'No sym angle' pointing to the right, indicating the direction without any symmetry angle applied. The diagram visually demonstrates how the robot's orientation changes relative to the original destination orientation based on different symmetry angles.

This function would solve the problem for vision process applications. This function would solve the problem for pelletize applications. This function would also help ease the burden of programming time, thus reducing the application process time.

- Input:

- The pick/drop position is taught with Tool Center Point at exact symmetric center of the work piece.
- User specifies the symmetric part angle depending on the shape of the part. A rectangular part is 180 degrees. A square part is 90 degrees. A cylindrical part is 0 degrees.
- User enables this feature.
- User sets those conditions either in a Macro or in a regular instruction.

- Output:

- The robot move with a minimum rotation of the Tool Center Point from the current position to the target position.

<!-- PDF page 1845 -->

#### 14.60.1 System Variables for Symmetric Parts

- $SYM_PART[group]

: Input for the function

— $SYM_ANGLE: This specify the symmetric of the part.
— $SYM_ENABLE: This enable the symmetric part function.

- $SYMR_STAT[group]: Output Status for this function

— $SYM_A_OFST: This value indicate how many degree was reduced from original orientation.
— $SYM_LINE_N: The line number that symmetric part is currently activated on.
— $SYM_ROS_TIK: Ros Tick for symmetric part activation

$SYMCFG:

— $GROUP_MASK: This is a bit mask to specify which group will facilitate for this function.
— $DEBUG: Debug flag
— $OPT_ENB: used by system internal function.
— $APP_ENB: used by system internal function.

#### 14.60.2 Program Examples for Symmetric Part

For a typical pick and place program

! pick part
L PR[2] 2000 mm/sec CNT100
L PR[3] 2000 mm/sec CNT0 TB R[20], Call VAC_ON
L PR[2] 2000 mm/sec CNT100

Set the system variable \(SYM_PART[group].\)SYM_ANGLE according to the symmetric of the workpiece. For example if the workpiece is a rectangle, \(SYM_PART[group].\)SYM_ANGLE to 180. Set \(SYM_PART[group].\)SYM_ENABLE to TRUE before run the pick program.

You can create a sub program/macro such as SYM180, SYM_ON and SYM180_OFF.

!SYM180
$SYM_PART[1].$SYM_ANGLE = 180

!SYM_ON
$SYM_PART[1].$SYM_ENABLE = 1

!SYM_OFF
$SYM_PART[1].$SYM_ENABLE = 0

<!-- PDF page 1846 -->

Call SYM180 and SYM_ON before call pick program and call SYM_OFF after calling pick program.

With above program, the robot will not move more than 90 degree TCP orientation regardless that starting position

### 14.61 TCP SPEED OUTPUT (OPTION)

#### 14.61.1 Overview

TCP speed output is a function that outputs a value proportional to the TCP speed to a *target* that can be an analog output, a group output, or a register.

The proportional rate is decided by four parameters: Max value, Max speed, Min value, and Min speed.

- When the TCP speed is less than Min speed, the value has Min value.
- When the TCP speed is greater than Max speed, the value has the Max value.

See Figure 14–251.

Figure 14–251. Max Value

> **Image description -- img-104.jpeg:** The image is a line graph depicting the relationship between TCP Speed (horizontal axis) and Value (vertical axis). The horizontal axis is labeled 'TCP Speed' and ranges from 'Min Speed' to 'Max Speed'. The vertical axis is labeled 'Value' and ranges from 'Min Value' to 'Max Value'. The graph shows a linear increase in value as TCP speed increases from Min Speed to Max Speed. At Min Speed, the value is at Min Value, and at Max Speed, the value reaches Max Value. The graph indicates a direct proportionality between TCP Speed and Value, with no intermediate steps or plateaus.

- The Max value can be less than the Min value. In this case the proportional rate is negative. See Figure 14–252.

<!-- PDF page 1847 -->

Figure 14–252. Max Speed

> **Image description -- img-105.jpeg:** The image is a line graph depicting the relationship between TCP Speed (horizontal axis) and Value (vertical axis). The horizontal axis is labeled 'TCP Speed' with two marked points: 'Min Speed' on the left and 'Max Speed' on the right. The vertical axis is labeled 'Value' with two marked points: 'Min Value' near the bottom and 'Max Value' near the top. The graph shows a downward-sloping curve starting from the 'Min Value' at 'Min Speed' and gradually decreasing until it flattens out near the 'Max Value' at 'Max Speed'. The curve indicates that as TCP Speed increases from Min Speed to Max Speed, the Value decreases from Max Value to Min Value, eventually stabilizing at Min Value. The graph visually represents an inverse relationship between TCP Speed and Value.

- When Max speed is less than Min speed, the value is always 0.

You can define up to 10 targets (outputs) to which the system will output the TCP speed proportional value.

- Every target can have individual proportional parameters.
- Every target can be disabled individually.
- When a target is disabled, the value is not set to the target.

The specified targets are set by the function only while a motion instruction is being executed. Otherwise the specified target values keep their respective Min values.

### 14.61.2 Setting Up TCP Speed Output

Use Procedure 14-95 to set up TCP Speed Output.

#### Procedure 14-95 Setting up TCP Speed Output

##### Steps

1. Press MENU.
2. Select 5, I/O.
3. Press F1, TYPE
4. Select TCP Speed. You will see a screen similar to the following:

<!-- PDF page 1848 -->

TCP speed output
List 1/10
Enable Target Min (Val/Spd) Max
1 ON AO[ 1] 100/ 10 4095/ 2000
2 OFF AO[ 2] 0/ 0 0/ 0
3 OFF AO[ 3] 0/ 0 0/ 0
4 OFF AO[ 4] 0/ 0 0/ 0

5. The TCP speed output List menu allows you to enable a target that has already been assigned.

The list menu shows the setting of all 10 targets. Min value, min speed, max value and max speed are all displayed as integer values. You can enable targets in this menu, but you cannot change other items.

To enable a target, move the cursor to the target you want and press F4, ON.

6. To set up details of a target, press F3, DETAIL. You will see a screen similar to the following:

TCP speed output
TCP_SPD[1]
1 Enable: ON
2 Target: AO[ 1]
3 Min. value: 10.000
4 Max. value: 4096.000
5 Min. speed (mm/sec): 100.000
6 Max. speed (mm/sec): 2000.000

The Detail menu allows you to set all the parameters of a target. The min value, min speed, max value, and max speed are all displayed as real values.

You can change the type of the target to AO, GO, or R in this menu.

To return to the List menu, press F3, LIST, or press the PREV key.

7. To set prediction time, at the List menu press F2, SETUP. You will see a screen similar to the following:

TCP speed output
Setup
1 Prediction time (msec): 0

The Setup menu allows you to set a TCP speed prediction time for all targets.

When you set a TCP speed prediction time, all targets will report what the TCP proportional speed will be at a specified future time, for example, 10ms. There is only one prediction time setting for the entire system. You cannot set individual prediction times for each target.

<!-- PDF page 1849 -->

If you do not set a TCP speed prediction time, each target will report the actual TCP proportional speed as it occurs, according to the proportional parameters that were set for that target.

To return to the last menu, press F3, LIST, or press the PREV key.

#### 14.61.3 TCP Speed Output Program Instruction

The TCP speed output function can be set up by TP program instructions. The TCP_SPD item is available under the Register and I/O instructions when Mixed logic is selected. The format of the instruction is the following.

target_type [ target_index ] = ( TCP_SPD [ index ] )

- The ‘target_type’ is the type of the target: AO, GO, or R.
- The ‘target_index’ is the index of the target.
- The ‘TCP_SPD’ is the word used to enable the TCP speed output function.
- The ‘index’ is the line number of the target on the List menu.

When the following instruction is executed, 'Enable' of TCP_SPD[1] will be turned on and 'Target' of TCP_SPD[1] will be set to AO[1].

AO[1]=(TCP_SPD[1])

Register and I/O instructions are also used to disable TCP speed output function. When the following instruction is executed, 'Enable' of TCP_SPD[1] will be turned off and the output value of AO[1] will be forced to be 100.

AO[1]=100

##### TCP Speed Output Instructions

“TCP_SPD” is treated as mixed logic instructions. You can put TCP_SPD only in the area specified by parentheses.

Use Procedure 14-96 to add TCP Speed Output instructions to a teach pendant program.

##### Procedure 14-96 Adding TCP Speed Output Instructions to a Program

1. In the EDIT menu, press F1, INST.
2. Select Registers.
3. Select . . . = ( . . . )
4. To add a Register Statement, select R[ ].

<!-- PDF page 1850 -->

If you want to add a GO Statement, select GO [ ], or to select an AO Statement, select AO [ ].

5. Enter the index number for the Register, GO, or AO.

Mixed logic JOINT 10 %
1 UI[] 5 WI[]
2 UO[] 6 WO[]
3 RI[] 7 TCP_SPD[]
4 RO[] 8 --- next page ---
1 R[1]=(...)
[END]

Select TCP_SPD[ ].

Mixed logic JOINT 10 %
1 UI[] 5 WI[]
2 UO[] 6 WO[]
3 RI[] 7 TCP_SPD[]
4 RO[] 8 --- next page ---
1 R[1]=(TCP_SPD[...])
[END]

6. Enter 1 to assign the first target.

Mixed logic JOINT 10 %
1 UI[] 5 WI[]
2 UO[] 6 WO[]
3 RI[] 7 TCP_SPD[]
4 RO[] 8 --- next page ---
1 R[1]=(TCP_SPD[1])
[END]

<!-- PDF page 1851 -->

### 14.62 TCP SPEED PREDICTION (OPTION)

#### 14.62.1 Overview

The TCP Speed Prediction option provides the predicted value of the TCP speed continuously as the robot is moving. Some robot applications require that you know the Tool Center Point (TCP) speed of the robot ahead of time. This is especially useful for applications that dispense or spray material from a gun attached to the robot arm, where dispensing or spraying equipment cannot be turned on instantaneously. A delay, called the equipment delay, occurs before the flow of fluid becomes effective or before its rate, called the flow rate, changes. If the TCP speed is known ahead of time by the equipment delay time, the flow rate can be adjusted accordingly to increase or decrease depending upon the TCP speed. This provides better quality of dispensed material on the workpiece.

You must enable the TCP Speed Prediction option and set the equipment delay using the system variables described in this section. The TCP Speed Prediction software then computes the predicted value and sets it in another system variable. Your application can access these predicted values through teach pendant or KAREL programs and use them to control equipment precisely.

Although there are a few system variables related to this option, the following are the most important:

- $TCPPIR.$enable_tcpp - enables or disables the TCP Speed Prediction option
- $TCPPIR.$tcdelay - sets the prediction or equipment delay time
- $TCPPSPEED.$speed - this is where the output or the TCP predicted value is output continuously

You use the TCP Speed Prediction option by setting system variables that control how the option works. This section contains the following information:

- An overview of the TCP Speed Prediction option to help you decide when you can use the option - Section 14.62.2
- TCP Speed Prediction system variables that you set to the appropriate values to use TCP Speed Prediction - Section 14.62.3

#### 14.62.2 Setting Up and Running TCP Speed Prediction

This section contains an overview of the TCP Speed Prediction option in the following areas:

- Software setup
- Execution
- Limitations

<!-- PDF page 1852 -->

# Software Setup

You must set several TCP Speed Prediction system variables properly in order to use TCP Speed Prediction. In particular, you must set the $enable_tcpp and $tcdelay fields in the $TCPPIR system variable structure properly. Refer to Section 14.62.3 for details.

# Execution

After you have enabled TCP Speed Prediction using the system variables, TCP Speed Prediction runs automatically as a background task and does not require any additional user input or action. However, to take advantage of TCP Speed Prediction, an application task should be written that monitors the $TCPPSPEED system variable structure (typically the $speed field) for the predicted speed values, and performs whatever processing is required to generate application process control signals.

If the Remote TCP option is used, TCP Speed Prediction shifts its reference frame automatically as an application program switches to the Remote TCP mode and back again. Therefore, no user action is required. However, you must understand that the speed reference - the $TCPPSPEED.$vspeed and $TCPPSPEED.$speed variables in particular - are with respect to the Remote TCP frame instead of the WORLD frame during Remote TCP motions.

# Limitations

The TCP Speed Prediction option has the following limitations:

- Prediction is supported only for group 1 motion. Multiple motion groups can exist and be programmed, but are not supported for TCP Speed Prediction.
- Prediction for non-integrated extended axes is not supported.
- Prediction for JOINT motions is approximated as if the motions were Cartesian motions. Such estimation is generally good enough if the JOINT motion is not too large. If predicted speed accuracy is important, linear motion is recommended.
- Prediction becomes invalid during instances of speed and motor limit conditions and other motion warnings and errors. In these cases, you could correct the programmed path to remove the error conditions. Prediction also becomes temporarily invalid during instances of dynamic speed override changes.
- You can change the prediction time delay ($TCPPIR.$tcdelay) on-the-fly. However, this might cause a momentary discontinuity in the value of the predicted speed output.
- TCP Speed Prediction has no knowledge of WAIT or other system delay instructions that might interrupt robot motion. Therefore, TCP Speed Prediction will continue to predict the speed based upon subsequent motion commands in these cases. However, TCP Speed Prediction will resynchronize itself properly after the delay condition has been met and motion resumes.
- TCP Speed Prediction is not compatible with any of the general tracking options, such as seam tracking and line tracking.
- Transitions between normal TCP Speed Prediction and Remote TCP Speed Prediction include a change of reference frame from WORLD frame to USER (REMOTE TCP) frame. When this transition takes place, the TCP Speed Prediction task will "blend" this change of reference

<!-- PDF page 1853 -->

frame. This might cause the predicted speed signal to show an apparent speed decrease during the blending period.

### 14.62.3 System Variables

Three system variable structures are generated when you load the TCP Speed Prediction option. These structures control the state and configuration of this option, and provide the speed and other output values for user program access. These variables are described in this section:

- $TCPPIR structure
- $TCPPSPEED structure
- $TCPP_CFG structure

### $TCPPIR STRUCTURE

Name: TCP Speed Prediction Instruction Record System Variable Structure

Description: This set of variables allows the user to enable the TCP Speed Prediction softpart and set the equipment delay (prediction) time. The individual fields within this structure are defined below.

User Interface Location: SYSTEM Variables screen

<!-- PDF page 1854 -->

$TCPPIR.$enable_tcpp

Minimum: FALSE

Default: FALSE

Maximum: TRUE

KCL/Data: RW

Program: RW

GET/SET_VAR: RW

Data Type: BOOLEAN

Name: TCP Speed Prediction Enable Switch

Description: This allows you to enable or disable the TCP Speed Prediction softpart. A predicted speed output is generated when the softpart is enabled. This variable is initially set FALSE at the time of loading, and must be set TRUE by the user prior to using the speed prediction values.

Power Up: This value initializes to FALSE and maintains its previous value over subsequent power cycles.

User Interface Location: SYSTEM Variables screen

<!-- PDF page 1855 -->

# $TCPPIR.$tcdelay

Minimum: -5000.0

Default: 200.0

Maximum: 5000.0

KCL/Data: RW

Program: RW

GET/SET_VAR: RW

Data Type: REAL

Name: TCP Speed Prediction (Equipment) Delay Time (milliseconds)

Description: This value allows the user to specify the equipment delay time to be used as the prediction time by the TCP Speed Prediction softpart. This variable is initially set to 200 at the time of loading, but should be set to an appropriate positive value by the user prior to using the speed prediction values.

Power Up: This value initializes to 200 (msec) and maintains its previous value over subsequent power cycles.

User Interface Location: SYSTEM Variables screen

NOTE: Modified values of this variable will take effect immediately if $TCPP_CFG.$otf_tim_enb is TRUE, but will not take effect until all robot motion has stopped if $TCPP_CFG.$otf_tim_enb is FALSE.

# $TCPPSPEED STRUCTURE

Name: TCP Speed Prediction Speed Output System Variable Structure

Description: These are the output system variables that involve the predicted =speed of the robot Tool Center Point (TCP). These variables are updated by the TCPP task softpart at the interval specified by the value of $TCPP_CFG.$tcpp_time. The individual fields within this structure are defined below.

User Interface Location: SYSTEM Variables screen

See Also: $TCPP_CFG.$tcpp_time

<!-- PDF page 1856 -->

$TCPPSPEED.$accel

Minimum: 0 Default: 0

Maximum: 1000.0

KCL/Data: RO

GET/SET_VAR: RO

Name: TCP Speed Prediction Warning Message Enable

Description: This system variable when true allows the posting of warning level error messages. These are warnings only, not faults, which you might want not to be displayed. Currently these messages include the following: - TCPP-011 "Pred time skips first motion" - TCPP-018 "Begin Error Mode at line:nn" - TCPP-019 "Speed Ovrd Mode at line:nn"

Power Up: This value initializes to TRUE and maintains its previous value over subsequent power cycles.

User Interface Location: SYSTEM Variables screen

### 14.63 TEACH PENDANT SHIM

### 14.63.1 Overview

The teach pendant shim (TP Shim) utility allows you to adjust individual positions of a teach pendant by a small amount in either the x, y, or z direction. It also allows you to track those adjustments and recall shims already applied to that position using the History screen. You can shim positions in one group or positions in multiple groups. The teach pendant shim varies from the Program Adjust Utility in that Program Adjust moves multiple positions in a program while the shim moves only one. Also, Program Adjust does not allow you to track previous adjustments.

### A TP Shim Example

Typically, you should shim positions in order, one after the other. This allows the shims to be additive and sequential. If you start off with the following position: X:0.000 Y:0.000 Z:800.000 Shims: 0/0 and you apply a shim of 1 mm in the x direction, the position changes and the shim number and shim maximum increment by one. The new shimmed position is: X:1.000 Y:0.000 Z:800.000 Shims: 1/1.

<!-- PDF page 1866 -->

Apply another shim of 2 mm in the x direction, the position changes, and the shim number and shim maximum increment by one. The new current position is now: X:3.000 Y:0.000 Z:800.000 Shims: 2/2.

Apply another shim of 3 mm in the x direction, the position changes, and shim number and shim maximum increment by one. The new current position is: X:6.000 Y:0.000 Z:800.000 Shims: 3/3 See Figure 14–253.

Figure 14–253. Typical TP Shim Example

> **Image description -- img-106.jpeg:** A vertical flowchart diagram showing the current teach pendant positions for a robotic system. The diagram consists of four labeled positions arranged sequentially from top to bottom: 'Start' at X:0.000, Y:0.000, Z:800.000; 'Shim 1' at X:1.000, Y:0.000, Z:800.000; 'Shim 2' at X:3.000, Y:0.000, Z:800.000; and 'Shim 3' at X:6.000, Y:0.000, Z:800.000. Each position is represented by a circle with an arrow pointing downward to the next position, indicating a sequential progression. The X, Y, and Z coordinates are provided for each position, showing changes only in the X-axis while Y and Z remain constant at 0.000 and 800.000 respectively. The diagram visually represents the spatial progression of the teach pendant along the X-axis for different shim positions.

#### An Advanced TP Shim Example Using USEMAST

TP Shim allows you to shim from the original position using F3, USEMAST.

When you press F3, USEMAST, the original position is restored in the teach pendant program. At this point you can start shimming from that point without disturbing the previously applied shims.

For example,

1. Press F3, USEMAST, and F4, YES, to restore the original position. The new current position is: X:0 Y:0 Z:800 Shims: 0/3.
2. Apply a shim of 1 mm in the y direction, the position changes, and the shim number and shim maximum increment by one. The new current position is: X:0.000 Y:1.000 Z:800.000 Shims: 4/4.
3. Apply a shim of 1 mm in the y direction, the position changes, and the shim number and shim maximum increment by one. The new current position is: X:0.000 Y:2.000 Z:800.000 Shims: 5/5.

### 14.64 TIME BEFORE/AFTER MOTION OPTION INSTRUCTION

#### 14.64.1 Overview

Normally, when a teach pendant program is executed, the instruction that follows a motion instruction is not executed until the motion has been completed. The TIME BEFORE/AFTER motion option instruction allows you to specify a teach pendant program that is to be called or an output that is to be set at a specified time before or after the completion of a motion instruction.

For example, you might specify that a teach pendant program CLS_GRIP is to be called 600 ms before the completion of the move. CLS_GRIP might consist of the instruction DOUT[GRIP]=ON.

This function can reduce external device communication time and improve cycle time. This section contains information on the following:

- Program execution
- Execution timing
- Recording a TIME BEFORE or TIME AFTER instruction
- TIME BEFORE instruction program example
- Programming

Note The Time Before/After Motion Option only exists if the Condition Monitor Option is loaded.

#### 14.64.2 Program Execution

The motion instruction and the sub program (called by the main program) are executed in parallel. Because of this, the execution of the sub program does not affect the robot motion in the main program.

The instruction that follows a TIME BEFORE or TIME AFTER instruction will not be executed until the subprogram specified in the TIME BEFORE or TIME AFTER instruction has been executed.

You must specify the called program in the TIME BEFORE/AFTER instruction and specify the time when the CALL instruction is to be executed (execution timing). If the execution timing is 0 sec, this indicates that the robot has stopped moving. The exact time that the robot stops is determined by the termination type (FINE, CNT 100 and so forth).

The action and the execution timing are taught in the motion option instruction. See Figure 14–256.

<!-- PDF page 1874 -->

Figure 14–256. TIME BEFORE / TIME AFTER Motion Option Instructions

> **Image description -- img-109.jpeg:** The image is a diagram illustrating the timing of motion execution in a programming context, specifically for a subprogram call. It shows a flowchart with the following components: 

1. **Motion Timing**: A horizontal timeline labeled 'TIME BEFORE (TB)' and 'TIME AFTER (TA)', indicating the execution timing of a motion. 'TIME BEFORE' refers to the execution of the action before the motion is done, while 'TIME AFTER' refers to the execution of the action after the motion is done.

2. **Subprogram Call Structure**: A box on the right side details the structure of a subprogram call, including:
   - `CALL<subprogram>`: The command to call a subprogram.
   - `CALL<subprogram>()`: A variation of the call command.
   - `DO[1]=...`: Placeholder for a DO instruction with an index.
   - `GO[1]=...`: Placeholder for a GO instruction with an index.
   - `AO[1]=...`: Placeholder for an AO instruction with an index.
   - `WO[1]=...`: Placeholder for a WO instruction with an index.

3. **Example Usage**: Below the diagram, there are two examples demonstrating the timing of a subprogram call:
   - The first example shows a joint position command `J P[1] 100% FINE` with `TB 0.1sec, CALL HANDOPEN`, indicating the subprogram 'HANDOPEN' is called 0.1 seconds before the motion is completed.
   - The second example shows the same joint position command `J P[1] 100% FINE` with `TA 0.1sec, CALL HANDOPEN`, indicating the subprogram 'HANDOPEN' is called 0.1 seconds after the motion is completed.

The diagram visually explains how to schedule subprogram execution relative to the completion of a motion, with clear labels and examples for 'TIME BEFORE' and 'TIME AFTER' scenarios.

#### Robot TCP Path

With TB instruction, robot TCP path varies with the value of $timebf_ver.

$timebf_ver = 1: Execution of the next line will start without waiting for the completion of the TB action;

$timebf_ver = 2: Execution of the next line will not start until the completion of the TB action;

For example,

1 L P[1] 2000 mm/sec FINE
2 L P[2] 2000 mm/sec CNT100 TB 0.5 sec. DO[1]=ON
3 L P[3] 2000 mm/sec FINE

with $timebf_ver = 2, the execution of line 3 does not start until DO[1] is turned ON. With $timebf_ver=1, line 3 is executed as if there were no TB motion option.

$timebf_ver = 3: The system will automatically determine the behavior based on TB action routine itself:

- If TB action routine is not too long and does not contain WAIT statement, then execution of the next line will start without waiting for the completion of the TB action (the same as when $timetbf_ver = 1);
- If TB action routine is lengthy or has WAIT statement, then execution of the next line will not start until the completion of the TB action (the same as when $timebf_ver=2);

Note With $timebf_ver = 1, 2, or 3, constant path feature is not guaranteed. That is, the TCP path of a robot may vary with the time value in the TB instruction and the time in a WAIT statement of the action (if the action has a WAIT statement);

$timebf_ver = 4: the system tries to maintain constant path. That is, robot TCP path can be maintained the same regardless of the time value in TB instruction, regardless of the time in WAIT statement in TB action and regardless of speed override, as shown in the following figure:

<!-- PDF page 1875 -->

Figure 14–257. Normal Execution when $timebf_ver=4

> **Image description -- img-110.jpeg:** The image is a diagram illustrating a robot motion path with labeled points (P2, P3, P4, P5, P6, P7) and associated program instructions. The robot follows a path from P2 to P7, with specific instructions for each segment. The instructions include movement speed (2000 mm/sec), controller type (CNT100), and time-based (TB) wait commands with varying time values. The diagram highlights that the robot executes normal motion along the path but stops at the corner of the line (P3) if the wait time in the TB instruction is too long. The instructions are as follows: L P[2] 2000 mm/sec CNT100, L P[3] 2000 mm/sec CNT100 TB x sec call ACTION, L P[4] 2000 mm/sec CNT100, L P[5] 2000 mm/sec CNT100, L P[6] 2000 mm/sec CNT100, and L P[7] 2000 mm/sec FINE. The diagram also includes annotations explaining the effect of different time values in the TB instruction and the robot's behavior based on these values.

# Warning

During Hold, E-stop, and Resume, robot TCP path will not be maintained the same path, no matter what the value of $timebf_ver is!

# Single Step Execution

If you are single stepping through a TIME BEFORE/AFTER instruction, the motion is paused when the sub program is called. The robot moves to the destination position as you single step through the sub program.

# Power Fail Recovery

If Hot start is enabled and the controller is turned off while the sub program is executing, the sub program will resume execution from the same line the next time the controller is turned on. Because of this, the execution timing of the sub program is different from normal execution.

<!-- PDF page 1876 -->

### 14.64.3 Execution Timing

Execution timing is the specified time when the CALL instruction is to be executed. Execution timing can be specified as:

• TIME BEFORE : 0 to 30.0 sec
• TIME AFTER : 0 to 0.5 sec

The execution timing begins counting from the time robot motion is completed. Execution timing is not related to override.

If execution timing is set to 0 sec, the sub program is executed at almost the same time as the statement following the MOVE instruction. When 0 sec is set, the next line of the main program can be executed before the sub program starts to execute. The execution timing acts as follows:

Specify [ n sec ] in the TIME BEFORE instruction. See Figure 14–258 .

Figure 14–258. Timing Sequence (TIME BEFORE instruction)

#### 14.64.6 Programming Hints

The following programming hints apply to the TIME BEFORE or TIME AFTER instruction.

- The sub program called from the TIME BEFORE or TIME AFTER instruction cannot contain motion instructions. The motion group mask of the program must be [*,*,*,*,*,*,*,].
- Until the called program has finished executing, the next line cannot be executed.
- There is no limit to the number of lines in a sub program.
- You can use the TIME BEFORE or TIME AFTER instruction in combination with any other motion option instructions, except application instructions such as the Arc Start[] instruction or the SKIP instruction.
- Only one TIME BEFORE or TIME AFTER instruction can be used with a single motion instruction.
- If you add CNT to a motion instruction, the timing when the motion instruction is completed is changed by the value of CNT. Even if 0 sec is specified in the TIME BEFORE instruction, the sub program might be executed too soon. You might need to use the TIME AFTER instruction to adjust the execution timing.

<!-- PDF page 1880 -->

- When the TIME BEFORE or TIME AFTER instruction is used in the last line of the program, the sub program might not be called. This is because the execution of the main program is completed before the sub program is called. Therefore, do not teach the TIME BEFORE or TIME AFTER instruction on the last line.

### 14.65 TORQUE LIMIT

#### 14.65.1 Introduction

The torque limit instruction allows you to limit the maximum torque value of the specified motor.

This function has two advantages, as shown by the example of the servo controlled gripper.

> **Image description -- img-115.jpeg:** The image depicts a mechanical setup involving a servo motor connected to a hand-like structure. The servo motor is positioned centrally and is connected via a linkage mechanism to the hand. The hand is shown in two states: one with fingers spread open and the other with fingers closed, indicating that the servo motor controls the opening and closing of the hand. The linkage system translates the rotational motion of the servo motor into linear motion, which in turn moves the fingers of the hand. The image includes a label pointing to the servo motor, identifying it as the component responsible for the motion, and a caption stating, 'The hand is opened or closed by the servo motor.' The setup appears to be a simplified representation of a robotic hand or gripper mechanism.

- Advantage 1. Simple teaching

The taught point is only one (the point at which the fingers close completely) regardless of the size of part.

- Advantage 2. Holding force is adjustable.

The output of motor can be limited to an arbitrary value and therefore holding force is adjustable and constant.

# (1) Operation without torque function

Each part must have its own position for the part closed position. If sufficient force is applied to hold the part, errors could occur during operation. If the part were to crush slightly during handling, the force on the part would not be maintained and it might be dropped. Also, it is inconvenient in terms of maintenance (part size might change slightly from one part to the next).

> **Image description -- img-116.jpeg:** The image consists of three sequential diagrams, each depicting a process involving a blue robot and a grid-based environment. Each diagram shows a grid with a robot positioned at the top, a smaller inset grid below it, and a sequence of arrows indicating movement or transformation. In the first diagram, the robot is at the top of a 5x5 grid, with an inset grid showing a blue square in the center. The second diagram shows the robot at the top of a 5x5 grid with an inset grid displaying a red vertical rectangle. The third diagram depicts the robot at the top of a 5x5 grid with an inset grid containing a 3x3 grid filled with yellow and green squares. The arrows between the diagrams suggest a progression or transformation from one state to another, likely representing a step-by-step process or algorithm involving the robot and the grid configurations.

The taught point must be changed because the size of the workpiece varies.

<!-- PDF page 1881 -->

##### (2) Operation with torque function

With the torque function feature enabled, only the open and closed positions must be programmed. As the gripper starts to close, the fingers of the gripper will stop when they encounter the part to be picked up. The force of the grip is programmable and is maintained until the gripper is opened.

> **Image description -- img-117.jpeg:** The image shows three sequential diagrams, each depicting a step in a process involving a grid of squares and a series of colored blocks. Each diagram consists of a horizontal row of colored blocks (blue, purple, yellow, and green) positioned above a grid of squares. The first diagram shows the blue block aligned with the leftmost column of the grid, the second diagram shows the purple block aligned with the second column, and the third diagram shows the yellow block aligned with the third column. Below each grid, there is a smaller inset grid with a highlighted (shaded) square, indicating a specific cell of interest. The diagrams appear to represent a process where a colored block moves from left to right across the top row, and the corresponding grid below shows a highlighted cell that changes position in sync with the block's movement. The operational meaning suggests a step-by-step interaction where the position of the colored block determines the highlighted cell in the grid below.

##### (3) Holding force is adjustable.

The maximum value of motor torque can be programmed in the torque limit instruction. Therefore the holding force can be adjusted from 1 to 100% of the maximum motor torque.

#### 14.65.2 Specification

- This function is designed to limit the maximum value of torque generated for a servo-controlled gripper.
- The limit on torque is a percentage of a maximum value of motor torque.

Syntax:

TORQ_LIMIT t% (t:0.0 ~ 100.0)

- The following system variables are used to set the axis that the torque limit is applied to. The default value is 7th axis of group 1.

\(TORQUE_LMT.\)GROUP[i]: This system variable represents the group number that the torque limit is applied to, where i is the group number. If this system variable is set to True for a group, it means that the torque limit is applied to that particular group.

i: group number

\(TORQUE_LMT.\)GAi[j]: This system variable represents the group and the axis number for the motor to which torque limitation is applied.

i: group number,
j: axis number

For example, if the motor is the first axis of group 2, \(GA2[1]\) is set to TRUE and others are set to FALSE.

\(TORQUE_LMT.\)GROUP[2] = TRUE
\(TORQUE_LMT.\)GA2[1] = TRUE

<!-- PDF page 1882 -->

\(TORQUE_LMT.\(GA2[2]\) = FALSE
:
\(TORQUE_LMT.\(GA2[9]\) = FALSE

— GA1[1] to GA1[6] are normally robot axes and are not set TRUE.
— Multiple axes can be set TRUE.

- You must determine the optimal value of force for each part. The part weight and gripped surface may affect the torque required to hold the part firmly.
- During torque limit, the maximum of motor torque is not changed until the next torque limit instruction is reached.

Example.

1: J P[1] 100% FINE
2: TORQ_LIMIT 20.0% <- Torque limitation is set to 20%.
3: J P[2] 100% FINE
4: L P[2] 500mm/sec CNT100 <- Maximum Torque is limited to 20%.
6: TORQ_LIMIT 100.0% <- Torque limitation is set to 100%.

- If the torque limit instruction lowers the motor torque too much, the axis might not be able to reach the taught point. The value of the following system variable should be large enough that errors do not occur during normal operation.

— $PARAM_GROUP[group].$STOPTOL[axis]
— $PARAM_GROUP[group].$STOPERLIM[axis]
— $PARAM_GROUP[group].$MOVER_OFFST[axis]

- You can specify the maximum value of torque limit by using the following system variable.

$TORQUE_LMT.$MAX_TRQ_LMT = Upper limit

Lower limit is 0.1 fixed value.

#### 14.65.3 Restriction

# Warning

Because this function can also be applied to the robot axis, special care should be taken in NOT enabling this function for an axis that could fall due to the robot's own mass, for instance a gravity loaded axis.

<!-- PDF page 1883 -->

- This function only limits the maximum value of motor torque and, consequently, has no effect on the output torque of motor.
- This function is designed for the FANUC servo motors only. Special considerations and extensive care are needed if the motor is manufactured by another company than FANUC.

### 14.66 TOUCH SKIP (formerly known as Collision Skip)

#### 14.66.1 Overview

This function can perform a SKIP by monitoring the disturbance of multiple axes. When this option is ordered,

- the SETUP/ TOUCH.SKIP screen can be displayed.
- Touch Skip programs can be called.

Note You must load option J921 (Touch Skip) in order for Touch Skip macros to be available for use.

Note Note that the system variable $MISC_MSTR.$HPD_ENB must be TRUE when Touch Skip is used. If $MISC_MSTR.$HPD_ENB is not TRUE, please set $MISC_MSTR.$HPD_ENB TRUE and cycle power.

Note The Touch Skip function is an option. Some robot models do not support this function.

#### 14.66.2 Touch Skip Screen

In Touch Skip screen, conditions to decide the touch are set.

#### Procedure 14-100 Displaying the Touch Skip Screen

1. Press MENU.
2. Select SETUP.
3. Press F1, [TYPE].
4. Select TOUCH SKIP. You will see a screen similar to the following.

<!-- PDF page 1884 -->

SETUP/ TOUCH SKIP JOINT 95 % 1/7
Scd. No. [10]
Max. threshold(A) / Min. threshold(A)
J1: 0.00[dis] / 0.00[dis]
J2: 0.00[dis] / 0.00[dis]
J3: 17.80[enb] / 0.00[dis]
J4: 0.00[dis] / 0.00[dis]
J5: 0.00[dis] / -1.78[enb]
J6: 0.00[dis] / 0.00[dis]
[ TYPE ]

5. To change the schedule number, enter a value in "Scd. No." field.
6. Set values and enable/disable of thresholds of each axis in lines below. Please check the disturbance during the motion by STATE -> AXES -> DISTURBANCE screen and please add margins if necessary.

Note In the example above, a condition of “J3 disturbance is larger than 17.8[A] or J5 disturbance is smaller than -1.78[A]” is set.

#### 14.66.3 Touch Skip Programs

The following programs can be called:

- SETSKCOL(s, g) — is is a program to set schedule No. [s], which is set on Touch Skip screen, on threshold of group [g].
- CLSKP_Gg — These are programs to set skip condition “disturbance exceeds threshold in an axis of group [g]”. For example, you can use these programs as follows.

AAA JOINT 10 %
3/178
3: CALL SETSKCOL(10,1)
4: CALL CLSKP_G1
5:
6: J P[12] 10% CNT3 SKIP, LBL[9]
7: JUMP LBL[8]
8:
9: LABEL[8:touch occurred]
10: J P[13] 10% FINE
11: PAUSE
12:
13: LABEL[9:touch did not occur]
14: J P[14] 10% FINE
DIRECT INDIRECT

- In line3, schedule No. [10] which is set on Touch Skip screen is set on threshold of group [1].

<!-- PDF page 1885 -->

- In line4, skip condition “disturbance exceeds threshold in an axis of group [1]” is set. Same as other skip conditions, this condition has been effective until program ends or another skip condition is set.
- A motion with skip instruction in line6 works all the same as other skip conditions. When disturbance exceeds threshold in an axis of group [1], the next line (line 9) is executed. And the jump to the label [9] is executed when the motion is done without any excess of disturbance in an axis of group [1]. Motions with quick skip instruction (SKIP, LBL, PR) work all the same.

### 14.66.4 Cautions

- To decrease impact of stopping when skip condition is satisfied, speed limit is set for the motion with touch skip instruction. The speed limit is adjusted for each robot models. When taught speed exceeds the limit, speed limit works automatically. When speed limit works, the following warning is displayed.

MOTN-560 Hspd.skip speed limit (G:group number)

- Some robot models decreased stop when high-speed skip instruction is executed. With such a robot, touch skip function can not be used. When touch skip function is executed with such a robot, the following alarm is displayed.

MOTN-561 Touch skip NOT available (G:group number)

- Touch skip can not be used with skip instruction (Skip, LBL). When touch skip is executed with skip instruction (Skip, LBL), the following alarm is displayed. When you use touch skip function, you must teach high-speed skip instruction (Skip, LBL, PR).

MOTN-561 Touch skip NOT available (G:group number)

### 14.67 XVR ACCESS FUNCTION

### 14.67.1 Overview

XVR – The XML VR (Variable) Access function provides a function to import and export system and KAREL variables in the form of an XML file.

This function has the following benefits.

- Selected Variable Update – May not want to load sysvar.sv
- Fixing customer systems by changing XML and importing it
- Customer may want ASCII readable file

<!-- PDF page 1886 -->

### 14.67.2 Configuration

The configuration file have to be loaded to the controller before the XML file can be imported/exported.

#### Configuration File

The configuration file will appear as shown below. It can have any name with extension “.CVR” e.g. MYSV.CVR. These configuration files will be loaded to Mem Device (MD:).

Naming Convention: <file_name>.cvr

<XMLCFG>
    <PROG name="*SYSTEM*">
    <VAR name="$SYSTEM_TIME" />
    <VAR name="$SCR.$DUMMY162" />
    </PROG>
</XMLCFG>

#### Procedure 14-101 Loading Configuration Files Using the FILE Menu

1. Set the default device to the device you want:

a. Press MENU.
b. Select FILE.
c. Press F1, [TYPE].
d. Select File.
e. Press F5, [UTIL].
f. Select Set Device.

g. Move the cursor to the device you want and press ENTER.

2. To load the configuration file, move the cursor to the item "* CVR (all CVR files)" and press ENTER to display the file name in the device, move the cursor to the name of the file you want to load, and press NEXT, >, and then press F2, COPY.
3. Press F4, [CHOICE], to select the device to which the file will be copied.
4. Move the cursor to Mem Device (MD:) and press ENTER.
5. Press F1, DO_COPY.

### 14.67.3 Export Function (Backup)

The export mechanism will take a configuration as an input and it will output the XML file containing all the system and KAREL variables. You can modify the values of any variables and import them back using the mechanism below to update the values.

<!-- PDF page 1887 -->

# Output File

The corresponding XML file, generated from the above configuration, appears as shown below. It will have the name with extension .XVR e.g. MYSV.XVR.

Naming Convention: <file_name>.xvr</file_name>

<XMLVAR version="V9.1013 4/12/2017">
<PROG name="*SYSTEM*">
<VAR name="$SYSTEM_TIME">
<ARRAY name = "$SYSTEM_TIME[1]">
<FIELD name="PWR_TOT" prot="RO">379</FIELD>
<FIELD name="PWR_LAP" prot="RO">0</FIELD>
<FIELD name="SRV_TOT" prot="RO">379</FIELD>
<FIELD name="SRV_LAP" prot="RO">0</FIELD>
<FIELD name="RUN_FLG" prot="RO">0</FIELD>
<FIELD name="RUN_TOT" prot="RO">0</FIELD>
<FIELD name="RUN_LAP" prot="RO">0</FIELD>
<FIELD name="WIT_FLG" prot="RO">0</FIELD>
<FIELD name="WIT_TOT" prot="RO">0</FIELD>
<FIELD name="WIT_LAP" prot="RO">0</FIELD>
<FIELD name="SHM_TOT" prot="RO">0</FIELD>
<FIELD name="SHM_LAP" prot="RO">0</FIELD>
</ARRAY>
</VAR>
<VAR name="$SCR.$DUMMY162" prot="RW">255</VAR>
</PROG>
</XMLVAR>

# Procedure 14-102 Exporting XVR Using the FILE Menu

1. Set the default device to Mem Device (MD):

a. Press MENU.
b. Select FILE.
c. Press F1, [TYPE].
d. Select File.
e. Press F5, [UTIL].
f. Select Set Device.
g. Move the cursor to Mem Device (MD:) and press ENTER.

2. To export the output file, move the cursor to the item "* XVR (all XVR files)" and press ENTER to display the file name in Mem Device (MD:), move the cursor to the name of the file you want to copy, and press NEXT, >, and then press F2, COPY.
3. Press F4, [CHOICE], to select the device to which the file will be copied.
4. Move the cursor to the device name you want and press ENTER.
5. Press F1, DO_COPY.

<!-- PDF page 1888 -->

#### 14.67.4 Import Function (Restore)

The import function reads the XVR file and will update the corresponding system or KAREL variables. Import function will be ignored if the variable data is uninitialized. The following message will be displayed:

VARS-217 [Variable Name] Variable is uninitialized.

##### Procedure 14-103 Importing XVR Using the FILE Menu

1. Set the default device to the device you want:

a. Press MENU.
b. Select FILE.
c. Press F1, [TYPE].
d. Select File.
e. Press F5, [UTIL].
f. Select Set Device.

g. Move the cursor to the device you want and press ENTER.

2. To import the XVR file, move the cursor to the item “* XVR (all XVR files)” and press ENTER to display the file name in the device, move the cursor to the name of the file you want to import, and press NEXT, >, and then press F2, COPY.
3. Press F4, [CHOICE], to select the device to which the file will be copied.
4. Move the cursor to Mem Device (MD:) and press ENTER.
5. Press F1, DO_COPY.
6. To overwrite, press F4, YES, otherwise press F5, NO.

##### Variable Protection

The system variable “$XVRCFG.$PROT_OVRD” sets the read-only variable to be write protected. It is set to FALSE by default. If variables are read-only, then they will be ignored by the system.

If you need to update any read-only variables, then this system variable “$XVRCFG.$PROT_OVRD” needs to be set to TRUE and modify prot = "RO" to prot = "RW" in the XVR file.

# Positional Data

Transform representation will be output like Cartesian representation but representation will be preserved so during import data is converted back to actual format. For all other representations, if representation mismatch is found, import function will be ignored for that positional item, and the following message will be displayed:

VARS-216 [Variable Name] Representation mismatch

If an invalid group number is specified for the position data, import function will be ignored for that positional item, and the following message will be displayed:

## 15.1 OVERVIEW

The FANUC Sensor Interface is an optional feature that enables the controller to communicate with an external sensor device through the RS-232-C serial port. The sensor device provides the controller with position offset data. The controller uses the position offset data for robot motion compensation.

Usually, a sensor has a coordinate system that differs from the coordinate system used by the robot. Because of this difference, the offset data must be transformed so the result reflects a valid offset for the coordinate system of the robot.

After the controller receives the offset data, you can use the offset data to compensate any taught position in your program.

Refer to Section 15.3 for more information about programming.

## 15.2 COMMUNICATION PROTOCOL

### 15.2.1 Overview

The FANUC Sensor Interface has a proprietary software flow control mechanism and uses its own data format. This communication protocol is similar to Xmodem protocol, but uses a very simple control sequence. It has a fixed data format and is equipped with a block checksum character for error detection.

### 15.2.2 Flow Control Mechanism

Four different flow control codes are available:

- ENQ
- ACK
- NAK
- EOT

ENQ (enquiry) 0x05 in hex representation

For every transmitted packet, the sending end sends an ENQ request to the receiving end to begin the data exchange. The sending end waits for the receiving end to respond with an ACK signal. If the sending end does not receive any acknowledgement from the receiving end within a predefined period of time, an error occurs.

<!-- PDF page 1893 -->

# ACK (acknowledgement) 0x06 in hex representation

The receiving end sends ACK when it is ready for data transmission. If the receiving end receives an ENQ but is not ready for data exchange, it sends a NAK.

# NAK (not acknowledged) 0x95 in hex representation

The receiving end sends a NAK if it is not ready for data exchange when an ENQ arrives.

# EOT (end of transmission) 0x84 in hex representation

After the sending end sends all the data in a packet, it notifies the receiving end that the packet sending session is finished by sending an EOT.

# 15.2.3 Data Format

The FANUC Sensor Interface recognizes five different fixed length packet formats:

0X55
0X5A
0X36
0X3A
0X6C

These packet formats are composed as shown in Figure 15-1 and are detailed in Table 15-1.

Figure 15-1. Composition of FANUC Sensor Data Packet

> **Image description -- img-118.jpeg:** The image depicts a horizontal rectangular block divided into four equal segments, each labeled with a specific term. From left to right, the segments are labeled as follows: "TCC", "Count", "Data", and "BCC". Each label is centered within its respective segment. The labels likely represent distinct fields or components in a structured data format or communication protocol, where "TCC" and "BCC" could denote control or checksum fields, "Count" might indicate a numerical value or counter, and "Data" represents the payload or information content.

# TCCTransfer Control Character1 Byte

The receiving end uses the TCC to interpret the corresponding data in the packet.

# Count1 Byte

The Count is the number of bytes that follows in the Data section. (BCC is not included.)

# DataMultiple Bytes

The Data section represents the data to be exchanged. The Data section allows multiple bytes, but the number of bytes is fixed for each TCC.

<!-- PDF page 1894 -->

# BCCBlock Checksum Character1 Byte

The BCC is computed by taking Exclusive-Or (XOR) of all bytes in the Count and data section.
This is an even parity checking mechanism for error detection.

Table 15-1. FANUC Sensor Data Formats

### 15.2.4 Handshaking

There are five handshaking sequences for each packet:

- Send the contents of a register to the sensor.
- Receive a register number and its data.
- Receive data for a position register.

<!-- PDF page 1895 -->

- Receive three point data.
- Receive the transformation matrix.

Figure 15–2 through Figure 15–6 illustrate each of these handshaking sequences.

Figure 15–2. Handshaking When the Contents of a Register is Sent to the Sensor

> **Image description -- img-119.jpeg:** The image depicts a communication protocol sequence diagram between a ROBOT and a SENSOR. The diagram shows a series of labeled signals and data exchanges with corresponding hexadecimal values. The sequence begins with the ROBOT sending an ENQ (enquiry) signal (0x05) to the SENSOR, which responds with an ACK (acknowledgment) signal (0x06). The ROBOT then sends a SEND REG (send register) command (0x55 03 DATA BCC) to the SENSOR, which again responds with an ACK (0x06). Finally, the ROBOT sends an EOT (end of transmission) signal (0x84) to the SENSOR, concluding the communication sequence. The arrows indicate the direction of the signals, with the ROBOT initiating all commands and the SENSOR providing acknowledgments. The hexadecimal values represent the specific codes or data being transmitted at each step.

### 15.3 PROGRAMMING

There are four program instructions associated with the FANUC sensor interface:

- SEND R[*]
- RCV R[*], LBL[*]
- RCV R[*] LBL[x] TIMEOUT, LBL[y]
- CALMATRIX

SEND R[*] sends out a packet with TCC = 0X5A. RCV R[*], LBL[*] waits for input until the register is set, then continues to the OFFSET condition instruction. If a communication error occurs, program execution will jump to LBL[1]. CALMATRIX computes the transformation matrix for offset data.

The OFFSET program element can then be used in your program to compensate the motion of any recorded robot position. Refer Chapter 7 PROGRAM INSTRUCTIONS for more information about program instructions.

In the programming example shown in FANUC Sensor Interface Program Example, sensor will send all the offset data to the position registers. At the end, sensor set R[2] to 1 so program execution will continue. At that point, P[1], P[2], and P[3] will be offset by the sensor input.

# Caution

Recorded positions are not affected by UFRAME and UFRAME has no affect during playback. However, position registers are recorded with respect to UFRAME. If you change UFRAME, any recorded position registers will also change.

# FANUC Sensor Interface Program Example

1: R[1] = 2
2: R[2] = 0
3: !Notify sensor to use R[2] to terminate comm
4: SEND R[1]
5: !Get the input, at the end set R[2] to 1
6: RCV R[2], LBL[1]
7: OFFSET CONDITION PR[1]
8: J P[1] 100% FINE OFFSET
9: J P[2] 100% FINE OFFSET
10: J P[3] 100% FINE OFFSET

### 15.4 SENSOR SETUP AND HARDWARE CONNECTIONS

To use an external sensor device with the controller, you must:

<!-- PDF page 1898 -->

- Set up the RS-232-C port.
- Connect the RS-232-C port to an external sensor.

You set up the port using the Port Init screen in the SETUP menu. The external sensor device uses the following default communications setting:

- 4800 baud
- 1 stop bit
- Odd parity

Refer to Section 12.1.4 for information on how to set up a port.

You use a NULL modem cable to connect the RS-232 port to a sensor device. Refer to Table 15–2 for the pin connector layout.

Table 15–2. NULL Modem Cable Pin Connector Layout
