## 16.1 OVERVIEW

### 16.1.1 Overview

The /RCalibration options are a family of products that relate to robot accuracy. Refer to Table 16–1 for information about the functions each option performs.

Table 16–1. Relation of /RCalibration Options

[tbl-140.md](tbl-140.md)

<!-- PDF page 1902 -->

[tbl-141.md](tbl-141.md)

** Frame Shift, TCP Shift, and Master Recovery functions for production maintenance and recovery require some operation during the setup phase.

Use the following steps to set up and use the iRCalibration options:

1. Install robot and workcell hardware and software, including an iRCalibration Mastering or iRCalibration TCP fixture (you can use the same fixture or different fixtures for iRCalibration Mastering and iRCalibration TCP).
2. Use iRCalibration Master Set for initial Mastering; Use iRCalibration Master Recovery for mastering reference. iRCalibration Master Set can also compute the initial TCP value.
3. Use iRCalibration TCP Set for initial TCP setting; Use iRCalibration TCP Shift for TCP referencing.iRCalibration Mastering and iRCalibration TCP do not necessarily need to use the same tooling and fixturing, so a separate referencing of iRCalibration TCP is needed.
4. Use iRCalibraiton Frame Set to set the initial user frame; Use iRCalibration Frame Shift to set the frame referencing.iRCalibration Frame Shift can also be used as a quick check to detect misaligned fixtures or tooling.
5. Teach all required robot programs, using iRCalibration TCP Shift periodically to verify and correct the TCP whenever inadvertent collisions occur during jogging and test running of programs.
6. During production, execute iRCalibration TCP Shift in automatic mode to maintain an accurate TCP or to signal when the TCP becomes inaccurate.
7. Use iRCalibration Frame Shift to quickly check the location of one or more points on the tooling, fixture, or part.
8. When recovering from a crash or major hardware maintenance:

- If mastering is lost on one or more axes, use iRCalibration Master Recovery to recover mastering.
- If the TCP becomes mis-aligned, recover the TCP with iRCalibration TCP Shift.
- If the cell fixturing becomes mis-aligned, recover the user frame with iRCalibration Frame Shift.

<!-- PDF page 1903 -->

### 16.1.2 Torque Observer Sensor and Electrical Continuity Sensing

The Torque Observer Sensor (TOS) can detect the contact between a robot tool and an object without the use of external sensors, signals, or I/O. This technology uses motor torque signals and other information to detect such contact using a very light contact force. TOS is especially useful for applications such as waterjet cutting where other detection methods might not be practical. There are two kinds of TOS: TOS Wrist and TOS All Axes.

TOS All Axes is the default method and is recommended when the I/O method is not used.

TOS All Axes monitors the motor torque signals for all axes. This method requires more contact force for contact detection, but it does not have the limitation of TOS Wrist regarding the TCP placement. TOS All axes is recommended for all standard six-axis articulated robots, but naturally, it is generally much more sensitive and requires less force to detect contact with small robots than with large robots. TOS is not available for all robots. Refer to the Software Release Note for specifics. The torque threshold setting in the detection schedule may need to be adjusted in some cases

The TOS All Axes method performs a small learning motion before each search, so the tooling should have clearance to allow this learning motion to complete without contact. The learning speed and distance can be changed on the Detection Schedule Setup Screen. Refer to Table 16–10, Table 16–16, or Table 16–25.

TOS Wrist monitors the signals from the wrist axes so that contact between the tool and an object is detected very quickly using very light contact force. For this reason, if the line between the contact point on the tool and the wrist center is parallel to the search direction, the detection requires much more force. Normally this situation does not occur for tooling such as waterjet cutting where the TCP is away from the faceplate (J6) axis and where the tool shaft is not parallel to the faceplate (J6) axis, but care should be taken if you are using TOS with a tool that does not meet this constraint. TOS Wrist works best with six-axis, smaller-payload robots.

TOS Wrist is very sensitive and can be more prone to false detections in certain cases than the more robust TOS All Axes method. TOS Wrist is not recommended except for special cases where it can verified that false detections will not occur.

All of the applications that use TOS technology can use I/O as an alternate signal to TOS. These applications can work on any robot regardless of tooling configuration or payload by using the I/O detection method. Many processes, such as arc welding, some laser cutting, and some spot welding, have an I/O contact detection means as part of the process equipment. For these processes, use the I/O method instead of the TOS unless some of the contact points (tool orientation, for example) do not have the I/O contact detection capability.

If the I/O signal detection method is used by the /RCalibration option, then a corresponding output signal is provided so that user circuitry can enable the input signal in the situations where it is desired to have the I/O active only while the /RCalibration option is being used. The I/O method can be used by charging the tooling (for example, for arc welding or laser cutting) and detecting the change from a being in a charged state to being in a grounded state where the contact plate is grounded to the I/O ground. Alternatively, the contact plate can be electrically isolated and charged and the contact detected by grounding the contact plate through the normal grounding capability on the robot tooling. The advantage of the charged plate method is that no additional circuitry needs to be on the robot arm itself.

<!-- PDF page 1904 -->

Note Because of compliance, robot dressout, axis configuration, and other factors, the Torque Observer Sensor may not yield the same results in different areas of the workcell with the same threshold setting. This is generally not an issue for iRCalibration TCP Shift and iRCalibration Master Recovery because they use the same configuration for mastering and recovery.

For initial TCP and initial Robot Calibration, each detection motion has a similar and opposite detection motion, thereby minimizing any such effects. However, for iRCalibration Frame Shift where large configuration changes of the robot axes may exist in some cases between mastering and recovery motions, care should be taken in the choice of detection motion. For this case, having symmetric and opposing detections will minimize the error.

#### 16.1.3 iRCalibration TP Instructions

- Calib Start[n]
- Utool Start[n]
- Uframe Start[n]
- Detect Point[m] frame[dir]
- Detect Circle[m,xyoff,zoff] frame[dir]
- Detect Joint[m] axis[num,dir]
- Utool End type
- Uframe End type
- Update Frame
- Update TCP
- Calib End

The iRCalibration Options all use TP programs as a basis of their execution. Each iRCalibration Option has its own start instruction, Calib Start for iRCalibration Mastering, UTool Start for iRCalibration TCP, and UFrame Start for iRCalibration Frame. All the start instructions include a schedule number that allows different acceptance tolerances, limits, and register numbers associated with that option.

# Detection Instructions

Two detection instructions, Detect Point and Detect Circle, are used by all the iRCalibration Options. A third instruction, Detect Joint, is supported only by iRCalibration Mastering for single axis recovery.

The Detect Point instruction has three parameters:

- The first parameter is a detection schedule index
- The second parameter is the search frame, one of WORLD, UFRAME, or UTOOL.
- The last parameter is search direction, plus or minus XYZ in the specified search frame. During the search motion the robot will move along the search direction until contact is detected or until the search distance specified in the detection schedule is reached.

The Detect Circle instruction has five parameters:

- The first parameter is the detection schedule index.

<!-- PDF page 1905 -->

- The second parameter is the XY Offset which is the distance perpendicular to the search direction the robot will move in order to detect the surface.
- The third parameter is the Z offset which is the offset past the plate surface that the robot will move before performing the circle search.
- The fourth parameter is the search frame, one of WORLD, UFRAME, or UTOOL.
- The fifth parameter is the search direction, plus or minus XYZ in the specified search frame. This is the direction the robot will move to detect the plate surface if XY Offset and Z offset are non-zero. If the XY Offset and Z offset are zero then the robot must be taught inside the hole and no search for the plate surface is performed.

# Update Instructions

The Update Tool instruction will apply a partial update to a TCP calibration recovery program. All the detections before the Update Tool are applied. This is useful in determining a Tool Z direction, for instance before searching the X or Y directions to ensure the proper Z height for the latter instructions. Multiple Update Tool instructions are allowed.

Update Tool instructions are not included in the generated iRCalibration TCP Shift programs, but can be added manually after generation.

The Update Frame instruction, similar to the Update Tool instruction will apply a partial update to a UFrame calibration recovery program. All the detections before the Update Frame are applied. This is useful in determining a UFrame Z direction, for instance before searching the X or Y directions to ensure the proper Z height for the latter instructions. You could also do three Z searches then apply the Update Frame instruction to get the partial orientation of that plane. Then the remaining X and Y searches will be in the correct Z distance.

Update Frame instructions are not included in the generated iRCalibration Frame Shift programs, but can be added manually after generation.

# 16.2 IRCALIBRATION MASTER SET

# 16.2.1 Overview

Note iRCalibration Master Set is not available for all robots. Refer to Software Release Note for specifics.

iRCalibration Master Set, formerly RobotCal, is the 3rd generation of calibration software FANUC America Corporation has offered. It follows the AccuSight (1989) and AccuCal (1997) products with updated user interface and TOS technology.

iRCalibration Master Set is an optional calibration option that can do initial calibration of a robot.

iRCalibration Master Set uses a wizard-style menu. It shows the steps that need be done to complete the robot calibration process. Each step of the process has its own status display that shows where you are in the setup process. You cannot skip steps and you cannot go to the next

<!-- PDF page 1906 -->

step without completing the current step. iRCalibration Master Set also includes a menu item, View Result, that lets you review the previous calibration result and log history.

- iRCalibration Master Set uses teach pendant programs for all execution. These programs are typically generated by iRCalibration Master Set, but can also be created or modified by the user.
- iRCalibration Master Set supports initial mastering
- iRCalibration Master Set supports schedule based sensor setup and can use a different schedule for different searches.
- Because iRCalibration Master Set uses very large axis rotations, the TCP and mastering values are very accurate.
- iRCalibration Master Set supports all robot motion groups.

It is recommended that iRCalibration Master Set calibration be performed on all robots before any points are taught. The axes that normally require calibration are J2, J3, J4, and J5. In general, J1 and J6 are not calibrated under initial calibration because a taught UFrame and UTool will completely correct for any error in these axes.

The same program used for iRCalibration Master Set can later be used to recover mastering for any or all robot axes, J1 through J6. If iRCalibration Master Set is not performed, but iRCalibration Master Recovery mastering is performed, it is recommended to both master and recover at least J2, J3, J4, and J5. It is not recommended to recover a different set of axes than were mastered, except it is OK to recover J1 and J6 as described in Table 16–3. Also, see the special requirements regarding J2 for robots with linear J1 axis.

### Hardware Requirements

The following hardware is required to use iRCalibration Master Set:

- Calibration tooling. Refer to Section 16.2.2.
- Six-axis robot (except as indicated in the Software Release Note)
- User-supplied circuitry for using I/O sensor (for robots with delicate tooling)

If the standard tooling is used, iRCalibration Master Set can generate a program to perform initial mastering of robot axes 2 through 5, usually without any user point teaching. Standard tooling is available for most robots to support the default calibration program generated by iRCalibration Master Set.

### Using iRCalibration Mastering

To use iRCalibration Master Set, you must do the following:

1. Install the iRCalibration Master Set software option and any required hardware.
2. Set up iRCalibration Master Set.
3. Create a robot calibration program.
4. Run iRCalibration Master Set to set up initial mastering.

<!-- PDF page 1907 -->

### 16.2.2 Preliminary Setup

# **Standard /RCalibration Master Set Hardware**

Standard /RCalibration Master Set hardware is available. It includes the following components:

- Calibration Tool to attach to the faceplate of the robot. An adapter plate may be required.
- Calibration Arm with one or two calibration plates to attach to the base of the robot
- I/O cable to attach to the robot EE connector

The standard hardware available includes the following:

- EE connector cable to support the I/O detection method of the Calibration Options. Cables are available to support both 5-pin and 24-pin EE connectors.

— EE-5770-020-040 (4 meters).
Cable Assembly for End Effector Touch Sensor w / 24 Pin Connector
— EE-5770-021-025 (2.5 meters).
Cable Assembly for End Effector Touch Sensor w / 5 Pin Connector

- Calibration tool assembly to mount to the robot faceplate. The calibration tool assembly consists of a base to mount to the faceplate, a supporting tube extending away from the base, an attached nonconducting block, and a calibration pointer supported by the non-conducting block. The angle between the J6 axis and the calibration pointer is 70 degrees for the short tool and 45 degrees for the long tool. Multiple tools and adapters are available to support most robots.

1. MO-1800-943 Calibration Tool Assembly – Short
2. MO-1800-944 Calibration Tool Assembly – Long
3. MO-1800-945-001 Calib. Tool Adapt. - M710/20L

7. MO-1800-945-005 Calib. Tool Adapt. - Arc Tregasis
8. MO-1800-945-006 Calib. Tool Adapt. - Arc Binzel

- Calibration arm to mount to the robot base. The calibration arm assembly includes two calibration plates and a mounting bracket. /RCalibration Master Set, depending on robot model and configuration, uses one or both of the plates. Multiple calibration arms are available to support most robots.

— MO-1800-940 Calibration Arm Assembly –Standard
— MO-1800-941 Calibration Arm Assembly – Short

Note The standard calibration arm, MO-1800-940, can be used on any robot which is supported by the short calibration arm, MO-1800-941.

*The M710iB/20L-SA does not currently have a Standard Calibration Tool assembly available.

Some robots, for example the top loader series of robots, do not have an available standard calibration arm. For these cases, iRCalibration Master Set can still generate the standard iRCalibration Master Set program if the user installs the standard calibration tool to the robot faceplate and installs a calibration plate at the proper location for the generated calibration program.

Robots that cannot do FRONT/BACK configuration change or FLIP/NOFLIP configuration change require two calibration plates. For all robots, the first calibration plate must be located parallel to the robot World Y-Z plane with the hole centered at the Uframe coordinates.

If the robot requires two plates, the second plate must be located in the X-Y plane with the hole centered at these values: (Uframe.x – 56, Uframe.y-82, Uframe.z+57). The two-plate method of initial calibration is more accurate for robots that cannot change configuration than the single plate method. The two-plate method generates 11 calibration points on the first plate and 6 on the second plate.

The Standard iRCalibration Master Set calibration plate(s) are attached (by a calibration arm) to the mastering holes located on front of the robot base. The calibration arm is located along the +Y direction of robot World frame. The calibration plates are not precisely located; iRCalibration Master Set will fine tune the actual location of the calibration plates.

Refer to Procedure 16-13 for information on installing and aligning the Touch Plate and for setting up the Touch Plate for use with iRCalibration Master Set.

<!-- PDF page 1909 -->

Note If there is significant mastering correction or if the generated program positions are not centered on the calibration plate hole, you should run iRCalibration Master Set twice.

### 16.2.3.1 Setting Up iRCalibration Master Set

iRCalibration Master Set uses a wizard-style menu. It shows the steps that need be done to complete the robot calibration process. Each step of the process has its own status display that shows where you are in the setup process. You cannot skip steps and you cannot go to the next step without completing the current step.

iRCalibration Master Set also includes a menu item, View Result, that lets you review the previous calibration result and log history. Both iRCalibration Master Set and iRCalibration Master Shift share the same calibration log.

iRCalibration Master Set should be used:

- Before you teach any points or run any programs on a new robot you should select iRCalibration Master Set to generate extremely accurate calibration data. After you run the calibration program you should use the Update menu to update the robot's mastering data.

#### 16.2.4 Creating a Robot Calibration Teach Pendant Program

In order to master a robot with iRCalibration Master Set, you must first create a robot mastering teach pendant program. You can create the program manually or you can have iRCalibration Master Set create the program for you automatically. When iRCalibration Master Set setup is complete, the iRCalibration Master Set main menu will be displayed with the cursor at Teach Points.

For most six-axis robots

- you can have iRCalibration Master Set create a standard iRCalibration Master Set Calibration program automatically,
- you can customize an automatically generated program, or
- you can create your own custom program.

If yours is not a six-axis robot, you can create a custom program, but iRCalibration Master Set cannot create a standard iRCalibration Master Set program automatically.

<!-- PDF page 1919 -->

If a robot is not supported for the Standard iRCalibration Master Set program creation, the menu goes directly to the CUSTOM calibration menu. You can also go to this page by pressing F4, CUSTOM, at the Program Creation menu.

If you cannot use the Standard iRCalibration Master Set generated program because of robot limits, workspace restrictions, or other reasons, you should use the CUSTOM program creation method. You can touch up generated points from either the Standard or Custom generated programs to meet the specific restrictions of the workcell. However, the final program must contain significant rotations of all axes in order to get the best results.

To disable the Standard iRCalibration Master Set program creation menu, set the system variable $CB_VARS.$STDCAL_ENB = FALSE. If the Standard iRCalibration Master Set program creation menu is disabled, when you select Teach Points from the main menu you will go directly to the custom iRCalibration Master Set program creation menu.

# Teaching Points

Creating a standard iRCalibration Master Set program automatically can usually be done without teaching any points. If you are creating a custom program to perform or recover mastering with iRCalibration Master Set, you must first teach several points to be used in your robot mastering teach pendant program. Refer to Section 16.2.4.2.

5 Create Program (Done)
6 Run: RCAL_G1 (Not Done)
7 Update Master CT (Not Done)
8 View Result

##### 16.2.4.2 Custom Program Creation

The custom program menu will generate programs supporting only the first, vertically oriented, calibration plate. The custom program creation menu does not support generating programs using two calibration plates.

##### Guidelines for Creating a Custom Robot Calibration Program

Review the following guidelines before you begin to teach points.

- If the starting TCP is all zero, an estimated TCP will be created and applied when the calibration program is created. The seven taught points are also modified to reflect the new

<!-- PDF page 1923 -->

estimated TCP. The user must take care that the rotations during program motion do not cause collisions to occur and must insert additional points if needed.

- If the starting TCP is not all zero, then no estimated TCP is used and all program rotations will occur with respect to the starting TCP. The user must take care that the rotations during program motion do not cause collisions to occur and must insert additional points if needed.
- The calibration of Axis 1 and Axis 6 require that both the UFrame and UTool be known. If fixturing with known dimensions is used then the user can set UFrame and UTool to be the correct values and disable solving for UFrame and UTool and enable calibration of J1 and J6.
- If the robot cannot reach a BACK configuration, then the calibration tool dimensions and the location of the touch plate are important. For this case, the calibration tool must be large enough and the touch plate located such that all the axes have significant range of motion (greater than 90 degrees) during the calibration.
- Careful teaching of the calibration points such that they are centered above the touch plate holes and the with the tool shaft oriented perpendicular to the touch plate surface will improve calibration.
- If the initial robot calibration correction is large then repeating the calibration process a second time (after touching up the calibration points) will improve initial calibration.

There are seven taught points. They are described in Table 16–6.

Refer to Figure 16–2 and Figure 16–6 for illustrations of the first six taught points.

The blue cylinder remains stationary in all three stages, serving as a base or reference point for the robotic arm's actions.

Note These examples show an M-16 series robot which is capable of the FRONT/BACK and FLIP/NOFLIP configuration change. When the robot can achieve these configuration changes there is a great deal of latitude in the placement of the calibration plate.

The placement shown is not acceptable for robots such as the M-6 series which do not support the FRONT/BACK configuration change. For these robots, we recommend using the Standard Program Creation method using the calibration plate location and UTool that is generated in UFrame[9] and UTool[10] when the iRCalibration Master Set program is created. It is recommended that the tooling hardware be constructed to support calibration at these locations.

Six additional points are created by iRCalibration Master Set:

- Two additional points are created between the approach position and orientation position on each side of the plate, for a total of four additional orientation points.
- One additional point is created where the wrist changes configuration (Flip to Noflip, or vice versa). The user must ensure that no collisions occur during the change of Flip/Noflip configuration and must insert additional points if needed.
- One additional point is created where the robot changes Front to Back configuration if possible. If the robot cannot achieve this configuration, then an additional Front configuration point is created. The user must take care that no collisions occur during the change of Front/Back configuration and must insert additional points if needed.

#### 16.2.5 Running the /RCalibration Master Set Program

When all the points are taught and the program has been created, the Create Program status will be Done and the cursor will move automatically to Run.

- /RCalibration Master Set provides accurate initial calibration of the robot axes before any points have been taught. After you run the calibration program you should update the robot's mastering data by using the Update Master CT menu.

<!-- PDF page 1930 -->

It is recommended to run iRCalibration Master Set at least twice to get optimal results. Especially if there were significant orientation correction to the taught points, the second execution of iRCalibration Master Set can result in a better calibration and lower calibration errors.

You should always verify the generated calibration program by stepping through it at a low override. Be careful that the robot does not collide with objects, especially for the large rotations generated between the FRONT/BACK and FLIP/NOFLIP configurations. During single-step the detection instructions are not executed, so verifying the program is relatively quick.

You can modify the generated program, but any modifications will be lost if you regenerate the program. Also, certain modifications could prevent iRCalibration Master Set from loading the program positions, should you want to regenerate it. It is always a good idea to keep a backup before modifying a generated iRCalibration Master Set program.

It is recommended to run iRCalibration Master Set at least twice to get optimal results. Especially if there were significant orientation correction to the taught points, the second execution of iRCalibration Master Set can result in a better calibration and lower calibration errors.

### 16.2.7 Viewing the Calibration Result

The /RCalibration Master Set View menu allows you to see the results of previous calibrations. You can access the view menu at any time to review what has been done with /RCalibration Master Set earlier, even after a cold start. The screen you see will be based on the calibration type selected in the main menu

The calibration log is a buffer that holds previous mastering information. It has a fixed size of 20 entries. When the buffer is full, it will replace the oldest data in the buffer with the new logged data. If you want to view mastering information, you can display the Calibration Result screen. To display the calibration result screen, use Procedure 16-6.

### 16.3 iRCALIBRATION MASTER RECOVERY

#### 16.3.1 Overview

Note iRCalibration Mastering is not available for all robots. Refer to Software Release Note for specifics.

iRCalibration Master Recovery is an optional calibration option that allows you to recover the mastering of one of more robot axes after a motor change or a crash.

iRCalibration Master Recovery uses a wizard-style menu. It shows the steps that need be done to complete the robot calibration process. Each step of the process has its own status display that shows where you are in the setup process. You cannot skip steps and you cannot go to the next step without completing the current step. iRCalibration Master Recovery also includes a menu item, View Result, that lets you review the previous calibration result and log history.

- iRCalibration Master Recovery uses teach pendant programs for all execution. These programs are typically generated by iRCalibration Master Recovery, but can also be created or modified by the user.
- iRCalibration Master Recovery supports schedule based sensor setup and can use a different schedule for different searches.
- The iRCalibration Master Recovery reference data is stored in the teach pendant program; system variables are not used to store reference data.
- iRCalibration Master Recovery supports all robot motion groups.
- iRCalibration Master Recovery supports single-axis detection and recovery

The same program used for iRCalibration Master Set initial setup can later be used to recover mastering for any or all robot axes, J1 through J6. If iRCalibration Master Set is not performed, but iRCalibration Master Set mastering is performed, it is recommended to both master and recover at least J2, J3, J4, and J5. It is not recommended to recover a different set of axes than were mastered, except it is OK to recover J1 and J6 as described in Table 16–9. Also, see the special requirements regarding J2 for robots with linear J1 axis.

<!-- PDF page 1937 -->

# Hardware Requirements

The following hardware is required to use /RCalibration Master Recovery:

- Calibration tooling. Refer to Section 16.3.2.
- Six-axis robot (except as indicated in the Software Release Note)
- User-supplied circuitry for using I/O sensor (for robots with delicate tooling)

If the standard tooling is used, /RCalibration Master Recovery can generate a program to perform mastering recovery of robot axes 2 through 5, usually without any user point teaching. Standard tooling is available for most robots to support the default calibration program generated by /RCalibration Mastering.

# Using /RCalibration Master Recovery

To use /RCalibration Master Recovery, you must do the following:

1. Install the /RCalibration Master Recovery software option and any required hardware.
2. Set up /RCalibration Master Recovery.
3. Create a robot calibration program.
4. Run /RCalibration Master Recovery.
5. Run Mastering Recovery as needed.

# 16.3.2 Preliminary Setup

# Standard /RCalibration Mastering Hardware

Standard /RCalibration Mastering hardware is available. It includes the following components:

- Calibration Tool to attach to the faceplate of the robot. An adapter plate may be required.
- Calibration Arm with one or two calibration plates to attach to the base of the robot
- I/O cable to attach to the robot EE connector

The standard hardware available includes the following:

- EE connector cable to support the I/O detection method of the Calibration Options. Cables are available to support both 5-pin and 24-pin EE connectors.

EE-5770-020-040 (4 meters).
Cable Assembly for End Effector Touch Sensor w / 24 Pin Connector
EE-5770-021-025 (2.5 meters).
Cable Assembly for End Effector Touch Sensor w / 5 Pin Connector

- Calibration tool assembly to mount to the robot faceplate. The calibration tool assembly consists of a base to mount to the faceplate, a supporting tube extending away from the base, an attached nonconducting block, and a calibration pointer supported by the non-conducting block. The angle between the J6 axis and the calibration pointer is 70 degrees for the short

<!-- PDF page 1938 -->

tool and 45 degrees for the long tool. Multiple tools and adapters are available to support most robots.

1. MO-1800-943 Calibration Tool Assembly - Short
2. MO-1800-944 Calibration Tool Assembly -Long
3. MO-1800-945-001 Calib. Tool Adapt. - M710/20L
4. MO-1800-945-002 Calib. Tool Adapt. - R2000
5. MO-1800-945-003 Calib. Tool Adapt. - M900
6. MO-1800-945-004 Calib. Tool Adapt. - Arc Solution Arm
7. MO-1800-945-005 Calib. Tool Adapt. - Arc Tregasis
8. MO-1800-945-006 Calib. Tool Adapt. - Arc Binzel

- Calibration arm to mount to the robot base. The calibration arm assembly includes two calibration plates and a mounting bracket. IRCalibration Mastering, depending on robot model and configuration, uses one or both of the plates. Multiple calibration arms are available to support most robots.

— MO-1800-940 Calibration Arm Assembly –Standard
— MO-1800-941 Calibration Arm Assembly – Short

Note The standard calibration arm, MO-1800-940, can be used on any robot which is supported by the short calibration arm, MO-1800-941.

Table 16–8. Calibration Hardware

[tbl-154.md](tbl-154.md)

<!-- PDF page 1939 -->

*The M710iB/20L-SA does not currently have a Standard Calibration Tool assembly available.

Some robots, for example the top loader series of robots, do not have an available standard calibration arm. For these cases iRCalibration Master Recovery can still generate the standard iRCalibration Mastering program if the user installs the standard calibration tool to the robot faceplate and installs a calibration plate at the proper location for the generated calibration program.

Robots that cannot do FRONT/BACK configuration change or FLIP/NOFLIP configuration change require two calibration plates. For all robots, the first calibration plate must be located parallel to the robot World Y-Z plane with the hole centered at the Uframe coordinates.

If the robot requires two plates, the second plate must be located in the X-Y plane with the hole centered at these values: (Uframe.x – 56, Uframe.y-82, Uframe.z+57). The two-plate method of initial calibration is more accurate for robots that cannot change configuration than the single plate method. The two-plate method generates 11 calibration points on the first plate and 6 on the second plate.

The Standard iRCalibration Mastering calibration plate(s) are attached (by a calibration arm) to the mastering holes located on front of the robot base. The calibration arm is located along the +Y direction of robot World frame. The calibration plates are not precisely located; iRCalibration Mastering will fine tune the actual location of the calibration plates.

Refer to Procedure 16-13 for information on installing and aligning the Touch Plate and for setting up the Touch Plate for use with iRCalibration Mastering.

### 16.3.3 iRCalibration Master Recovery Setup

The first time you run the recovery program, iRCalibration Master Recovery masters the recovery program by storing golden data into the teach pendant program. For mastering, no update is

<!-- PDF page 1940 -->

required. After the teach pendant program has been mastered, you can recover mastering data by running the iRCalibration Mastering program again and using the Update menu to update the robot's mastering data.

iRCalibration Master Recovery can recover mastering data by running the mastered teach pendant program after a motor has been replaced. The iRCalibration Master Recovery computes the offset between the new contact positions with the golden data and convert the offset to pulse counts to adjust the zero position for that motor. After the mastering data of that motor has been updated, the robot is re-mastered and no touch up is required for production teach pendant programs.

Setting up and running iRCalibration Master Recovery includes the following:

- Setting up the Mastering Schedule. Refer to Table 16–9 for descriptions of the items on the Mastering Schedule screen.
- Setting up the Detection Schedule. Refer to Table 16–10 for descriptions of the items on the Detection Schedule screen.
- Creating the robot calibration program. Refer to Section 16.3.4.
- Running the calibration program. Refer to Section 16.3.5.
- Updating the master count (Master CT) with the calibration result obtained from running the robot calibration program. Refer to Section 16.3.7.

Note There are 10 Mastering Schedules.

Table 16–9. iRCalibration Mastering Schedule Screen Description

### 16.3.3.1 Setting Up /RCalibration Master Recovery

/RCalibration Master Recovery uses a wizard-style menu. It shows the steps that need be done to complete the robot master recovery process. Each step of the process has its own status display that shows where you are in the setup process. You cannot skip steps and you cannot go to the next step without completing the current step.

/RCalibration Master Recovery also includes a menu item, View Result, that lets you review the previous calibration result and log history.

For a robot that has all its programs taught, /RCalibration Master Recovery allows you to recover the robot's mastering data when necessary. You run the recovery program initially to "master" the data in the program. No update is necessary at this time. Then, when you need to recover the mastering data, you run the program again and use the Update menu to update the mastering data.

### 16.3.4 Creating a Robot Calibration Teach Pendant Program

In order to master a robot with /RCalibration Master Recovery you must first create a robot mastering teach pendant program. You can create the program manually or you can have /RCalibration Mastering create the program for you automatically. When /RCalibration Master Recovery setup is complete, the /RCalibration Master Recovery main menu will be displayed with the cursor at Teach Points.

For most six-axis robots

- you can have /RCalibration Master Recovery create a standard /RCalibration Mastering Calibration program automatically,
- you can customize an automatically generated program, or
- you can create your own custom program.

If yours is not a six-axis robot, you can create a custom program, but /RCalibration Master Recovery cannot create a standard /RCalibration Master Recovery program automatically.

If a robot is not supported for the Standard /RCalibration Master Recovery program creation, the menu goes directly to the CUSTOM calibration menu. You can also go to this page by pressing F4, CUSTOM, at the Program Creation menu.

If you cannot use the Standard /RCalibration Master Recovery generated program because of robot limits, workspace restrictions, or other reasons, you should use the CUSTOM program creation method. You can touch up generated points from either the Standard or Custom generated programs to meet the specific restrictions of the workcell. However, the final program must contain significant rotations of all axes in order to get the best results.

To disable the Standard /RCalibration Master Recovery program creation menu, set the system variable $CB_VARS.$STDCAL_ENB = FALSE. If the Standard /RCalibration Mastering program creation menu is disabled, when you select “Teach Points” from the main menu you will go directly to the custom /RCalibration Master Recovery program creation menu.

### Teaching Points

Creating a standard /RCalibration Master Recovery program automatically can usually be done without teaching any points. If you are creating a custom program to recover mastering with /RCalibration Mastering, you must first teach several points to be used in your robot mastering teach pendant program. Refer to Section 16.3.4.2.

##### 16.3.4.2 Custom Program Creation

The custom program menu will generate programs supporting only the first, vertically oriented, calibration plate. The custom program creation menu does not support generating programs using two calibration plates.

##### Guidelines for Creating a Custom Robot Calibration Program

Review the following guidelines before you begin to teach points.

- If the starting TCP is all zero, an estimated TCP will be created and applied when the calibration program is created. The seven taught points are also modified to reflect the new estimated TCP. The user must take care that the rotations during program motion do not cause collisions to occur and must insert additional points if needed.
- If the starting TCP is not all zero, then no estimated TCP is used and all program rotations will occur with respect to the starting TCP. The user must take care that the rotations during program motion do not cause collisions to occur and must insert additional points if needed.
- The calibration of Axis 1 and Axis 6 require that both the UFrame and UTool be known. If fixturing with known dimensions is used then the user can set UFrame and UTool to be the correct values and disable solving for UFrame and UTool and enable calibration of J1 and J6.
- If the robot cannot reach a BACK configuration, then the calibration tool dimensions and the location of the touch plate are important. For this case, the calibration tool must be large enough and the touch plate located such that all the axes have significant range of motion (greater than 90 degrees) during the calibration.

<!-- PDF page 1954 -->

- Careful teaching of the calibration points such that they are centered above the touch plate holes and the with the tool shaft oriented perpendicular to the touch plate surface will improve calibration.

There are seven taught points. They are described in Table 16–12.

Refer to Figure 16–5 and Figure 16–6 for illustrations of the first six taught points.

Table 16–12. Robot Calibration Program Taught Points

[tbl-161.md](tbl-161.md)

<!-- PDF page 1955 -->

Figure 16–5. Example of First Three Positions

> **Image description -- img-128.jpeg:** The image shows a sequence of three 3D diagrams illustrating the movement of a robotic arm through different positions. Each diagram is labeled below with a description of the position: 'Approach Position 1', 'Center Position 1', and 'Rotate Position 1'. The robotic arm is depicted in yellow with blue components, including a gripper or tool at the end. In the first diagram, the arm is in the 'Approach Position 1', extending downward toward a target. In the second diagram, the arm is in the 'Center Position 1', aligned more directly with the target. In the third diagram, the arm is in the 'Rotate Position 1', where it appears to be rotating or adjusting its orientation relative to the target. The diagrams collectively demonstrate the arm's motion from an initial approach, through a centered alignment, to a rotational adjustment.

Figure 16–6. Example of Second Three Positions

> **Image description -- img-129.jpeg:** The image shows three sequential stages of a robotic arm performing a task involving a yellow object and a blue cylindrical object. In the first stage labeled 'Approach Position 2,' the robotic arm is positioned above the yellow object, which is placed on a surface, with the blue cylinder nearby. In the second stage labeled 'Center Position 2,' the robotic arm has moved to center itself over the yellow object, aligning its gripper directly above it. In the third stage labeled 'Rotate Position 2,' the robotic arm has rotated or adjusted its gripper to interact with the yellow object, likely preparing to grasp or manipulate it. The blue cylinder remains stationary in all three stages. The labels indicate the progression of the robotic arm's movement and positioning relative to the objects.

Note These examples show an M-16 series robot which is capable of the FRONT/BACK and FLIP/NOFLIP configuration change. When the robot can achieve these configuration changes there is a great deal of latitude in the placement of the calibration plate.

<!-- PDF page 1956 -->

The placement shown is not acceptable for robots such as the M-6 series which do not support the FRONT/BACK configuration change. For these robots, we recommend using the Standard Program Creation method using the calibration plate location and UTool that is generated in UFrame[9] and UTool[10] when the iRCalibration Mastering program is created. It is recommended that the tooling hardware be constructed to support calibration at these locations.

Six additional points are created by iRCalibration Master Recovery:

- Two additional points are created between the approach position and orientation position on each side of the plate, for a total of four additional orientation points.
- One additional point is created where the wrist changes configuration (Flip to Noflip, or vice versa). The user must ensure that no collisions occur during the change of Flip/Noflip configuration and must insert additional points if needed.
- One additional point is created where the robot changes Front to Back configuration if possible. If the robot cannot achieve this configuration, then an additional Front configuration point is created. The user must take care that no collisions occur during the change of Front/Back configuration and must insert additional points if needed.

#### 16.3.5 Running the iRCalibration Master Recovery Program

When all the points are taught and the program has been created, the Create Program status will be Done and the cursor will move automatically to Run.

iRCalibration Master Recovery

- Allows you to recover mastering after an event such as a motor change or collision. The first time you run the recovery program, iRCalibration Mastering does the “Mastering” of the teach pendant Calibration program. No update is required.

After the teach pendant program has been mastered, you can recover mastering data by running the calibration program again and using the Update Master CT menu to update the mastering data.

iRCalibration Master Recovery can recover mastering in one of two ways

— Multiple axis recovery. This requires a program either generated by iRCalibration Mastering or written and/or modified by the user. All the detection instructions must be DETECT CIRCLE instructions and a calibration plate is required. It is recommended that the program creation menu be used to generate this iRCalibration Mastering program. There must be significant (at least 60 degrees) motion on all axes except perhaps J4. It is highly recommended for robots capable of FRONT/BACK configuration change that the calibration program contain both configurations as well as a FLIP/NOFLIP configuration.

These constraints will guarantee sufficient motion on each axis. If the robot does not support such configuration changes, either by robot joint limits or by dressout limitations, then special care must be taken in choosing a calibration tool and locating the calibration plate. Special calibration tooling may be required.

— Single axis recovery. This requires a program written by the user to detect contact by moving a single axis. The axis that moves is the axis that can be recovered. This program must be mastered with Master Recovery. This method will work with either robot axes, positioner axes, or aux axes. There must be exactly one DETECT JOINT instruction in the user-written iRCalibration Mastering program. Refer to Section 16.3.6.

<!-- PDF page 1961 -->

You should always verify the generated calibration program by stepping through it at a low override. Be careful that the robot does not collide with objects, especially for the large rotations generated between the FRONT/BACK and FLIP/NOFLIP configurations. During single-step the detection instructions are not executed, so verifying the program is relatively quick.

You can modify the generated program, but any modifications will be lost if you regenerate the program. Also, certain modifications could prevent iRCalibration Master Recovery from loading the program positions, should you want to regenerate it. It is always a good idea to keep a backup before modifying a generated iRCalibration Master Recovery program.

It is recommended to run iRCalibration Master Recovery at least twice to get optimal results. Especially if there were significant orientation correction to the taught points, the second execution of iRCalibration Mastering can result in a better calibration and lower calibration errors.

#### 16.3.6 Single Axis Mastering Recovery

iRCalibration Master Recovery can recover mastering by a very simple program with only a single axis to move and cause detection. You must write a program for each axis to be calibrated; iRCalibration Master Recovery does not generate programs for single axis recovery.

The following is an example program for single axis recovery:

1:J P[1:Approach Point] 5% FINE
2:L P[2:Detect Point] 100mm/sec FINE
3: Calib Start[1]
4: Detect Joint[1] Axis(1,+)

<!-- PDF page 1963 -->

5: Calib END[Recovery]
6:L P[1:Approach Point] 100mm/sec FINE

You can write a similar program to recover mastering any axis, including robot axes, aux axes, and positioners. The parameter of Detect Joint[] is the detection schedule number. The first parameter of Axis() is the axis number. The second parameter is the direction of motion of that axis, either plus or minus for the detection motion.

If more than one axis is to be recovered (one at a time), it is recommended that care be used in determining the locations of detections. You should not have two detections on the same mechanical unit to search in approximately the same direction and use the same contact point. You can use any point on the unit to make contact, it does not need to be near the TCP. If using this method on a multiple axis robot or positioner, it is beneficial to have the contact on the link immediately next to the axis being calibrated. Then by recovering from the base axis out each axis has the benefit of the previous axes being already calibrated.

#### 16.3.7 Updating the Master Count

The iRCalibration Master Recovery View menu allows you to see the results of previous calibrations. ### 16.4 IRCALIBRATION TCP SET

#### 16.4.1 Overview

Note /RCalibration TCP Set is not available for all software application Tools.

The /RCalibration TCP Set option, formerly TCPCal, provides a cost effective, easy-to-use solution to set the Tool Center Point (TCP) automatically.

When you use /RCalibration TCP Set you start with a fully functional system and an unknown or inaccurate TCP. You then set up /RCalibration TCP Set to generate an accurate TCP.

/RCalibration TCP Set works with any robot and tool where the TCP is at the end of cylindrically-shaped tooling. If the normal tooling is not cylindrical, or if the TCP is away from the tooling, a teach tip can be installed.

To use /RCalibration TCP Set, you must do the following:

1. Install the /RCalibration TCP Set software option and any required hardware.
2. Set up /RCalibration TCP Set.
3. Create a TCP calibration TP program.

<!-- PDF page 1968 -->

4. Run iRCalibration TCP Set to set the initial TCP value.

### 16.4.2 Preliminary Setup

Before you can set up and use iRCalibration TCP Set you must do the following:

- install the iRCalibration TCP Set software option. Refer to the Software Installation Manual for more information about installing software options.
- Install the touch plate on a stationary object in the robot workcell. Refer to Section 16.4.2.1

You will then use the iRCalibration TCP Set software to set up the initial tool center point. The following figures show typical arc welding and waterjet tool definition.

### Procedure 16-13 Installing and Aligning the Touch Plate

#### Conditions

- The TOOL frame has been set up correctly.

Refer to “Frames Setup” in the application-specific Setup and Operations Manual for more information.

#### Steps

1. Install the touch plate (touch pointer for Cal-Plate calibration) on a flat level surface well within the workcell. See Figure 16–10.

The touch plate or touch pointer should be securely fastened to a firm surface. If the touch plate position changes due to collisions or other events, the recovered TCP will be incorrect. There should be ample clearance below the plate so that the tooling can be inserted through the circular opening in the touch plate.

<!-- PDF page 1971 -->

Figure 16–10. Installing the Touch Plate

> **Image description -- img-133.jpeg:** The image depicts a technical diagram of a mechanical assembly involving a cylindrical component and a rectangular base. The cylindrical component is positioned vertically above the rectangular base, with a threaded shaft extending downward from its bottom end. The shaft appears to pass through a hole in the rectangular base. The base has two visible circular features, likely mounting holes or alignment guides, positioned symmetrically near its edges. The cylindrical component has a hexagonal nut or bolt head at its top, suggesting it can be rotated or secured. The diagram is a simplified, isometric line drawing without color or shading, focusing on the structural relationship between the parts.

2. For /RCalibration TCP Set, /RCalibration Master Set, and /RCalibration Master Recovery, the touch plate is typically oriented in a vertical plane as shown in Figure 16–11 and Figure 16–12. This vertical orientation (with the plate typically parallel to the robot WORLD x-z or y-z plane) makes it easier to orient the tool so it can touch both sides of the plate with the proper orientation and without encountering axis limits.

In most applications, the typical TCP definition is that the TOOL z axis is along the shaft used by /RCalibration TCP Set. For arc welding applications, the TOOL +z direction extends from the TCP location into the torch body. For other applications, the TOOL +z direction extends away from the shaft at the TCP location. /RCalibration TCP Set works with any TOOL frame definition.

If a touch pointer is used for Cal-Plate calibration, align the pointer so it is pointing in one of the world X, -X, Y, -Y, Z or -Z directions.

Installation and alignment of the touch plate is now complete.

- Updating the UTool with the calibration results obtained from running the calibration program. Refer to Procedure 16-17.

##### 16.4.3.2 Creating a TCP Calibration Teach Pendant Program

In order to create a new TCP frame with iRCalibration TCP Set, you must first create a TCP calibration teach pendant program. You can create the program manually or you can have iRCalibration TCP Set create the program for you automatically. When iRCalibration TCP Set setup is complete, the iRCalibration TCP Set main menu will be displayed with the cursor at Teach Points.

- To have iRCalibration TCP Set create the teach pendant program automatically, refer to Procedure 16-15.

# Teaching Points

In order to set a TCP with iRCalibration TCP Set, you must first teach certain points to be used in your TCP calibration teach pendant program.

Review the following guidelines before you begin to teach points.

<!-- PDF page 1981 -->

- If the starting TCP is all zero, an estimated TCP will be created and applied when the Initial TCP calibration program is created. The six or seven taught points are also modified to reflect the new estimated TCP. Be very careful that the rotations during program motion do not cause collisions. You might need to insert additional points to accomplish this.
- If the starting TCP is not all zero, then no estimated TCP is used and all program rotations will occur with respect to the starting TCP. Be very careful that the rotations during program motion do not cause collisions. You might need to insert additional points to accomplish this.
- To improve calibration, teach the calibration points carefully to be sure they are centered above the touch plate holes and with the tool shaft oriented perpendicular to the touch plate surface.
- Set the payload accurately, especially when the iRCalibration TCP Set reference positions are at extreme points of the robot's reach.

After you have established the iRCalibration TCP Set, you can use it in new and existing programs. You can apply iRCalibration TCP Set easily to new or existing programs without having to redefine positions as long as the original programs were created with an accurate tool center point.

You will need to teach positions for your program.

### New TCP Program

For creating a New TCP, (including Cal-Plate calibration), there are six or seven taught points. Refer to Table 16–17 for a description of the points to be taught.

Note For New TCP, all points except the Orientation point are taught centered on and above the hole in the calibration plate,

Table 16–17. New TCP Program Points

<!-- PDF page 1982 -->

[tbl-172.md](tbl-172.md)

The Center position 1 defines the side of the plate where the TCP will reside. The final TCP will be at the surface of the plate and centered on the hole on the side 1–4 1. where the first contact is made. The position must be taught so the plate is approximately perpendicular to the contact pointer.

For NEW-XYZ or NEW-XYZWPR you must record 7 positions:

# Procedure 16-15 Teaching Points (Creating the iRCalibration TCP Set Teach Pendant Program Automatically)

# Conditions

- iRCalibration TCP Set Setup has been completed.

#### 16.4.5 Displaying the UTool Log Screen

The iRCalibration TCP Set view menu allows you to see previous calibration results stored in the UTool log.

### 16.4.6 /RCalibration TCP Set Error Recovery

If a /RCalibration TCP Set error occurs during TCP calibration, the robot goes back to the starting position and an error message is displayed. Review the error message, correct the problem, then restart the TCP calibration program.

### 16.4.6.1 Redoing a /RCalibration TCP Set Adjustment

To redo a /RCalibration TCP Set adjustment and restart /RCalibration TCP Set,

1. Review the error message for an indication of the problem.
2. Correct the problem.
3. Abort any program that is paused.
4. Enter the /RCalibration TCP Set program name in the setup screen.
5. Press DONE to exit.
6. When /RCalibration TCP Set asks "Program exists, skip Teach/Create?", reply YES.

<!-- PDF page 1993 -->

7. Run the iRCalibration TCP Set program: move the cursor to Run and press ENTER.

## 16.5 iRCALIBRATION TCP SHIFT

### 16.5.1 Overview

Note iRCalibration TCP Shift is not available for all software application Tools.

The iRCalibration TCP Shift option, formerly TCPCal, provides a cost effective, easy-to-use solution to recover the Tool Center Point (TCP) automatically.

When you use iRCalibration TCP Shift you start with a fully functional system and an unknown or inaccurate TCP. You then set up iRCalibration TCP Shift to generate an accurate TCP.

iRCalibration TCP Shift works with any robot and tool where the TCP is at the end of cylindrically-shaped tooling. If the normal tooling is not cylindrical, or if the TCP is away from the tooling, a teach tip can be installed.

To use iRCalibration TCP Shift, you must do the following:

1. Install the iRCalibration TCP Shift software option and any required hardware.
2. Set up iRCalibration TCP Shift.
3. Create a TCP calibration TP program.
4. Run iRCalibration TCP Shift to recover the current TCP.

### 16.5.2 Preliminary Setup

Before you can set up and use iRCalibration TCP Shift you must do the following:

- install the iRCalibration TCP Shift software option. Refer to the Software Installation Manual for more information about installing software options.
- Install the touch plate on a stationary object in the robot workcell. Refer to Section 16.4.2.1

You will then use the iRCalibration TCP Shift software to recover the current tool center point. The following figures show typical arc welding and waterjet tool definition.

### Procedure 16-19 Installing and Aligning the Touch Plate

#### Conditions

- The TOOL frame has been set up correctly.

Refer to “Frames Setup” in the application-specific Setup and Operations Manual for more information.

#### Steps

1. Install the touch plate (touch pointer for gripper) on a flat level surface well within the workcell. See Figure 16–19.

The touch plate or touch pointer should be securely fastened to a firm surface. If the touch plate position changes due to collisions or other events, the recovered TCP will be incorrect. There should be ample clearance below the plate so that the tooling can be inserted through the circular opening in the touch plate.

<!-- PDF page 1998 -->

Figure 16–19. Installing the Touch Plate

> **Image description -- img-145.jpeg:** The image depicts a technical diagram of a mechanical assembly involving a cylindrical component and a rectangular base. The cylindrical component is positioned vertically above the rectangular base, with a threaded section visible at the bottom of the cylinder. The base has two circular holes, likely for mounting or attachment purposes. The cylinder appears to be hollow, with a smaller inner cylinder or rod extending downward, aligned with the holes in the base. The diagram uses simple line art to represent the parts, with no visible labels, values, or additional annotations.

2. In most applications, the typical TCP definition is that the TOOL z axis is along the shaft used by iRCalibration TCP Shift. For arc welding applications, the TOOL +z direction extends from the TCP location into the torch body. For other applications, the TOOL +z direction extends away from the shaft at the TCP location. iRCalibration TCP Shift works with any TOOL frame definition.

Installation and alignment of the touch plate is now complete.

### 16.5.3 iRCalibration TCP Shift Setup

Before you can use iRCalibration TCP Shift to recover the TCP, you must perform some setup procedures. Setup involves the initial setting of menu options within iRCalibration TCP Shift software.

Setting up and running iRCalibration TCP Shift includes the following processes:

- Selecting the motion group you want to calibrate
- Selecting the teach pendant program, the UTool you want to calibrate, and the calibration mode: XYZWPR, XYZ-align, XYZ, XY, Z, Gripper. Refer to Table 16–19 for details of the calibration modes.

- Setting up the detection schedule. Refer to Table 16–21 for a description of the items on the /RCalibration TCP Shift Detection Schedule Detail Screen.
- Teaching points for the teach pendant calibration program. Refer to Procedure 16-21.
- Creating the teach pendant calibration program from the taught points and running the calibration program. You can have /RCalibration TCP Shift create the program for you automatically (refer to Procedure 16-21.
- Updating the UTool with the calibration results obtained from running the calibration program. Refer to Procedure 16-23.

### 16.5.3.2 Creating a TCP Calibration Teach Pendant Program

In order to master a TCP with /RCalibration TCP Shift, you must first create a TCP calibration teach pendant program. You can have /RCalibration TCP Shift create the program for you automatically. When /RCalibration TCP Shift setup is complete, the /RCalibration TCP Shift main menu will be displayed with the cursor at Teach Points.

- To have /RCalibration TCP Shift create the teach pendant program automatically, refer to Procedure 16-21.

### Teaching Points

In order to recover a TCP with /RCalibration TCP Shift, you must first teach certain points to be used in your TCP calibration teach pendant program.

Note If the calibration type is Gripper, you have to create the TCP calibration program,. The /RCalibration TCP Shift software can not create a gripper recovery program

### TCP Recovery Program

For creating a TCP Recovery Program, there are four taught points. Refer to Table 16–22 for a description of the points to be taught.

Table 16–22. New TCP Program Points

[tbl-181.md](tbl-181.md)

Teach four points on the other side of the touch plate: the approach position 2, the center position 2, the rotate position 2, and the orientation position (not shown in Figure 16–12). The orientation position is taught with the tool shaft extended through the circle.

For Cal-Plate calibration, you must teach 6 positions. See Figure 16–13 for an example.

When /RCalibration TCP Shift setup is complete, the /RCalibration TCP Shift main menu will be displayed with the cursor at Teach Points.

##### 16.5.3.3 Custom iRCalibration TCP Shift Program Creation

iRCalibration TCP Shift is very flexible for custom iRCalibration TCP Shift program creation. Custom programs can be used for TCP Recovery in any combination of X, Y, Z translational directions. Custom iRCalibration TCP recovery programs for partial orientation are not supported. If you need to recover a TCP with orientation by custom programming you must use the Gripper mode and recover six degrees of freedom.

<!-- PDF page 2012 -->

For custom TCP XYZ recovery, it is not necessary to have special UFrame settings. However, if a UFrame is used it cannot change location with respect to the contact surface from the time of mastering to the time of recovery.

iRCalibration TCP Shift supports the recovery types of XYZ, XY, and Z. These types indicate how many searches are allowed for the recovery. XYZ requires three searches, XY requires two searches, and Z requires one search. However, the actual search directions do not need to correspond to the indicated directions. Each search direction must be perpendicular to the others, though.

Note that using custom iRCalibration TCP Shift programming, a wide variety of sensors can be used. If TOS is used, the touch surface can be virtually any rigid object. The touch points do not need to be near each other, but must be perpendicular to each other with respect to the UTool. You can even use a single proximity sensor and rotate the tool 90 degrees between searches but use the same World search direction for each search.

Figure 16-21. Example of Manually Created XYZ Search TPP Program

1: UFRAME_NUM=1
2: UTOOL_NUM=1
3:L P[1:Home Position] 100mm/sec FINE
4: UTool Start[1]
5:L P[2:Via Pos 1] 100mm/sec FINE
6:L P[3:Search Pos 1] 100mm/sec FINE
7: Detect Point[4] UFrame[X]
8:L P[4:Via Pos 2] 100mm/sec FINE
9:L P[5:Search Pos 2] 100mm/sec FINE
10: Detect Point[4] UFrame[Y]
11:L P[6:Via Pos 3] 100mm/sec FINE
12:L P[7:Search Pos 3] 100mm/sec FINE
13: Detect Point[4] UFrame[-Z]
14: UTool End XYZ
15:L P[8:Via Pos 4] 100mm/sec FINE
16:L P[9:Home Position] 100mm/sec FINE

The three searches can be in any order, but they must all be perpendicular to each other. This could also be done with a single Find Circle instruction with XY and Z parameters, or a Find Circle with parameters both zero and another search perpendicular to the plane of the circle.

Figure 16-22. Example of Manually Created XY Search TP Program

1: UFRAME_NUM=1
2: UTOOL_NUM=1
3:L P[1:Home Position] 100mm/sec FINE
4: UTool Start[1]
5:L P[2:Via Pos 1] 100mm/sec FINE
6:L P[3:Search Pos 1] 100mm/sec FINE
7: Detect Point[4] UFrame[X]
8:L P[4:Via Pos 2] 100mm/sec FINE
9:L P[5:Search Pos 2] 100mm/sec FINE

<!-- PDF page 2013 -->

10: Detect Point[4] UFrame[-Z]
11: UTool End XY
12:L P[6:Via Pos 3] 100mm/sec FINE
13:L P[7:Home Position] 100mm/sec FINE

Notice the UTool End XY instruction on line 8. This tells /RCalibration TCP Shift that this program will find two perpendicular corrections along the search direction axes, UFrame X and UFrame -Z. It does not mean that the correction will necessarily be in any frame X or Y direction.

Figure 16–23. Example of Manually Created Z Search Teach Pendant Program

1: UFRAME_NUM=1
2: UTOOL_NUM=1
3:L P[1:Home Position] 100mm/sec FINE
4: UTool Start[1]
5:L P[2:Via Pos 1] 100mm/sec FINE
6:L P[3:Search Pos 1] 100mm/sec FINE
7: Detect Point[4] UFrame[X]
8: UTool End Z
9:L P[4:Via Pos 2] 100mm/sec FINE
10:L P[5:Home Position] 100mm/sec FINE

Notice the UTool End Z instruction on line 8. This tells /RCalibration TCP Shift that this program will find a single correction along the search direction axis, UFrame X. It does not mean that the correction will necessarily be in any frame Z direction.

Figure 16–24. Example of Manually Created XYZ Search TP Program Using Detect Circle Instruction (with XY and Z offsets)

1: UFRAME_NUM=1
2: UTOOL_NUM=1
3:L P[1:Home Position] 100mm/sec FINE
4: UTool Start[1]
5:L P[2:Via Pos 1] 100mm/sec FINE
6:L P[3:Search Pos 1] 100mm/sec FINE
7: Detect Circle[4] (30.00, 10.00)
UFrame[X]
8: UTool End XYZ
9:L P[4:Via Pos 2] 100mm/sec FINE
10:L P[5:Home Position] 100mm/sec FINE

Notice the Detect Circle instruction on line 7. The parameter of 30 (the XY offset parameter) indicates that the robot will move the tool 30mm perpendicular to the search direction (i.e. it will move in the UFrame YZ plane) before performing a search along the UFrame X direction. After detecting the surface, the robot will return to P3. Then it will move along the UFrame X direction until it is 10mm (the Z offset parameter) past the point where the surface was detected in the first search. Then the robot will perform four searches in the UFrame YZ plane to find the center of the circle then return to P3.

<!-- PDF page 2014 -->

Figure 16–25. Example of Manually Created XY Search TP Program Using Detect Circle Instruction (without XY and Z offsets)

1: UFRAME_NUM=1
2: UTOOL_NUM=1
3:L P[1:Home Position] 100mm/sec FINE
4: UTool Start[1]
5:L P[2:Via Pos 1] 100mm/sec FINE
6:L P[3:Search Pos 1] 100mm/sec FINE
7: Detect Circle[4] (0.00, 0.00)
UFrame[X]
8: UTool End XYZ
9:L P[4:Via Pos 2] 100mm/sec FINE
10:L P[5:Home Position] 100mm/sec FINE

Notice the Detect Circle instruction on line 7. The parameters of  \( (0.00, 0.00) \)  indicate that the robot will not perform the surface detection. The robot tool must already be inside the circle. The robot will perform four searches in the UFrame YZ plane to find the center of the circle then return to P3.

Figure 16–26. Example of Standard iRCalibration TCP Shift-Generated Program with Update Frame Added

1: UFRAME_NUM=1
2: UTOOL_NUM=1
3:L P[1:Approach pos.] 100mm/sec FINE
4: UTool Start[1]
5:L P[2:Plate position] 100mm/sec FINE
6: Detect Point[4] World[Y]
7: Update Tool
8:L P[3:Approach pos.] 100mm/sec FINE
9:L P[4:Center 1 inside] 100mm/sec FINE
10: Detect Circle[4](0.00, 0.00)World[Y]
11: Update Tool
12:L P[5:Center 2 inside] 100mm/sec FINE
13: Detect Circle[4](0.00, 0.00)World[Y]
14:L P[6:Approach pos.] 100mm/sec FINE
15: UTool End XYZWP

Notice the Update Tool instruction at line 7 and line 11. The first Update Tool will compensate for the detection in the plate direction. This method is especially important if there is a large variation in the Tool Z direction. Then the next detection, Detect Circle on line 10 will have the proper amount of the tool protruding through the circle. After this detection, the second Update Tool instruction is executed to help center the tool on the circle. This update may or may not be useful. If the TCP deviation was due to a significant orientation change of the tool then this Update Tool may actually make the next Detect Circle instruction closer to the edge of the circle. Regardless of this, for large orientation changes it is recommended to run iRCalibration TCP Shift twice.

<!-- PDF page 2015 -->

### 16.5.3.4 Gripper Program Creation

The following is an example of a TCP Gripper recovery program. This program is manually created and must contain at least six searches where at least three are non-colinear and have a common search direction, at least two have a common search direction approximately perpendicular to the others and at least on with a search direction approximately perpendicular to the others. The points should be separated from each other.

The UFrame used must be located at the contact point. Typically the contact point is a pointer type object with UFrame set to the tip. The TCP Shift program searches cause the gripper to make contact with the pointer tip. Any of the detection methods can be used.

Multiple UFrames and multiple detection points can be used in the same TCP Shift gripper program. Each UFrame must correspond to the current detection point. This is useful for large grippers or for where unidirectional sensors such as proximity sensors are used for detection.

1: UFRAME_NUM=1
2: UTOOL_NUM=1
3:L P[1:Home Position] 100mm/sec FINE
4: UTool Start[1]
5:L P[2:Via Pos 1] 100mm/sec FINE
6:L P[3:Search Pos 1] 100mm/sec FINE
7: Detect Point[4] UFrame[X]
8:L P[4:Via Pos 2] 100mm/sec FINE
9:L P[5:Search Pos 2] 100mm/sec FINE
10: Detect Point[4] UFrame[X]
11:L P[6:Via Pos 3] 100mm/sec FINE
12:L P[7:Search Pos 3] 100mm/sec FINE
13: Detect Point[4] UFrame[X]
14:L P[8:Via Pos 4] 100mm/sec FINE
15:L P[9:Search Pos 4] 100mm/sec FINE
16: Detect Point[4] UFrame[Y]
17:L P[10:Via Pos 5] 100mm/sec FINE
18:L P[11:Search Pos 5] 100mm/sec FINE
19: Detect Point[4] UFrame[Y]
20:L P[12:Via Pos 6] 100mm/sec FINE
21:L P[13:Search Pos 6] 100mm/sec FINE
22: Detect Point[4] UFrame[-Z]
23: UTool End Gripper
24:L P[14:Via Pos 7] 100mm/sec FINE
25:L P[15:Home Position] 100mm/sec FINE

This is an example of a simple six point program for recovering a gripper UTool. The searches can be done in any order but in this example the first three searches have a parallel search direction. They must not be colinear and must have significant distance between them. The next two searches have a search direction perpendicular to the first three and have a significant distance between them. The last search direction is perpendicular to all the other search directions. More points can be used. It is recommended to run TCP Shift iteratively until the UTool correction is small.

<!-- PDF page 2016 -->

1: UFRAME_NUM=1
2: UTOOL_NUM=1
3:L P[1:Home Position] 100mm/sec FINE
4: UTool Start[1]
5:L P[2:Via Pos 1] 100mm/sec FINE
6:L P[3:Search Pos 1] 100mm/sec FINE
7: Detect Point[4] UFrame[X]
8:L P[4:Via Pos 2] 100mm/sec FINE
9:L P[5:Search Pos 2] 100mm/sec FINE
10: Detect Point[4] UFrame[X]
11:L P[6:Via Pos 3] 100mm/sec FINE
12: UFRAME_NUM=2
13:L P[7:Search Pos 3] 100mm/sec FINE
14: Detect Point[4] UFrame[X]
15:L P[8:Via Pos 4] 100mm/sec FINE
16: UFRAME_NUM=3
17:L P[9:Search Pos 4] 100mm/sec FINE
18: Detect Point[4] UFrame[Y]
19:L P[10:Via Pos 5] 100mm/sec FINE
20:L P[11:Search Pos 5] 100mm/sec FINE
21: Detect Point[4] UFrame[Y]
22:L P[12:Via Pos 6] 100mm/sec FINE
23:L P[13:Search Pos 6] 100mm/sec FINE
24: Detect Point[4] UFrame[-Z]
25: UTool End Gripper
26:L P[14:Via Pos 7] 100mm/sec FINE
27: UFRAME_NUM=1
28:L P[15:Home Position] 100mm/sec FINE

Notice that on line 12 and 16 different UFrame numbers are set. The TCP Shift Gripper method supports using multiple UFrame numbers. However, each UFrame location must closely correspond to the sensor location or contact surface location. This example shows one way of recovering the UTool of a large gripper with minimal robot motion and rotation by using multiple sensors corresponding to multiple UFrame numbers. You must not change the UTool number in any iRCalibration TCP Shift program.

### 16.5.6 /RCalibration TCP Shift Error Recovery

If a /RCalibration TCP Shift error occurs during TCP calibration, the robot goes back to the starting position and an error message is displayed. Review the error message, correct the problem, then restart the TCP calibration program.

### 16.5.6.1 Redoing a /RCalibration TCP Shift Adjustment

To redo a /RCalibration TCP Shift adjustment and restart /RCalibration TCP Shift,

1. Review the error message for an indication of the problem.
2. Correct the problem.
3. Abort any program that is paused.
4. Enter the /RCalibration TCP Shift program name in the setup screen.
5. Press DONE to exit.
6. When /RCalibration TCP Shift asks "Program exists, skip Teach/Create?", reply YES.
7. Run the /RCalibration TCP Shift program: move the cursor to Run and press ENTER.
