### 16.6 iRCALIBRATION FRAME SHIFT

#### 16.6.1 Overview

iRCalibration Frame Shift, formerly CellCal, is a calibration option that compensates for frame changes by establishing a MASTER frame that runs a frame search teach pendant program. After the frame is changed, iRCalibration Frame Shift runs the same frame search teach pendant program again and computes the frame offset.

iRCalibration Frame Shift allows you to set up a cell, work, or part frame by using Torque Observer Sensor technology or Digital I/O using contact or proximity sensing. iRCalibration Frame Shift provides a simple utility to compensate for change of tooling during production. iRCalibration Frame Shift reduces production down time by eliminating the time-consuming process of touching up all positions in all part programs.

iRCalibration Frame Shift also makes cell cloning possible by compensating for the differences in tooling in a different cell. By combining iRCalibration Frame Shift with iRCalibration Master Set and iRCalibration TCP Set software, a part program that has been taught in Cell 1 can usually be transferred and run in Cell 2 without any touch-ups.

# **Limitations**

The following limitations apply to iRCalibration Frame Shift.

- iRCalibration Frame Shift cannot be used with Line Tracking and other options that use a different run-time reference frame other than the current $MNUFRAME. Coordinated motion is supported only when Dynamic-UFrame is used. Refer to Section 16.6.5 and the Coordinated Motion Setup and Operations manual for more information.
- iRCalibration Frame Shift instructions will not be executed in single step test run mode.
- The TCP must be located near the contact surface of the tool. The relationship between the TCP and the contact surface cannot change from the time a iRCalibration Frame Shift program is mastered until it is used. iRCalibration TCP Set can be used, and is recommended, to maintain this relationship between the TCP and the physical tooling.
- The TCP can change in a iRCalibration Frame Shift program to reflect a different contact surface on the tool. The UFrame cannot change in a iRCalibration Frame Shift program.

# **Compatibility**

iRCalibration Frame Shift is compatible with the following:

- iRCalibration Frame Shift can be used with robots with extended axes.
- iRCalibration Frame Shift can be used with multiple groups in single-group programs.

<!-- PDF page 2023 -->

# Hardware Requirements

The following hardware is required to use /RCalibration Frame Shift.

- Teaching tip, if desired (highly recommended for arc welding)
- I/O circuitry, if used

# Software Requirements

The following software is required to use /RCalibration Frame Shift.

- /RCalibration Frame Shift software option

# Installation

You must install the /RCalibration Frame Shift software option before you can use /RCalibration Frame Shift. Refer to the Software Installation Manual for more information about installing software options.

You do not need to install any hardware if TOS (Torque Observer Sensor) is used for contact detection. You will need to set up I/O ports for contact detection if you use I/O for contact detection. Refer to the "I/O Setup" chapter in this manual for information on setting up I/O ports.

You might also need to install a teaching tip as the robot's TCP before running the frame search teach pendant program, and take the teaching tip out after the frame search teach pendant program is complete.

# 16.6.2 Preliminary Setup

FANUC America Corporation recommends that you set up /RCalibration Frame Shift prior to starting production.

Note /RCalibration Frame Shift always uses the current program's $MNUTOOL and $MNUFRAME for searching and position recording.

Perform the following steps prior to using /RCalibration Frame Shift:

1. Define a Tool Center Point (TCP), including WPR if you will be performing tool-relative searches. Refer to the "Frames Setup section" or Section 16.4, "/RCalibration TCP Shift".
2. Install a teaching tip, if desired. This is highly recommended for arc welding and other applications in which the tooling is not conducive to repetitive contact with a part.
3. You must define a UFRAME. $MNUFRAMENUM[group_num] for that particular group must be non-zero This UFRAME will be adjusted when recovery is done to compensate for a change in part or tooling location.
4. If you are using I/O for detection, install and set up circuitry.
5. If you are using Analog Sensor, you must have a data file that resides in the FRS: directory. The data file has a fix name: cb_ainX,dt, where X is a digit from 1 to 9., The data file is very

<!-- PDF page 2024 -->

similar to the analog data file supported in the touch sensing option. It has the following format:

AinPortNumber 2
MaxAnalogInput 1000
MinAnalogInput 100
TotalDataPair 4
DistSensorToPart AnalogInput
400.0 100
200.0 400
100.0 700
-100.0 1000

The maximum allowed TotalDataPair is 10

6. Set up iRCalibration TCP Shift for maintaining the same relationship between the tool frame and the physical TCP. Since iRCalibration Frame Shift determines the UFRAME based on touching surfaces with the robot tool, any misalignment of the tool frame and physical TCP will adversely affect the accuracy of the recovered UFRAME. iRCalibration TCP Shift should be used to recover the tool frame after every minor collision. Very often there is a slight change to the tool even when there seems to be no damage.

Note Refer to Figure 16–27 for Arc Weld tool definition and Figure 16–28 for a typical Waterjet tool definition.

<!-- PDF page 2025 -->

Figure 16–27. Typical Arc Weld Tool Definition

The diagram includes two identical diamond-shaped plates positioned at an angle to each other, connected by a vertical cylindrical shaft in the center. ### 16.6.3 iRCalibration Frame Shift Setup

Before you can use iRCalibration Frame Shift to master or recover a frame, you must perform some setup procedures. Setup involves the initial setting of menu options within iRCalibration Frame Shift software.

Refer to Section 16.6.2 for preliminary setup recommendations.

Setting up and running iRCalibration Frame Shift includes the following processes:

1. Selecting the motion group you want to calibrate
2. Selecting the teach pendant program, the UFRAME you want to calibrate, and the calibration mode (standard or dynamic UFrame). Refer to Section 16.6.5 for information about using iRCalibration Frame Shift with dynamic UFrame.

<!-- PDF page 2027 -->

3. Setting up the Frame schedule. Refer to Table 16–24 for a description of the items on the Frame Schedule Detail Screen.
4. Setting up the detection schedule. Refer to Table 16–25 for a description of the items on the iRCalibration Frame Shift Detection Schedule Detail Screen.
5. Teaching points for the teach pendant calibration program. Refer to Procedure 16-26.
6. Creating the teach pendant calibration program from the taught points and running the calibration program. Refer to Section 16.6.4.
7. Updating the UFrame with the calibration results obtained from running the calibration program. Refer to Procedure 16-29.

### 16.6.3.1 Setting up iRCalibration Frame Shift

# Guidelines for Creating a Frame Calibration Teach Pendant Program Manually

Be familiar with the following guidelines as you create the frame search teach pendant program.

- The contact surface should be relatively flat.
- The search direction must be approximately perpendicular to the contact surface.
- The robot will return to the starting point (or as specified by "return distance" in the detection schedule) after each search.
- Multiple searches (in different directions) can be done at the same starting point as long as the search direction is approximately perpendicular to the contact surface.
- If the contact surface is not approximately perpendicular to a UFRAME or WORLD axis then search frame must be TOOL. You must orient the tool so that one of the TOOL axes is perpendicular to the contact surface.
- The "Update Frame" instruction can be used to apply an incremental frame update.

The "Update Frame" instruction will always update the current UFRAME regardless of the value of the "Auto Update" field in the Frame Schedule.
- When "Update Frame" is used, the final error and position change value only applies to the detection points since the last "Update Frame" instruction was executed.
Multiple"Update Frame" instructions can be included in a program.
- All searches before an "Update Frame" instruction must be either parallel or perpendicular to each other.
If "Update Frame" instruction is used, no more than three parallel searches can be executed before the instruction.

- Search directions can be mixed in the same program (UFRAME, UTOOL, or WORLD can be used).
- The UFRAME cannot be changed in the calibration program.
- The order that you teach the points does not matter, however, it is important that each search direction has enough points that are far from each other.

This program is very similar to the one created automatically by iRCalibration Frame Shift. It has fewer Via points and has two extra instructions, Update Frame, on line 11 and 15.

- The first Update Frame instruction on line 11 allows the XY plane to be corrected for orientation. So, the searches in the X and Y directions are at the proper height with respect to the top of the plane.
- The second Update Frame instruction on line 15 provides an additional update for the new detection in the Y direction. This allows the detections on lines 19 and 20 to be at the proper location with respect to P6.

You can have as few as one and as many as 24 detections in a iRCalibration Frame Shift program, although it is rare to have more than 12. You can intermix Detect Circle and Detect Point instructions. If there are fewer than six points before Uframe End or before an Update Frame instruction, then the points must meet the following restrictions:

- All searches must be approximately perpendicular or parallel to each other
- There must be no more than three parallel searches
- There must be no more than two parallel searches that are colinear
- There must be significant distance between all parallel searches

# 16.6.5 Using /RCalibration Frame Shift with Dynamic-Uframe

Dynamic-Uframe is a feature of coordinated motion where a specified Uframe of the follower group is attached to the Leader Frame of the leader group. When the leader group moves, the follower group's Uframe changes dynamically.

/RCalibration Frame Shift can work with a Dynamic-Uframe similarly to the normal static Uframe. For the case of Dynamic-Uframe, /RCalibration Frame Shift updates the Leader frame which is attached to the faceplate or positioner top of the leader group. This allows positioning errors of parts held by the leader to be compensated with respect to the leader faceplate or positioner top.

Once the Dynamic-Uframe is set up and enabled, /RCalibration Frame Shift programs can move both leader and follower groups. The detection instructions move only the follower group. However, both groups can move between detection instructions.

<!-- PDF page 2048 -->

The Dynamic-Uframe iRCalibration Frame Shift program can also be a single group program that contains only the follower group. The iRCalibration Frame Shift program will use the current Dynamic-Uframe.

Refer to the Coordinated Motion Setup and Operations manual for more information on how to set up and use a Dynamic-Uframe.

### 16.7 iRCALIBRATION SIGNATURE

Note The iRCalibration Signature option cannot be used on robots that have offset wrists, such as the P-250iB. Refer to the Software Structure Diagram for supported robot models.

<!-- PDF page 2052 -->

### 16.7.1 Overview

#### 16.7.1.1 Product Concept

With the latest machining technologies and advancements in product design and analysis tools, it is still not possible to eliminate the deflection of a robot arm or to assemble mechanical parts without error. Therefore, to achieve absolute robot accuracy, software is required to compute and compensate for an individual robot's inherited errors, and the iRCalibration Signature option (A05B-2600-R726) is the software that can improve the absolute accuracy of a robot.

#### 16.7.1.2 High Accuracy Factory Calibration

For all robots ordered with the iRCalibration Signature software, FANUC performs high accuracy factory calibration as part of the manufacturing process. The signature calibration measures hundreds of robot positions in the entire robot work envelope and computes the coefficients that compensate for the errors of the robot. The result is a robot that is capable of achieving a high level of accuracy for the entire working space that cannot be obtained by robots without calibration. For the robot that has gone through the calibration process, a label like the one shown in Figure 16–34 is affixed and accuracy evaluation data is delivered as an attachment. Note that high accuracy factory calibration is model-specific. Contact FANUC for a list of supported robot models.

Once a robot is signature calibrated, the robot runs in signature compensated mode for all types of motion with very minor restrictions (refer to Section 16.7.8.2). In signature compensated mode, all teach pendant program motion instructions benefit from the high accuracy compensation built into FANUC's motion system and there is no special treatment required for these TP programs to perform high-accuracy motions. Use the robot as you would a standard robot and the iRCalibration Signature software will make sure that the robot reaches its taught positions as accurately as possible.

Figure 16–34. Label for High Accuracy Calibration

> **Image description -- img-151.jpeg:** The image is a rectangular warning label with a black background and white text. It features a triangular warning symbol on the left side, consisting of a black exclamation mark inside a yellow triangle with a black border. To the right of the triangle, the text reads 'HIGH ACCURACY CALIBRATED' in all capital letters. The label appears to indicate that a device or instrument has been calibrated to a high level of accuracy.

#### 16.7.1.3 Custom Signature Calibration

To maintain the best accuracy of a robot, it is recommended to check its accuracy regularly for the life of the robot and to perform calibration of the robot if required. In addition, if a robot went through reducer or motor replacement, you will have to recalibrate the robot to get the robot back to its known accuracy. In either case, you can use the custom signature calibration function provided by the iRCalibration Signature software to calibrate the robot at your own facility to get the robot back into production with reduced down time.

<!-- PDF page 2053 -->

Figure 16–35. Overview of the Custom Calibration Function

> **Image description -- img-152.jpeg:** The diagram illustrates a calibration process workflow for a FANUC system within a customer's facility. It begins with 'Factory Calibration' (highlighted in a blue box), which is the initial calibration performed at the factory. This is followed by the addition of a 'Signature option' (indicated by a yellow box), which is a specific feature added to the system. The next step is 'Retrofit Calibration' (highlighted in a green box), which involves updating or adjusting the calibration to accommodate new or modified components. This step is followed by 'Enhanced Calibration' (highlighted in a purple box), which optimizes the system for specific operational conditions such as area, payload, and installation type. If a repair is needed (e.g., for a motor or reducer), the process moves to 'Repair' (highlighted in a yellow box), and then to 'Calibration Recovery' (highlighted in a blue box), which restores the calibration to its proper state post-repair. The arrows indicate the flow and sequence of these steps, showing how the calibration process is maintained and adjusted throughout the lifecycle of the equipment within the customer's facility.

To perform custom signature calibration, you will need a laser tracker and a laser beam reflector as the target for the laser tracker. The reflector is mounted on the tool of the robot and should be fixed during the calibration process. Similar to factory calibration, this calibration requires measuring the reflector at various robot positions. Different calibration types have different requirements for the number of measurements needed. Once the measurement is completed and the measured data is loaded onto the controller, the iRCalibration Signature software computes the new compensation parameters and notifies you of the calibration result. If the result is acceptable, the controller then loads the new compensation parameters and the robot is back in production.

# Note

1. A laser tracker and measurement software are required to perform custom calibration. In addition, the operator should have training in metrology and know how to set up measurement frames. Contact FANUC if you need help.
2. The custom signature calibration function has to be conducted by FANUC personnel or personnel trained and certified by FANUC to ensure that the correct procedure is followed. Contact FANUC the first time custom signature calibration must be performed.

### 16.7.1.4 Signature Compensation

Once signature calibration parameters have been applied to the robot controller, the software compensates the motor position in real time to achieve better accuracy regardless of motion type, position representation, or motion modifier. Therefore, the signature calibrated robot can be used in a wide range of applications.

Note Similar to gravity compensation, iRCalibration Signature uses payload information to compute the bending of the robot arm due to gravity loading. Refer to Section 14.22.2 to set an accurate payload to take advantage of the full benefits of the signature compensation function.

<!-- PDF page 2054 -->

### 16.7.2 Benefits of a Signature Calibrated Robot

#### 16.7.2.1 Simplified off-line programming

A signature calibrated robot makes Teach Pendant (TP) programs generated off-line much easier to adopt in the real controller. The example in Figure 16–36 shows the steps involved in converting an off-line generated TP program to a program on the factory floor. (A) Measure the robot installation position and jig location using a laser tracker and (B) Shift the off-line created TP program based on the measured value in the simulation. (C) Download the shifted TP program to the controller. (D) Verify the TP program and touch up when necessary.

#### 16.7.2.2 Easy Robot Replacement

Most FANUC robot models have locating pin holes in the base as shown in Figure 16–37. By using these locating pin holes, a new robot can be installed at the same location as an old robot. These pin holes are used in FANUC factory calibration as a reference. Therefore, when replacing a signature calibrated robot with a new signature calibrated robot and using the location pin holes to place the new robot in the correct location, the new robot requires minimal touch-ups. This drop-in replacement can reduce the downtime of a production line significantly when a robot is damaged during production.

### 16.7.3 Custom Signature Calibration

#### 16.7.3.1 Calibration System

To perform signature calibration, the following hardware and software are required:

- Laser Tracker
- Measurement reflector
- PC for measurement software
- Robot
- Robot controller loaded with /RCalibration Signature software
- Calibration program that contains the positions that you want to measure

After running through the calibration program and measuring a variety of robot positions, a measurement data file from the PC is loaded onto the robot controller via a memory device (such as a USB). The robot controller then computes the signature calibration parameters using the loaded 3–D measurement data to minimize robot errors. Note that the laser tracker, measurement reflector, PC, and measurement PC software are third-party products that you should obtain before conducting the calibration.

<!-- PDF page 2056 -->

Figure 16–38. Calibration System

> **Image description -- img-158.jpeg:** The image depicts a setup for a laser tracking system used to measure and calibrate the motion range of a robot. The key components and their labels are as follows: (A) Laser Tracker, which emits a laser beam to track the robot's movements; (B) Reflector, attached to the robot to reflect the laser beam back to the tracker; (C) PC for measurement, connected to the laser tracker to process and record the measurement data; (D) Robot, whose motion range is being calibrated and measured; and (E) Robot Controller, which controls the robot's movements. The diagram shows the laser tracker positioned on a table, the reflector mounted on the robot, and the robot controller and PC connected to the system. The calibration range is indicated as the area where the robot's motion is tracked, and the robot motion range is the broader area encompassing the robot's operational workspace.

### 16.7.3.2 Calibration Type

In addition to the high accuracy factory calibration, custom signature calibration provides the following calibration types to maintain absolute accuracy during the life cycle of the robot:

#### Retrofit Calibration

Retrofit calibration is a function to perform signature calibration for robots that have not been calibrated before being installed in a customer's facility. This function computes optimized signature calibration data using limited space, after installation.

#### Enhanced Factory Calibration (Enhanced Calibration)

Enhanced factory calibration is a function to perform signature calibration in addition to the existing factory calibration. This function computes optimized signature data in actual installation conditions (such as upside-down and angle mount) by measuring additional robot positions to improve accuracy for specific robot configurations.

#### Calibration Recovery

When a signature calibrated robot needs a repair, such as replacing a reducer or motor, the calibration recovery function can return the robot to accuracy similar to its previous accuracy.

#### TCP/Uframe Calibration

TCP/Uframe calibration computes the robot installation position and the measurement reflector position mounted on the robot's tool.

#### Note

- Since retrofit calibration is equivalent to factory calibration, it has to be conducted by FANUC personnel or personnel trained and certified by FANUC to ensure that the correct procedure is followed and an acceptable result can be obtained for this particular robot.

<!-- PDF page 2057 -->

- Retrofit calibration, enhanced calibration, and calibration recovery are available in 7DC1/32 (V8.10P/32), 7DC3/62 (V8.30P/62), 7DF3/18 (V9.30P/18), 7DF5/15 (V9.40P15) or later. Contact FANUC for the status in 7DC2 (V8.20P) or 7DF1(V9.10P).
- In 7DC3 (V8.30P) or later, the signature calibration type has the same features as the retrofit calibration type in the software versions in which retrofit calibration has not been supported. Functionality is improved in retrofit calibration. Therefore, it is recommended that you update the software to the latest version.

In this step, the system checks if TCP (Tool Center Point) is calibrated (Yes/No), if the World Frame is calibrated (Yes/No), and allows settings for the Reference Frame and Calibration Recovery. The 'View/Apply Calibration Result' step allows viewing the calibration result and applying the signature calibration data to the robot. Finally, the 'Save SYSMAST.SV' step saves the system state file including the signature calibration data, leading to the 'FIN' (finish) step.

### 16.7.3.5 Coordinate Systems

# Coordinate Systems in Signature Calibration

As shown in Figure 16–44, this function uses a (L) laser tracker frame, (W) World frame, (M) measurement frame, (F) mechanical interface frame, and (T) Tool Frame.

Figure 16–44. Coordinate Systems in Signature Calibration

> **Image description -- img-165.jpeg:** The image depicts a mechanical setup involving a robotic arm and a cylindrical object. The robotic arm, colored yellow, is mounted on a base and appears to be in the process of manipulating or interacting with the cylindrical object, which is green with red and yellow circular components attached to its ends. The setup is placed on a flat surface with a grid pattern. Two coordinate systems are visible: one on the left side of the image, labeled with axes X, Y, and Z, and another on the right side, also labeled with axes X, Y, and Z. The left coordinate system is associated with the robotic arm, while the right coordinate system is associated with the cylindrical object. The image includes labels for force (F) and torque (T) on the right side, indicating the directions of these mechanical interactions. The robotic arm's end effector is positioned near the cylindrical object, suggesting a task involving precise positioning or manipulation.

# Laser Tracker Frame (L)

A laser tracker frame is a coordinate system integrated in the laser tracker itself. Therefore, the laser tracker frame can be used as a measurement frame.

# World Frame (W)

The World Frame is a standard Cartesian coordinate system fixed in a workspace. The coordinate system is fixed at a position determined by the robot.

# Measurement Frame (M)

- The measurement PC software in general is capable of setting up a measurement frame using its alignment function.
- It is possible to set the measurement frame consistently using multiple fixed measurement points with known design values in a production line. The measurement frame is thus reproducible by measuring those points when setting up the laser tracker.
- Set the position and orientation (x,y,z,w,p,r) of the measurement frame (with respect to the robot's World Frame) into the User Frame for signature calibration.

<!-- PDF page 2062 -->

# Mechanical Interface Frame (F)

The mechanical interface frame is a standard Cartesian coordinate system defined for the mechanical interface of the robot (the surface of the wrist flange). When setting up a Tool Frame, the Tool Frame references the mechanical interface frame.

# Tool Frame (T)

- The Tool Frame defines the position of the tool center point (TCP) seen from the mechanical interface frame.
- Set the position (x,y,z) of the measurement reflector into the Tool Frame used for signature calibration.

# Setup of Measurement Frame and its Features

The features in Figure 16–45 can be obtained by setting the measurement frame to fit the World Frame or User Frame.

Figure 16–45. Setup of Measurement Frame and its Features

> **Image description -- img-166.jpeg:** The image is a flowchart or decision diagram that explains the relationship and calibration requirements between three types of frames: Measurement Frame, World Frame, and User Frame. The diagram is divided into two main sections: the left side shows the frames and their calibration status, while the right side lists the features or outcomes based on the calibration. 

On the left side:
- The Measurement Frame is the starting point and is connected to the World Frame and User Frame.
- The World Frame has a decision point labeled "Setting of 'Is world frame calibrated'" with two possible outcomes: "Yes" or "No."
- If the answer is "Yes," the World Frame is calibrated; if "No," the User Frame is considered.

On the right side, under the "Features" heading, the outcomes are described:
- If the World Frame is calibrated (Yes), the feature states: "Require the measurement frame to matches the world frames precisely."
- If the World Frame is not calibrated (No), two features are listed:
  1. "No need to fit two frames precisely. Measurement frame setup is easy."
  2. "User frame can be optimized simultaneously with the robot."

# World Frame Calibration

- When the measurement frame is aligned with the World Frame precisely, the status is set to show that World Frame calibration has been done.
- If World Frame calibration has been done, set (x,y,z,w,p,r) = (0,0,0,0,0,0) into the User Frame used for signature calibration. If World Frame calibration has not been done, set the position and orientation (x,y,z,w,p,r) of the measurement frame as seen from the robot's World Frame into the User Frame used for signature calibration.
- In the setup of signature calibration, when “Is world frame calibrated” is set to Yes, signature calibration parameters are computed assuming that the measurement frame matches the robot’s World Frame precisely. When “Is world frame calibrated” is set to No, the measurement

<!-- PDF page 2063 -->

frame seen from the robot's World Frame is computed simultaneously with the robot's signature calibration parameters and is applied to the User Frame.

- In retrofit calibration and enhanced factory calibration, it is recommended that you set the World Frame calibration to Not done. In calibration recovery, it is recommended that you set the World Frame calibration to Done, because the World Frame calibration must be done when recovering a parameter related to J1.

# Calibration of User Frame

- When a User Frame has been defined on a jig of the production line and used in a TP program, for example, the software can calibrate the User Frame as part of signature calibration.
- In this case, the answer to the "Is world frame calibrate" question in the Signature Setup menu is No.
- When "Is world frame calibrated" is set to No, the actual User Frame position (with respect to the robot's World Frame) is computed
- If the User Frame is calibrated as part of signature calibration, there is no need to adjust an off-line TP program's User Frame to correct the actual jig positions.

# Tool Frame Setup and Calibration

- The Tool Frame for signature calibration is defined as the measurement reflector location with respect to the robot's mechanical interface frame.
- If the measurement reflector location is known exactly, select YES for the question "Is TCP Calibrated" in the Signature Setup screen. Go to the MENU > SETUP/Frame screen to enter the known (x, y, z) value for the designated UTOOL. If the measurement location is unknown, answer NO for the question "Is TCP Calibrated". Go to the MENU > SETUP/Frame to enter an estimated (x, y, z) value so that the actual location is within a 10 mm radius of the estimated location for the designated UTOOL.
- When "Is TCP Calibrated?" is set to YES, signature calibration assumes that the measurement reflector's position is known and will not compute an offset to the Tool frame. If "Is TCP Calibrated" is set to NO, signature calibration will compute the offset to the Tool Frame as part of the signature computation.

##### 16.7.4.5 Run Calibration Program Screen

# Run Calibration Program Screen

Follow the descriptions shown on the screen to select a calibration TP program from the program selection screen, run the program, and transfer the measurement data file to the robot controller.

Note Before running the calibration program, make sure that the following items are set correctly:

- The measurement reflector is attached and its location is properly set in the Tool Frame.
- The correct payload number is selected and its payload information is based on the current physical payload.
- The laser tracker is securely tied down and will not move during measurement.
- The medium for recording measurement data is inserted and the current device is correctly selected.
- If the robot has secondary encoders, make sure that secondary encoder control is enabled.

# Outline of the Calibration TP Program

The example program shown in Figure 16–52 is created using Procedure 16-34. In this example, lines 1-4 and lines 86-87 are special instructions added for signature calibration and they should not be edited. Lines 5-85 are added for the measurement point based on the position program and a call instruction to a measurement TP program is added. Touch up or add teaching points as appropriate.

Figure 16-52. Outline of the Calibration TP Program

[tbl-195.md](tbl-195.md)

Figure 16–53 shows the measurement TP program which is automatically loaded when entering the Run Calibration Program screen. The program will pause at the PAUSE instruction in line 3. Measure the measurement reflector position using the laser tracker at this time. After one measurement, press the START button to move the robot to the next position.

Figure 16-53. RECD_CAL_POS.TP program

[tbl-196.md](tbl-196.md)

Note Recording internal data at line 2 and measurement by the laser tracker at line 3 must be executed at same robot position. ACAL-150 “Near Singularity, Skip Meas.” could occur during the execution of line 2 when the measurement position is around a singularity position. In this case, recording the internal data of line 2 is not performed. Therefore, you must also skip the laser tracker measurement in line 3.

# Loading Measurement Data on the Robot Controller

After taking measurements at all measurement points and the calibration program has finished running, eject the memory device from the robot controller and plug the memory device into the PC. Note that the calibration software created a directory on the memory device and for this example, the directory is named SIG_CAL_G1. Do not change the contents of this directory. Copy the measurement data file to the root (top) directory of the memory device. After copying the file, insert the memory device back into the robot controller. The measurement data file should have the following characteristics:

<!-- PDF page 2070 -->

- The file name should be cb_measxyz.txt.
- Each row indicates the X, Y, Z position (units: mm) of the measurement data. Use space to separate each item.

### 16.7.5.1 Calibration Recovery

#### Calibration Recovery Setup

Calibration recovery is a function for performing signature calibration after parts have been replaced. This function computes optimized signature calibration parameters related to the

<!-- PDF page 2075 -->

replaced parts. In addition to the setup items described in Section 16.7.4.3, the Recover Mastering related Data and Recover all related axis items are selectable for each axis.

Figure 16–60. Custom Calibration Custom Setup Screen

Refer to Table 16–31 to set up the items to be recovered according to the parts that have been replaced. You can select multiple recovery items.

Table 16–31. Selection of recovery items according to the replaced parts

[tbl-198.md](tbl-198.md)

# Position Program

As described in Section 16.7.3.4, the position program should include various positions that cover most of the motion ranges of all axes.

To accurately recover mastering related parameters, the position program should include a wide motion range of the axis to be recovered. For example, assuming that the J2 motor has been replaced, you need to move J2 as much as possible within the constraints of the production environment. For World Frame calibration, the measurement points should not be on the same plane.

<!-- PDF page 2076 -->

For Tool Frame calibration, the measurement positions should include various orientation changes in order to compute an accurate Tool Frame.

# Recovery of J1 Signature Calibration Parameters

World Frame calibration must be done when recovering signature J1 calibration parameters after replacing parts such as motors or reducers. Before falling into maintenance due to breakage, the measurement frame used for calibration recovery seen from the robot World Frame must be known by TCP/Uframe Calibration in advance and saved into the User Frame. By setting the User Frame number as the reference frame number, World Frame calibration can be set to done using the reference frame function. Refer to Section 16.7.5.2 and Section 16.7.5.3 for details.

### 16.7.5.2 TCP/Uframe Calibration

TCP/Uframe Calibration computes the robot installation position and measurement reflector position mounted on the robot's tool. Figure 16–61 shows a schematic of TCP/Uframe calibration.

Figure 16–61. Schematic of TCP/Uframe Calibration

> **Image description -- img-180.jpeg:** The image depicts a mechanical setup involving a robotic arm interacting with a cylindrical object. The setup includes a robotic arm mounted on a base, with a gripper or end-effector attached to its free end. The cylindrical object is positioned on a table or platform in front of the robotic arm. The image includes coordinate axes labeled +X, +Y, and +Z, indicating the spatial orientation of the system. The robotic arm is shown in two states: one where it is extended toward the cylindrical object (highlighted in yellow) and another where it is retracted (highlighted in green). The gripper or end-effector is shown in a closed position around the cylindrical object. Additionally, there is a force (F) vector indicated near the cylindrical object, suggesting the application of force during the interaction. The setup appears to be part of a robotic manipulation or automation experiment, likely involving force control or precision handling.

The measurement reflector location is calculated as (T) Tool Frame seen from (F) Mechanical Interface Frame. The calculated User Frame is the position and rotation of (M) measurement frame seen from (W) the robot's World Frame.

To calculate the Tool frame, three or more measurement points that include tool orientation changes are required. To calculate the User Frame, four or more measurement points are required, and all of the points must not be on the same plane.

The Setup screen and View Calibration Result screen for TCP/Uframe Calibration are different from the other calibration types described in Section 16.7.4.

# Note

<!-- PDF page 2077 -->

- To calibrate the Tool Frame, a rough estimate of the measurement reflector's position (x, y, z) with respect to the mechanical interface frame is required. The estimated position should be within a 10 mm radius of the actual TCP position.
- To compute the User Frame, it is required to have an estimated UFRAME value (x, y, z, w, p, r) before calibration. A rough position and orientation (x, y, z, w, p, r) within 100 mm and 10 deg is sufficient.

##### 16.7.5.3 Reference Frame Function

The reference frame function is a function to convert the measurement data of the measurement frame (M) to the World Frame (W) when the position and rotation of the measurement frame (M) seen from the World Frame (W) is known. As shown in Figure 16–64, four reference points (measurement reflector holder) are placed on a jig whose positional relationship with the robot is fixed. The measurement frame (M) can be set consistently by measuring four reference points. In this case, you can use TCP/Uframe calibration to calculate the relationship between M and W and save the data into a User Frame. Once the User Frame is known, by using the reference frame function, the measurement data on the measurement frame (M) can be handled internally as data in the World Frame (W) and can be used for signature calibration. By using this feature, accuracy of calibration recovery can be improved by setting the World Frame calibration to done.

<!-- PDF page 2079 -->

Figure 16–64. Schematic of the Reference Frame Function

> **Image description -- img-183.jpeg:** The image depicts a 3D coordinate system diagram with labeled axes and reference points. The coordinate system is defined by three orthogonal axes: x (green), y (red), and z (blue), with their positive directions indicated by arrows. The origin of the coordinate system is marked as (L). Three reference points are labeled as Reference point 1, Reference point 2, and Reference point 3, each represented by red dots. Reference point 1 is located along the positive x-axis, Reference point 2 is positioned in the positive y direction, and Reference point 3 is placed in the positive z direction. The diagram also includes a small illustration of a person holding a light source, suggesting the direction of illumination or observation. The coordinate system is labeled with (W) near the origin, and (M) near Reference point 1, indicating possible measurement or observation points. The spatial relationships between the reference points and the coordinate axes are clearly illustrated, showing their positions relative to the origin.

# Procedure 16-41 Enabling the Reference Frame Function

# Conditions

##### 16.7.5.4 Enable/Disable iRCalibration Signature Compensation

For a given TP program position, the robot may reach a different physical position when it is in signature compensated mode than when it is not in signature compensated mode, due to the applied compensation. If you need to put the robot in or out of signature compensated mode, you can use the following KAREL programs in your TP program using the technique described in this section.

Note The robot position will change slightly when signature compensation is enabled or disabled.

The Signature function can be enabled or disabled by executing the following KAREL programs:

- CALL ACCU_START(1) : Enable the Signature function
- CALL ACCU_END(1) : Disable the Signature function

You can create sub-TP programs such as the ones shown in Table 16–32 and Table 16–33 and call them from your main TP program. A DO[] = ON instruction is used to indicate that the robot is in high accuracy mode.

### 16.7.7 Mastering

#### 16.7.7.1 Mastering the Signature Calibration Robot

FANUC factory mastering is performed with disabled signature compensation, which means that the robot is not in high accuracy mode when it is mastered. When a signature calibrated robot needs to be re-mastered due to parts replacement or other reasons, it is also necessary to take the robot out of signature compensated mode. Refer to Procedure 16-43 to disable signature compensation.

Note If you attempt to master a robot when the robot is in signature compensated mode, a message will prompt you to take the robot out of signature compensated mode. Follow the instructions in the displayed message to disable signature compensation.

Note When a signature calibration robot is not in signature compensated mode, all zero position marks match when the robot moves all of its joints to zero degrees.

After mastering has been correctly performed, enable signature compensated mode using Procedure 16-43 and validate the accuracy of the robot. If the accuracy is not acceptable, refer to Section 16.7.5.1 to perform calibration recovery.

#### 16.7.7.2 Quick Mastering

The robot can lose its pulse count due to removing the battery, disconnecting the Pulsecoder cable, or for other reasons. The pulse count is composed of two numbers: the number of revolutions and the Pulsecoder value within the revolution. When a robot has lost its pulse counts, it loses the number of revolutions value but keeps the pulse value within the revolution data. Quick mastering uses this fact to quickly re-establish the pulse counts correctly. Therefore, quick mastering does not affect the accuracy of a signature calibrated robot.

Note When a Pulsecoder is replaced, quick mastering cannot be applied to regain the correct pulse count. Therefore, the robot will need to be recalibrated to maintain its accuracy.

#### 16.7.7.3 Monitoring the Change of Mastering Data

When a signature calibrated robot needs to be mastered again, it is necessary to validate the robot's accuracy after performing the mastering procedure. If the robot has more error than expected, calibration recovery is required. When iRCalibration Signature software is installed, the software will monitor the change of mastering data and display a notification icon when mastering data has changed from the data at signature calibration. If the change of mastering data is intentional, the change can be approved using Procedure 16-44.

#### Procedure 16-44 Approving Mastering Data

1. Display the iRCalibration Signature Status Screen. (Procedure 16-42)

#### 16.7.8 Cautions

##### 16.7.8.1 Accuracy Around Singularity

In general, a robot in its singularity position means either that the robot is fully extended or that two or more robot axes are in a straight line. When a robot is close to its singularity position, the robot's accuracy is deteriorated compared to when the robot is far away from its singularity position. This is true even for signature calibrated robots. To maintain the accuracy of the robot, it is recommended to design the robot's tool and production cell layout to avoid positions that are close to the robot's singularity. Figure 16–69 shows the four singularity areas that should be avoided.

### 16.7.8.2 Restrictions

The iRCalibration Signature option can be used in combination with other software options, with the following restrictions:

- Multi-arm configuration could require a special operation in the FANUC manufacturing process. Contact your local FANUC representative for the required configuration.
- Auxiliary axis is supported. Integrated Rail is not supported.

## 17.1 OVERVIEW

Note Some descriptions in this chapter might apply only to the use of this option with the SpotTool+ product and not the HandlingTool product.

The Material Handling option provides the controller with the ability to set up, configure, and control the functioning of vacuum or clamp-style material handling valves. You define the tooling valve type, characteristics, and I/O. Then you can control the tooling valve using specific macro commands that are called from within a teach pendant program, run from the Manual Functions screen, or run by pressing a teach pendant user key.

The following terms are used in the descriptions of setting up and operating the Material Handling Tool. Review them for a better understanding of the Material Handling Option.

### Tooling

This is a "gripper-like" mechanism controlled by valves.

### Vacuum Tool

This is a mechanism that picks up objects using vacuum suction cups.

### Clamp Tool

This is a mechanism that picks up objects using clamps.

### Part Present

This is a sensor that indicates whether an object is being held by a tool.

### Vacuum Input

This is a sensor that indicates whether the vacuum suction is on.

### Valve n to A

This is a signal that indicates whether the tooling valve is in the A position. When the signal is on, the tooling valve is in the A position. The A and B positions must be opposite.

### Valve n to B

This is a signal that indicates whether the tooling valve is in the B position. When the signal is on, the tooling valve is in the B position. The A and B positions must be opposite.

<!-- PDF page 2089 -->

### 17.2.1 Overview

You set up the Material Handling Tool by doing the following:

1. Set up tooling valve information.
2. Set up tooling valve signals.

After you have set up this information, you can also control valve I/O.

Note There are no material handling program instructions; macros are used instead. You can combine material handling macros with either SpotTool+ application program instructions or DispenseTool application program instructions.

Note Refer to Section 8.8 for information on setting up and executing macros.

## 17.5 PRODUCTION

When you have the Material Handling Plug-in, production operation has the following features, if they have been enabled:

<!-- PDF page 2115 -->

- Tryout mode
- Disable for 20 cycles
- Alarms

### 17.5.1 MH Tryout Mode

MH Tryout Mode enables and disables the ability of the robot to execute material handling commands in a tryout, or dry run, mode. You enable and disable MH Tryout Mode on the TEST CYCLE Spot Weld menu after you set up the cell interface I/O. Refer to Section 13.10.2.

You can also enable MH Tryout Mode by setting the system variable $SHELL_WRK.$tryout_mode to TRUE.

When MH Tryout Mode is enabled, it does the following:

- Disables checking for feedback signals.
- Changes the checking for part present signals. When MH Tryout Mode is enabled on the TEST CYCLE Spot Weld menu, the part present signals must never be on.
- Allows the robot to run the program with all other material handling alarms and conditions enabled.

### 17.5.2 Disable for 20 Cycles

When you use the Disable Fault Checking feature, you can specify that the robot ignore tooling valve inputs, clamps, and part present alarms for 20 cycles. After 20 cycles, an error message will be re-enabled and, if the alarm occurs again, will pause the program until it is reset by the operator.

You can use the Disable Fault Checking feature to disable each tooling valve PAUSE alarm for 20 cycles. When a material handling pause alarm occurs, you will be able to choose Disable Alarm on the error recovery screen to disable this particular alarm for 20 cycles. Refer to Section 9.2.5 for more information about using the Disable Fault Checking feature to do this.

### 17.5.3 Alarms

All Material Handling alarms turn on the MH Fault output, if the controller is not in MH Tryout Mode. The output will be turned off when a FAULT RESET is given.

The MH Alert output turns ON when a fault that has been disabled for 20 cycles occurs. The output will be turned OFF when a FAULT RESET is given.

# PAINT PLUG-IN OPTION

# Contents

[tbl-232.md](tbl-232.md)

<!-- PDF page 2118 -->

## 18.1 Overview

The Paint Plug In option for HandlingTool and LR HandlingTool is used to simplify the integration of robots that do not require the features included with PaintTool. PPS[] (Paint Start) and PPE (Paint End) application instructions are used within the user taught program to control the application I/O. Additionally, PAUSE and RESUME functionality is included with the Paint Plug In option. The application processing is carried out by a teach pendant TPE program that is provided in the system for each event (PPS, PPE, Pause, and Resume). This enables you to customize the application processing depending on the application requirements by modifying the system provided teach pendant programs. See Section 18.1.3.

It is also possible to adjust the timing where PPS or PPE processing starts by setting the anticipation time value (Time Before). See Section 18.3.

### 18.1.1 Application Instructions

The following instructions are included with the Paint Plug In option:

- PPS[index] Initiate Paint Start sequence using the associated index 1-999.
- PPE End Paint Start sequence.

Below is an example of a typical paint start and end sequence:

1:L P[1] 250mm/sec CNT100 PPS[1]
2:L P[3] 250mm/sec CNT100
3:L P[2] 250mm/sec CNT100 PPE

The Robot Digital output 1 will turn on (RO[1]=ON) when the PPS[1] instruction is executed, and turn RO[1]=OFF when the PPE instruction executes. The index parameter provides an option for you to perform different actions based on the parameter. For example, the application might require setting some analog outputs before setting the RO. This can be accomplished by using index 1 to set the analogs, and index 2 to set the RO as shown below.

1:L P[1] 250mm/sec CNT100 PPS[2]
2:L P[3] 250mm/sec CNT100
3:L P[2] 250mm/sec CNT100 PPE

Note PPS instructions should not be used standalone (i.e. 1:PPS[2]). They should always be attached to a motion line (i.e. 1:L P[1] 250mm/sec CNT100 PPS[2]).

The teach pendant programming editor includes the above instructions within the Painting section of the instruction menu as follows:

<!-- PDF page 2119 -->

Instruction Joint 10%
1 Registers 5 WAIT
2 I/O 6 JMP/LBL
3 PAINTING 7 CALL
4 IF/SELECT 8 ---next page---

The instructions are also accessible from the Motion Modify menu as shown below:

Motion Modify Joint 10%
1 No Option 5 ACC
2 PPS[] 6 Skip, LBL[]
3 PPE 7 BREAK
4 Wrist Joint 8 ---next page---

The instructions have also been added to the default instruction menu at the bottom of the select screen as follows:

PROC1 Joint 10%

1:L P[1] 250mm/sec CNT100 PPS[1]
2:L P[3] 250mm/sec CNT100
3:L P[2] 250mm/sec CNT100 PPE
POINT PNT_STR PNT_END TOUCHUP

PNT_STR includes the motion data in addition to the PPS[index] instruction. PNT_END will include the motion data as well as the PPE instruction.

#### 18.1.2 Configuration

By default, the Paint Plug In is configured to control a single trigger via Robot Digital Output 1 (RO[1]), and no setup is required. Registers are used within the Plug-in to perform specific tasks. The default registers used are as follows:

- R[GROUP] - Contains index specified by PPS[index] instruction.
- R[101] - Saved state of RO[1] used during resume.

Note GROUP = 1 in the default configuration.

The R[GROUP] setting can be changed to use a different register via the Paint Plug In Setup screen.

#### 18.1.3 Custom Setup

The Paint Plug In option includes the following teach pendent programs:

- Paint_Start.TP – Program called when PPS[index] instruction executes.
- Paint_End.TP – Program called when PPE instruction executes.
- Paint_Pause.TP – Called when error occurs between paint start, end sequence.

<!-- PDF page 2120 -->

- Paint_Resum.TP – Called when cycle start received after an error and reset. Only occurs during a paint start, end sequence.
- Proc1.TP – Called from Paint_Start.TP when index of PPS[index] instruction is 1.

These programs are set up by default to control Robot Digital Output RO[1] when the PPS[] and PPE instructions are used. When additional I/O needs to manipulated, these programs will need to be modified. The following procedure is an example of what is required if the application requires different analog settings or other I/O throughout the path.

The taught path used in this example is as follows:

1:L P[1] 250mm/sec CNT100 PPS[x]
2:L P[3] 250mm/sec CNT100
3:L P[2] 250mm/sec CNT100 PPE

1. Create a ProcX.TP file for each unique index or schedule required.
2. Modify Proc1.TP and the newly created ProcX.TP to control the appropriate IO. In this example Proc1.TP will now control the analog IO and ProcX.TP will control the trigger or RO[1].

Note Except where noted in Section 18.1.2, the registers used in the following program are shown for example purposes only. You must determine which registers are used in your application.

Proc1.tp

1: ! Set non trigger process control ;
2: AO[1]=100 ;
3: AO[2]=200 ;
4: AO[3]=300 ;
5: ! Save IO states for Pause/Resume sequence ;
6: R[111] = AO[1] ;
6: R[112] = AO[2] ;
6: R[113] = AO[3] ;

ProcX.tp

1: ! Turn ON the TRIGGER ;
2: RO[1]=ON ;
3: ! Save settings to register ;
4: ! for PAINT_RESUME.TP ;
5: R[101]=RO[1] ;

3. Modify the Paint_Start.tp program to call the newly created ProcX.tp program when R[1] = X.

1: IF R[1]=1, CALL PROC1;
2: IF R[1]=X, CALL PROCX;

<!-- PDF page 2121 -->

4. Modify Paint_Pause.tp to clear the appropriate I/O on a fault:

1: RO[1]=Off;
2: AO[1]=0;
3: AO[2]=0;
4: AO[3]=0;

5. Modify Paint_Resum.tp to restore the appropriate I/O on the cycle start or resume.

1: RO[1]=R[101];
2: AO[1]=R[111];
3: AO[2]=R[112];
4: AO[3]=R[113];

6. Modify Paint_End.tp to change the state of I/O as desired.

The above steps can be repeated as many times as necessary for the application although the current index range is 1 - 999.

##### 18.1.3.1 Event Teach Pendant Program Requirements

The Group Mask Attribute cannot be used with these teach pendant programs, and must be set to *,*,*,*. These programs must exist on the controller even if the PPS[] and PPE instructions are not used. It is very important that these programs execute as quickly as possible. Be careful when you are performing the teach pendant programming. As an example, if a WAIT of 2 seconds is inserted into the ProcX.TP program, an error would occur because execution took too long. However, a WAIT of .2 seconds would be acceptable. The current requirement is that the program finishes within .5 seconds.

Figure 18–1 shows an overview of the Paint_Start and Paint_End teach pendant files used within the application.

<!-- PDF page 2122 -->

Figure 18-1. Paint Start and Paint End

> **Image description -- img-192.jpeg:** The image depicts a flowchart or diagram illustrating the relationship and interaction between different program modules or plugins in a control system, likely related to a painting process. The diagram includes three main labeled boxes: 'CustomerPartProgram.TP', 'Paint_Start.TP', and 'Paint_End.TP'. 

1. **CustomerPartProgram.TP**: 
   - Contains three program steps (P[1], P[2], P[3]) each calling a CNT100 instruction with different parameters (PPS[1], PPS[2], PPE).

2. **Paint_Start.TP**: 
   - This is identified as a Paint Plug-in.
   - It processes the program PPS[1].
   - It is called by CustomerPartProgram.TP.
   - It creates a schedule for PPS[1] and PPE.
   - It requires a change to Paint_Start.TP.
   - It creates a new process for each PPS[1] and PPE.
   - It registers the schedule automatically.
   - It updates the current schedule when the PPE instruction gets executed.
   - It sets non-trigger process control and application attributes.
   - It turns off the trigger and can be created and called above.

3. **Paint_End.TP**: 
   - This is also identified as a Paint Plug-in.
   - It processes the program PPE.
   - It is called by CustomerPartProgram.TP.
   - It gets executed when the PPE instruction is called.
   - It sets the following program attributes: Group Mask, application, and turns off the trigger.

The right side of the image contains detailed notes about the Paint_Start.TP module, explaining its functions, attributes, and operational steps. The notes include specific instructions and conditions for its operation, such as setting registers, turning triggers on/off, and handling process control.

The normal execution sequence of the PPS[] and PPE instructions in the above example is as follows:

1. Cycle start initiates execution of CustomerPartProgram.tp.
2. As the robot approaches P[1], the PPS[1] instruction is executed.
3. Paint_Start.tp is called.
4. R[1] is evaluated and thus calls Proc1.TP because index = 1.
5. Proc1.tp sets RO[1] = On thus turning on the Trigger.
6. Proc1.tp saves the state of the trigger to R[101].
7. Steps 2 thru 6 are repeated as robot approaches P[2].
8. Paint_End.TP is called when the robot approaches P[3], RO[1] = Off.

If a Pause or greater severity error occurs while the robot is within the PPS[] and PPE sequence, the following occurs:

1. Paint_Pause.tp is executed and RO[1] is set to Off.
2. When the alarm is cleared, the controller is reset and Cycle Start is inhibited, Paint_Resum.tp is executed.
3. The state of RO[1] saved during the Paint_Pause.tp is restored and robot motion is resumed.

<!-- PDF page 2123 -->

Figure 18–2 shows the Paint_Resum and Paint_Pause teach pendant programs.

Note After Paint_start.tp has been called, it will finish its execution before Paint_pause.tp is called even if an error occurs during Paint_start.tp execution.

Figure 18–2. Paint_Pause and Paint_Resum Teach Pendant Programs

## 19.1 OVERVIEW

### 19.1.1 1-1 Feature of function

#### What is a servo tool?

A servo tool is a tool having an axis that is driven by a servo motor controlled by a robot controller.

- It is possible to switch more than two servo tools without power off.
- Switching the air drive tool and the servo tool is also available.

### 19.1.2 1-2 Basic specification

Table 19–1. Basic Specifications

[tbl-246.md](tbl-246.md)

(*1) The period includes the internal processing period, not include the period of robot motion for changing the tools.

### 19.1.3 Restrictions

#### Restrictions matters

- Switching is possible only between servo tools that are set within the same motion group.
- The tool change function cannot be used with a servo tool having more than one axis.
- Because servo tools that do not have a battery for tool axis pulse value backup require calibration after they are attached, these tools require longer processing time for tool change than battery-equipped tools.
- The motor of the tool change must be controlled by the same amp.
- The tool change instruction can not used by multi task. (The tool change instruction can not be execute by plural tasks at the same time)

#### Prohibition matters

- Do not force to detach the tool while the controller is off.
- Line tracking can not used with tool change function.

<!-- PDF page 2134 -->

# Notes on using the batteryless type

- When calibration motion type 1 or 2 is selected, calibration cannot be interrupted by a hold or emergency stop. (Program execution must not be stopped during tool attach processing.)
- When calibration motion type 3 or 4 is selected, the stroke limit must be expanded so that the tool axis touches the open limit.
- When calibration motion type 5 or 6 is selected, a detection switch such as a limit switch must be installed in the tool.

### 19.1.4 1-4 System Configuration

Servo tool change system is constructed as follows.

Figure 19–1. Example: Servo tool is the 2nd group and the number of tools is four

> **Image description -- img-193.jpeg:** The diagram illustrates a robotic system with two motion groups. Motion group 1 consists of a single robotic arm labeled 'Robot = Motion group 1,' which is connected to a controller. The robotic arm has a detachable tool interface, allowing tools to be attached or detached as needed. Motion group 2 comprises up to nine tools arranged in a row, labeled Tool 2, Tool 3, Tool 4, etc., each with its own tool interface. The tools are positioned on a base labeled J1 and J4, indicating their placement or joint axes. Arrows indicate the direction of tool attachment and detachment from the robotic arm. The controller manages the operations of both motion groups, enabling the robotic arm to interact with the tools in motion group 2. The overall concept demonstrates a modular tool system where the robotic arm can switch between different tools to perform various tasks.

You can replace the servo tool with the air tool by switching on the controller.

> **Image description -- img-194.jpeg:** The diagram illustrates a control system involving two types of actuators connected to a central controller. On the left side, there is a mechanical arm or lever system with a pivot point, indicating a physical movement or positioning mechanism. This system is connected to two separate actuator units labeled 'Servo tool (example: controller 1)' and 'Air tool (example: controller 2)'. The servo tool is driven by a servo motor (motion group = 2) and can be set to any open position, suggesting precise control over its movement. The air tool is driven by an ON/OFF air actuator (no motion group), indicating it operates in a binary fashion, either fully on or off. Both actuators are connected to the same controller, which manages their operation. The diagram conveys a system where a single controller can manage both continuous (servo) and discrete (air) actuators, highlighting the integration of different types of motion control in a unified setup.

### 19.2 INITIAL SETUP

The following initial setup is needed to install the servo tool change system.

- Motion parameter setup (Independent Axes setup) of servo tool axes
- The configuration setup of servo tool number
- Enable the tool change function.

Note These setup must be done at the beginning of system installation.

These setup must be done only one time.

These setup is done at the controlled start. See Section 19.11.1 for detail information.

### 19.3 PRELIMINARY TOOL ATTACH OPERATION

When “Tool Change” is enabled as described in Section 19.2, tools assigned to a target operation group are all detached.

Note Only when the tool change software is installed in a system in which servo tools have already been operated and a tool used previously is left attached, the tool is attached. In this case, preliminary tool attach steps xxx 1 to 9 explained below are unnecessary.

When using a tool for the first time, be sure to follow the steps below to perform the preliminary attach operation, then proceed to Section 19.4.

1. Press the MENUS key to display the screen menu.
2. Select 6, SETUP.
3. Press F1, TYPE to display the screen switch menu.
4. Select "Tool Change." The tool change list screen appears.

SETUP TOOL CHANGE G2 JOINT 10 %
Tool Change / Group:2
AXS Comment BatteryType
1 TOOL[ 1: Part A ] ON[---]
2 TOOL[ 1: Part B ] ON[---]
3 TOOL[ 1: Part C ] ON[---]
[ TYPE ] GROUP DETAIL

5. From the list, select one tool, and press F3,DETAIL. The tool change setup detail screen then appears.
6. On the tool change setup detail screen, temporarily set the battery to ON. (Even when the actual tool has no battery, select ON in this step. This item is to be set again after the preliminary attach operation is completed.)

<!-- PDF page 2137 -->

SETUP TOOL CHANGE G1 JOINT 10 %
Tool Change / Group:2 Tool:1 1/4
1 Comment: [Part A ]
2 Attach signal: SDI[ 1]
3 Identify signal: SDI[ 2]
4 Battery: ON
[ TYPE ] LIST

7. Attach a target tool to the tool changer.
8. Create a program to teach an attach instruction.

1 TOOL ATTACH[ 1 ] ;

9. Execute the TOOL ATTACH instruction to attach the tool temporarily.
10. After the TOOL ATTACH instruction is executed, the following are issued:

• SRVO-075 Pulse not established
• SRVO-062 BZAL alarm

11. On the calibration screen, press F3, RES_PCA, and select YES.

System Master/Cal G2 JOINT 10 %
1 FIXTURE POSITION MASTER
2 ZERO POSITION MASTER
3 QUICK MASTER
4 SINGLE AXIS MASTER
5 SET QUICK MASTER REF
6 CALIBRATE

[TYPE] LOAD RES_PCA DONE

12. Turn the power off then on.
13. Jog the servo tool axis. Continue jogging the servo tool axis until the following message disappears when the reset button is pressed: SRVO-075 Pulse not established.

<!-- PDF page 2138 -->

System Master/Cal G2 JOINT 10 %

1 FIXTURE POSITION MASTER
2 ZERO POSITION MASTER
3 QUICK MASTER
4 SINGLE AXIS MASTER
5 SET QUICK MASTER REF
6 CALIBRATE

14. In the same manner as for ordinary servo tools, perform zero-position mastering for the servo tool axis at the position where the stationary-side tip and the movable-side tip touch.
15. After completing tool change setup and reference position setting for the first tool, detach the first tool by using the TOOL DETACH instruction, then perform the preliminary attach operation for the second and subsequent tools.

### 19.4 TOOL CHANGE SETUP

The tool change setup must be done for each tool.

1. Press MENU.
2. Select "6 SETUP".
3. Press F1 [TYPE].
4. Select "Tool change"

SETUP TOOL CHANGE G2 JOINT 10 %
Tool Change / Group:2
AXS Comment BatteryType
1 TOOL[ 1: Part A ] ON[---]
2 TOOL[ 1: Part B ] ON[---]
3 TOOL[ 1: Part C ] ON[---]

### Calibration Motion Type Selection Criteria

#### Types 1, 2

Select these types on systems capable of holding the tool detachment position as a result of braking the servo tool axis motor up to the next servo tool attachment.

Note With type 1 and 2, if calibration is interrupted by a hold or emergency stop, reference position data is lost. In such a case, see Section 19.13.2.

When these types are set, the position where the tool is detached is automatically memorized as the reference position, and calibration is carried out at that position after the tool is attached. For this reason, the position when the tool is attached must be the same as position when it is detached.

The allowable errors of the detach and attach positions must fall within the respective following ranges for the direct-acting axis and rotary axis:

<!-- PDF page 2140 -->

- Direct-acting axis: ±(gear ratio/2)mm or less around the detach position
- Rotary axis: ±((360/gear ratio)/2)deg or less around the detach position

Note that positional misalignment occurs during tool attachment if the above ranges are exceeded.

The difference between types 1 and 2 is in the operating direction during calibration. (See Table 19–3 and Figure 19–3.)

Type 1: Specify this type when the tool is detached at a position where it is impossible to move the tool in the positive direction of manual feed by two or more turns of the motor.

Type 2: Specify this type when the tool is detached at a position where it is impossible to move the tool in the negative direction of manual feed by two or more turns of the motor.

### Types 3, 4

Select these types on systems not capable of holding the tool detachment position as a result of the servo tool axis motor not having a brake up to the next servo tool attachment. On such a system, the reference position must be set to another position as the tool detachment position cannot be used as the reference position.

With these types, contact of the tool axis with the open limit is detected by using the motor torque, and the contact position is set as the reference position. (This is because, in the standard setting, the calibration motion causes the tool axis to move in the negative direction of manual feed.) For details on how to set the reference position, see Section 19.5.

The difference between types 3 and 4 is in the operating direction during calibration. (See Table 19–3 and Figure 19–3.)

Type 3: Specify this type when the tool is detached at a position where the distance to the open limit is two or more turns of the motor.

Type 4: Specify this type when the tool is detached at a position where the distance to the open limit is two or less turns of the motor.

Note In the calibration, to move the tool axis in the positive direction of manual feed (to use the limit on the positive side of manual feed), change the following system variable to 0: $SVTCTOOLxx.$CLOSDIR = 1 —> 0 (xx: Tool number)

Note With types 3 and 4, it is necessary to expand the stroke limit so that the tool axis touches the open limit.

### Types 5, 6

Like types 3 and 4, specify these types on systems not capable of holding the tool detachment position as a result of the servo tool axis motor not having a brake up to the next servo tool attachment. With types 5 and 6, however, a detection signal must be provided on the tool by means of a limit switch, and the contact position must be set as the reference position. Install the detection switch in such a place that the detection switch is turned on when the tool axis is moved in the negative direction of manual feed (this is because, in the standard setting, the calibration

<!-- PDF page 2141 -->

motion causes the tool axis to move in the negative direction of manual feed). For details on how to set the reference position, xxx see Section 19.5.

The difference between types 5 and 6 is in the operating direction during calibration. (See Table 19–3 and Figure 19–3.)

Type 5: Specify this type when the tool is detached at a position where the distance to the position where the detect signal turns ON is two or more turns of the motor.

Type 6: Specify this type when the tool is detached at a position where the distance to the position where the detect signal turns ON is two or less turns of the motor.

Note In the calibration, to move the tool axis in the positive direction of manual feed, change the following system variable to 0: $SVTCTOOLxx.$CLOSDIR = 1 -> 0 (xx: Tool number)

Note With types 5 and 6, a switch such as a limit switch must be installed in the tool.

Table 19–3. Calibration Motion Type

2: With types 1 and 2, the system automatically memorizes the position where the servo tool is detached as the reference position. This memorized reference position is used in calibration when the same tool is next attached. For this reason, when types 1 or 2 are selected, the detachment position and the attachment position must be the same. Do not select types 1 or 2 when a motor with a brake is used for the servo tool axis.

## 19.5 SETTING THE REFERENCE POSITION

### 19.5.1 Battery-less type tools

On battery-less tools, the position (pulse value) is lost when the tool is detached. So, calibration must be carried out when tool is attached.

The position taken as the reference for calibration is called the "reference position."

On battery-less tools, the reference point must be set before the tool is detached. How the reference point is set differs according to the calibration motion type.

- Types 1, 2
The system automatically sets the reference position when the servo tool is detached.
- Types 3, 4
Create a program for detecting the reference position using the touch torque, and execute this program to calculate the reference position. For details, refer to Section 19.12.1.
- Types 5, 6 Create a program for detecting the reference position using the detection signal, and execute this program to calculate the reference position. For details, refer to Section 19.12.2.

### 19.5.2 Battery-mounted type tools

On battery-mounted type tools, the position (pulse value) is not lost even if the tool is detached. Therefore, the reference position used for calibration when the tool is attached need not be set as it needs to be on a battery-less type tool. However, that we recommend setting a reference position for quick mastering by marking a line or alignment mark as shown in the figure below for extra safety in the event that the battery comes loose. For details on how to set the reference position for quick mastering, refer to Section 19.12.3.

## 19.6 TOOL CHANGE INSTRUCTION

For changing servo tools, the following instructions are provided.

<!-- PDF page 2146 -->

### 19.6.1 TOOL DETACH instruction

This instruction can detach the servo tool without power off.

Format : -
TOOL DETACH[i]

i : Tool number (1 -> 6)
Specify the tool number which you want to detach.
R[ ] and AR[ ] can be used.

Ex)

TOOL DETACH[1]
TOOL DETACH[R[2]]
TOOL DETACH[AR[1]]

### 19.6.2 TOOL ATTACH instruction

This instruction can attach the servo tool without power off. In case of batteryless tool, the mastering and calibration are performed automatically.

Format : -
TOOL ATTACH[i]

i : Tool number (1 -> 6)
Specify the tool number which you want to detach.
R[ ] and AR[ ] can be used.

Ex)

TOOL ATTACH[5]
TOOL ATTACH[R[3]]
TOOL ATTACH[AR[1]]

### 19.6.3 Sample program

1: J P[1:Approach] 100% FINE
2: L P[2:TOOL1 SET] 100mm/sec FINE
3: TOOL DETACH[1]
4: L P[1:Approach] 100mm/sec FINE
:
11:J P[11: Approach] 100% FINE
12: L P[12:TOOL2 SET] 100mm/sec FINE
1: Move to approach position
2: Set tool axis to 0 positio n
3: Detach tool 1
4: Release tool1

<!-- PDF page 2147 -->

13: TOOL ATTACH[2] 13: Attach tool 2

:

### 19.6.4 Foward execution

It is necessary to check that the tool number of instruction is same as the actual tool. And in the case of attach instruction, the calibration motion type must be set correct type. In the case of batteryless tool, the calibration motion (3 in the following figure) is done.

> **Image description -- img-198.jpeg:** The image is a three-step diagram illustrating a calibration process for a robotic tool attachment system. In the first panel, a robotic arm is shown moving to an attached position, indicated by an arrow pointing to a specific location on the arm. The second panel depicts the tool being attached to the robotic arm, with a label stating 'Tool attach' and 'Mastering Calibration finished.' The third panel shows the robotic arm performing a calibration motion, specifically for the tool axis, as indicated by the label 'Calibration motion (Tool axis only).' The diagram visually represents the sequence of actions required to attach and calibrate a tool on a robotic arm, emphasizing the movement to the correct position, the attachment of the tool, and the subsequent calibration of the tool axis.

Note In the case of calibration motion type is Type 1 or Type 2, if the motion is stopped by e-stop or HOLD during the calibration motion, the mastering data is lost. If the mastering data is lost, please do the zero mastering and calibration by manual again.

Otherwise,

1. The current position on TP is not matched to the actual position.
2. If the motion instruction is executed, the following alarm is occurred. "MOTN-049 Attempt to move w/o calibrated"
3. The TOOL DETACH instruction does not work until manual mastering and calibration are finished.

In the case of TOOL DETACH instruction, both robot and servo tool do not move at all.

### 19.6.5 Backward execution

Both the TOOL ATTACH and the TOOL DETACH instructions can not be executed by backward execution.

## 19.7 TOOL CHANGE SEQUENCE

Figure 19-4. Tool Change Sequence

> **Image description -- img-199.jpeg:** The image is a timing diagram illustrating the sequence of operations and signals involved in the process of detaching and attaching a tool on a robot. The diagram is divided into two main sections: TOOL DETACH and TOOL ATTACH, separated by a vertical blue line. The horizontal axis represents time, progressing from left to right. 

Key elements and their states are shown along the vertical axis:

1. **Robot motion**: Indicates the robot's movement state, transitioning from 'moving' to 'STOP' during both detach and attach operations.

2. **Robot lock of servo tool motion group is ON / SRDY of servo tool motor**: Shows the servo tool motor's readiness state, switching from OFF to ON during the detach operation and from ON to OFF during the attach operation.

3. **Tool attach signal**: Indicates the signal for tool attachment, turning ON during the attach operation and OFF during the detach operation.

4. **Tool attach verification signal**: Reflects the verification signal for tool attachment, turning ON during the attach operation and OFF during the detach operation.

5. **Motor power line (MCC)**: Displays the motor power line state, switching from OFF to ON during the attach operation and from ON to OFF during the detach operation.

6. **Motor power line GND line**: Shows the ground line state for the motor power, switching from OFF to ON during the attach operation and from ON to OFF during the detach operation.

7. **Pulse coder line +5V**: Indicates the pulse coder power line state, switching from OFF to ON during the attach operation and from ON to OFF during the detach operation.

8. **Pulse coder line 0V**: Shows the pulse coder ground line state, switching from OFF to ON during the attach operation and from ON to OFF during the detach operation.

9. **Detach/Attach status**: Summarizes the overall status of the tool operation, transitioning from 'Tool Attach' to 'Tool Detaching' during the detach operation and from 'Non gun' to 'Tool Attaching' during the attach operation.

The diagram visually represents the synchronization and timing of these signals and states to ensure proper tool detachment and attachment, with clear transitions and interactions between the different components and signals.
